(8.17) writes "$\psi \to (F\psi), s(\psi))$" for $\psi \mapsto (F(\psi), s(\psi))$ (possible misprint) (Findings, Chapter 8, items 71, 72) (pp. 396–398 (2017 pp. 286–287)).

**Lemma 8.6.2 (2017: 8.10)** (V8.40) ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.lemma_8_6_2⟧. *For isomorphic $x, x'$ the isomorphism classes of $F^{-1}(x)$ and $F^{-1}(x')$ correspond one to one, and isomorphic $y \in F^{-1}(x)$, $y' \in F^{-1}(x')$ lie in corresponding classes $\Theta_j$, $\Theta'_j$ for exactly one $j$.* **The text** argues before the lemma by lifting a morphism $x \to x'$ through Definition 8.5.1 (3) (2017: 8.8). **The formalized proof** does the same: every $y \in F^{-1}(x)$ is the source of a lift of $\varphi : x \to x'$, whose target lies in $F^{-1}(x')$ and is isomorphic to $y$ ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.exists_isomorphic_of_isomorphic⟧. So the index sets in $|Y|$ agree ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.fiberIndex_eq⟧, and with the classes indexed by their images in $|Y|$ the unique common index of $y$ and $y'$ is their common image. As a bijection between the sets of classes the correspondence is ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.lemma_8_6_2_equiv⟧ (Findings, Chapter 8, items 71, 73) (2017 p. 287).

**Lemma 8.6.3 (2017: 8.11)** (V8.41) ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.lemma_8_6_3⟧. *For isomorphic $x, x'$, $\#\Theta_j = \#\Theta'_j$ and $\#F^{-1}(x) = \#F^{-1}(x')$.* As in the text: $\#\Theta_j = \#G_x / \#G_{y_0}$ by Lemma 8.6.1 (2017: 8.9), $\#G_x = \#G_{x'}$, and $\#G_{y_0} = \#G_{y'_0}$ for $y_0 \in \Theta_j$, $y'_0 \in \Theta'_j$, isomorphic points having conjugate isotropy groups; the division is by $\#G_{y_0} \ge 1$. For an index outside both index sets both classes are empty. The fibre is the disjoint union of its classes ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.ncard_fiber_eq_sum⟧ ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.ncard_fiber_eq_of_isomorphic⟧. Possible misprints: after Lemma 8.6.2 (2017: 8.10), "the third claim of Lemma 8.10" for that of Lemma 8.6.1 (2017: 8.9), which has the claim $\#G_x = \#G_{y_0} \cdot \#\Theta_j$; and in the lemma, $\sum_{i=1}^q \#\Theta_j$ sums over $i$ with summands indexed by $j$ (Findings, Chapter 8, item 73) (2017 p. 287).

### VIII.24 Proposition 8.6.4 (2017: 8.4): the number of sheets

**Proposition 8.6.4 (2017: 8.4)** (V8.42) ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.proposition_8_6_4⟧. *$\#F^{-1}(x)$ is constant on the preimage of every connected component of $|X|$, and $x \mapsto \#F^{-1}(x)$ is an sc-smooth functor $X \to \mathbb N$.* **The text** argues that under small perturbations of $x$ "the structure of isomorphism classes stays the same". **The formalized proof** uses only the local constancy of $\#F^{-1}(x)$. *Step 1.* For $x' \in U(x)$, Definition 8.5.1 (2) (2017: 8.8) gives the bijection $y \mapsto (F|U(y))^{-1}(x')$ from $F^{-1}(x)$ onto $F^{-1}(x')$, the $U(y)$ being disjoint and covering $F^{-1}(U(x))$; so $\#F^{-1}$ is locally constant on $X$ ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.eventually_ncard_fiber_eq⟧ ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.isLocallyConstant_ncard_fiber⟧. *Step 2.* By Lemma 8.6.3 (2017: 8.11) it descends to $|X|$ ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.fiberCardOrbit⟧, where it is locally constant in the quotient topology, a level set upstairs being open ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.isLocallyConstant_fiberCardOrbit⟧, hence constant on connected components. *Step 3, the functor.* $\mathbb N$ is Lean's, with $0$, as the trivial ep-groupoid of the discrete M-polyfold ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.trivial⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · discretePolyfold⟧; a morphism $\varphi$ goes to the unit of $\#F^{-1}(s\varphi) = \#F^{-1}(t\varphi)$, and the object map is sc-smooth because it is locally constant ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.fiberCardFunctor⟧. The values are $\ge 1$, $F$ being surjective, which matches the text's $\mathbb N = \{1, 2, \dots\}$ ⟦Chapter8/ProperCovering · EpFunctor.IsProperCovering.one_le_ncard_fiber⟧ (Findings, Chapter 8, item 74) (2017 p. 288).

### VIII.25 Appendix §8.6.2 (2017 §8.5.2): the structure of strong bundle coverings

**§8.6.2 (2017 §8.5.2)** (V8.43) ⟦Chapter8/EpStrongBundle · EpStrongBundle.section_8_5_2⟧. *For a proper strong bundle covering functor $A$ over $F$, $A(\varphi, w) = (F(\varphi), A_{s(\varphi)}(w))$ with topological linear isomorphisms $A_y : W_y \to V_{F(y)}$, and $\mu_X(F(\varphi)) \circ A_{s(\varphi)} = A_{t(\varphi)} \circ \mu_Y(\varphi)$: $y \mapsto A_y$ is a natural transformation $\mu_Y \to \mu_X \circ F$ of functors into $\mathrm{Ban}$.* **The text** writes the morphism map in this form and computes $t(A(\varphi, w)) = A(t(\varphi, w))$. **The formalized proof** does the same. *Step 1.* The morphism map has the form $(\varphi, w) \mapsto (F(\varphi), A(w))$, as for every strong bundle functor (§VIII.13) ⟦Chapter8/EpStrongBundle · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering.mor_val⟧, and the fibre maps $A_y$ are topological linear isomorphisms by Definition 8.5.9 (1) (2017: 8.10), the local strong bundle isomorphisms having linear inverses ⟦Chapter8/EpStrongBundle · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering.fiberEquiv⟧. *Step 2.* A strong bundle functor commutes with the targets, $\nu(F(\varphi), A(w)) = A(\mu(\varphi, w))$ ⟦Chapter8/EpStrongBundle · EpStrongBundle.IsStrongBundleFunctor.μ_comm⟧, which is the text's computation. The natural transformation is stated as its naturality identity; the fibres $Q^{-1}(F(s\varphi))$ and $Q^{-1}(s(F\varphi))$ are identified through their values in $V$, and the category $\mathrm{Ban}$ is not formalized. Only the strong bundle functor part of Definition 8.5.9 (2017: 8.10) enters the identity (Findings, Chapter 8, item 75) (2017 pp. 288–289).

### VIII.26 Witnesses and counterexamples

Every hypothesis of the chapter is shown satisfiable, and each statement that does not hold as we read it has a counterexample (Findings, Chapter 8, items 100–105, 125, 130).

**Covering functors** (Definition 8.5.5 (2017: 8.9)). The identity of `SingleObj G` is a covering functor for every group $G$ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.isCoveringFunctor_id⟧; for non-trivial $G$ the functor sending every morphism to $1$ is not ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.not_isCoveringFunctor_one⟧; the empty groupoid gives a covering functor, with a geometric lift for which Proposition 8.5.7 (2017: 8.3) does not hold as we read it ⟦Chapter8/GeometricLiftEmpty2021 · CoveringExamples.not_proposition_8_5_7_empty⟧ (§§VIII.20, VIII.40). Theorem 8.5.8 (2017: 8.6) applies to the identity functor of every ep-groupoid in every universe ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.theorem_8_5_8_id⟧.

**A geometric lift, and Proposition 8.5.7 (2017: 8.3) applied.** $\mathbb Z/2 = \mathbb Z^\times$ acting on $\mathbb R$ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.rCat⟧ by $y \mapsto \pm y$ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.reflectionDiffeo⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.reflectionHom⟧ is a geometric lift of the identity of `SingleObj` $\mathbb Z^\times$, with $L_D = L_C$ and $\tau = 1$ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.reflectionLift⟧. Proposition 8.5.7 (2017: 8.3) makes it a proper covering functor onto the translation groupoid $\mathbb Z/2 \ltimes \mathbb R$, with non-trivial isotropy at $0$ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.isProperCovering_reflectionLift⟧.

**Identities and trivial strong bundles.** The identity functor of every ep-groupoid is a proper covering functor ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpFunctor.isScDiffeoOn_fibredMap_id⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpFunctor.isProperCovering_id⟧. Every strong bundle over an M-polyfold is a strong bundle over its trivial ep-groupoid with $\mu(z, w) = w$ (Definition 8.3.1 (2017: 8.4)) ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpStrongBundle.trivial⟧; the identity is a strong bundle map and a strong bundle functor (Definitions 8.3.2, 8.3.3 (2017: 8.5, 8.6)) ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpStrongBundle.isMap_id⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpStrongBundle.isStrongBundleFunctor_id⟧, and the identity of every strong bundle over an ep-groupoid is a proper strong bundle covering functor ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · StrongBundle.isStrongBundleIsoOn_id⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpStrongBundle.isStrongBundleIso_fibredLift_id⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpStrongBundle.isProperStrongBundleCovering_id⟧. Over a trivial ep-groupoid every section is functorial ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpStrongBundle.isFunctorialSection_trivial⟧, so $\Gamma$, $\Gamma^+$ and the sc-Fredholm section functors are Part I's sc-smooth, sc⁺- and sc-Fredholm sections ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpStrongBundle.mem_sectionFunctors_trivial⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpStrongBundle.mem_plusSectionFunctors_trivial⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · EpStrongBundle.mem_fredholmSectionFunctors_trivial⟧. The witnesses use that maps of pull-backs $(z, y) \mapsto (g(z), \Phi(y))$ are strong bundle maps ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · pullbackMap⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · StrongBundle.isStrongBundleMap_pullbackMap⟧.

**A strong bundle over an ep-groupoid in `Type`.** Part I's trivial strong bundle $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R^n$ ⟦Chapter3/NonVacuity · TrivialBundle.bundle⟧ over the trivial ep-groupoid of $\mathbb R^n$ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · TrivialBundle.epBundle⟧ has an ep-groupoid as functorial picture ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · TrivialBundle.epBundleEpGroupoid⟧, its identity is a proper strong bundle covering functor ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · TrivialBundle.epBundle_isMap_id⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · TrivialBundle.epBundle_isProperStrongBundleCovering⟧, $0 \in \Gamma^+$ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · TrivialBundle.fiberZero_mem_plusSectionFunctors_epBundle⟧, and for a smooth $\phi : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^k$ the graph section lies in $\Gamma$ and is sc-Fredholm ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · TrivialBundle.graphSection_mem_sectionFunctors_epBundle⟧ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuityBundle · TrivialBundle.graphSection_mem_fredholmSectionFunctors_epBundle⟧, from Part I's results on graph sections ⟦Chapter3/NonVacuity · TrivialBundle.isScSmoothSection_graphSection⟧.

**Tangent witnesses.** The tangent of the trivial ep-groupoid of $\mathbb R^n$ is tame ⟦Chapter8/TangentTame · EpGroupoid.isTame_tangentEpGroupoid_trivial_rn⟧ (Lemma 8.1.9 (2017: 8.8); the trivial ep-groupoid itself is tame by Chapter 7 ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isTame_trivial_rn⟧), and the tangent of the trivial ep-groupoid of any M-polyfold has a paracompact orbit space ⟦Chapter8/TangentOrbit · EpGroupoid.hasParacompactOrbitSpace_tangent_trivial⟧ (Theorem 8.1.15 (2017: 8.4); its hypothesis is Chapter 7's ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.hasParacompactOrbitSpace_trivial⟧).

**Theorem 8.5.3 (5) (2017: 8.5) as printed.** For the identity functor of $\mathbb Z/2 \ltimes \mathbb R$ (§VII.30) ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · EpGroupoid.Examples.reflectionEpGroupoid⟧, every chart of Theorem 8.5.3 (2017: 8.5) at $0$ has, in the sheet of $\psi_0 = (-1, 0)$, a morphism $\psi$ with $F(s(\psi)) \ne t(F(\psi))$ ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.theorem_8_5_3_five_as_printed⟧, and such charts exist ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.theorem_8_5_3_five_as_printed_nonvacuous⟧ (§VIII.17).

**Remark 8.1.10 (2017: 8.1), the bare-map reading.** On the trivial $\mathbb Z/3$-action every $T\varphi$ is the identity, and $(\varphi, h) \mapsto (T\varphi, Ts(h))$ is not injective ⟦Chapter8/TangentEpNotInjective · EpGroupoid.Examples.remark_8_1_10_not_injective⟧ (§VIII.6).

**Forms.** The constant $0$-forms are forms on every ep-groupoid ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EpGroupoid.constForm_mem_epForms⟧, and on an ep-groupoid with $s = t$ every form of the object M-polyfold is one ⟦Chapter11/EpPoincareLemma · EP.epFormsInftyToObj_surjective_of_src_eq_tgt⟧ (§§VIII.35, VIII.37).

*What the witnesses do not exercise.* "A sufficiently small $U(x)$" is a chart datum, and charts exist inside every open $V \ni x$, so part (c) of Theorem 8.5.8 (2017: 8.6), which quantifies over all charts, is not vacuous; no hypothesis of the form "for all compatible charts" is made in the chapter. But every proper covering functor constructed has one-point fibres $F^{-1}(x)$ (identities, and the functor of the reflection lift, whose $D$ has one object), so the even coverings of Definitions 8.5.1 (2) and 8.5.9 (2) (2017: 8.8 and 8.10) are met with one sheet and the counting of §8.6.1 (2017 §8.5.1) only with $q = 1$, $\#\Theta_1 = 1$; no proper strong bundle covering functor other than identities is constructed, and $\Gamma^+$ is witnessed by the zero section only (Findings, Chapter 8, item 105).

### VIII.27 What is not formalized

Every gap of the chapter is closed (G.74, G.75, G.86–G.89, §§VIII.34–VIII.40). What remains:

- **The degeneracy remark for non-tame $X$, $Y$** (pp. 379–385 (2017 pp. 275–276); row V8.28, narrower): only $d_{\mathbf X \times Y} \le 2\,d_{\mathbf Y}$ along the image of $L_F$; equality without tameness is open in the project, Part I proving the product formula only for tame M-polyfolds (§VIII.15; Findings, Chapter 8, item 51).
- **The statements that do not hold as we read them**, each with a counterexample: Theorem 8.5.3 (5) (2017: 8.5) as printed, where the square with $s$ on both vertical arrows and the companion square with $t$ on both are proved (§VIII.17; Findings, Chapter 8, item 54); Proposition 8.5.7 (2017: 8.3) for $D = \emptyset$ (§§VIII.20, VIII.40; Findings, Chapter 8, items 59, 130); and Remark 8.1.10 (2017: 8.1) in the bare-map reading (§VIII.6; Findings, Chapter 8, item 10).
- **The local bundle model in the proof of Theorem 8.1.15 (2017: 8.4)** (2017 p. 268): the sc-isomorphism of $TU(x_z)$ with $TO \to O^1$ and the linearity of the bundle action of $G_{x_z}$; not needed by the proof here (§VIII.9; Findings, Chapter 8, items 21, 113).
- **$W[1]$ as an ep-groupoid**: Proposition 8.4.1 (3) needs only its orbit space, which is built directly (§VIII.39; Findings, Chapter 8, item 133).
- **Remarks without formal content**: the naturality remarks of Remark 8.5.4 (2017: 8.2) (b), strong bundle maps over open subsets of the base, the closing sentence of Definition 8.5.9 (2017: 8.10), "the structure of isomorphism classes stays the same" before Proposition 8.6.4 (2017: 8.4), and the category $\mathrm{Ban}$ of §8.6.2 (2017 §8.5.2); none is used elsewhere in the chapter, so none is given a gap (Findings, Chapter 8, item 113).

### VIII.28 What the formalization taught us

**Fibre injectivity replaces calculus on fibred products.** The text proves the groupoid laws of $T(X, \mathbf X)$, Theorem 8.1.11 (2017: 8.2) and Proposition 8.1.14 (2017: 8.1) by differentiating identities on $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$, which needs the tangent of a fibred product. Since $s$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism, a vector of $T\mathbf X$ is determined by its base point and its image under $Ts$; base points are computed in $\mathbf X$ and images under $Ts$ by Lemma 8.1.3 (2017: 8.2). Only one identity of §8.1, the target formula of Lemma 8.1.3 (2017: 8.2), is genuinely differentiated, and the identification $T(\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X) = T\mathbf X\,{}_{Ts}{\times}_{Tt}\,T\mathbf X$ is never needed (§§VIII.3, VIII.7, VIII.8).

**The tangent calculus of §8.1 lives on open sets.** Every proof of §8.1 differentiates a map defined only near a point: a local inverse of $s$, the map $\alpha$ of Lemma 8.1.3 (2017: 8.2), $\hat\psi$. Part I differentiates only globally sc-smooth maps. Tangents of maps on open sets, with the chain rule and the tangents of local sc-diffeomorphisms, are the infrastructure the chapter rests on, and Lemma 8.1.7's (2017: 8.6) "by construction" is exactly their last property (§VIII.1).

**Definition 8.5.1 (3) (2017: 8.8) carries Theorem 8.5.3 (2017: 8.5).** The text builds the sheets $\mathbf U(\psi_0)$ from natural representations of the groups $G_y$ in $Y$ and never invokes condition (3). With (3), the sheets are images of the continuous sections $z \mapsto L_F^{-1}(\Gamma(g, F z), z)$ of $s$, and connectedness of $U(y)$ does the rest; neither the finiteness of the fibre nor condition (1) is used. The same condition counts the morphisms over a fibre in §8.6.1 (2017 §8.5.1) and gives the unique lifting behind Theorem 8.5.8 (2017: 8.6) (§§VIII.17, VIII.21, VIII.23).

**A functor commutes with $s$, not with "$s$ on one side and $t$ on the other".** Theorem 8.5.3 (5) (2017: 8.5) as printed equates $F(s(\psi))$ with $t(F(\psi))$; a non-trivial element of $G_x$ moves points, so the square fails for the reflection of $\mathbb R$ in every chart at $0$. The two squares that functoriality gives, with $s$ on both sides and with $t$ on both sides, are what the proofs downstream use (§VIII.17).

**Empty groupoids and non-tame products.** Two statements needed a hypothesis that the text does not state: Proposition 8.5.7 (2017: 8.3) needs $D \ne \emptyset$, because Definition 8.5.5 (2017: 8.9) admits the empty groupoid, over which the functor of Proposition 8.5.7 (2017: 8.3) is not surjective; and the degeneracy remark after Definition 8.5.1 (2017: 8.8) needs tameness, the only form of the product formula $d_{\mathbf X \times Y} = d_{\mathbf X} + d_Y$ that Part I proves. In both cases the hypothesis holds where the text uses the statement (§§VIII.15, VIII.20).

**Metrizability is the shorter road to paracompactness, again.** As for Proposition 7.5.3 (2017: 7.12), Theorem 8.1.15 (2017: 8.4) follows from Smirnov's theorem pulled back along $|TX| \to |X^1|$: $|TX|$ is metrizable, which is stronger than paracompact, and the closed paracompact sets $\tilde A_z$, the regularity of $|TX|$ and Proposition 2.7.4 (2017: 2.17) drop out. What remains of the text's argument is the metrizability of $|TU(x_z)|$, and for it the open embedding $G_x\backslash TU(x) \to |TX|$, which the text leaves implicit (§VIII.9).

**Strong bundles over ep-groupoids need more of Part I than Part I states.** A global notion of strong bundle map, the atlas and universal property of the pull-back on both levels $[0]$ and $[1]$, the sum of sc-smooth sections, and the strong bundle structure on $\mathbf V\,{}_s{\times}_A\,W$ are all used in §8.3 and Definition 8.5.9 (2017: 8.10) without being defined or proved in Part I. With them in place, the claims of §8.3 that the text states without proof, the functorial picture and the identity of Definitions 8.3.2 and 8.3.3 (2017: 8.5 and 8.6), are routine (§§VIII.10–VIII.14, VIII.22).

**Compatibility with morphisms is $s^*\omega = t^*\omega$.** Definition 8.2.1 asks $(T\varphi)^*\omega_y = \omega_x$ for every morphism. Since $T\varphi = Tt \circ (Ts|T_\varphi\mathbf X)^{-1}$, this is the equality of the pull-backs of $\omega$ by the two global sc-smooth maps $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$. In that form every closure property of §8.2 — under $d$, the wedge product, restriction to $X^1$, pull-back by functors — is one line, from the naturality of pull-backs in Part I; the text's local maps $t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi_0))^{-1}$ are not needed (§VIII.35).

**The Poincaré lemma on an ep-groupoid is a statement about equivalences.** The text averages a primitive over $G_x$ and extends it to the saturation by morphisms. Both steps are instances of general facts: averaging works for any finite family of self-functors covering the morphisms of a groupoid, and the extension is the push-forward of forms along the equivalence $G_x \ltimes U(x) \to X|\pi^{-1}(\pi(U(x)))$ of §11.2. So the proof of Proposition 8.2.3 rests on Chapter 11 (§VIII.37).

**Vertical vectors are the derivative the text takes.** Proposition 8.1.16 differentiates (8.16) and uses that $T\tau_X$ is onto. On the vertical vectors of $T(TX)$ the tangent of an isotropy element of $TX$ acts as $Tg$, and that suffices; no surjectivity is used (§VIII.38).

### VIII.29 The 2021 additions to §8.1: Propositions 8.1.16 and 8.1.17, the Zhou condition and LUC for $TX$

The Springer edition (2021) adds Propositions 8.1.16, 8.1.17, Definition 8.3.5, §8.4, Example 8.5.6, condition (0) of Definition 8.5.9 and Lemma 8.5.10; Sections VIII.29–VIII.33 retell them, with the 2021 numbers and pages (V8.44–V8.52). The conditions of Chapter 7's §7.4 are those of §§VII.35–VII.39.

**Proposition 8.1.16** (V8.44) ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.proposition_8_1_16⟧. *If $X$ satisfies (ZHOU), so does $TX$.* **The text's proof**: an isotropy element of a smooth $b \in TX$ over $x$ is a pair $(g, h)$, $g \in G_x$; differentiating (8.16) and using that $T\tau$ is onto, $T(g, h) = \mathrm{id}$ gives $Tg = \mathrm{id}$, so $g \in T_x$ by (ZHOU), and then $(g, h) \in T_b$. **The formalized proof.** *Step 1.* A smooth point of $TX$ lies over a smooth point of $X$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · MPolyfold.levelVal_tangentProj_mem_smoothSet⟧, and the base $p(k)$ of an isotropy element $k$ of $b$ is an isotropy element of $p(b)$. *Step 2.* The step "$T(g, h) = \mathrm{id}$ implies $Tg = \mathrm{id}$" needs the second tangent bundle $T(TX)$ and $T\tau$, which are not formalized; it was the hypothesis ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.TangentZhouReflect⟧ in the first reading, and holds for every ep-groupoid by §VIII.38 (gap G.88, closed). *Step 3.* (ZHOU) for $X$ puts $p(k)$ in $\mathbf X^T$, and if $s = t$ near $p(v)$ then $Ts = Tt$ near $v$, so $k \in (T\mathbf X)^T$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.mem_nonEffectivePart_tangent⟧. As in Chapter 7, $Tg$ is a set map on the fibre, no linear structure is used (§VII.37). For every trivial ep-groupoid the tangent of a morphism is the identity and the hypothesis holds ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.tangentMor_trivial⟧ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.tangentZhouReflect_trivial⟧ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.Examples.proposition_8_1_16_point⟧ (Findings, Chapter 8, item 115) (p. 369).

**Proposition 8.1.17** (V8.45) ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.proposition_8_1_17_one⟧. *(1) If $X^1$ has LUC, so has $TX$, with $(T\mathbf X)^T = p^{-1}((\mathbf X^1)^T)$. (2) (SLUC) for $X$ gives (SLUC) for $TX$.* *(1).* If $v \in (T\mathbf X)^T$, then $Ts = Tt$ on a neighbourhood $O$ of $v$, and $s = t$ on the open set $p(O)$, $p$ being open: $p(v) \in (\mathbf X^1)^T$. Conversely, $(\mathbf X^1)^T = (\mathbf X^T)^1$ by Appendix 7.6.4 (§VII.36), and Step 3 of Proposition 8.1.16 applies ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.nonEffectivePart_tangent_eq⟧. So $(T\mathbf X)^T$ is closed as a preimage of the closed $(\mathbf X^1)^T$ (Proposition 7.2.21 for $X^1$), and $TX$ has LUC by Proposition 7.2.21 for $TX$. The hypotheses are those of Appendix 7.6.4 — $U(x) \cap X_1$ connected in $X^1$ and dense in $U(x)$ (the density is gap G.73) — and the openness of $p : T\mathbf X \to \mathbf X^1$ (gap G.8); both now hold for every ep-groupoid (§VII.45), and the proposition without them is §VIII.40. They are satisfied by the point ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.isOpenMap_tangentProj_of_subsingleton⟧ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.Examples.proposition_8_1_17_one_point⟧. *(2)* for $(TX)^0 = TX$ is (1) ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpGroupoid.proposition_8_1_17_two⟧; for every $(TX)^i$ it needs $(TX)^i = T(X^i)$, which is §VIII.33 (gap G.88, closed) (Findings, Chapter 8, items 116, 124, 126) (p. 371).

### VIII.30 Definition 8.3.5, Proposition 8.4.1 and Definition 8.4.2: auxiliary norms, paracompactness, local regularity

**Definition 8.3.5** (V8.46) ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsAuxNorm⟧. *An auxiliary norm for a strong bundle over an ep-groupoid is a continuous $N : W_{0,1} \to [0, \infty)$, a complete norm on every fibre, with $h_k \to 0_x$ whenever $P(h_k) \to x$ and $N(h_k) \to 0$, and invariant: $N(h) = N(k)$ if $h = \mu(\varphi, k)$.* The first three conditions are Part I's auxiliary norm (Definition 5.1.1) on the underlying strong bundle, so $N$ lives on its level-one space; values in $[0, \infty)$ follow from (1). In (3), $h \in W_{0,1}$ is given and $h = \mu(\varphi, k)$ is an equation in $W$; it is not vacuous, since $\mu(\varphi, k) \in W_{0,1}$ for $k \in W_{0,1}$ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.exists_oneVal_eq_μ⟧. Over the trivial ep-groupoid every auxiliary norm of Part I is one ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.exists_isAuxNorm_trivial⟧, and $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R^n$ has one ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · TrivialBundle.exists_isAuxNorm_epBundle⟧ (Findings, Chapter 8, item 117) (p. 379).

**Proposition 8.4.1** (V8.47) ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.proposition_8_4_1_two_imp_one⟧. *$|X|$, $|W[0]|$ and $|W[1]|$ are paracompact together.* *(2) ⇒ (1).* $\mu(\varphi, 0_{s(\varphi)}) = 0_{t(\varphi)}$ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.μ_fiberZero⟧, so the zero section induces $|0| : |X| \to |W[0]|$ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.zeroOrbitMap⟧, continuous ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.continuous_zeroOrbitMap⟧, with left inverse $|P|$ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.leftInverse_zeroOrbitMap⟧, hence a topological embedding ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.isEmbedding_zeroOrbitMap⟧. The text concludes as a closed subset of a paracompact space; the formalized proof goes through metrizability: $|W[0]|$ paracompact is metrizable by Theorem 7.3.1 and Smirnov's theorem (§VII.23), so is its subspace $|X|$, hence paracompact. (1) ⇒ (2) and the statements on $|W[1]|$ are §VIII.39, without bundle charts (gap G.86, closed) (Findings, Chapter 8, items 118, 127, 133) (p. 380).

**Definition 8.4.2** (V8.48) ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpStrongBundle.IsLR⟧. *The strong bundle has the local regularity property if every $x$ has arbitrarily small $U(x)$ such that every strong bundle isomorphism $B$ of $W|U(x)$ with $|B(w)| = |w|$ is $w \mapsto g * w$ for some $g \in G_x$*, the natural lift $g * w = \mu(\Gamma(g, P(w)), w)$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpStrongBundle.natLift⟧. As for Definition 8.5.9 (§VIII.22), the strong bundle isomorphism is read as a strong bundle map $W \to W$ that is Part I's strong bundle isomorphism on $W|U(x)$, "arbitrarily small" as "inside every open $O \ni x$", and $|B(w)| = |w|$ as equality of orbits in $(W, \mathbf W)$, as for (LR) (§VII.39). Every strong bundle over a trivial ep-groupoid has it ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhou · EpStrongBundle.isLR_trivial⟧. Proposition 8.4.3, effective $X$ with (LR) gives the property, is §VIII.39, with the openness of $P$ from Chapter 10 (Findings, Chapter 8, items 119, 128) (p. 382).

### VIII.31 Example 8.5.6, Definition 8.5.9 in the 2021 form, and Lemma 8.5.10

**The remark after Definition 8.5.5 and Example 8.5.6** (V8.49) ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · example_8_5_6⟧. *For a covering functor $f : D \to C$, $f : G_d \to G_{f(d)}$ is injective* ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · IsCoveringFunctor.injective_map_end⟧ — by the bijectivity required in Definition 8.5.5 — *but need not be surjective*: $D$ with two objects and one morphism between any two ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · Example856D⟧, mapped to $\mathbb Z^\times$ as a one-object category with $f(\varphi) = f(\varphi^{-1}) = -1$ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · example856Functor⟧, is a covering functor whose $G_a$, $G_b$ are trivial while $G_x \cong \mathbb Z/2$ (Findings, Chapter 8, item 120) (p. 388).

**Definition 8.5.9, 2021 form** (V8.50) ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021⟧. *A strong bundle map $A : W \to V$ over an ep-functor $F$ with $Q \circ A = F \circ P$ is a proper strong bundle covering functor if (0) $\tau(F(\psi), A(w)) = A(\mu(\psi, w))$ and (1)–(3) of the 2017 definition hold.* It is stated for the object map, (0) being the strong bundle map property of Definition 8.3.2 (2017: 8.5); (1)–(3) are those of §VIII.22. The reading of §VIII.22 had taken 2017's "strong bundle map $A$" as a strong bundle functor, which contains (0); the two are equivalent ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.isProperStrongBundleCovering2021_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering.isProperStrongBundleCovering2021⟧: the functor is determined by its object map, on morphisms $(\psi, w) \mapsto (F(\psi), A(w))$. Identities are witnesses ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.isProperStrongBundleCovering2021_id⟧ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · TrivialBundle.epBundle_isProperStrongBundleCovering2021⟧ (Findings, Chapter 8, items 70, 121) (p. 394).

**Lemma 8.5.10** (V8.51) ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.lemma_8_5_10⟧. *$B : W \to F^*V$, $w \mapsto (P(w), A(w))$, is a strong bundle isomorphism over $Y$ for $\mu_{F^*V}(\varphi, (y, v)) = (t(\varphi), \mu_X(F(\varphi), v))$, with (8.23) $B \circ \mu_Y = \mu_{F^*V} \circ B$, and $A = \bar A \circ B$.* $F^*V$ is Part I's pull-back, whose paracompactness always holds, and $\mu_{F^*V}$ is its formula ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.pullbackμ⟧. *Step 1.* $B$ lands in $F^*V$ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.bundleB⟧ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.bundleB_val⟧, and (8.23) is (0) ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.bundleB_μ⟧. *Step 2, bijective.* On the fibre over $y$, $A$ is the linear isomorphism $A_y : W_y \to V_{F(y)}$ of a local strong bundle isomorphism of Definition 8.5.9 (1) at $y$, so $B$ is bijective ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.bijective_bundleB⟧. *Step 3, the inverse.* Near every point, $B^{-1}(y, v) = \Psi(v)$ for the inverse $\Psi$ of a local strong bundle isomorphism of Definition 8.5.9 (1), whose base map is injective ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.eq_of_isStrongBundleIsoOn⟧ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.bundleBInv⟧ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.bundleBInv_eq_of⟧, so $B$ and $B^{-1}$ are strong bundle maps ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.isStrongBundleMap_bundleB⟧ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.mapsTo_oneSet_bundleBInv⟧ ⟦Chapter8/Book2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.isStrongBundleMap_bundleBInv⟧. "Strong bundle isomorphism over the ep-groupoid $Y$" is read as a strong bundle isomorphism $W \to F^*V$ covering the identity, with (8.23); that $\mu_{F^*V}$ makes $F^*V$ a strong bundle over the ep-groupoid $Y$, and $B$ an isomorphism of strong bundles over $Y$, is §VIII.40 (gap G.89, closed) (Findings, Chapter 8, items 122, 129) (p. 395).

### VIII.32 The 2021 additions: what is not formalized, and what they taught us

Every gap of the 2021 additions is closed:

- **Proposition 8.1.16 without `TangentZhouReflect`** (gap G.88, closed): through the vertical vectors of $T(TX)$ (§VIII.38; Findings, Chapter 8, items 115, 126). Proposition 8.1.17 (2) for every $(TX)^i$ is §VIII.33; of $(TX)^i = T(X^i)$ the compatibility with unit, inverse and composition is not formalized, since LUC does not use it (Findings, Chapter 8, item 124).
- **Proposition 8.2.3** (p. 373; gap G.87, closed): the Poincaré lemma, as printed, with the forms of §8.2 (gap G.74, closed) (§§VIII.35–VIII.37; Findings, Chapter 8, items 110, 123, 132).
- **Proposition 8.4.1 and Proposition 8.4.3** (gap G.86, closed): (1) ⇔ (2) ⇔ (3), with $|W[1]|$ built as an orbit space, and the local regularity of strong bundles (§VIII.39; Findings, Chapter 8, items 118, 119, 127, 128, 133).
- **$F^*V$ as a strong bundle over the ep-groupoid $Y$** in Lemma 8.5.10 (gap G.89, closed) (§VIII.40; Findings, Chapter 8, items 122, 129).

**The tangent inherits the Chapter 7 conditions through the base.** Both propositions of §8.1 reduce to Chapter 7: a vector of $T\mathbf X$ is in $(T\mathbf X)^T$ as soon as its base is in $(\mathbf X^1)^T$, and the openness of $p$ gives the converse. The passage from $T(g, h)$ to $Tg$ needs the second tangent bundle; it goes through the vertical vectors of $T(TX)$ (§VIII.38).

**Condition (0) was already in the reading.** The 2021 Definition 8.5.9 adds (0); the first reading had read 2017's "strong bundle map" as a strong bundle functor, which contains it, and the two forms are equivalent (§VIII.31).

### VIII.33 Proposition 8.1.17 (2) for every $(TX)^i$

**Equivalences of ep-groupoids** (V8.52) ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EpGroupoid.EpEquiv⟧. The text's "naturally $(TX)^i = T(X^i)$" is used only to carry LUC from $T(X^i)$ to $(TX)^i$. For that it suffices to have sc-diffeomorphisms of the object and of the morphism M-polyfolds commuting with source and target; an sc-diffeomorphism is a homeomorphism ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · MPolyfold.ScEquiv.toHomeomorph⟧. Such equivalences compose and contain the identities ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EpGroupoid.EpEquiv.refl⟧ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EpGroupoid.EpEquiv.trans⟧, pass to the index raises ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EpGroupoid.EpEquiv.shift⟧, map $\mathbf X^T$ onto $\mathbf X'^T$, since $s = t$ near a morphism is preserved ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EpGroupoid.EpEquiv.nonEffectivePart_eq⟧, and so transport LUC, by the characterization of Proposition 7.2.21 ($\mathbf X^T$ closed) ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EpGroupoid.EpEquiv.isLUC⟧. The compatibility with unit, inverse and composition is not formalized, since LUC does not use it.

**$T(X^i) \cong (TX)^i$** (V8.52) ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EP.tangentLiftEpEquiv⟧. Part I's Proposition 2.3.17 for $i = 1$, on the object and the morphism M-polyfold, gives an equivalence $T(X^1) \cong (TX)^1$, commuting with $s$ and $t$ by the naturality of the inclusion $T(X^1) \to TX$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EpGroupoid.tangentShiftEpEquiv⟧. By recursion, composing with the index raise of the previous equivalence, $T(X^i) \cong (TX)^i$ for every $i$, for the bundled tangent ep-groupoid ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EP.tangentEP⟧, as Part I's $\Phi_i$ for M-polyfolds ⟦Chapter2/TangentLiftAll · BundledMPolyfold.tangentLiftEquiv⟧ ⟦Chapter2/TangentLiftAll · proposition_2_3_17_all⟧.

**Proposition 8.1.17 (2)** (V8.52) ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EP.proposition_8_1_17_two_all⟧. *If $X$ has (SLUC), so has $TX$.* **The text's proof**: (SLUC) gives LUC for every $X^{i+1} = (X^i)^1$; by (1) every $T(X^i)$ has LUC; and $(TX)^i = T(X^i)$. **The formalized proof** is the same: (1) applied to $X^i$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EP.isLUC_tangent_lift⟧, then the equivalence. The hypotheses of (1) — natural representations with $U(x) \cap (X^i)_1$ connected in $(X^i)^1$ and dense in $U(x)$ (gap G.73), and the openness of $p : T(\mathbf X^i) \to (\mathbf X^i)^1$ (gap G.8) — are taken on every $X^i$; both hold for every ep-groupoid (§VII.45), and the proposition without them is §VIII.40 ⟦Chapter7/SmoothRegularAssembly · EP.isLUC_tangent_lift_of_isSLUC⟧. They hold for the point ep-groupoid and all its lifts ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EpGroupoid.hasConnectedDenseLevelOneReps_of_subsingleton⟧ ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouLevels · EpGroupoid.Examples.proposition_8_1_17_two_all_pointEP⟧ (gap G.88, closed for (2)) (Findings, Chapter 8, item 124) (p. 371).


### VIII.34 Lemma 8.1.2 (2017: 8.1) as printed, and the M-polyfold of pairs of Remark 8.1.10 (2017: 8.1)

§VIII.2 proved Lemma 8.1.2 in the form the construction of $T\mathbf X$ uses: the composition (8.5) is defined through the local sc-diffeomorphisms $Ts$, $Tt$, and $T\mathbf X$ is an ep-groupoid. The text states more: under the identification of $T(\mathbf X \,{}_s{\times}_t\, \mathbf X)$ with $T\mathbf X \,{}_{Ts}{\times}_{Tt}\, T\mathbf X$, the multiplication of $T\mathbf X$ is $Tm$. This is now formalized as printed (V8.4; gap G.75, closed).

**The M-polyfold $\mathbf X \,{}_s{\times}_t\, \mathbf X$** ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · EpGroupoid.compPolyfold⟧ is the sub-M-polyfold of $\mathbf X \times \mathbf X$ of Definition 7.1.3 (4); its second projection $\pi_2$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism, since $s$ is one ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · EpGroupoid.isLocalScDiffeo_compSnd⟧, and the multiplication $m$ is sc-smooth by condition (4) ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · EpGroupoid.compMul⟧.

**The identification** ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · EpGroupoid.tangentCompPairs⟧ is $v \mapsto (T\pi_1 v, T\pi_2 v)$. *Step 1.* As $\pi_2$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism, $T\pi_2$ is bijective on the fibres, and a vector $v$ of $T(\mathbf X \,{}_s{\times}_t\, \mathbf X)$ is determined by its base point and $T\pi_2 v$. *Step 2.* $T\pi_1(v)$ is the vector over $\pi_1$ with $Ts(T\pi_1 v) = Tt(T\pi_2 v)$, by the chain rule for $s \circ \pi_1 = t \circ \pi_2$. So the identification is injective with range the pairs $(k, h)$ with $Ts(k) = Tt(h)$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · EpGroupoid.range_tangentCompPairs⟧. *Step 3, $Tm$ is the composition.* $Tm(v)$ lies over $m(\pi_1 v, \pi_2 v)$ and $Ts(Tm\, v) = Ts(T\pi_2 v)$, by the chain rule for $s \circ m = s \circ \pi_2$; since $Ts$ is injective on the fibres of $\mathbf X$, this characterizes the composition (8.5): $Tm(v) = T\pi_1(v) \circ T\pi_2(v)$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · EpGroupoid.lemma_8_1_2_tangentMul⟧. In the text's words: for $Ts(k) = Tt(h)$ there is exactly one $v$ over $(k, h)$, and $k \circ h = Tm(v)$, a vector over $p(k) \circ p(h)$ with $Ts(k \circ h) = Ts(h)$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · EpGroupoid.lemma_8_1_2_book⟧; the multiplication of the tangent ep-groupoid on its fibred product is $Tm$ transported by the identification ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · EpGroupoid.lemma_8_1_2_compMul⟧. *Step 4, as M-polyfolds.* The identification is an sc-diffeomorphism onto the sub-M-polyfold $T\mathbf X \,{}_{Ts}{\times}_{Tt}\, T\mathbf X$ of $T\mathbf X \times T\mathbf X$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · EpGroupoid.isScDiffeoOn_tangentCompPairs⟧: it is a bijection which, composed with the local sc-diffeomorphism $T\pi_2$ on the right side, gives the local sc-diffeomorphism $T\pi_2$ on the left, and such a map is a local sc-diffeomorphism ⟦Chapter8/TangentFibred · MPolyfold.isLocalScDiffeo_of_comp_eq⟧. **A reading.** The text derives $Ts(k \circ h) = Ts(h)$ by differentiating $s(m(\psi, \varphi)) = s(\varphi)$; the proof above uses the same identity, in the form $s \circ m = s \circ \pi_2$ on the M-polyfold of pairs (p. 359).

**Remark 8.1.10, the M-polyfold of pairs** (V8.12). §VIII.6 formalized the bijection of the remark between morphisms of $T\mathbf X$ and pairs $(T\varphi, a)$ with the label $\varphi$ in place of the bare map $T\varphi$ (as a bare map the assignment is not injective, §VIII.6). Here $T\varphi$, defined as $Tt \circ (Ts|T_\varphi\mathbf X)^{-1}$, is the tangent at $s(\varphi)$ of the local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1}$, as the text has it ⟦Chapter9/Tangent · EpGroupoid.tangentMor_eq_tangentMapOn_hat⟧, a bijection $T_{s(\varphi)}X \to T_{t(\varphi)}X$ with inverse $T(\varphi^{-1})$ ⟦Chapter7/TangentMorphism · EpGroupoid.bijOn_tangentMor⟧, represented in charts by mutually inverse bounded linear maps ⟦Chapter7/TangentMorphism · EpGroupoid.tangentMor_chart_iso⟧. The remark also says that the pairs form an M-polyfold for which the bijection is an sc-diffeomorphism. *The pairs* $(\varphi, a)$, $\varphi \in \mathbf X^1$, $a \in T_{s(\varphi)}X$, form the fibred product $\mathbf X^1 \,{}_s{\times}_p\, TX$, a sub-M-polyfold of $\mathbf X^1 \times TX$ by Proposition 2.5.20, $s : \mathbf X^1 \to X^1$ being a local sc-diffeomorphism ⟦Chapter8/TangentPairs · EpGroupoid.tangentPairsPolyfold⟧. *The map* $G(v) = (p(v), Ts(v))$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentPairs · EpGroupoid.remarkGInto⟧ is an sc-diffeomorphism $T\mathbf X \to \mathbf X^1 \,{}_s{\times}_p\, TX$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentPairs · EpGroupoid.remark_8_1_10_scDiffeo⟧, by the argument of Step 4: it is bijective and commutes with the local sc-diffeomorphisms $Ts : T\mathbf X \to TX$ and $\pi_2 : \mathbf X^1 \,{}_s{\times}_p\, TX \to TX$. *The triples.* $v \mapsto (Ts\, v, p(v), Tt\, v)$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentPairs · EpGroupoid.remarkTriple⟧ is injective, with range the triples $(a, \varphi, b)$ with $a \in T_{s(\varphi)}X$ and $b = T\varphi(a)$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentPairs · EpGroupoid.remark_8_1_10_triples⟧, the text's "$(a, T\varphi, b)$" with $\varphi$ recorded (pp. 364–365). The row stays narrower only for the reading of $T\varphi$ as a label (Findings, Chapter 8, item 131).

### VIII.35 Definition 8.2.1 (2017: 8.2): sc-differential forms on ep-groupoids

§VIII.27 of the first reading recorded §8.2 as not formalized, since Part I's forms (§4.4) were not yet available. With them (Part IV), Definition 8.2.1 is formalized as printed (V8.53; gap G.74, closed).

**The condition** ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EpGroupoid.IsMorCompatible⟧. *An sc-differential $k$-form on the ep-groupoid $(X, \mathbf X)$ is an sc-differential $k$-form $\omega$ on the object M-polyfold, Definition 4.4.1, with $(T\varphi)^*\omega_y = \omega_x$ for every morphism $\varphi : x \to y$*, $T\varphi$ being the bounded linear isomorphism $T_xX \to T_yX$ of Definition 7.1.4 (§VIII.6). The forms satisfying it form the vector space $\Omega^k_{ep}(X)$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EpGroupoid.epForms⟧. **The key reformulation**: $\omega$ is compatible with the morphisms iff $s^*\omega = t^*\omega$ on the morphism M-polyfold $\mathbf X$, the pull-backs being Part I's pull-backs by the sc-smooth maps $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EpGroupoid.isMorCompatible_iff_formPullback⟧; for $T\varphi = Tt \circ (Ts)^{-1}$ on the fibre over $\varphi$ is the definition of §VIII.6. Every closure property follows from this form. *(a)* A form on $X$ is a form on $X^1$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EpGroupoid.formLower_mem_epForms⟧. *(b)* $d\omega$ is compatible with the morphisms: $s^*d\omega = d\,s^*\omega = d\,t^*\omega = t^*d\omega$, by the naturality of Part I's $d$; so $d : \Omega^k_{ep}(X) \to \Omega^{k+1}_{ep}(X^1)$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EpGroupoid.extD_mem_epForms⟧. The text argues with the local sc-diffeomorphisms $f = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi_0))^{-1}$ and $f^* d = d f^*$; the global maps $s$, $t$ give the same in one line. *(c)* Wedge products ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EpGroupoid.formWedge_mem_epForms⟧. *(d)* For an sc-smooth functor $F : X \to Y$, $F^*$ maps $\Omega^k_{ep}(Y)$ to $\Omega^k_{ep}(X)$, as $s_Y \circ F = F \circ s_X$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EpGroupoid.formPullback_mem_epForms⟧, and naturally equivalent functors (Definition 8.1.13) have the same pull-back: for $\theta : F \to F'$, $F = s \circ \theta$ and $F' = t \circ \theta$, so $F^*\omega = \theta^* s^*\omega = \theta^* t^*\omega = F'^*\omega$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EpGroupoid.formPullback_eq_of_natTrans⟧. The constant $0$-forms are a witness (§VIII.26).

**The direct limit.** For the index lifts $X^i$ (an ep-groupoid by Proposition 7.3.9), $\Omega^k_{ep}(X^i)$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epForms⟧, with the pull-backs by the inclusions as the maps of a directed system ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epFormsMap⟧, and $\Omega^k_{ep,\infty}(X)$ is its direct limit ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epFormsInfty⟧, Mathlib's direct limit of modules. Every class has a representative on some $X^i$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.exists_epFormsInftyOf_eq⟧, and two forms on $X^i$, $X^j$ represent the same class iff their pull-backs to some $X^l$, $l \ge i, j$, agree ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epFormsInftyOf_eq_iff⟧, as the text says. *The exterior derivative* $d[\omega] = [d\omega]$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epFormsInftyD⟧ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epFormsInftyD_of⟧ is well defined since $d$ commutes with the steps, and $d \circ d = 0$ from Part I ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epFormsInftyD_comp_epFormsInftyD⟧. **Readings.** "An sc-smooth map $\oplus_k TX \to \mathbb R$, linear in each argument and skew-symmetric" is Part I's Definition 4.4.1, as the text says ("already introduced in Section 4.4"), so a form is a family of alternating maps on the fibres; compatibility on level $i$ is with the morphisms of $X^i$ on level one, that is of $\mathbf X_{i+1}$; and $T_yY$ in the definition is read as $T_yX$ (Findings, Chapter 8, items 110, 132) (pp. 372–373).

### VIII.36 Definition 8.2.2 (2017: 8.3): the sc-de Rham complex, and pull-backs by functors

**The complex** (V8.54). $\Omega^*_{ep,\infty}(X) = \oplus_k \Omega^k_{ep,\infty}(X)$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epFormsInftyGraded⟧ with $d$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epFormsInftyGradedD⟧ and $d \circ d = 0$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epFormsInftyGradedD_comp_self⟧ is the sc-de Rham complex; its cohomology $\ker d / \operatorname{im} d$ ⟦Chapter8/EpForms · EP.epDeRham⟧ is that of the same complex as a cochain complex of real vector spaces ⟦Chapter8/EpFormsObj · EP.epDeRhamComplex⟧. *It is a subcomplex of Part I's complex of the object M-polyfold.* The text defines $d$ as "the exterior derivative of an sc-differential form on the object M-polyfold". The inclusion $\Omega^k_{ep,\infty}(X) \to \Omega^k_{\infty}(\mathrm{Ob}\,X)$, the object M-polyfold of $X^i$ being the lift $(\mathrm{Ob}\,X)^i$ of Part I, is injective ⟦Chapter8/EpFormsObj · EP.epFormsInftyToObj⟧ ⟦Chapter8/EpFormsObj · EP.epFormsInftyToObj_injective⟧ and commutes with $d$ ⟦Chapter8/EpFormsObj · EP.formsInftyD_comp_epFormsInftyToObj⟧ (p. 373).

**Pull-backs by sc-smooth functors.** Used by Proposition 8.2.3 and by §11.2 (Part XI), and stated in Theorem 11.2.1 (1), (2): for $F : X \to Y$ with index raises $F^i : X^i \to Y^i$, $F^*[\omega] = [(F^i)^*\omega]$ ⟦Chapter8/EpFormsFunctor · EP.epFormsInftyPullback⟧, well defined since the $(F^i)^*$ commute with the steps; it commutes with $d$ ⟦Chapter8/EpFormsFunctor · EP.epFormsInftyD_comp_epFormsInftyPullback⟧, and naturally equivalent functors give the same map, by §VIII.35 (d) on every level, applied to the index raises of the natural transformation ⟦Chapter8/EpFormsFunctor · EP.epFormsInftyPullback_eq_of_natTrans⟧. The inclusion into the forms of the object M-polyfold commutes with these pull-backs ⟦Chapter11/EpPoincareLemma · EP.epFormsInftyToObj_epFormsInftyPullback⟧.

### VIII.37 Proposition 8.2.3 (new in the 2021 edition; the 2017 text promised it for later): the Poincaré lemma

**Proposition 8.2.3** (V8.55; gap G.87, closed) ⟦Chapter11/EpPoincareLemma · EP.proposition_8_2_3⟧. *Every object $x$ of an ep-groupoid $X$ has saturated open neighbourhoods $V \subseteq U$ such that every closed $[\omega] \in \Omega^k_{ep,\infty}(X|U)$, $k \ge 1$, is $d[\sigma]$ on $V$ for some $[\sigma] \in \Omega^{k-1}_{ep,\infty}(X|V)$.* Here $X|U$ is the restriction of Proposition 7.1.22 ⟦Chapter11/SubGroupoidModel · EP.sub⟧, $k \ge 1$ is written $k + 1$, and "on $V$" is the pull-back by the inclusion functor $X|V \to X|U$ ⟦Chapter11/SubGroupoidModel · EP.subIncl⟧. The proposition holds also inside every saturated open neighbourhood $U$ given in advance ⟦Chapter11/EpPoincareLemma · EP.proposition_8_2_3_of_isOpen⟧; the statement above takes $U = X$. **The text's proof**: Lemma 4.4.8 on the object M-polyfold gives a primitive $\tau$ on a neighbourhood $V'(x)$ invariant under $G_x$; the average $\tau' = \frac{1}{\# G_x}\sum_g g^*\tau$ is invariant with $d\tau' = \omega$, and is extended to the saturation by $\sigma(y) = \psi^*\tau'(x')$ for a morphism $\psi : x' \to y$. **The formalized proof** follows these steps; the extension is the push-forward along an equivalence.

*Step 1, the object M-polyfold.* Lemma 4.4.8 ⟦Chapter4/Poincare2021b · lemma_4_4_8⟧, applied to the image of $a$ in the forms of the object M-polyfold of $X|U$, gives an open $V_0 \ni x$ and a primitive among the forms of the object M-polyfold on $V_0$ ⟦Chapter8/EpPoincare · EP.proposition_8_2_3_object⟧.

*Step 2, the translation groupoid.* Theorem 7.1.13 ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.theorem_7_1_13⟧ gives a natural representation of $G_x$ on an open $U(x) \subseteq V_0$, and with it the translation ep-groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$, the M-polyfold $U(x)$ with only the unit morphisms, the functor $J : U(x) \to G_x \ltimes U(x)$, the identity on objects ⟦Chapter11/TranslationAverage · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.unitsFunctor⟧, the functors $\Phi_g : y \mapsto g * y$ of $U(x)$ ⟦Chapter11/TranslationAverage · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.smulFunctor⟧ and the natural transformations $\theta_g : J \to J \circ \Phi_g$, $y \mapsto (g, y)$ ⟦Chapter11/TranslationAverage · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.smulNatTrans⟧. In an ep-groupoid with $s = t$, such as $U(x)$ with its units, every form of the object M-polyfold is a form of the ep-groupoid ⟦Chapter11/EpPoincareLemma · EP.epFormsInftyToObj_surjective_of_src_eq_tgt⟧, so the primitive of Step 1, restricted to $U(x)$, is a $\beta \in \Omega^k_{ep,\infty}(U(x))$ with $d\beta = J^*c$, $c$ the pull-back of $a$ to $G_x \ltimes U(x)$; $\beta$ need not be invariant.

*Step 3, averaging.* This is done for any $J : W \to T$ which is a bijective local sc-diffeomorphism on objects, with a finite family $\Phi_g$ closed under composition up to permutations $\sigma_g$ of the index set ($\Phi_h \circ \Phi_g = \Phi_{\sigma_g(h)}$), and $\theta_g : J \to J \circ \Phi_g$ whose values exhaust the morphisms of $T$ ⟦Chapter11/FormAveraging · EP.exists_primitive_of_average⟧. On every level $i$ the sum $\sum_g (\Phi_g^i)^*\beta$ is invariant under every $(\Phi_h^i)^*$, by the permutations, and is therefore $(J^i)^*\tau$ for a form $\tau$ of the ep-groupoid $T^i$: compatibility with a morphism $\theta_g(y)$ of $T$ is invariance under $\Phi_g$ ⟦Chapter11/FormAveraging · EP.exists_epForms_sum_pullback⟧. Dividing by $\# G_x$, $J^*(d\tau) = d J^*\tau = J^*c$, and $J^*$ is injective since $J$ is a surjective local sc-diffeomorphism on objects ⟦Chapter11/FormAveraging · EP.injective_epFormsInftyPullback_of_surjective⟧; so $c = d\tau$ with $\tau$ the text's $\tau'$ ⟦Chapter11/TranslationAverage · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.exists_primitive_translation⟧.

*Step 4, extension to the saturation.* The functor $G_x \ltimes U(x) \to X|\pi^{-1}\pi(U(x))$ ⟦Chapter11/SubGroupoidModel · EP.modelFunctor⟧ is an equivalence ⟦Chapter11/SubGroupoidModel · EP.isEquivalence_modelFunctor⟧: full and faithful by the uniqueness property of $\Gamma$ (Theorem 7.1.13), essentially surjective by the definition of the saturation, and a local sc-diffeomorphism on objects. If $E : T \to Z$ is an equivalence and $E^*a = d\tau$, then $a = d(E_*\tau)$, with $E_*$ the push-forward of Definition 11.2.3 ⟦Chapter11/EquivalenceFormsInfty · EP.epFormsInftyPush⟧ ⟦Chapter11/FormAveraging · EP.exists_primitive_of_equivalence⟧; $E_*\tau$ at $y$ is $\psi^*\tau(x')$ for a morphism $\psi : x' \to y$, the text's $\sigma$. So $V = \pi^{-1}\pi(U(x))$, saturated, open and contained in $U$. No hypothesis is added (Findings, Chapter 8, items 123, 132) (pp. 373–374).

### VIII.38 Proposition 8.1.16 without added hypothesis: vertical vectors

§VIII.29 proved Proposition 8.1.16 with the step "$T(g, h) = \mathrm{id}$ implies $Tg = \mathrm{id}$" as the hypothesis `TangentZhouReflect`. The step holds for every ep-groupoid ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouReflect2021 · EpGroupoid.tangentZhouReflect⟧, so *(ZHOU) for $X$ gives (ZHOU) for $TX$* with the text's hypothesis only ⟦Chapter8/TangentZhouReflect2021 · EpGroupoid.proposition_8_1_16_2021⟧ (V8.44; gap G.88, closed).

**Vertical vectors.** For a smooth $\alpha \in T_xX$ (level one of $TX$) and $w \in T_xX$, the vertical vector $\mathrm{vert}_\alpha w \in T_\alpha(TX)$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentVertical2021 · MPolyfold.vert⟧ is the vector with chart representative $(T\varphi(\alpha), (0, h))$, $h$ the representative of $w$, in a chart of $TX$ at $\alpha$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentVertical2021 · MPolyfold.vertChart⟧; it does not depend on the chart, its representative in every chart has the same form ⟦Chapter8/TangentVertical2021 · MPolyfold.tangentChartMap_vert⟧. $w \mapsto \mathrm{vert}_\alpha w$ is injective ⟦Chapter8/TangentVertical2021 · MPolyfold.vert_injective⟧ and natural: $T(Tf)(\mathrm{vert}_\alpha w) = \mathrm{vert}_{Tf\alpha}(Tf\, w)$ for sc-smooth $f$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentVertical2021 · MPolyfold.tangentMap_tangentMap_vert⟧. The local form is $D(Tf)(x, h)(0, v) = (0, Df(x)v)$, from the linearity of $Tf$ in the fibre ⟦Chapter8/TangentVertical2021 · IsSc1.scDeriv_tangentMap_vert⟧.

**The proof.** Let $k = (g, h)$ be in the isotropy group of a smooth $b \in TX$ over $x$, with $Tk = \mathrm{id}$, and let $v \in T_xX$. Choose $u \in T_g\mathbf X$ with $Ts(u) = v$ ($Ts$ is bijective on the fibres) and put $V = \mathrm{vert}_k u \in T_k(T\mathbf X)$. By naturality, $T(Ts)V = \mathrm{vert}_b v$ and $T(Tt)V = \mathrm{vert}_b(Tt\, u)$. $Tk$ sends $T(Ts)V$ to $T(Tt)V$, so $Tk = \mathrm{id}$ gives $\mathrm{vert}_b(Tt\, u) = \mathrm{vert}_b v$, hence $Tt(u) = v$ by injectivity, that is $Tg(v) = Tt(u) = v$. This is the text's "differentiate (8.16)" restricted to the vertical directions of $T_b(TX)$, on which $Tk$ acts as $Tg$; the surjectivity of $T\tau$ is not used. Steps 1 and 3 of §VIII.29 are unchanged (Findings, Chapter 8, items 115, 126) (p. 369).

### VIII.39 Propositions 8.4.1 and 8.4.3

**Proposition 8.4.1** (V8.47; gap G.86, closed) ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.proposition_8_4_1⟧. *For a strong bundle $P : W \to X$ over an ep-groupoid, the following are equivalent: (1) $|X|$ is paracompact; (2) $|W[0]|$ is paracompact; (3) $|W[1]|$ is paracompact.* (2) ⇒ (1) is §VIII.30.

*(1) ⇒ (2)* ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompact2021 · EpStrongBundle.proposition_8_4_1_one_imp_two⟧. *Step 1, the local action.* For a natural representation of $G_x$ on $U(x)$, $G_x$ acts on $W|U(x) = P^{-1}(U(x))$ by $g * w = \mu(\Gamma(g, P(w)), w)$, the text's lift on p. 382, by homeomorphisms ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompact2021 · EpStrongBundle.bundleMulAction⟧. *Step 2.* Two points of $W|U(x)$ have the same orbit in $|W|$ iff they are $G_x$-related ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompact2021 · EpStrongBundle.π_eq_π_iff_exists_smul⟧, so $G_x \backslash (W|U(x)) \to |W|$ is an open embedding ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompact2021 · EpStrongBundle.isOpenEmbedding_bundleOrbitQuotientMap⟧ onto $|P|^{-1}(|U(x)|)$ ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompact2021 · EpStrongBundle.range_bundleOrbitQuotientMap⟧. *Step 3.* The quotient of a metrizable space by a finite group of homeomorphisms is metrizable, by the metric $\hat\rho$ of Lemma 7.3.2 ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompact2021 · metrizableSpace_orbitRel_quotient_finite⟧; $W$ is metrizable as an M-polyfold, so every $|P|^{-1}(|U(x)|)$ is metrizable. *Step 4.* $|X|$ paracompact is metrizable (Theorem 7.3.1), and Smirnov's theorem, pulled back along $|P|$ as for $TX$ in §VII.23, makes $|W[0]|$ metrizable ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompact2021 · EpStrongBundle.metrizableSpace_orbitSpace⟧, hence paracompact ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompact2021 · EpStrongBundle.proposition_8_4_1_one_iff_two⟧. This replaces the text's closed cover and Proposition 2.7.4 by the partition-of-unity form of Smirnov's theorem; no bundle charts are needed, only the continuity of $\mu$.

*(1) ⇔ (3).* $W[1]$ is not built as an ep-groupoid in the project; $|W[1]|$ is taken as the orbit space of the groupoid $(W[1], \mathbf X \,{}_s{\times}_P\, W[1])$, the quotient of the M-polyfold $W[1]$ by $w \sim \mu(\varphi, w)$ ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.OrbitSpaceOne⟧ ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.πOne_eq_πOne_iff⟧, its ep-groupoid structure being unused by the statement. The quotient map is open, as in Proposition 7.1.8 ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.isOpenMap_πOne⟧. The action of $G_x$ on $W[1]|U(x)$ is continuous for the level-one topology, since $\mu : \mathbf X \,{}_s{\times}_P\, W[1] \to W[1]$ is sc-smooth (part of "strong bundle map") ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.continuous_bundleOneSmul⟧, and Steps 2–4 repeat ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.isOpenEmbedding_bundleOneOrbitQuotientMap⟧ ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.metrizableSpace_orbitSpaceOne⟧: (1) ⇒ (3) ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.proposition_8_4_1_one_imp_three⟧. Conversely the zero section is an sc$^+$-section, so $|0| : |X| \to |W[1]|$ is continuous with continuous left inverse $|P[1]|$ and closed image ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.isClosedEmbedding_zeroOrbitMapOne⟧, and $|X|$ is paracompact as a closed subspace: (3) ⇒ (1) ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.proposition_8_4_1_three_imp_one⟧ ⟦Chapter8/BundleOrbitParacompactOne · EpStrongBundle.proposition_8_4_1_one_iff_three⟧. No hypothesis beyond the text's (Findings, Chapter 8, items 118, 127, 133) (p. 380).

**Proposition 8.4.3** (V8.48) ⟦Chapter8/BundleLocalRegularity2021 · EpStrongBundle.proposition_8_4_3⟧. *If $X$ is effective and has (LR), the strong bundle has the local regularity property of Definition 8.4.2.* Take $U(x)$ from (LR) for $X$, and a strong bundle isomorphism $\Phi$ of $W|U(x)$ with $|\Phi(w)| = |w|$, over $\beta = g * \cdot$ by (LR). *Step 1.* $|\Phi(w)| = |w|$ gives a morphism $(\psi, w) : w \to \Phi(w)$, $\psi : P(w) \to \beta(P(w))$ ⟦Chapter8/BundleLocalRegularity2021 · EpStrongBundle.exists_mor_of_π_eq⟧. *Step 2.* At a regular object two morphisms with the same source and target are equal ⟦Chapter8/BundleLocalRegularity2021 · EpGroupoid.eq_of_isRegular_src⟧, so over a regular $P(w)$, $\psi = \Gamma(g, P(w))$ and $\Phi(w) = \mu(\psi, w) = g * w$ directly (the text's $C(w) = w$). *Step 3.* The regular points are open and dense (Proposition 7.2.4), and $P$ is an open map ⟦Chapter10/LocalizationLREffectiveBundle · StrongBundle.isOpenMap_proj⟧, so $P^{-1}(X_{reg})$ is dense in $W|U(x)$, and the closed set where $\Phi(w) = g * w$ is all of $W|U(x)$. The uniqueness of $g$, which the text takes from effectiveness, is not needed (Findings, Chapter 8, items 119, 128) (p. 382).

### VIII.40 Lemma 8.5.10, Proposition 8.5.7 for $D = \emptyset$, Theorem 8.5.8 in every universe, Proposition 8.1.17 without added hypotheses

**Lemma 8.5.10, $F^*V$ over the ep-groupoid $Y$** (V8.51; gap G.89, closed). §VIII.31 proved the lemma with $F^*V$ as Part I's pull-back and $\mu_{F^*V}$ as a formula. *The strong bundle.* For every sc-smooth functor $F : Y \to X$ and strong bundle $Q : V \to X$, $(F^*Q, \mu_{F^*V})$ is a strong bundle over the ep-groupoid $Y$ (Definition 8.3.1: $\mu_{F^*V}$ is a surjective strong bundle map covering $t$, a local sc-diffeomorphism, with the unit and composition laws) ⟦Chapter8/PullbackStrongBundle2021 · EpStrongBundle.pullbackBundle2021⟧: it is Chapter 10's pull-back along $F$ (Part X), and its structure map is the text's formula $\mu_{F^*V}(\varphi, (y, v)) = (t(\varphi), \mu_X(F(\varphi), v))$ ⟦Chapter8/PullbackStrongBundle2021 · EpStrongBundle.pullbackBundle2021_μ⟧, so the text's sentence "defines the strong bundle" holds ⟦Chapter8/PullbackStrongBundle2021 · EpStrongBundle.pullbackBundle2021_isStrongBundle⟧. *The isomorphism.* For a proper strong bundle covering functor, $B(w) = (P(w), A(w))$ and $B^{-1}$ are strong bundle maps of strong bundles over ep-groupoids (Definition 8.3.2) covering the identity functor of $Y$ ⟦Chapter8/PullbackStrongBundle2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.isMap_bundleB⟧ ⟦Chapter8/PullbackStrongBundle2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.isMap_bundleBInv⟧, the compatibility with $\mu$ being (8.23); so $B$ is a strong bundle isomorphism over the ep-groupoid $Y$ ⟦Chapter8/PullbackStrongBundle2021 · EpStrongBundle.IsProperStrongBundleCovering2021.lemma_8_5_10_full⟧ (Findings, Chapter 8, items 122, 129) (p. 395).

**Proposition 8.5.7 for $D = \emptyset$** (V8.35). Definition 8.5.5 allows $D = \emptyset$, and then Proposition 8.5.7 does not hold as we read it ⟦Chapter8/GeometricLiftEmpty2021 · CoveringExamples.not_proposition_8_5_7_empty⟧. The functor from the empty category to $\mathbb Z^\times$, as a one-object category, is a covering functor, both sides of the bijection of Definition 8.5.5 being empty ⟦Chapter8/GeometricLiftEmpty2021 · CoveringExamples.emptyCover⟧; with $L_C(\star) = \mathbb R$, $\mathbb Z/2$ acting by reflection, it has a geometric lift ⟦Chapter8/GeometricLiftEmpty2021 · CoveringExamples.emptyLift⟧. The induced $F : \emptyset \to \mathbb Z/2 \ltimes \mathbb R$ is not surjective on objects, hence not a proper covering functor. The project's Proposition 8.5.7 carries $D \ne \emptyset$, which the text presumably intends (§VIII.20; Findings, Chapter 8, item 130) (p. 390).

**Theorem 8.5.8 in every universe** (V8.36). The first reading proved Theorem 8.5.8 for ep-groupoids in `Type` only. Read with Definition 8.5.5 in one universe — $D$, $G$ and the category $\mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$ in which the lift takes values — no proof changes, and $X$, $Y$ share the universe because $\mathrm{Diff}_{sc}$ is one category (§VIII.21). The identity of a one-object category, with its geometric lift, is a witness ⟦Chapter8/NonVacuity · CoveringExamples.theorem_8_5_8_id⟧ (Findings, Chapter 8, item 125) (p. 392).

**Proposition 8.1.17 without added hypotheses** (V8.45, V8.52). The hypotheses of §VIII.29 and §VIII.33 — natural representations with $U(x) \cap X_1$ connected in $X^1$ and dense in $U(x)$ (gap G.73), and the openness of $p : T\mathbf X \to \mathbf X^1$ (gap G.8) — hold for every ep-groupoid (§VII.45): the first ⟦Chapter7/SmoothConnectedReps · EpGroupoid.hasConnectedDenseLevelOneReps⟧, the second by Part I ⟦Chapter2/TangentProjOpen · MPolyfold.isOpenMap_tangentProj⟧. With only the second still taken as an assumption the proposition is ⟦Chapter7/SmoothConnectedReps · EpGroupoid.proposition_8_1_17_one_of_isOpenMap⟧; with none: *(1) if $X^1$ has LUC, so has $TX$, and $(T\mathbf X)^T = p^{-1}((\mathbf X^1)^T)$* ⟦Chapter7/SmoothRegularAssembly · EpGroupoid.proposition_8_1_17_one_of_isLUC⟧ ⟦Chapter7/SmoothRegularAssembly · EpGroupoid.nonEffectivePart_tangent_eq_of_isLUC⟧; *(2) if $X$ has (SLUC), $TX$ has LUC* ⟦Chapter7/SmoothRegularAssembly · EP.proposition_8_1_17_two_of_isSLUC⟧, *every $T(X^i)$ has LUC* ⟦Chapter7/SmoothRegularAssembly · EP.isLUC_tangent_lift_of_isSLUC⟧, *and $TX$ has (SLUC)* ⟦Chapter7/SmoothRegularAssembly · EP.proposition_8_1_17_two_all_of_isSLUC⟧, through $(TX)^i \cong T(X^i)$ of §VIII.33 (Findings, Chapter 8, items 116, 124, 126) (p. 371).

## Part IX. Branched ep⁺-subgroupoids (HWZ Chapter 9, §§9.1–9.5 and §9.6.1 (2017 §§9.1–9.5))

Chapter 9 continues Part II; its numbers and pages are those of the book (Springer 2021, pp. 401–458), with the 2017 text's in parentheses (2017 pp. 291–332). It introduces the objects that will carry the solution sets of perturbed sc-Fredholm sections with symmetries: functors $\Theta : X \to \mathbb Q^+$ on an ep-groupoid that are, near every point of their support, finite weighted sums of indicator functions of properly embedded smooth finite-dimensional submanifolds. §9.1 gives the definition (Definition 9.1.2 (2017: 9.1)), the local closedness of the orbit support (Lemma 9.1.5 (2017: 9.1)), symmetric local branching structures (Lemma 9.1.7 (2017: 9.2)) and the dimensional decomposition (Propositions 9.1.11 (2017: 9.2) and 9.1.12, the latter new in 2021 with its proof in Appendix §9.6.1). §9.2 attaches to $\Theta$ a section $T_\Theta$ of formal sums of tangent spaces (Theorem 9.2.1 (2017: 9.1)), proved through good and bad points and a graph representation of the sheets near a bad point (Proposition 9.2.8, Lemmas 9.2.9–9.2.11 (2017: 9.3, 9.6–9.8)); it defines the tangent $T\Theta$ (Definition 9.2.12 (2017: 9.6)) and, through the position of a submanifold relative to $\partial X$ (Lemma 9.2.13 (2017: 9.9)), the boundary $\partial\Theta$ (Proposition 9.2.15, Definition 9.2.16 (2017: 9.4, 9.7)). §9.3 orients $\Theta$ (Definition 9.3.2 (2017: 9.8)), compares orientations at good points (Lemma 9.3.4 (2017: 9.10)), gives an example (Example 9.3.5 (2017: 9.1)) and the boundary orientation (Definitions 9.3.6–9.3.10). §9.4 studies essential points and sets of measure zero of the sheets and decomposes an oriented structure (Propositions 9.4.9, 9.4.10 (2017: 9.5, 9.6)). §9.5 integrates sc-differential forms and proves Stokes' theorem: the sets of measure zero in $|\mathrm{supp}(\Theta)|$ and the σ-algebras $L(S)$, $L(\partial S)$ (Definitions 9.5.1, 9.5.3, 9.5.14, Lemma 9.5.2 (2017: Definitions 9.15–9.17, Lemma 9.16)), the branched integrals (Theorems 9.5.4, 9.5.5 (2017: 9.2, 9.3), Definition 9.5.6, Lemmas 9.5.7, 9.5.9–9.5.11 (2017: 9.17–9.19), Proposition 9.5.13), the boundary measures (Theorems 9.5.15, 9.5.16 (2017: 9.4, 9.5)) and Stokes' theorem (Theorems 9.5.17, 9.5.18 (2017: 9.6, 9.7)). Every gap of §§9.1–9.4 is closed and §9.5 is formalized with the text's hypotheses, except part of Remark 9.5.20; §§IX.26–IX.39 hold the later material.

**What is proved, and what is not.** All definitions of §§9.1–9.5 and §9.6.1 are formalized. Of the eighteen gaps of the chapter, seventeen are closed (G.93–G.109) and one is formalized in part (G.110, for Remark 9.5.20 only); none is open and none has nothing to formalize. *§§9.1–9.4.* The facts of level-0 sc-calculus that the first version of this part took as hypotheses on a general M-polyfold (the local constancy of the dimension of Remark 9.1.1, the graph representation of Lemmas 9.2.9–9.2.11, invariance of domain, the level-1 continuity of frames) are theorems on every M-polyfold (§IX.27). So Proposition 9.1.12, Theorem 9.2.1 (2017: 9.1), Lemma 9.2.7 (2), Lemma 9.6.4 and Proposition 9.6.5 hold for every branched ep⁺-subgroupoid of every ep-groupoid, Lemma 9.3.4 (2017: 9.10) for every $n$-dimensional one, and $T\Theta$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid of $TX$ when $|X|$ is paracompact (§IX.11). Also proved: Remark 9.1.4, Proposition 9.1.9 (2017: 9.1) and Remark 9.1.10 (§IX.26); the global decomposition of Proposition 9.1.11 (§IX.4); the footnote to Definition 9.1.2 (§IX.1); the classification of the orientations of Example 9.3.5 (§IX.29); a tame sheet as a Mathlib manifold with corners, the boundary operation built from the sheet, the continuity of $o_{\partial M}$, the boundary stratum and Figure 9.1 (§IX.30); Lemma 9.4.3 (§IX.18); Lemmas 9.4.4 and 9.4.6 for the sheets of an M-polyfold, with no hypothesis (§IX.28). Lemmas 9.1.5, 9.1.7, 9.2.3, 9.2.5, 9.2.7 (1), 9.3.7, 9.4.2, 9.4.8, 9.6.1, 9.6.2, Propositions 9.2.15, 9.3.9, 9.4.9, 9.4.10 and the remarks with formal content are proved, several in a stronger form. *§9.5.* The Lebesgue null sets of the sheets of an M-polyfold are built (Hausdorff measure in the charts), and Lemma 9.5.2 holds for $n$-dimensional $\Theta$ (§IX.28); Theorems 9.5.4 and 9.5.5 hold as printed for the integral of sc-differential forms, with "oriented, tame" read as: near every point of the support an oriented tame structure describes $\hat T_\Theta$ (§§IX.31–IX.32); (9.21), (9.22), Lemmas 9.5.7, 9.5.9–9.5.11 and Proposition 9.5.13 hold as identities of measures (§§IX.31, IX.33); $L(\partial S)$ is built with $(n-1)$-dimensional null sets (§IX.34). Theorems 9.5.15–9.5.18 are proved as printed, with the text's hypotheses only, for every $n \ge 1$ (G.109 closed, V9.67 and V9.68 restated): the class conditions `hcov` and `hcovS` of the first proofs (§§IX.34–IX.35) are derived (§IX.36), the local formula of Theorems 9.5.15 and 9.5.16 holds for every oriented tame structure (§IX.37), and for $n = 1$ the 0-forms are integrated over the finite sets of oriented boundary points (§IX.38). Witnesses with nonempty boundary, with the local unique continuation property, are the closed upper hemisphere ($n = 2$) and the closed half-circle ($n = 1$) (§§IX.35, IX.38). **Formalized in part** (G.110): Remark 9.5.20. Its M-polyfold $X$, $\partial X$, $\mathbb Z_3 \ltimes X$ and the effective isotropy at $\partial X$, three read in $X$ and one read in $\partial X$, are proved; $\Theta$, $\oint_{\hat\Theta} df$ and the two boundary integrals are not (§§IX.24, IX.39).

**Narrower than printed, and why.** V9.2: the dimension is measured in a chart. V9.9 (Proposition 9.1.11): the uniqueness among all decompositions does not hold as we read it; it holds among local decompositions, and local finiteness off the support needs a bound on the dimensions (§IX.4). V9.27 (Definition 9.2.16): the uniqueness does not hold as we read it; the characterization is unique with (2) asked on the larger support (§IX.13). V9.32 (Lemma 9.3.4): $\Theta$ is $n$-dimensional; for mixed dimensions the lemma does not hold as we read it (§IX.15). V9.33 (Example 9.3.5): "otherwise different" does not hold as we read it, and "four possibilities" holds for each structure but not for $\Theta$, which has infinitely many orientations, six of them with integer weights (§§IX.15, IX.29). V9.42 (Lemma 9.4.4): the sheets have one dimension (§IX.17). V9.65 (Remark 9.1.10): one dimension $n$, since a Mathlib manifold has one model space; the composition of the groupoid is sc-smooth only, Mathlib having no orbifolds (§IX.26). V9.67 and V9.68 (Theorems 9.5.15–9.5.18) are restated (§§IX.36–IX.38). **Statements that do not hold as we read them**, each with a Lean counterexample: the uniqueness in Proposition 9.1.11 (§IX.4); Lemma 9.2.13 (2) ⇒ (1) at interior points (§IX.12); the uniqueness in Definition 9.2.16 (§IX.13); Lemma 9.3.4 for mixed dimensions and two claims of Example 9.3.5 (§§IX.15, IX.29); the footnote to Definition 9.1.2 for $\Theta = 0$ (§IX.1); Lemma 9.4.4 and the transfer of null sets in Lemma 9.5.2 across dimensions (§§IX.17, IX.19, IX.28).

**Seven structural choices.** (1) *Tangent sets, linear algebra in charts.* When this part was first written, Part I's $T_xX$ carried no linear structure (gap G.7, since closed). The tangent space $T_yM$ of a submanifold is the set of tangent vectors fixed by the tangent of the retraction that presents $M$, and $\mathrm{Gr}(x)$ is generated by such sets; in a chart the image of $T_yM$ is a linear subspace of the right dimension, and every argument that needs linear algebra is carried out there (§IX.6). (2) *Functors as functions.* $\Theta$ is a function on objects with $\Theta(s(\varphi)) = \Theta(t(\varphi))$, valued in $\mathbb Q$, nonnegativity a field. (3) *Dimension labellings.* The splitting by dimension is done with labellings $\mathrm{dim} : I \to \mathbb N$, unique when they exist (§IX.1); since the dimension is locally constant on every M-polyfold, a labelled structure exists at every point of the support (§IX.27). (4) *Slices instead of sequences.* Proposition 9.2.8 is used in the text to count the weights of a class of tangent sheets by the values of $\Theta$ at good points; the formalization counts them on one finite slice transverse to the class (§IX.9). The same device proves Proposition 9.6.5 (§IX.22). (5) *Hypotheses first, then theorems.* The facts of the text's §9.2 that need level-0 sc-calculus inside a partial quadrant were first named hypotheses (`HasGraphChartAt`, `HasLocallyConstantDimAt`, `HasDomainInvarianceAt`, `HasContinuousLevelOneOn`), proved on $\mathbb R^m$; they are now theorems on every M-polyfold, with the graph representation in the weaker form of one cone per tangent space, which is all the slice arguments use (§IX.27). The statements under the hypotheses are kept. (6) *Sheet geometry and null sets as structures.* §9.4 is formalized for Mathlib manifolds with corners and, through the structure `SheetGeometry`, for sheets in an M-polyfold (§IX.17); the null sets of §9.5 are a structure `SheetNullSets` (§IX.19). Both are now instantiated on every M-polyfold by the $n$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of the chart images (§IX.28). (7) *Integration as a structure.* The integral of a form over a measurable part of an oriented sheet enters §9.5 through a structure `SheetIntegration` with the properties the text uses (linearity, countable additivity, vanishing on null sets, the comparison of two sheets, invariance under morphisms); Theorems 9.5.4 and 9.5.5 and the lemmas before them are proved for every such structure (§IX.31), and the structure is then built for sc-differential forms by integrating in graph charts (§IX.32).

Throughout, $X = (X, \mathbf X)$ is an ep-groupoid as in Part VII, $s, t$ its source and target, $\pi : X \to |X|$ the orbit map, $X^\infty$ the full subcategory of smooth objects, $G_x$ the isotropy group of $x$ with a natural representation $(\Phi, \Gamma)$ on a neighbourhood $U(x)$ (§VII.4). A *submanifold* is a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold in the sense of Part I (§IV.2): the image, near each of its points, of an sc⁺-retraction. For $\Theta : X \to \mathbb Q$, $\mathrm{supp}(\Theta) = \{\Theta > 0\}$ and $|\mathrm{supp}(\Theta)| = \pi(\mathrm{supp}(\Theta))$. A local branching structure at $x$ is $(U(x), (M_i)_{i \in I}, (\sigma_i)_{i \in I})$ as in Definition 9.1.2; we write $I_y = \{i \mid y \in M_i\}$ and $M_U = \bigcup_i M_i$.

### IX.1 Definition 9.1.2 (2017: 9.1), and the dimension of a submanifold (Remark 9.1.1 (2017: 9.1))

**Definition 9.1.2 (2017: 9.1)** (V9.1) ⟦Chapter9/Basic · EpGroupoid.IsBranchedEpSubgroupoid⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Basic · EpGroupoid.LocalBranchingStructure⟧. A branched ep⁺-subgroupoid is a functor $\Theta \ge 0$ ⟦Chapter9/Basic · EpGroupoid.IsFunctorial⟧ with $\mathrm{supp}(\Theta) \subseteq X_\infty$ ⟦Chapter9/Basic · EpGroupoid.supp⟧, $|\mathrm{supp}(\Theta)|$ paracompact ⟦Chapter9/Basic · EpGroupoid.orbitSupp⟧, and a local branching structure at every point of the support. The formalization reads the paracompactness of the induced topology as a `ParacompactSpace` instance on the subtype $|\mathrm{supp}(\Theta)|$, and "the inclusion $M_i \to U(x)$ is proper" as `IsProperMap` of the inclusion of subtypes. For a closed $M_i$ in $U(x)$ the latter is automatic ⟦Chapter9/Symmetric · isProperMap_inclusion_iff⟧. Witnesses: the zero functor ⟦Chapter9/Basic · EpGroupoid.isBranchedEpSubgroupoid_zero⟧ and the indicator of a smooth point of $\mathbb R^n$, a $0$-dimensional submanifold ⟦Chapter9/Basic · rnPolyfold_isSmoothSubmanifold_singleton⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Basic · EpGroupoid.localBranchingStructure_indicator⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Basic · EpGroupoid.isBranchedEpSubgroupoid_indicator⟧. The 2017 text refers in (4) to "(ii) and (iii)", the 2021 text to (2) and (3).

**The dimension** (V9.2). Remark 9.1.1 says that $m \mapsto \dim T_mM$ is locally constant. With $T_mM$ a set of tangent vectors, the dimension is measured in a chart: $M$ has dimension $k$ at $a$ if the tangent space at the chart image of $a$ of the sub-retract presenting $M$ is $k$-dimensional ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · MPolyfold.HasDimAt⟧. *Step 1, chart independence.* A germ of sc-diffeomorphisms between retracts restricts to a linear isomorphism of the tangent spaces of sub-retracts ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · finrank_span_tangentSpace_eq⟧, so the value is the same for every chart and every presentation ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · MPolyfold.finrank_tangentSpace_chart_change⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · MPolyfold.HasDimAt.finrank_eq⟧; it is unique ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · MPolyfold.HasDimAt.unique⟧ and exists at every point ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · MPolyfold.IsSmoothSubmanifold.exists_hasDimAt⟧. *Step 2, invariance.* It is unchanged by intersecting with an open set and by sc-diffeomorphisms ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · MPolyfold.hasDimAt_inter_isOpen_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · MPolyfold.hasDimAt_image_iff⟧. *Step 3, local constancy* ⟦Chapter9/AppendixSlices · MPolyfold.HasLocallyConstantDimAt⟧ holds on every M-polyfold ⟦Chapter9/GeneralLevelZero · MPolyfold.hasLocallyConstantDimAt⟧: in a chart the dimension is the rank of $Dt$ for the chart sc⁺-retraction $t$ presenting the submanifold ⟦Chapter9/GeneralLevelZero · hasDimAt_finrank⟧, and this rank is locally constant along the retract ⟦Chapter9/GeneralLevelZero · eventually_finrank_eq⟧ (§IX.27). On $\mathbb R^m$ it was proved first: $T_yM$ is the range of the projection $Ds(y)$, whose rank is its trace, continuous in $y$ and integer valued ⟦Chapter9/AppendixSlices · MPolyfold.hasLocallyConstantDimAt_rn⟧. The dimensions of the sheets of one structure enter as labellings; all sheets of one structure pass through $x$, so a labelling is unique ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.LocalBranchingStructure.dim_unique⟧, and by local constancy every point of the support has a labelled structure ⟦Chapter9/GeneralCorollaries · hasLabelledBranchingAt_general⟧.

**$n$-dimensional $\Theta$.** The 2021 text says the sheets "can be taken" $n$-dimensional (2017: are $n$-dimensional), and this is the formal reading: some local branching structure at each point of the support has only $n$-dimensional sheets ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.LocalBranchingStructure.IsOfDim⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.IsNDimensional⟧. The zero functor is $n$-dimensional for every $n$ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.isNDimensional_zero⟧. **The footnote**, that an $n$-dimensional $\Theta$ is not $m$-dimensional for $m \ne n$, is proved for $\Theta$ with nonempty support ⟦Chapter9/LocallyEquidimensional2021 · definition_9_1_2_footnote⟧ ⟦Chapter9/LocallyEquidimensional2021 · definition_9_1_2_footnote_of_ne_zero⟧. *Step 1.* At a point of the support two structures, one with $n$-dimensional and one with $m$-dimensional sheets, give the same tangent sum (Theorem 9.2.1, now unconditional, §IX.10), so some sheet of the first has the tangent space of some sheet of the second ⟦Chapter9/LocallyEquidimensional2021 · exists_submanifoldTangent_eq⟧. *Step 2.* Equal tangent spaces have equal dimensions, so $m = n$ ⟦Chapter9/LocallyEquidimensional2021 · isOfDim_unique⟧. For $\Theta = 0$ the footnote does not hold as we read it, the zero functor being $n$-dimensional for every $n$ ⟦Chapter9/LocallyEquidimensional2021 · definition_9_1_2_footnote_zero⟧. "Locally equidimensional" is formalized in both readings, which agree: at every point of the support some structure has sheets of one dimension ⟦Chapter9/LocallyEquidimensional2021 · IsLocallyEquidimensional⟧, iff at every such point there is an $n$ such that every structure there, restricted to a small enough neighbourhood, has only $n$-dimensional sheets ⟦Chapter9/LocallyEquidimensional2021 · isLocallyEquidimensional_iff⟧, the book's "sufficiently small"; nearby points of the support then have structures of the same dimension ⟦Chapter9/LocallyEquidimensional2021 · IsLocallyEquidimensional.exists_isOpen_isNDimensionalAt⟧ (gap G.93, closed).

**Submanifolds of $\mathbb R^n$** (V9.3). The witnesses of the chapter are built from closed submanifolds of $\mathbb R^n$. The image of a smooth idempotent $s$ is one, of dimension $\mathrm{rank}\,Ds(a)$ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · rnPolyfold_isSmoothSubmanifold_range⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · rnPolyfold_hasDimAt_range⟧. The graph of a smooth $\beta : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ is the image of $(s, t) \mapsto (s, \beta(s))$ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · graphRetraction⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · rnPolyfold_isSubmanifoldOfDim_graph2⟧. Finite weighted sums of closed submanifolds, and indicators of locally closed ones, are branched ep⁺-subgroupoids of the trivial ep-groupoid ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.isBranchedEpSubgroupoid_sum_rn⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.isNDimensional_sum_rn⟧ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.isBranchedEpSubgroupoid_indicator_rn⟧, whose orbit space is $\mathbb R^n$, so the paracompactness is free ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.paracompactSpace_orbitSupp_trivial_rn⟧.

### IX.2 Remark 9.1.3 (b) (2017: 9.2 (b)), Lemma 9.1.5 (2017: 9.1), Definitions 9.1.6 and 9.1.8 (2017: 9.2 and 9.3)

**Remark 9.1.3 (b) (2017: 9.2 (b))** (V9.4) ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.remark_9_1_3_b⟧.
