The lemma is not used by the formal proof of Lemma 15.1.5 (§XV.5); it is formalized as stated.

### XV.5 Lemma 15.1.5 (2017: 15.2): local dichotomy of finitely many maps

**Statement** (stronger) ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.lemma_15_1_5⟧. In a pseudo-metric space, let $s_i$, $i \in I$ finite, be maps continuous on a ball $B_\varepsilon(y)$, $\varepsilon > 0$, with values in a Hausdorff space. Then there are $z$ with $d(z, y) < \varepsilon$, $\delta > 0$ and a surjective partition $e : I \to \{1, \dots, p\}$ such that (1) $B_\delta(z) \subseteq B_\varepsilon(y)$, (2) $s_i = s_{i'}$ on $B_\delta(z)$ when $e(i) = e(i')$, and (3) $s_i(w) \ne s_j(w)$ for $w \in B_\delta(z)$ when $e(i) \ne e(j)$. The text (pp. 685–686) states it for the sections of a local sc⁺-section structure on $O$; the formal maps need only be continuous, with no linear or sc-structure.

**The topological form** ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.exists_isOpen_dichotomy⟧: for finitely many maps continuous on a nonempty open set $V$ of a topological space, with values in a Hausdorff space, there is a nonempty open $W \subseteq V$ on which every pair of maps either coincides everywhere or differs everywhere.

*Proof.* By induction over a finite set $S$ of pairs $(i, j)$, the claim being that some nonempty open $W \subseteq V$ has the dichotomy for the pairs in $S$. For $S = \emptyset$ take $W = V$. For the step, let $W$ serve the pairs of $S$ and add the pair $(i, j)$. The map $w \mapsto (s_i(w), s_j(w))$ is continuous on $W$, and the complement of the diagonal is open because the target is Hausdorff, so
$$W' = \{w \in W : s_i(w) \ne s_j(w)\}$$
is open. If $W'$ is empty, then $s_i = s_j$ on $W$, and $W$ serves $S \cup \{(i, j)\}$. If $W'$ is nonempty, then $W'$ serves the new pair (the maps differ everywhere on it) and still serves the pairs of $S$, since coincidence or difference everywhere on $W$ passes to the subset $W'$. Applying this to the set of all pairs gives the claim.

*The lemma from the topological form.* Apply it to the ball, open and nonempty: it gives $W$ and a point $z \in W$; $d(z, y) < \varepsilon$ since $W$ lies in the ball. As $W$ is open, some $B_\delta(z) \subseteq W$, which gives (1). The partition is that of the values at $z$ ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.exists_fin_partition⟧: $e(i) = e(j)$ iff $s_i(z) = s_j(z)$. For (2), if $e(i) = e(i')$ the pair cannot differ everywhere on $W$ (it agrees at $z$), so it coincides on $W \supseteq B_\delta(z)$. For (3), if $e(i) \ne e(j)$ the pair cannot coincide on $W$ (it differs at $z$), so it differs everywhere on $W$.

*How this departs from the text's proof.* The text builds the pieces one at a time: it fixes $i_1$, considers the closed sets $\Sigma_j = \{s_j = s_{i_1}\}$, uses Lemma 15.1.4 when they cover the ball, moves the point slightly, and repeats with $i_2 \notin I_1$ on a ball of a quarter of the radius. The formal proof goes through the pairs instead of the pieces and shrinks the open set at each step to where the new pair differs, if that set is not empty. The argument for a single pair is the one observation that the set where two continuous maps into a Hausdorff space differ is open; if it is empty on an open set, the maps agree there. So Lemma 15.1.4 is not needed. The same form gives the locally dichotomous points used in §§XV.3, XV.6 and XV.7 ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.exists_isLocDich_mem⟧.

### XV.6 Remark 15.1.6: modifying the sequence

The remark, new in the 2021 edition (p. 686), makes two observations: a sequence with the properties of Proposition 15.1.3 can be obtained from any sequence $x'_k \to 0$ by modifying it "slightly" and passing to a subsequence; and modifying such a sequence slightly keeps the properties. Both are formalized, with "slightly" made explicit (restated).

**First part** ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.remark_15_1_6⟧. In a metric space, for finitely many maps continuous on an open $V$ with values in a Hausdorff space and any sequence $x'_k \to x_0$ in $V$, there are $x''_k \in V$ with $d(x'_k, x''_k) < 1/(k + 1)$ and $x''_k \to x_0$, a strictly increasing $\phi$, and a partition $e$ with the separation property at every $x''_{\phi(k)}$. *Proof.* For each $k$ the set $B_{1/(k+1)}(x'_k) \cap V$ is open and nonempty (it contains $x'_k$), so it contains a locally dichotomous point $x''_k$ (§XV.3, Step 1). Then $d(x''_k, x_0) \le d(x''_k, x'_k) + d(x'_k, x_0)$, and both terms tend to $0$, the first being below $1/(k + 1)$; by squeezing, $x''_k \to x_0$. The subsequence and the partition come from the pigeonhole step of §XV.3 ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.exists_isSeparatedAt_subseq⟧. "Slightly" is the bound $1/(k + 1)$, which gives the text's $d(x'_k, x''_k) \to 0$. The modified points need not differ from $x_0$; if $x'_k \ne x_0$ is wanted as well, one removes $x_0$ from the open sets as in §XV.3.

**Second part** ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.IsSeparatedAt.eventually⟧. If the separation property holds at $z$ for a partition $e$ and the maps are continuous at $z$, it holds at every $z'$ in a neighbourhood of $z$. *Proof*, pair by pair, finitely many conditions each holding on a neighbourhood. For a pair in one piece, $s_i = s_j$ on a neighbourhood $N$ of $z$; on the open interior of $N$ both clauses hold at every point, (1) because the values agree and (2) because the germs agree. For a pair in different pieces, $s_i(z) \ne s_j(z)$, so $(s_i(z), s_j(z))$ lies off the diagonal, which is closed in a Hausdorff space; by continuity of $w \mapsto (s_i(w), s_j(w))$ at $z$, the values differ on a neighbourhood, and (1) holds there while (2) is vacuous for the pair. So small moves of the points of a separating sequence keep it separating, which is the text's second observation; "slightly" means "inside this neighbourhood".

### XV.7 Proof of Theorem 15.1.1: the core lemma, the model, the chart, the change of chart

The proof follows the text's reduction to a local model and its limit argument, with three changes: the separation runs in the level-$1$ topology, the two structures are separated together without halving weights, and the formal sums compared are of pairs (value, derivative) over all branches. The steps are (a) a limit lemma for finite formal sums, (b) the comparison at a separated point, (c) the core lemma in a topological space, (d) the model, (e) the chart, (f) the change of chart and the intrinsic statement.

**(a) The limit step** ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.wsum_eq_of_frequently⟧. Let $a_i(z)$, $b_j(z)$ be finitely many points of a Hausdorff space $Q$, depending on $z$ in a topological space and continuous at $x_0$, with weights $\sigma_i$, $\tau_j$. If the formal sums $\sum\sigma_i \cdot a_i(z)$ and $\sum\tau_j \cdot b_j(z)$ agree for $z$ frequently near $x_0$ (that is, in every neighbourhood of $x_0$ there is such a $z$), they agree at $x_0$. *Proof.* Fix $q \in Q$. For each point $p \ne q$ choose disjoint neighbourhoods $N_p \ni q$ and $V_p \ni p$ (Hausdorff); for $p = q$ take $N_q = V_q = Q$. Let $N_0$ be the intersection of the finitely many $N_p$ for $p$ among the values $a_i(x_0)$, $b_j(x_0)$: a neighbourhood of $q$. For $z$ near $x_0$, and each $i$: if $a_i(x_0) = q$, then $N_0$ is a neighbourhood of $a_i(x_0)$ and $a_i(z) \in N_0$ by continuity; if $a_i(x_0) = p \ne q$, then $a_i(z) \in V_p$, which is disjoint from $N_p \supseteq N_0$. So eventually $a_i(z) \in N_0 \iff a_i(x_0) = q$, for all $i$, and likewise for the $b_j$. Choose $z$ with this property at which the two formal sums agree. Then the mass of $N_0$ under the first sum at $z$ is the coefficient of $q$ in the first sum at $x_0$, the mass under the second is that of the second, and the two masses are equal because the formal sums at $z$ are (§XV.1) ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.mass_eq_of_wsum_eq⟧. This is the text's convergence "in the weak topology" of the formal sums: the points cluster near their limits, and a neighbourhood that separates one limit from the others carries the limit's coefficient.

**(b) At a locally dichotomous point** ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.wsum_pair_eq_at_of_isLocDich⟧. Let the branches $c_\alpha$, $\alpha \in I \sqcup K$, of two families with weights $\sigma$ on $I$ and $\tau$ on $K$ give the same weighted count of every value at $u$, let $u$ be locally dichotomous for the combined family, and let the "derivatives" $D_\alpha(u)$ depend only on germs: $c_\alpha = c_\beta$ near $u$ implies $D_\alpha(u) = D_\beta(u)$. Then the formal sums of the pairs $(c_\alpha(u), D_\alpha(u))$ over $I$ and over $K$ agree. *Proof.* Fix a pair $(v, L)$. Two branches through $v$ at $u$ cannot differ at $u$, so by dichotomy they coincide near $u$, and by locality they have the same $D$. Hence there is one $L_v$ with $D_\alpha(u) = L_v$ for every branch through $v$ (any $L$ if there is none). For such a family, the coefficient of $(v, L)$ is the coefficient of $v$ if $L = L_v$ and $0$ otherwise ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.wsum_pair_of_const⟧: the pairs with first entry $v$ are exactly $(v, L_v)$. Applying this to both families, with the same $L_v$ since it was chosen for the combined family, the coefficients are the counts of $v$, which agree.

**(c) The core lemma** ⟦Chapter15/SeparationLemmas · Linearization15.wsum_pair_eq_of_isLocal⟧. Let both families be continuous on an open $V$, with equal weighted counts of every value at every point of $V$, and let the $D_\alpha$ be continuous on $V$ and depend only on germs at every point of $V$. Then at every $x_0 \in V$ the formal sums $\sum\sigma_i \cdot (c_i, D_i)(x_0)$ and $\sum\tau_j \cdot (c_j, D_j)(x_0)$ agree. *Proof.* The maps $z \mapsto (c_\alpha(z), D_\alpha(z))$ are continuous at $x_0$, so the limit step (a) applies once the sums agree frequently near $x_0$. Given a neighbourhood $N$ of $x_0$, the set $\operatorname{int}(N) \cap V$ is open and contains $x_0$, so it contains a point $u$ locally dichotomous for the combined family (§XV.3, Step 1); by (b) the sums agree at $u$. *Departure from the text.* The text forms the union of the two structures with halved weights, applies Proposition 15.1.3 to it, and compares multiplicities piece by piece along the sequence. Here the dichotomy is applied to the combined family $I \sqcup K$ directly, which needs no new structure and no weights. The points $u$ may include $x_0$ itself, so no sequence $x_k \ne x_0$ is needed and isolated points are covered; this is why Proposition 15.1.3 is not used and its failure at isolated points (§XV.3) does not reach the theorem.

**(d) On the model.** Two facts of the sc-calculus at level $1$ come first. *Continuity of values* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationModel · Linearization15.continuousOn_comp_toBase_one⟧: an sc⁰ map is continuous on $U_1$ in the level-$1$ topology, read in $F_0$ (it is continuous $U_1 \to F_1$, and $F_1 \to F_0$ is continuous). *Continuity of derivatives* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationModel · Linearization15.continuousOn_scDeriv_coe⟧: for an sc¹ map $g$, $u \mapsto Dg(u)$ is continuous on $U_1$ (level-$1$ topology) into the operators $E_0 \to F_0$ with the topology of pointwise convergence. This is Definition 1.1.15 (3), the continuity of $(u, h) \mapsto Dg(u)h$ on $U_1 \times E_0$, read one $h$ at a time. *Locality of the derivative* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationModel · Linearization15.scDeriv_eq_of_eventuallyEq_lvl⟧: if two sc¹ maps $g$, $g'$ on an sc-domain agree near a level-$1$ point $x$ in the level-$1$ topology, then $Dg(x) = Dg'(x)$. Both derivatives are Fréchet derivatives of $g \circ \iota$, $g' \circ \iota$ within $U_1$ at $x$; the two composites agree near $x$ within $U_1$, so they have the same derivatives there, and within an sc-domain the derivative within $U_1$ is unique; finally an operator on $E_0$ is determined by its values on the dense $E_1$.

*The comparison on the model* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationModel · Linearization15.wsum_model_eq⟧. Let the two structures have the same counts at every $y \in O \cap N$. Work on the space $Z = U_1$, the level-$1$ points of $U$ with the level-$1$ topology, and on its open subset $V = \{u : r(u) \in N\}$, open because $u \mapsto r(u)$ is continuous on $U_1$ (r is sc-smooth, so sc⁰). The combined family has branches $c_\alpha(u) = \hat s_\alpha(r(u))$ (the $\hat s_i$ and the $\hat t_j$ together) and derivatives $D_\alpha(u) = D((\hat f - \hat s_\alpha) \circ r)(u)$, regarded as functions $E_0 \to F_0$. The hypotheses of the core lemma hold. Continuity: the $c_\alpha$ by the first fact, since $\hat s_\alpha \circ r$ is sc-smooth; the $D_\alpha$ by the second, since $(\hat f - \hat s_\alpha) \circ r$ is sc-smooth, a difference of sc-smooth maps. Counts: at $u \in V$ they are the counts at $r(u) \in O \cap N$, equal by hypothesis. Locality: if $c_\alpha = c_\beta$ near $u$ in $U_1$, then $(\hat f - \hat s_\alpha) \circ r$ and $(\hat f - \hat s_\beta) \circ r$ agree near $u$ in $U_1$ (both are $\hat f \circ r$ minus the branch), so their derivatives agree at $u$ by the locality fact. The core lemma gives equal formal sums of pairs at the point $z$, which lies in $U_1$ because it lies over $O \subseteq U$, and in $V$ because $r(z) = z$ for $z \in O$.

*Theorem 15.1.1 on the model*, from the pairs. The coefficient of an operator $\ell : T_zO \to F_0$ in the formal sum of a structure is the mass, under the formal sum of pairs, of the set
$$N_\ell = \{(v, D) : v = \hat f(z),\ D(h) = \ell(h)\ \text{for all } h \in T_zO\}.$$
Indeed, the summand $i$ contributes $\sigma_i$ iff $\hat s_i(z) = \hat f(z)$ and $(\hat f - \hat s_i)'(z) = \ell$, and the latter, an equality of operators on $T_zO$, says that the full derivative $D((\hat f - \hat s_i) \circ r)(z)$ agrees with $\ell$ on $T_zO$, which is the membership of the pair in $N_\ell$ (with $r(z) = z$). Equal formal sums of pairs give equal masses (§XV.1), so the coefficients of $\ell$ agree for the two structures; this proves `theorem_15_1_1_model`. The form with an arbitrary map $\psi$ of operators is the same argument with the set $\{(v, D) : v = \hat f(z),\ \psi(L) = q'\ \text{for every operator } L \text{ with } L = D\}$: the derivative is recorded as a function, and $\psi$ is applied to the operator it determines.

*Two readings of the text's proof* (Findings, Chapter 15, items 1 and 2). (a) The text takes the points $x_k$ of Proposition 15.1.3 in the metric of $E_0$ and lets $T(f - s_i)(x_k)$ converge "in the weak topology". The derivative of an sc¹ map is continuous only on level $1$, and there only pointwise as an operator $E_0 \to F_0$. So the separation is run in the level-$1$ topology, where the branches are continuous and the separation lemmas hold equally (they are topological), and the "weak topology" is read as pointwise convergence of operators, which is the topology in which the derivatives are continuous. (b) The last display of the text sums $\sigma_i \cdot T(f - s_i)(0)$ over all $i$ and then uses $f(0) = s_i(0)$; this holds only for some $i$, and the sum is presumably over $\{i : f(0) = s_i(0)\}$. The formal proof compares the formal sums of the pairs $(s_i, (f - s_i)')$ over all $i$, where no such equation is needed, and selects the first entry $f(0)$ only at the end, by the mass of $N_\ell$.

**(e) In a strong bundle chart.** Let $c$ be a strong bundle chart of $P$ with base chart $\varphi$, model $O$ and fibre model $F$, and let $s$ be a section over $O_X \supseteq \operatorname{dom}(c)$. Its principal part $\hat s$ is the fibre component of $c \circ s \circ \varphi^{-1}$: $c(s(\varphi^{-1}(z))) = (z, \hat s(z))$ for $z \in O$ ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.apply_localSection⟧. *Principal parts are sc-smooth.* A local sc⁺-section on $O_X$ has $\hat s \circ r$ sc-smooth on $U$ in every chart of the atlas with domain in $O_X$ ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.IsScPlusSectionOn.isScSmooth_principal_comp_r⟧. The sc⁺-section is an sc-smooth map into $W_{0,1}$; composed with the sc-smooth inclusion $W_{0,1} \to W$ it is sc-smooth into $W$ on $O_X$; read in the chart, $z \mapsto (z, \hat s(z))$ is an sc-smooth retract map $O \to K$; composed with the base retraction $r : U \to O$ and projected to the second factor, $\hat s \circ r$ is sc-smooth. The same holds for an sc-smooth global section ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.isScSmooth_principal_comp_r⟧. *Counts in the chart* ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.IsLocalRepOn.count_eq⟧: for a local section structure of $\Lambda$ on $O_X \supseteq \operatorname{dom}(c)$ and $y \in O$, the weighted count $\sum_{i : \hat s_i(y) = v}\sigma_i$ equals $\Lambda(\Phi^{-1}(y, v))$ if $(y, v) \in K$, and $0$ otherwise. If $(y, v) \in K$, let $w = \Phi^{-1}(y, v)$, which lies over $\varphi^{-1}(y) \in O_X$; the defining formula of the structure gives $\Lambda(w) = \sum_{i : w = s_i(P w)}\sigma_i$, and $w = s_i(\varphi^{-1}(y))$ iff $\hat s_i(y) = v$, by injectivity of the chart and the formula for $\hat s_i$. If $(y, v) \notin K$, no branch can have $\hat s_i(y) = v$, since $(y, \hat s_i(y))$ is the chart image of $s_i(\varphi^{-1}(y))$ and lies in $K$. *The statement in a chart* ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.linSumChart_eq⟧: for two structures of $\Lambda$ on $O$ and $O'$ and a chart with domain in $O \cap O'$, both counts at every $y$ of the model equal $\Lambda(\Phi^{-1}(y, v))$ or $0$, so the model theorem applies with $N$ the whole space; Theorem 15.1.1 in a chart is this for sc-Fredholm section functors, which are sc-smooth ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.theorem_15_1_1⟧. Every object lies in such a chart ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.exists_chart_isLocalRepOn⟧: an sc⁺-multisection has a local section structure on the domain $U(x)$ of a natural representation around $x$, and any atlas chart around $x$ restricted to its domain intersected with $U(x)$ is a chart with domain in $U(x)$.

**(f) The change of chart, and the statement with intrinsic operators.** *Independence of the structure in $\mathrm{GrF}(x)$* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.linSumIntr_eq_of_isLocalRepOn⟧: in one chart with domain in $O \cap O'$, the intrinsic formal sums of two structures agree. This is the model theorem with the map $\psi$ that sends a chart operator to its intrinsic operator (§XV.1), at the level-$1$ point over $\varphi(x)$, with the counts of (e).

*The text's "without loss of generality $X = O$"* is, formally, the independence of the intrinsic operator $(f - s)'(x)$ from the chart. The proof makes $f - s$ a global section to which Part I's chain rule applies. *The section $f - s$ on $O_X$* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.sectionSubOn⟧: at $y \in O_X$ the difference $f(y) - s(y)$ in the fibre, and $f(y)$ elsewhere; a section ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.isSection_sectionSubOn⟧ whose principal part in a chart with domain in $O_X$ is $\hat f - \hat s$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.principal_sectionSubOn⟧, because the chart is linear on fibres. In such a chart $z \mapsto (z, \hat f(z) - \hat s(z))$ is an sc-smooth retract map $O \to K$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.isScSmoothRetractMap_sectionSubOn⟧: for every sc-smooth retraction $R'$ onto $O$, $\hat f \circ R'$ and $\hat s \circ R'$ are sc-smooth (as in (e)), and so is the pair $(R', \hat f \circ R' - \hat s \circ R')$; this is the chart-wise form of sc-smoothness that Part I's statements take. The derivative of $(\hat f - \hat s) \circ r$ at a level-$1$ point equals that of the principal part of $f - s$ composed with $r$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.scDeriv_sub_eq_sectionSubOn⟧, since the two maps agree on $U$ (derivatives of sc¹ maps agreeing on a relatively open set agree on its level-$1$ points).

*The values lie in the fibre* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.chartOp_mem_range⟧. At a zero $x$ of a global section $g$ whose principal part is sc-smooth in the chart, every value $D(\hat g \circ r)(z)(T\varphi\,\alpha)$ lies in $\Phi_x(W_x)$. Part I's lemma on the derivative at a zero ⟦Chapter3/LinearizationCharts · rho_scDeriv_comp_r⟧ says that the bundle projection $\rho(z)$ onto the fibre $K_z$ fixes $D(\hat g \circ r)(z)$ on $T_zO$ when $\hat g(z) = 0$; so the values lie in $K_z = \Phi_x(W_x)$. Hence the default branch of the intrinsic operator is never taken at the points of interest.

*The chain rule* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.toIntr_chart_independent⟧. At a zero $x \in X_1$ of a section $g$ whose principal parts are sc-smooth in two charts $c$, $c'$ around $x$, the intrinsic operators through $c$ and through $c'$ are equal. Part I's chain rule with the operators named ⟦Chapter3/LinearizationChartChange · linAt_chart_change_key⟧ provides a retraction $r_W$ onto the base overlap and the identity
$$D(\hat g' \circ r')(z')\big(D(\tau \circ r_W)(z)v\big) = \Gamma(z)\big(D(\hat g \circ r)(z)v\big),$$
with $\tau$ the base transition and $\Gamma(z)$ the fibre transition operator. Two further identities translate this to intrinsic operators: the chart vector of $\alpha \in T_xX$ in $c'$ is $D(\tau \circ r_W)(z)$ applied to its chart vector in $c$ (the transition of tangent fibres), and the fibre part of $c'$ is $\Gamma(z)$ composed with that of $c$. With these, $\Phi'_x$ applied to the operator through $c'$ equals $\Phi'_x$ applied to the operator through $c$, and $\Phi'_x$ is injective. This is the argument of Part I's chart independence of $f'(x)$ ⟦Chapter3/LinearizationIntrinsic · StrongBundle.linIntr_chart_independent⟧, with chart-wise hypotheses only, so that it applies to $f - s$, which is sc-smooth only over $O_X$.

*The formal sum does not depend on the chart* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.linSumIntr_chart_independent⟧. For one structure on $O_X$ and two charts with domains in $O_X$, the formal sums agree term by term. The selection condition is the same through both charts: $\hat s_i(\varphi(y)) = \hat f(\varphi(y))$ iff $s_i(y) = f(y)$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.principal_eq_iff⟧, by injectivity of the chart on the fibre. For a selected $i$, the operator $(f - s_i)'(x)$ through either chart is the intrinsic operator of the global section $f - s_i$ at its zero $x$ (by the derivative identity above), and the chain rule gives equality.

*Proof of the intrinsic statement.* Given structures on $O$, $O'$ and charts $c$, $c'$ with domains in $O$, $O'$ around $x \in X_1$, let $c''$ be $c$ restricted to $\operatorname{dom}(c) \cap O \cap O'$, a chart around $x$ with domain in $O \cap O'$. Then: the sum of $(s, \sigma)$ through $c$ equals that through $c''$ (chart independence, structure $s$); through $c''$ it equals the sum of $(t, \tau)$ (independence of the structure); and that equals the sum of $(t, \tau)$ through $c'$ (chart independence, structure $t$). Only the sc-smoothness of $f$ enters; the theorem is stated for sc-Fredholm section functors, as in the text.

### XV.8 Definition 15.1.7 (2017: 15.1): the linearization $T(f, \Lambda)$

**Definition** (restated) ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.linearization⟧. *Local data* at $x \in X_1$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.LocalLinData⟧ are an open set $O$, a local sc⁺-section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)_{i < k}$ of $\Lambda$ on $O$, and a strong bundle chart $c$ of the atlas around $x$ with domain in $O$; their formal sum is the intrinsic sum through $c$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.LocalLinData.sum⟧. $T(f, \Lambda)(x) \in \mathrm{GrF}(x)$ is the sum of some local data, chosen, and $0$ if there are none. The text calls $T(f, \Lambda)$ the linearization of $\Lambda \circ f$ "at the points in $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$" (p. 687); the formal definition is made at every level-$1$ point, with value $0$ off the support (§XV.2).

**Well-defined** ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.LocalLinData.sum_eq⟧: any two local data at $x$ give the same sum, by the intrinsic Theorem 15.1.1 (§XV.7 (f)). **Data exist** ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.nonempty_localLinData⟧ at every level-$1$ point of an sc⁺-multisection, from the chart of §XV.7 (e). **Theorem 15.1.1 (2)** ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.linearization_eq⟧: $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is the sum of *any* local data at $x$; so the value at $y$ may be computed from any structure around $x$ and any chart around $y$ with domain inside it, which is the text's (2) for all $y$ near $x$, smooth or of level $1$. **Theorem 15.1.1 (1) and Remark 15.1.2** ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.linearization_eq_zero⟧: where $\Lambda(f(x)) = 0$, $T(f, \Lambda)(x) = 0$. *Proof.* Take the chosen data $(O, s, \sigma, c)$. The point $(\varphi(x), \hat f(\varphi(x)))$ lies in $K$, and $\Phi^{-1}$ of it is $f(x)$; so by the count formula (§XV.7 (e)) the weighted count of $\hat f(\varphi(x))$ is $\Lambda(f(x)) = 0$. With positive weights, no branch has $\hat s_i(\varphi(x)) = \hat f(\varphi(x))$, and every summand of the formal sum vanishes.

**In a chart.** The formalization also keeps the chart-level definition: in a chart $c$, the formal sum of any structure on an open set containing the domain of $c$, and $0$ if there is none ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.linearizationIn⟧, equal to the sum of every such structure at every level-$1$ point ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.linearizationIn_eq⟧, and $0$ where $\Lambda(f(y)) = 0$ ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.remark_15_1_2⟧. It is the form used where an argument stays inside one chart.

The definition is the value of a section; that this section is a *functor* is the next subsection.

### XV.9 Theorem 15.1.1: the functor property

The text calls $T(f, \Lambda)$ a section functor of $\mathrm{GrF}(X) \to X_\infty$, i.e. $T(f, \Lambda)(t(\varphi)) = \varphi_*T(f, \Lambda)(s(\varphi))$ for every morphism, and gives no separate argument for it. The formalization proves it at every level-$1$ point (stronger than the text's smooth points), with no added hypothesis.

**The action of a morphism on $\mathrm{GrF}$.** For $\varphi : x \to y$, $\mu(\varphi, \cdot) : W_x \to W_y$ is a linear map ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.muLin⟧ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.muLin_apply⟧, linear because the action of a strong bundle over an ep-groupoid is linear on fibres. If $x$ is of level $1$ then so is $\varphi$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.mem_levelSet_one_of_src⟧ (a morphism lies in $\mathbf X_m$ iff its source lies in $X_m$), and then Chapter 7's tangent map $T\varphi : T_xX \to T_yX$ is a bounded linear isomorphism ⟦Chapter7/TangentMorphismLinear · EpGroupoid.tangentMorCLE⟧. An operator $L : T_xX \to W_x$ is carried to
$$\varphi_*L = \mu(\varphi, \cdot) \circ L \circ (T\varphi)^{-1} : T_yX \to W_y$$
⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.conjOp⟧ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.conjOp_apply⟧, which is the text's $\varphi_*L \circ T\varphi = \mu(\varphi, L(\cdot))$, and a formal sum to the push-forward of its coefficients along $L \mapsto \varphi_*L$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.grfPush⟧.

**Statement** (stronger, for this clause) ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.theorem_15_1_1_functor⟧. For an sc-Fredholm section functor $f$, an sc⁺-multisection $\Lambda$, a morphism $\varphi$ and level-$1$ points $x = s(\varphi)$, $y = t(\varphi)$: $T(f, \Lambda)(y) = \varphi_*T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ in $\mathrm{GrF}(y)$.

**Proof.** Since $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$ may be computed from *any* local data at $y$ (§XV.8), it suffices to carry local data at $x$ to local data at $y$ and to compare the two sums. The carrying uses the local strong bundle isomorphism attached to a morphism by its sheet, built in Chapter 12 (Part XII) ⟦Chapter12/MorphismIso · EpStrongBundle.morIso⟧: over the image $t(\text{sheet})$ of the sheet of $\varphi$ it consists of the base sc-diffeomorphism $\phi = s \circ (t|_{\text{sheet}})^{-1}$ onto $s(\text{sheet})$, with $\phi(y) = x$, and the fibre maps $\Phi$, $\Psi$ given by the action $\mu$ of the morphisms of the sheet.

*Step 1, data at $x$ inside the sheet.* Take local data $(O, s, \sigma, c)$ at $x$, restrict the chart to $\operatorname{dom}(c) \cap s(\text{sheet})$ and the structure to $O \cap s(\text{sheet})$ (a local structure restricts to open subsets ⟦Chapter11/MultisectionLocalStructure2021 · SBLocalization.IsLocalRepOn.mono⟧). Call the result $(O, s, \sigma, c)$ again.

*Step 2, carrying the sections* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.transSec⟧. A section $s$ near $x$ becomes $z \mapsto \Psi(s(\phi(z)))$ on $t(\text{sheet}) \cap \phi^{-1}(O)$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.transSet⟧, an open set ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.isOpen_transSet⟧ (the preimage of an open set under the continuous $\phi$), and the carried section is a section there ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.P_transSec⟧ because $\Psi$ covers $\phi^{-1}$. An sc⁺-section stays sc⁺ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.isScPlusSectionOn_transSec⟧: its level-$1$ lift is the composite of the lift of $s$ with $\phi$ and with the level-$1$ part of $\Psi$, all sc-smooth. A local section structure of a *functor* $\Lambda$ is carried to one of $\Lambda$, with the same weights ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.isLocalRepOn_transSec⟧: for $w$ over the new domain, $\Lambda(w) = \Lambda(\Phi(w))$ because $\Phi$ acts by $\mu$ of a morphism and $\Lambda$ is a functor ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.isWFunctor_morIso_Φ⟧; the formula of the structure at $\Phi(w)$, which lies over $\phi(P(w)) \in O$, counts the $i$ with $\Phi(w) = s_i(\phi(P w))$; and this holds iff $w = \Psi(s_i(\phi(P w)))$, since $\Phi$ and $\Psi$ are inverse on the relevant fibres.

*Step 3, carrying the chart.* The chart $c$ at $x$ is carried to the transported chart $c \circ \Phi$ at $y$ ⟦Chapter3/FredholmPullbackIso · StrongBundle.LocalIso.transportChart⟧, with base chart $\varphi \circ \phi$ and the same model; it is a chart of the atlas ⟦Chapter3/FredholmPullbackIso · StrongBundle.LocalIso.isChart_transportChart⟧. In it the principal parts of the carried sections are those of the given sections in $c$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.principal_transportChart_transSec⟧ (unwind $\Phi \circ \Psi = \mathrm{id}$ and $\phi \circ \phi^{-1} = \mathrm{id}$), and the principal part of $f$ is that of $f$ in $c$ ⟦Chapter3/FredholmPullbackIso · StrongBundle.LocalIso.principal_transportChart⟧, because a functorial section satisfies $f = \Psi \circ f \circ \phi$ on $t(\text{sheet})$ ⟦Chapter12/MorphismIso · EpStrongBundle.eqOn_morIso⟧, which is $f(t(\psi)) = \mu(\psi, f(s(\psi)))$ for the morphisms $\psi$ of the sheet.

*Step 4, the chain rule in the carried chart.* Two identities at the point. $T\varphi$ is the identity on chart vectors ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.chartVec_transport⟧: the chart vector of $T\varphi(\beta)$ in $c \circ \Phi$ equals the chart vector of $\beta$ in $c$. Indeed $T\varphi = T\hat\varphi$ at $x$ (Chapter 7's tangent map of a morphism is that of the local diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi = t \circ (s|_{\text{sheet}})^{-1}$), $T(\phi) \circ T(\hat\varphi) = \mathrm{id}$ near $x$ since $\phi \circ \hat\varphi = \mathrm{id}$, and the chart vector of $Tg(\alpha)$ in $c$ is that of $\alpha$ in $c \circ g$. And $\mu(\varphi, \cdot)$ followed by the fibre part of the carried chart at $y$ is the fibre part of $c$ at $x$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.fiberLin_transport_muLin⟧, because on $W_x$ the fibre map $\Psi$ is $\mu(\varphi, \cdot)$ and $\Phi$ undoes it; also the fibre part of the carried chart at $y$ takes values in that of $c$ at $x$ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.fiberLin_transport_mem_range⟧. Together ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.toIntr_transportChart⟧: for every chart operator $L$, the intrinsic operator through the carried chart is $\mu(\varphi, \cdot) \circ (\text{intrinsic operator through } c) \circ (T\varphi)^{-1}$. If the values of $L \circ T\varphi$ lie in the fibre for $c$, those through the carried chart lie in the fibre (the preimages are the $\mu(\varphi, \cdot)$-images), and the two sides agree after applying the injective fibre part; if not, neither do the carried ones, and both sides are $0$.

*Step 5, the sums correspond* ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationFunctor · SBLocalization.linSumIntr_transportChart⟧. The level-$1$ point of the carried chart over $y$ is the level-$1$ point of $c$ over $x$, since $\phi(y) = x$. Term by term: the selection condition is the same (the principal parts agree), and the derivative $D((\hat f - \hat s_i) \circ r)(z)$ is the same in both charts, the composites agreeing on $U$. So each term of the sum at $y$ is $\varphi_*$ of the corresponding term at $x$ by Step 4, and push-forward of formal sums is additive. With the carried data at $y$ and the given data at $x$, §XV.8 identifies both sides with $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$ and $\varphi_*T(f, \Lambda)(x)$.

*Not formalized.* That $\varphi \mapsto \varphi_*$ is itself functorial, $(\psi\varphi)_* = \psi_*\varphi_*$ and $1_* = \mathrm{id}$, which the text uses to speak of $\mathrm{GrF}(X)$ as a category, is not formalized and not needed for the theorem; it would follow from Chapter 7's functoriality of $T$ and the composition law of $\mu$, in about 60–100 lines.

### XV.10 Local sc⁺-sections, the sections $f - s_i$ on $W|_O$, and local solution sets (prerequisite for §15.2)

The proofs of Theorems 15.2.2 and 15.2.5 and of the sc-Fredholm property of the summands (§XV.11) apply Part I's implicit function theorem to $f - s_i$ near $x$, where $s_i$ is defined only on an open $O$. The formalization makes $f - s_i$ a section problem of Part I on the restricted strong bundle $W|_O$ (extra).

**Local sc⁺-sections in compatible charts.** Chapter 11 defines a local sc⁺-section on $O$ as a section over $O$ that is sc-smooth into $W_{0,1}$. Two chart facts are needed for charts that are only compatible with the atlas, such as restricted charts. In every such chart with domain in $O$, the principal part takes values in $F_1$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.IsScPlusSectionOn.principal_mem_range_of_isChart⟧: compare with an atlas chart around $s(x)$, in which this holds by Chapter 13's local form ⟦Chapter13/ScPlusSectionOn · SBLocalization.IsScPlusSectionOn.isScSmoothRetractMap_localRepOne⟧, through the transition, which preserves level $1$ in the fibre. And the level-$1$ representative $z \mapsto (z, \hat s_1(z))$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.localRepOne_eq_of_sub⟧ is an sc-smooth retract map $O \to K[1]$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.IsScPlusSectionOn.isScSmoothRetractMap_localRepOne_of_isChart⟧. The proof is local: near each point, the representative is the composite of the base transition into an atlas chart $c'$ around $s(x)$, the representative in $c'$ (sc-smooth by Chapter 13), and the level-$1$ part of the bundle transition back to $c$; the composite agrees with the representative on the overlap.

**Restriction to $O$** ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.IsScPlusSectionOn.restrictOpen⟧. A local sc⁺-section on $O$ is a global sc⁺-section of the restricted strong bundle $W|_O$, Part I's pull-back along the inclusion $O \to X$ ⟦Chapter3/RestrictOpen · StrongBundle.restrictOpen⟧: the charts of $W|_O$ are restrictions of charts with domain in $O$, and in them the two chart facts above are the conditions of an sc⁺-section. (The restricted bundle needs the paracompactness of $O$ and of the pulled-back total space as type-class data; they hold for open subsets of M-polyfolds and are supplied in the proofs.)

**The section $f - s$** ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.subSec⟧: $f + (-1)\cdot\bar s$, where $\bar s$ is $s$ extended by $0$ off $O$; a global section ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.isSection_subSec⟧ with principal part $\hat f - \hat s$ in every chart with domain in $O$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.principal_subSec⟧ and with zeros in $O$ exactly where $f = s$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.isZeroAt_subSec_iff⟧. Its restriction to $W|_O$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.subRestrict⟧ is a tame sc-Fredholm section when $f$ has Part I's tame germ data ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.isScFredholmSectionTame_subRestrict⟧. *Proof.* Restriction to an open set keeps tame germ data (Part I), so $f|_O$ is tame sc-Fredholm on $W|_O$; $-\bar s$ is an sc⁺-section on $O$ (Chapter 13: sc⁺-sections on $O$ are closed under constant multiples), hence a global sc⁺-section of $W|_O$ by the restriction above; and an sc⁺-perturbation of a tame sc-Fredholm section is one, by Part I's Theorem 3.1.18 in its tame form ⟦Chapter3/TameGermsAddG · theorem_3_1_18_tame⟧. Finally, the restriction of a sum of sections is the sum of the restrictions.

**The linearization in a chart.** At a level-$1$ point $z$ of a chart with domain in $O$, the chart operator of $(f - s)'$ is $D((\hat f - \hat s) \circ r)(z) : E_0 \to F_0$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.subDeriv⟧, the derivative of an sc¹ map ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.isSc1_sub_comp_r⟧, and "onto" means that it maps $T_zO$ onto the fibre $K_z = \{k : (z, k) \in K\}$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.ChartOnto⟧, Part I's "$f'(x)$ onto" read in the chart. *The intrinsic and the chart readings agree* ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.surjective_toIntr_subDeriv_iff⟧: at $x \in X_1$ with $f(x) = s(x)$, the intrinsic operator $(f - s)'(x) : T_xX \to W_x$ of §XV.1 is onto iff the chart operator maps $T_zO$ onto $K_z$, $z$ over $\varphi(x)$. The chart operator equals that of the global section $f - s$, whose values at its zero lie in the fibre (§XV.7 (f)); the fibre part of the chart maps $W_x$ bijectively onto $K_{\varphi(x)}$, and $T\varphi$ maps $T_xX$ onto $T_zO$, so surjectivity transfers in both directions. *And they are Part I's surjectivity on $W|_O$.* In the restricted chart of $W|_O$ the principal part of $(f - s)|_O$ composed with $r$ has the same derivative as $(\hat f - \hat s) \circ r$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.scDeriv_restrictTo_subRestrict⟧; so chart surjectivity gives Part I's surjective linearization of $(f - s)|_O$ at $x$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.isLinSurjAt_subRestrict⟧, and conversely, at a zero, Part I's surjectivity gives chart surjectivity in every chart with domain in $O$ and at every level-$1$ point over $\varphi(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.chartOnto_of_isLinSurjAt_subRestrict⟧, by the chart independence of Part I's notion.

**Local solution sets.** *At a point of good position* ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.exists_solutionSet_of_isGoodPosition⟧. If $(f - s)|_O$ is in good position at $x$ in the sense of Part I's Definition 3.6.6 in a tame chart, there is an open $V \ni x$ inside the domain of $c$ such that $\{y \in V : f(y) = s(y)\}$ is a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold of $X$ (Definition 4.2.1), and at each of its points $y$: $y$ is smooth, $(f - s)|_O$ is in good position at $y$, and the chart operator is onto at every level-$1$ point over $\varphi(y)$. *Proof.* Part I's Theorem 3.6.8 ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFTNearbyOntoG · theorem_3_6_8'⟧ for the tame sc-Fredholm section $(f - s)|_O$ at its zero $x$ gives an open $V_x \subseteq O$ on which every zero is in good position; on $W = V_x \cap \operatorname{dom}(c)$ the solution set is a smooth submanifold of $O$ by Part I's lemma on solution sets in good position ⟦Chapter5/GeneralPosition · StrongBundle.isSmoothSubmanifold_solutionSet_inter⟧, and its image under the sc-diffeomorphism $O \to X$ (the inclusion) is a smooth submanifold of $X$. Zeros of an sc-Fredholm section are smooth points; good position implies surjective linearization; and the converse direction above gives chart surjectivity. *At an interior point* ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.exists_solutionSet_interior⟧: if $d_X(x) = 0$, $f(x) = s(x)$ and the chart operator is onto at $x$, the same conclusion holds without "good position" in it. The restriction $(f - s)|_O$ has degeneracy index $0$ at $x$ (the index of an open subset is that of $X$), it has surjective linearization at $x$ by the transfer above, and at a point of index $0$ Part I's surjectivity gives good position ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFTIndexG · StrongBundle.isGoodPositionGerm_of_isLinSurjAt⟧; then the first case applies.

All of this rests on Part I's Theorem 3.6.8 for tame germ data; with the 2021 untamed notion that theorem does not hold as we read it (Part III), which is why $f$ carries the tame germ data here and in §15.2 (§XV.11).

### XV.11 Theorem 15.1.1 (2): the summands are sc-Fredholm

The text puts sc-Fredholm operators into $\mathrm{GrF}(x)$ and asserts that $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is an element of it: each $(f - s_i)'(x)$ with $f(x) = s_i(x)$ is sc-Fredholm, because $f - s_i$ is an sc⁺-perturbation of an sc-Fredholm section. The formalization proves this for the operators that occur, in a chart (narrower).

**The chart operator is sc-Fredholm** ⟦Chapter15/FredholmSummands · SBLocalization.subDeriv_isScFredholm⟧. Let $f$ have Part I's tame germ data, $s$ be sc⁺ on an open $O$ containing the domain of the chart $c$, $f(x) = s(x)$, and $z$ a level-$1$ point over $\varphi(x)$ in $U$. Then $D((\hat f - \hat s) \circ r)(z)$ is an sc-operator, $T_zO$ and $K_z$ are sc-subspaces, the operator maps $T_zO$ into $K_z$, and its restriction $T_zO \to K_z$ is sc-Fredholm, Fredholm on every level with the index of level $0$. *Proof.* By §XV.10, $(f - s)|_O$ is a tame sc-Fredholm section of $W|_O$ with a zero at $x$, and the restricted chart of $c$ is a chart of $W|_O$. Part I's statement that the linearization of an sc-Fredholm section at a zero is sc-Fredholm in every chart ⟦Chapter3/LinearizationChartsScG · StrongBundle.linAt_isScFredholm⟧ gives all the conclusions for the derivative of the restricted principal part composed with $r$, which is $D((\hat f - \hat s) \circ r)(z)$ by the derivative identity of §XV.10.

**Theorem 15.1.1 (2), the summands** (restated, with the inherited hypothesis) ⟦Chapter15/FredholmSummands · SBLocalization.linearization_summand_isScFredholm⟧. For $x \in X_1$ and any local data $(O, s, \sigma, c)$ (§XV.8), every operator $L$ in the support of $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is $(f - s_i)'(x)$, the intrinsic operator of $D((\hat f - \hat s_i) \circ r)(z)$, for some $i$ with $f(x) = s_i(x)$, and that chart operator is sc-Fredholm as above. *Proof.* $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is the sum of the given data (§XV.8); an operator in the support of that sum is the intrinsic operator of a branch through $f(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_support_linSumIntr_iff⟧ (positive weights, as in Remark 15.1.2); and the chart statement applies to that branch.

**Reading.** $T_xX$ and $W_x$ carry no sc-structure in the project: they are a tangent fibre and a fibre with their linear structures. "$(f - s_i)'(x) : T_xX \to W_x$ is sc-Fredholm" is therefore read in a chart, through the identifications $T_xX \cong T_zO$ and $W_x \cong K_z$ by which the intrinsic operator is defined. The sc-structure on $T_zO$ and $K_z$ is that of sc-subspaces of $E$ and $F$; that it does not depend on the chart is not formalized, and not needed, since the statement holds in every chart. $\mathrm{GrF}(x)$ is not cut down to sc-Fredholm operators (§XV.1); the lemma says what lies in the support.

**The hypothesis taken.** *Tame germ data for $f$* (Part I's notion, an sc-Fredholm section whose germs are conjugate to basic germs in tame charts) is not stated in §15.1, where $f$ is "an sc-Fredholm section". It is not new: it is inherited from Part I's Theorems 3.1.18 and 3.6.8, which are proved for tame germ data and on which the proof rests; with the 2021 untamed notion, Theorem 3.6.8 does not hold as we read it ⟦Chapter3/UntamedBundleTheorem · UntamedCorner.theorem_3_6_8_untamed_not⟧ (Part III). The same hypothesis is carried by all of §15.2 (§§XV.12–XV.16) and by the cylinder of Corollary 15.3.10 (§XV.30). Its witness is the graph section of $0$ over $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$, which has tame germ data by Part I ⟦Chapter3/NonVacuityG · isScFredholmSectionTame_graphSection⟧, with the zero multisection; there all hypotheses of the §15.2 theorems hold together ⟦Chapter15/InteriorPerturbationWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_2_hyp_witness⟧. The witness has zero fibres, so it shows that the hypotheses are consistent, not that the summands are non-trivially sc-Fredholm; the sc-Fredholm statement itself is a theorem for every $f$ with tame germ data.

### XV.12 Definition 15.2.1 (2017: Definition 15.2): transversality

§15.2 (pp. 688–691) is the local theory: what $T(f, \Lambda)$ says about $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$ near one point. Its tool throughout is the passage of §XV.10 from a branch $s_i$ of a local sc⁺-section structure, a section defined only on an open $O$, to the sc-Fredholm section $(f - s_i)|_O$ of the restricted strong bundle $W|_O$, to which Part I's implicit function theorems apply. The definitions come first.

**Statement** (restated). Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section functor and $\Lambda$ an sc⁺-multisection. At a level-$1$ point $x$, *$T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is onto* if every operator in the support of the formal sum $T(f, \Lambda)(x) \in \mathrm{GrF}(x)$ (Definition 15.1.7, §XV.8) is surjective onto $W_x$ ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.IsOntoAtLevel⟧. For an arbitrary object $x$ the same is said with the clause $x \in X_1$ built in, since $T(f, \Lambda)$ is defined only on $X_1$ ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.IsOntoAt⟧. $(f, \Lambda)$ is *transversal at $x$* if $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$ and $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is onto ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.IsTransversalAt⟧ (the text's (2)), and *transversal* if it is transversal at every point of $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$ ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.IsTransversal⟧ (the text's (1)).

The text phrases the condition twice: as "a nonzero combination of surjective sc-Fredholm operators", and, after "i.e.", as the surjectivity of all $(f - s_i)'(x)$ with $f(x) = s_i(x)$ for a local sc⁺-section structure $(s_i)$. The formal definition is the first phrasing minus the two words that turn out to be automatic; the two lemmas below recover the second phrasing and the word "nonzero", and §XV.11 the word "sc-Fredholm".

**The operators of the formal sum.** Fix local data at $x$ (§XV.8): a local sc⁺-section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)_{i \in I}$ of $\Lambda$ on an open $O$, with positive weights, and a strong bundle chart $c$ around $x$ with domain in $O$. Then an operator $L : T_xX \to W_x$ lies in the support of $\sum_{i : f(x) = s_i(x)}\sigma_i \cdot (f - s_i)'(x)$ iff $L = (f - s_i)'(x)$ for some $i$ with $s_i(x) = f(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_support_linSumIntr_iff⟧. *Proof.* The formal sum through $c$ is, by definition, the push-forward of the chart-level sum, whose filter is "the principal parts of $s_i$ and $f$ agree at $\varphi(x)$" (§XV.7). For sections over the chart domain this is the same as $s_i(x) = f(x)$, the chart being injective on fibres; this rewrites the filter. The coefficient of $L$ is then $\sum_i [s_i(x) = f(x) \wedge (f - s_i)'(x) = L]\,\sigma_i$, a finite sum of non-negative rationals; it is nonzero iff some term is nonzero, and a term is nonzero iff its condition holds, because $\sigma_i > 0$. So positivity of the weights is exactly what makes "occurs in the sum" the same as "is the derivative of some branch through $f(x)$".

**The text's reading** ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.isOntoAtLevel_iff⟧: for $f$ an sc-Fredholm section functor and any local data at $x \in X_1$, $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is onto iff every $(f - s_i)'(x)$ with $s_i(x) = f(x)$, computed through the chart of the data, is surjective. *Proof.* By Definition 15.1.7, $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is the formal sum of these data, whichever data are taken ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.linearization_eq⟧ (this is Theorem 15.1.1, §XV.7); the support is described by the previous lemma; the two directions are then immediate. The text's "if $(s_i)$ is a local sc⁺-section structure" is thereby read "for any", which Theorem 15.1.1 makes the same as "for some".

**"Nonzero" is automatic** ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.linearization_ne_zero⟧: at $x \in X_1$ with $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$, $T(f, \Lambda)(x) \neq 0$. *Proof.* Local data exist at every level-$1$ point ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.nonempty_localLinData⟧. The count formula of the local structure, evaluated at the point $f(x)$ of the fibre over $x$, gives $\Lambda(f(x)) = \sum_{i : s_i(x) = f(x)}\sigma_i$; if no branch passed through $f(x)$ the sum would be empty and $\Lambda(f(x)) = 0$. So some $i$ has $s_i(x) = f(x)$, the operator $(f - s_i)'(x)$ lies in the support of the formal sum, and a formal sum with nonempty support is not $0$.

**"sc-Fredholm" is automatic** as well, for $f$ with Part I's tame germ data: every operator of the support is, read in the chart, sc-Fredholm (§XV.11). So Definition 15.2.1 asks only for surjectivity, and that is what the formal definition says.

**Where the support lives.** $T(f, \Lambda)$ is defined on $X_1$, so the formal definition carries "$x \in X_1$". Under the tame germ data this costs nothing: every point of the support is smooth. *One branch* ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_smoothSet_of_eq⟧: if $s$ is sc⁺ on an open $O \ni y$ and $f(y) = s(y)$, then $y$ is a zero of the section $(f - s)|_O$ of $W|_O$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.isZeroAt_subSec_iff⟧, which is a tame sc-Fredholm section (§XV.10) ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.isScFredholmSectionTame_subRestrict⟧; zeros of sc-Fredholm sections are smooth points (Part I) ⟦Chapter3/TameGermsG · StrongBundle.IsScFredholmSection.mem_smoothSet_of_isZeroAt⟧, and a point of the open M-polyfold $O$ is smooth there iff it is smooth in $X$. *The support* ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_smoothSet_of_pos⟧: if $\Lambda(f(y)) > 0$, the count formula of a local structure around $y$ produces a branch with $f(y) = s_i(y)$, as in the previous proof, and the one-branch lemma applies. The same fact without tame germ data, $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f) \subset X_1$, is proved for Definition 15.3.5 in §XV.20 ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.mem_levelSet_one_of_pos⟧.

**A witness.** Over the trivial ep-groupoid of $\mathbb R^n$, the strong bundle $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$ with the graph section of $0$ and the trivial multisection $\Lambda_0$ (Chapter 13; $\Lambda_0(w) = 1$ on the zero vectors, $0$ elsewhere) is transversal, with $\Lambda_0(f(x)) = 1$ at every point ⟦Chapter15/InteriorPerturbationWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_2_hyp_witness⟧. The fibres are $\{0\}$, so every operator into a fibre is onto. The example has zero fibres: it shows that the definition is satisfiable with nonempty support, not more.

### XV.13 Theorem 15.2.2 (2017: Theorem 15.2): interior local perturbation

**Statement** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_2_hyp⟧. Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section functor *with Part I's tame germ data*, $\Lambda$ an sc⁺-multisection, $d_X(x) = 0$, and $(f, \Lambda)$ transversal at $x$. Then there are a natural representation $U(x)$ of $G_x$ (Theorem 7.1.13), a local sc⁺-section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)_{i \in I}$ of $\Lambda$ on an open $O$, and a strong bundle chart $c$ with $U(x) \subset \operatorname{dom}(c) \subset O$, such that, with $M_i = \{y \in U(x) : f(y) = s_i(y)\}$:

1. $d_X(y) = 0$ for all $y \in U(x)$;
2. $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$ is onto at every $y \in U(x)$ with $\Lambda(f(y)) > 0$;
3. (a) every $M_i$ is a smooth finite-dimensional submanifold of $X$ (Definition 4.2.1); (b) the inclusion $M_i \hookrightarrow U(x)$ is a proper map; (c) $\{y \in U(x) : \Lambda(f(y)) > 0\} = \bigcup_iM_i$; (d) $\Lambda(f(y)) = \sum_{i : f(y) = s_i(y)}\sigma_i$ on $U(x)$; (e) $T(f, \Lambda)(y) = \sum_{i : f(y) = s_i(y)}\sigma_i \cdot (f - s_i)'(y)$, the operators read in $c$, at every level-$1$ point $y$ of $\operatorname{dom}(c)$;

and, in addition, a branch meets $f$ in $U(x)$ only if it passes through $f(x)$: $f(y) = s_i(y)$ for some $y \in U(x)$ implies $s_i(x) = f(x)$.

*Narrower* only by the tame germ data. The text's hypothesis $x \in \operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$ is part of transversality at $x$.

**Proof.** The text's proof is four sentences: choose $U'(x)$ and a local structure on it; by assumption $f(x) = s_i(x)$ for all $i$; apply the implicit function theorem to each $f - s_i$; intersect. The Lean proof follows it, with two additions: the branches that do not pass through $f(x)$ are handled separately, and every step is read through one chart inside the domain of the structure, so that §§XV.8 and XV.10 apply.

*Step 1, a structure and a chart inside it.* Since $\Lambda$ is an sc⁺-multisection, there is a natural representation $U_0(x)$ with a local sc⁺-section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)_{i \in I}$ on $U_0(x)$ (Definition 13.2.5 in its 2021 reading, Part XIII). Choose any strong bundle chart $c_0$ around $x$ in the atlas and restrict it to $\operatorname{dom}(c_0) \cap U_0(x)$, which is open; the restriction is a chart of the atlas, and its domain lies in the domain of the structure. Call it $c$. The structure and $c$ are local data at $x$ in the sense of Definition 15.1.7 ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.LocalLinData⟧.

*Step 2, from transversality to the chart.* Transversality at $x$ gives $x \in X_1$ and $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ onto; by the text's reading (§XV.12) ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.isOntoAtLevel_iff⟧, every intrinsic $(f - s_i)'(x)$ with $s_i(x) = f(x)$ is surjective. The intrinsic operator is onto $W_x$ iff the chart operator $D((\hat f - \hat s_i) \circ r)(z)$ maps $T_zO$ onto the fibre $K_z$ at the level-$1$ chart point $z$ over $\varphi(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.surjective_toIntr_subDeriv_iff⟧ (§XV.10).

*Step 3, one branch* ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.exists_branch_interior⟧. For each $i$ there is an open $V_i \ni x$ inside $\operatorname{dom}(c)$ such that $\{y \in V_i : f(y) = s_i(y)\}$ is a smooth submanifold, every point $y$ of it is smooth and has the chart operator of $f - s_i$ onto at every chart point over $\varphi(y)$, and, if some $y \in V_i$ has $f(y) = s_i(y)$, then $s_i(x) = f(x)$. Two cases.

- *The branch passes through $f(x)$.* Then the chart operator is onto at $x$ (Step 2), and the interior local solution lemma of §XV.10 ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.exists_solutionSet_interior⟧ gives $V_i$: it is Part I's implicit function theorem (Theorem 3.6.8) for the tame sc-Fredholm section $(f - s_i)|_O$ of $W|_O$ at its zero $x$, where $d_X(x) = 0$ makes the good position automatic, read back in $X$ through the inclusion $O \to X$. The last clause holds trivially.
- *The branch does not pass through $f(x)$.* Then $V_i = \{y \in \operatorname{dom}(c) : f(y) \ne s_i(y)\}$. It is open ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.isOpen_sep_ne⟧: $f$ is continuous, $s_i$ is continuous on $O$ ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.IsScPlusSectionOn.continuousOn⟧ (an sc⁺-section is the composite of a continuous lift to $W_{0,1}$ with the continuous inclusion $W_{0,1} \to W$), and the set where two continuous maps into a Hausdorff space differ is the preimage of the complement of the closed diagonal. It contains $x$. The solution set in $V_i$ is empty, so it is a submanifold, and the remaining clauses hold vacuously.

The second case is where the formal statement departs from the text's proof, which says "by assumption, $f(x) = s_i(x)$ for $i \in I$". That holds only for the branches through $f(x)$; presumably the text means those, the others having empty solution sets near $x$. The formal statement keeps the whole index set, and the last clause of the theorem says that the other branches contribute nothing on $U(x)$.

*Step 4, the neighbourhood.* The set $\operatorname{dom}(c) \cap \bigcap_iV_i \cap \{d_X = 0\}$ is open, the last set being open because the degeneracy index is upper semicontinuous, and it contains $x$. A natural representation can be shrunk into any open neighbourhood of $x$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.exists_naturalRep_shrink⟧ (Theorem 7.1.13); this gives $U(x) \subset U_0(x)$. Property (1) holds by construction.

*Step 5, the count.* For $y \in U(x)$ the count formula of the structure at the point $f(y)$ gives (d), $\Lambda(f(y)) = \sum_{i : f(y) = s_i(y)}\sigma_i$. Since the weights are positive, $\Lambda(f(y)) > 0$ iff some branch passes through $f(y)$; this gives (c).

*Step 6, (2).* Let $y \in U(x)$ with $\Lambda(f(y)) > 0$. By Step 5 some $i$ has $f(y) = s_i(y)$; then $y$ lies in the solution set of Step 3 for that branch, hence is smooth and in particular at level $1$. The same structure with the chart $c$ is local data at $y$, so by the text's reading it suffices that each $(f - s_j)'(y)$ with $s_j(y) = f(y)$ is onto; Step 3 for the branch $j$ gives the chart operator onto at $y$, and §XV.10 turns this into the intrinsic surjectivity ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.surjective_toIntr_subDeriv_iff⟧.

*Step 7, (a) and (b).* $M_i = \{y \in V_i : f(y) = s_i(y)\} \cap U(x)$, the intersection of a smooth submanifold with an open set, which is again one. For (b), an inclusion of a subset is a proper map iff the subset is closed; $M_i$ is the set of points of $U(x)$ where the two continuous maps $f$ and $s_i$ agree, which is closed in $U(x)$.

*Step 8, (e).* At a level-$1$ point $y$ of $\operatorname{dom}(c)$, the structure and $c$ are local data at $y$, and Definition 15.1.7 gives $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$ as their formal sum ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.linearization_eq⟧. The last clause is the last clause of Step 3.

**Readings.** (i) "$d_{M_i} \equiv 0$ and therefore a natural (classical) smooth manifold structure" in (a) is read as Definition 4.2.1 inside $\{d_X = 0\}$, which (1) provides; Definition 4.2.1 allows boundary and corners and here has none. (ii) The text's (e) "for $y \in U(x)$" uses the structure on $U(x)$; the formal (e) is read in the chart $c$, which is no restriction, since the formal sum does not depend on the chart (§XV.7). (iii) The text's "$f_i(y) = s_i(y)$" in (e) is read $f(y) = s_i(y)$. (iv) The index set is that of the structure; $M_i = \emptyset$ for the branches not through $f(x)$.

**The added hypothesis.** *Tame germ data for $f$* (Part I's sc-Fredholm sections with germ data in tame charts), not stated in §15.2, which says only "$f$ an sc-Fredholm section functor". It is inherited, not new: the proof is Part I's Theorem 3.6.8 applied to $(f - s_i)|_O$, and Part I proves that theorem for tame germ data; with the untamed 2021 notion of an sc-Fredholm germ Theorem 3.6.8 does not hold as we read it ⟦Chapter3/UntamedBundleTheorem · UntamedCorner.theorem_3_6_8_untamed_not⟧ (Part III). The restriction to $O$ keeps tame germ data, and the sc⁺-perturbation by $-s_i$ keeps them by Part I's Theorem 3.1.18 (§XV.10). No ep-level counterexample to the untamed §15.2 was built. *Witness* of all hypotheses together ⟦Chapter15/InteriorPerturbationWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_2_hyp_witness⟧: the example of §XV.12, where the graph section of $0$ has tame germ data by Part I ⟦Chapter3/NonVacuityG · isScFredholmSectionTame_graphSection⟧, $\Lambda_0$ is an sc⁺-multisection, $d_X \equiv 0$ on $\mathbb R^n$, $\Lambda_0(f(x)) = 1$ and $(f, \Lambda_0)$ is transversal everywhere. The example has zero fibres: it witnesses consistency, and the solution sets are all of $\mathbb R^n$.

### XV.14 Remark 15.2.3 (2017: Remark 15.2): $\Lambda \circ f$ is locally branched; tame; the ep-groupoid $U(x)$

The remark says that on the ep-groupoid $U(x)$ the functor $z \mapsto \Lambda(f(z))$ is a branched, tame ep⁺-subgroupoid with support $M_{U(x)}$. The formalization proves it in three forms: as a local branching structure at a point of $X$, as a global statement on $X$, and on the ep-groupoid $U(x)$ itself, each also with "tame".

**Local form** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_hyp⟧. With tame germ data for $f$: at a point $y$ with $d_X(y) = 0$ where $(f, \Lambda)$ is transversal, $z \mapsto \Lambda(f(z))$ has a local branching structure at $y$ in the sense of Definition 9.1.2 (2)–(4) (Part IX): an open $U \ni y$, finitely many smooth submanifolds $M_j \subset U$ through $y$ with proper inclusions, and positive rational weights $\sigma_j$ with $\Lambda(f(z)) = \sum_{j : z \in M_j}\sigma_j$ on $U$. *Proof.* Theorem 15.2.2 at $y$ gives $U(y)$, the structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)_{i \in I}$, the sets $M_i$ and (a)–(d). The index set of the branching structure is the set of branches through $f(y)$, $\{i \in I : s_i(y) = f(y)\}$, so that every $M_j$ contains $y$, as Definition 9.1.2 asks; the submanifold property and properness are (a) and (b); the weights are positive. The count is computed in three rewrites: by (d), $\Lambda(f(z)) = \sum_{i \in I}[f(z) = s_i(z)]\,\sigma_i$; by the last clause of Theorem 15.2.2 every branch with $f(z) = s_i(z)$ for some $z \in U(y)$ passes through $f(y)$, so the sum may be restricted to the branches through $f(y)$; and that sum is the sum over the index set of the structure, after reindexing by the subtype.

**Global form** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_isBranchedEpSubgroupoid_hyp⟧. With tame germ data: if $(f, \Lambda)$ is transversal, $d_X = 0$ on $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$, and the orbit space $|\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)|$ is paracompact, then $\Lambda \circ f$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid of $X$ (Definition 9.1.2). *Proof*, field by field. The values are non-negative rationals. Functoriality: for a morphism $\varphi$, $f(t(\varphi)) = \mu(\varphi, f(s(\varphi)))$ because $f$ is a section functor, and $\Lambda(\mu(\varphi, w)) = \Lambda(w)$ because $\Lambda$ is a functor on $W$; so $\Lambda(f(t(\varphi))) = \Lambda(f(s(\varphi)))$. The support consists of smooth points (§XV.12) ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_smoothSet_of_pos⟧. The paracompactness of the orbit space of the support, Definition 9.1.2 (1), is the hypothesis. The local branching structures at the support points are the local form. *Narrower* also by that hypothesis: Definition 9.1.2 (1) is new in the 2021 edition, and the remark, being local, does not address it. *Witness* ⟦Chapter15/InteriorPerturbationWitness · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_isBranchedEpSubgroupoid_hyp_witness⟧: the example of §XV.12, with the paracompactness of the orbit space of any subset of the trivial ep-groupoid of $\mathbb R^n$ from Part IX ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.paracompactSpace_orbitSupp_trivial_rn⟧.

**"Tame".** A tame local branching structure (Definition 9.3.6) is a local branching structure whose domain is a natural representation with the properness property (Definition 7.5.8) and whose submanifolds $M_j$ have tame induced structures (Definition 2.5.18). At an interior point of transversality $(f, \Lambda)$ is in good position (Definition 15.2.4; the lemma is in §XV.15), and at a point of good position Theorem 15.2.5 produces a tame local branching structure (§XV.16). Hence *the local tame form* (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_tame_hyp⟧: at $y$ with $d_X(y) = 0$ and $(f, \Lambda)$ transversal at $y$, $z \mapsto \Lambda(f(z))$ has a tame local branching structure at $y$; and *the global tame form* (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_isTameBranched_hyp⟧: under the hypotheses of the global form, $\Lambda \circ f$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid and tame, by the global form of Theorem 15.2.5 (§XV.16) applied with good position at every support point. *Witness* ⟦Chapter15/TameWitness · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_isTameBranched_hyp_witness⟧: the example of §XV.12, with support all of $\mathbb R^n$.

**The ep-groupoid $U(x)$.** *Reading.* "The ep-groupoid $U(x)$" is read as the translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ of the natural action of the isotropy group on a natural representation, whose objects are the points of $U(x)$ and whose morphisms are the pairs $(g, y)$ from $y$ to $g * y$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translationEpGroupoid⟧. Part VII proves that it is an ep-groupoid and that the functor $\Gamma : G_x \ltimes U(x) \to X$ is fully faithful onto the full subcategory of $X$ on $U(x)$ (Theorem 7.1.13 (3)), with the same orbit space (Proposition 7.1.19). So the full subcategory on $U(x)$ is an ep-groupoid in this form. The restriction of a functor $\Theta$ on $X$ to it is $\Theta_U(y) = \Theta(y)$, and "with support $M_{U(x)}$" is then the definition of the support of $\Theta_U$.

**The generic step** (extra) ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isTameBranched_translation⟧. For any ep-groupoid $X$, natural representation $U(x)$ and functor $\Theta \ge 0$ on $X$ with closed support, such that every point of $\operatorname{supp}\Theta \cap U(x)$ is smooth and carries a tame local branching structure of $\Theta$, the restriction $\Theta_U$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid of $G_x \ltimes U(x)$, and tame. Unlike the global form on $X$, no paracompactness is assumed: on $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ it is proved. *Proof*, field by field.

- *Functoriality.* A morphism $(g, y)$ of the translation groupoid is carried by $\Gamma$ to a morphism of $X$ with source $y$ and target $g * y$, so $\Theta(g * y) = \Theta(y)$ by functoriality of $\Theta$ on $X$.
- *Smoothness.* A point of the open sub-M-polyfold $U(x)$ is smooth there iff it is smooth in $X$.
- *Paracompactness of the orbit space of the support* ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.paracompactSpace_orbitSupp_translation⟧. Let $S = \operatorname{supp}\Theta_U$, closed in $U(x)$, hence paracompact, and let $p : S \to |S|$ be the orbit map restricted to it, continuous and onto. Two facts about the orbit map $\pi$ of $G_x \ltimes U(x)$. It is closed ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isClosedMap_translation_π⟧: every closed subset $C$ of $U(x)$ is a proper subset of the translation groupoid in the sense of Definition 7.5.8 ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translation_isProperSubset⟧, because Part VII proves that the restriction of the source–target map to the morphisms over the closure of any subset is proper ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translation_isProperMap⟧, and the orbit of a proper subset is closed (Proposition 7.5.10 (1)) ⟦Chapter7/ProperSubsets · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_5_10_one⟧. Its fibres are finite ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.finite_fiber_translation_π⟧: two points of $U(x)$ have the same orbit iff they differ by the action of an element of $G_x$, so a fibre is the image of the finite group $G_x$ under $g \mapsto g * y$. Restricted to the closed set $S$, $p$ is again closed with finite fibres. Now Michael's criterion (Lemma 2.7.3) ⟦Chapter7/Michael · paracompactSpace_of_closed_refinement⟧: a regular space is paracompact if every open cover has a locally finite closed refinement that covers. Given an open cover of $|S|$, pull it back to $S$, take a locally finite closed precise refinement there ⟦Chapter7/Michael · exists_closed_precise_refinement⟧, and push it forward by $p$. The images are closed ($p$ closed), cover ($p$ onto), refine the cover, and form a locally finite family by the next lemma.
- *Closed maps with finite fibres* ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · locallyFinite_image_of_isClosedMap⟧: a closed map $p$ with finite fibres carries a locally finite family $(v_i)$ to a locally finite family $(p(v_i))$. *Proof.* Fix $y$. Each point $z$ of the finite fibre $p^{-1}(y)$ has a neighbourhood $N_z$ meeting only finitely many $v_i$. The union $W$ of the interiors of the $N_z$ is open and contains the fibre, so $y \notin p(W^c)$, and $(p(W^c))^c$ is an open neighbourhood of $y$, $p$ being closed. If $p(v_i)$ meets it, at a point $p(z)$ with $z \in v_i$, then $z \notin W^c$, so $z$ lies in some $N_{z'}$ and $v_i$ meets $N_{z'}$; there are finitely many such $i$ for each of the finitely many $z'$.
- *Tame local branching structures move into $U(x)$* ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.nonempty_tameBranching_translation⟧. Let $C$ be a tame local branching structure of $\Theta$ at $y \in U(x)$, with domain $C.U$. Theorem 7.1.13 for the translation groupoid ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.theorem_7_1_13⟧ gives a natural representation $U'$ of $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ at $y$ inside the preimage of $C.U$; its image in $X$ is open and inside $C.U \cap U(x)$. The structure $C$ is restricted to this image (the $M_j$ intersected with an open set stay submanifolds with tame induced structures), and moved into the M-polyfold $U(x)$ by the inclusion $U(x) \to X$, an sc-diffeomorphism onto its open image ⟦Chapter8/TangentLocal · MPolyfold.isScDiffeoOn_subtypeVal⟧; images of tame induced structures under sc-diffeomorphisms are tame. The properness property of $U'$ inside the translation groupoid holds for every open subset of $U(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translation_hasPropernessProperty⟧, since every closed subset is proper there.

**Remark 15.2.3 on the ep-groupoid $U(x)$** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_restricted_hyp⟧. With tame germ data: at $x$ with $d_X(x) = 0$ and $(f, \Lambda)$ transversal at $x$, there is a natural representation $U(x)$ with $d_X \equiv 0$ on it such that $z \mapsto \Lambda(f(z))$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid of $G_x \ltimes U(x)$, and tame. *Proof.* Theorem 15.2.2 at $x$ gives $U(x)$ with (1) and (2). Apply the generic step to $\Theta = \Lambda \circ f$: it is $\ge 0$ and a functor ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isFunctorial_comp⟧; its support is closed in $X$ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isClosed_supp_comp⟧, being locally the finite union of the closed sets $\{f = s_i\}$ (§XV.21); its support points are smooth (§XV.12); and at a support point $y \in U(x)$, $d_X(y) = 0$ by (1) and $(f, \Lambda)$ is transversal at $y$ by (2), so the local tame form above gives a tame local branching structure at $y$. *No paracompactness* is assumed: the remark holds on $U(x)$ exactly as stated, with the inherited tame germ data. *Witness* ⟦Chapter15/TameWitness · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_restricted_hyp_witness⟧: all hypotheses together at $0 \in \mathbb R^1$ in the example of §XV.12, with the conclusion.

### XV.15 Definition 15.2.4 (2017: Definition 15.3): good position

At a point with $d_X(x) \ge 1$ transversality is not enough: the kernels must also sit well against the boundary. The text calls Definition 15.2.4 "a version of Definition 3.6.6"; the formalization makes it exactly that, branch by branch.

**Statement** (restated). *One branch* ⟦Chapter15/BoundaryPerturbation · SBLocalization.IsBranchGoodPosition⟧: for $s$ sc⁺ on an open $O \ni x$, the branch $f - s$ is in good position at $x$ if the section $(f - s)|_O$ of $W|_O$ is in good position at $x$ in a tame chart, Part I's Definition 3.6.6 in its tame germ reading: germ data at $x$ in a tame chart of $W|_O$, a linearization at $x$ that is onto, and a kernel in good position to the partial quadrant (Definition 3.1.24). *The pair* ⟦Chapter15/BoundaryPerturbation · SBLocalization.IsGoodPositionAt⟧: $(f, \Lambda)$ is in good position at $x$ if $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$, $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is onto (Definition 15.2.1), and there is a local sc⁺-section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ of $\Lambda$ on an open $O \ni x$ such that every branch with $s_i(x) = f(x)$ is in good position at $x$.

**Readings.** (i) The text's (1), "$X$ is tame near $x$", and (3), "the kernels of the $L_i$ are in good position to $C_xX$", are read together per branch as Part I's good position of $(f - s_i)|_O$, which carries a tame chart at $x$ (giving (1)) and the kernel condition (giving (3)). (ii) The condition is asked for one local structure; the text does not say whether it depends on the structure chosen. Theorem 15.2.5 below propagates it with the same structure. (iii) The text assumes $x \in \partial X$; the formal definition does not, and everything below holds at any point where the condition holds.

**At an interior point, transversality is good position** (extra) ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.isGoodPositionAt_of_interior⟧: if $d_X(x) = 0$ and $(f, \Lambda)$ is transversal at $x$ ($f$ with tame germ data), then $(f, \Lambda)$ is in good position at $x$. *Proof.* Take the structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ on a natural representation $U_0(x)$ and a chart $c$ inside it, as in Step 1 of §XV.13. For a branch through $f(x)$, transversality and the text's reading give the chart operator onto at $x$ (Step 2 of §XV.13); this is Part I's surjectivity of the linearization of $(f - s_i)|_{U_0(x)}$ at $x$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.isLinSurjAt_subRestrict⟧ (§XV.10). The degeneracy index of $x$ in the open M-polyfold $U_0(x)$ is that in $X$, so $0$. Part I: at a zero with $d = 0$, an onto linearization is good position in a tame chart ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFTIndexG · StrongBundle.isGoodPositionGerm_of_isLinSurjAt⟧, since at an interior point the partial quadrant is the whole space and the kernel condition is empty. So every branch through $f(x)$ is in good position, which is Definition 15.2.4.

This lemma is what lets the tame forms of Remark 15.2.3 (§XV.14) be derived from those of Theorem 15.2.5 (§XV.16).

**Witness** ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_hyp_witness⟧: in the example of §XV.12, $(f, \Lambda_0)$ is in good position at every point of $\mathbb R^n$. *Proof.* There every pair is in general position (Definition 15.3.5), the fibres being $0$ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPosition_epSEP_zero⟧, and general position gives good position at every point of the support (Remark 15.3.6, §XV.20) ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionBranches · SBLocalization.remark_15_3_6_goodPosition_hyp⟧. Zero fibres: a consistency witness.

### XV.16 Theorem 15.2.5 (2017: Theorem 15.3) and Remark 15.2.6: boundary local perturbation, tame, and under general position

**Statement** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/BoundaryPerturbation · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_hyp⟧. Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section functor with tame germ data, $\Lambda$ an sc⁺-multisection, and $(f, \Lambda)$ in good position at $x$. Then there are a natural representation $U(x)$, a local sc⁺-section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ on an open $O$ and a chart $c$ with $U(x) \subset \operatorname{dom}(c) \subset O$ such that, with $M_i = \{y \in U(x) : f(y) = s_i(y)\}$: every $M_i$ is a smooth submanifold (Definition 4.2.1); (1) the inclusions $M_i \hookrightarrow U(x)$ are proper; $\{y \in U(x) : \Lambda(f(y)) > 0\} = \bigcup_iM_i$; (2) $(f, \Lambda)$ is in good position, with the same structure, at every $y \in U(x)$ with $\Lambda(f(y)) > 0$, so $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$ is onto with the branches in good position; (3) $\Lambda(f(y)) = \sum_{i : y \in M_i}\sigma_i$ on $U(x)$; $T(f, \Lambda)(y) = \sum_{i : f(y) = s_i(y)}\sigma_i \cdot (f - s_i)'(y)$ in $c$; and only the branches through $f(x)$ meet $f$ in $U(x)$. "Tame submanifolds" and "tame branched" are the tame form below. *Narrower* by the inherited tame germ data; $x \in \partial X$ is not required.

**Proof.** The text: "along the lines of the proof of Theorem 15.2.2", with Part I's implicit function theorem in good position. The Lean proof is that proof with the good-position lemma in place of the interior one.

*Step 1.* Good position at $x$ supplies the structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ on an open $O \ni x$ in which the branches through $f(x)$ are in good position. Take a chart $c_0$ around $x$ and restrict it to $\operatorname{dom}(c_0) \cap O$: a chart $c$ with domain in $O$. A natural representation $U_0(x)$ is taken from the multisection property of $\Lambda$; only its existence is used, for the shrinking in Step 3.

*Step 2, one branch* ⟦Chapter15/BoundaryPerturbation · SBLocalization.exists_branch_goodPosition⟧: for each $i$ an open $V_i \ni x$ in $\operatorname{dom}(c)$ with $\{y \in V_i : f(y) = s_i(y)\}$ a smooth submanifold, each of its points smooth, with the branch in good position there and the chart operator onto there, and only meeting $f$ if $s_i(x) = f(x)$. If the branch passes through $f(x)$ this is the good-position local solution lemma of §XV.10 ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.exists_solutionSet_of_isGoodPosition⟧: Part I's Theorem 3.6.8 for $(f - s_i)|_O$ at $x$ in good position, which gives an open set of the zeros of which each is in good position, read back in $X$; the chart surjectivity at those zeros comes from the good position there. If it does not, $V_i = \{y \in \operatorname{dom}(c) : f(y) \ne s_i(y)\}$, as in §XV.13 ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.isOpen_sep_ne⟧.

*Step 3.* Shrink $U_0(x)$ into the open set $\operatorname{dom}(c) \cap \bigcap_iV_i$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.exists_naturalRep_shrink⟧. No condition on $d_X$ enters.

*Step 4.* The count (3), the description of the support, the submanifolds $M_i$, the properness (1) and the formula for $T(f, \Lambda)$ are proved word for word as Steps 5, 7 and 8 of §XV.13.

*Step 5, (2).* At $y \in U(x)$ with $\Lambda(f(y)) > 0$: some branch passes through $f(y)$, so $y$ is smooth, hence at level $1$, by Step 2. The structure on $O$ and the chart $c$ are local data at $y$; every branch $j$ through $f(y)$ has its chart operator onto at $y$ (Step 2), so $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$ is onto by the text's reading of §XV.12 ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.surjective_toIntr_subDeriv_iff⟧; and every branch $j$ through $f(y)$ is in good position at $y$ (Step 2). These are the three clauses of Definition 15.2.4 at $y$, with the same structure.

**Tame local solution sets** (extra) ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.exists_tame_solutionSet_of_isBranchGoodPosition⟧. If a branch $f - s$ with $f(x) = s(x)$ is in good position at $x$, there is an open $V \ni x$ inside $O$ such that $\{y \in V : f(y) = s(y)\}$ is a smooth submanifold of $X$ with a tame induced structure (Definition 2.5.18). *Proof.* Part I's Theorem 3.1.26, the implicit function theorem in the boundary case, for the tame sc-Fredholm section $(f - s)|_O$ at its zero $x$ in good position ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFTNearbyOntoG · theorem_3_1_26'⟧, gives an open $U \subset O$ around $x$ whose zeros are smooth and in good position and whose zero set is a sub-M-polyfold with a tame induced structure. The zero set in $U$ is a smooth submanifold of $O$ ⟦Chapter5/GeneralPosition · StrongBundle.isSmoothSubmanifold_solutionSet_inter⟧, the zeros of $(f - s)|_O$ being the points with $f = s$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.isZeroAt_subSec_iff⟧. Both properties are carried to $X$ by the sc-diffeomorphism $O \to X$ onto the open set $O$ ⟦Chapter8/TangentLocal · MPolyfold.isScDiffeoOn_subtypeVal⟧; $V$ is the image of $U$.

**Theorem 15.2.5, tame** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_tame_hyp⟧.
