In good position at $x$, $z \mapsto \Lambda(f(z))$ has a tame local branching structure at $x$ (Definition 9.3.6): a natural representation $U(x)$ with the properness property, the sets $M_j = \{z \in U(x) : f(z) = s_j(z)\}$ over the branches through $f(x)$, each a smooth submanifold with a tame induced structure and a proper inclusion, the weights $\sigma_j$, and the count. *Proof.* For every branch choose $V_i$: the tame local solution set above if the branch passes through $f(x)$, and $\{y \in O : f(y) \ne s_i(y)\}$ otherwise. Every object has a neighbourhood $Q$ with the properness property (Definition 7.5.8) ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.exists_hasPropernessProperty⟧. Theorem 7.1.13 ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.theorem_7_1_13⟧ gives a natural representation $U(x)$ inside the open set $Q \cap O \cap \bigcap_iV_i$; it has the properness property, its closure lying in that of $Q$. The $M_j$ are the intersections of the tame solution sets with the open $U(x)$, which keeps both the submanifold property and the tame induced structure; properness and the count are as in the local form of Remark 15.2.3 (§XV.14), with the index set the branches through $f(x)$. This is the text's "by definition $\Lambda \circ f$ … is a tame branched ep⁺-subgroupoid, since it is represented by tame submanifolds".

**The global tame form** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_isTameBranched_hyp⟧: if $(f, \Lambda)$ is in good position at every point of the support and $|\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)|$ is paracompact, then $\Lambda \circ f$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid of $X$ and tame; the fields are those of the global form of Remark 15.2.3 (§XV.14), with functoriality ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isFunctorial_comp⟧ and the tame local branching structures just proved. The same assembly gives the global tame form of Remark 15.2.3 (§XV.14), and, through good position from general position (Remark 15.3.6), the tame forms of Remark 15.3.6 ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.remark_15_3_6_isTameBranched_hyp⟧ and of the "in particular" of Theorem 15.3.7 ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_in_particular_tame_hyp⟧ (§§XV.20–XV.21).

**On the ep-groupoid $U(x)$** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/RestrictedEp · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_restricted_hyp⟧: in good position at $x$, there is a natural representation $U(x)$ on whose translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ the functor $z \mapsto \Lambda(f(z))$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid, and tame. *Proof.* Theorem 15.2.5 gives $U(x)$ with good position at every support point in it; the generic step of §XV.14 applies, the tame local branching structures at those points coming from the tame form above. No paracompactness is assumed.

**The closing sentence: general position.** The text: the same conclusion holds if (2) is replaced by the requirement that the restrictions of $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$ to the reduced tangent spaces $T^R_yX$ are surjective, pointing ahead to Definition 15.3.5.

*Definition 15.3.5 at one point* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.IsReducedOntoAtLevel⟧ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.IsInGeneralPositionAt⟧: $(f, \Lambda)$ is in general position at $x$ if $x \in X_1$ and every operator $L$ of $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$, restricted to $T^R_xX$, is onto $W_x$, with $T^R_xX$ read in every chart around $x$ and every presentation of its partial quadrant (Part I's reduced tangent fibre). Definition 15.3.5 (§XV.20) is this condition at every point of the support ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPosition_iff_forall_at⟧, the support lying in $X_1$ ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.mem_levelSet_one_of_pos⟧.

*Reading.* "(2) replaced by general position" is read: the hypothesis "good position at $x$" is replaced by "general position at $x$", and the conclusion (2) by "general position at every point of $M_{U(x)}$". Good position at $x$ and on $M_{U(x)}$ still holds, so the formal conclusion gives both forms of (2).

Four lemmas connect general position of the pair to Part I's general position of the branches (Definition 5.3.9 for $(f - s_i)|_O$: the linearization at the zero is onto, with kernel transversal to $T^R$).

- *Part I, in every chart* (extra) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · StrongBundle.linKer_sup_reduced_eq_of_isGeneralPositionAt⟧: if a smooth submanifold $A$ of the solution set of a section $f$ is in general position at $y$ (Definition 4.2.10), then in every strong bundle chart around $y$, at every level-$1$ point $z$ over $\varphi(y)$ and for every presentation of the partial quadrant, $\ker\mathrm{Lin}(z) + T^R_zO = T_zO$. *Proof.* General position of $A$ gives, in the chart, a splitting $T_zO = N \oplus B$ with $N$ the tangent space of $A$ and $B \subset T^R_zO$. The tangent space of a submanifold of zeros lies in the kernel of the linearization, so $N \subset \ker\mathrm{Lin}(z)$; hence $T_zO = N + B \subset \ker\mathrm{Lin}(z) + T^R_zO \subset T_zO$. This is the converse of Part I's chart criterion ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · isGeneralPositionGerm_of_sup_eq⟧, and it holds in every chart, not only in the chart of the germ data.
- *From the pair to the branches* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.isGeneralPositionGerm_branch_at⟧: if $(f, \Lambda)$ is in general position at $x$, every branch $(f - s_i)|_O$ through $f(x)$ of any local structure on an open $O \ni x$ is in Part I's general position at $x$. *Proof.* The point $x$ is smooth (§XV.12) ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_smoothSet_of_eq⟧, so the tame germ data of $f$ provide a tame chart centred at $x$; restrict it to $O$. With the structure it is local data at $x$, so $(f - s_i)'(x)$ through this chart lies in the support of $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_support_linSumIntr_iff⟧ and is onto on $T^R_xX$ by hypothesis. The chart step of Remark 15.3.6 (§XV.20) ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionBranches · SBLocalization.isGeneralPositionGerm_subRestrict⟧ turns this into Part I's general position of $(f - s_i)|_O$: in the transported chart of $W|_O$ the intrinsic operator is the chart derivative of the branch, onto from $T_0O \cap T^R_0$ means onto with $\ker + T^R_0O = T_0O$, which is Part I's chart criterion.
- *Good position from general position* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.isGoodPositionAt_of_isInGeneralPositionAt⟧: general position at $x$ with $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$ gives good position at $x$. *Proof.* $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is onto, because each operator is already onto on the subspace $T^R_xX$, read in some chart with a presentation ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.exists_chart_presentation⟧. Take any local structure on an open $O \ni x$ ⟦Chapter13/MultisectionSupport · SBLocalization.IsScPlusMultisection.exists_isLocalRepOn⟧; each branch through $f(x)$ is in Part I's general position (previous lemma), hence in good position in a tame chart, by Part I's Lemma 5.26 ⟦Chapter5/Transversality · StrongBundle.IsGeneralPositionGerm.isGoodPositionGermTame⟧, the branch being a tame sc-Fredholm section of $W|_O$ with $x$ a zero.
- *From the branches back to the pair* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.isReducedOntoAtLevel_of_isGeneralPositionGerm⟧: if, for a local structure on $O \ni y$ and a chart $c$ around $y$ with domain in $O$, every branch through $f(y)$ is in Part I's general position at $y$, then $(f, \Lambda)$ is in general position at $y$. *Proof.* The reduced tangent fibre does not depend on the chart and presentation ⟦Chapter2/ReducedTangentIntrinsic · reducedTangentFiber_eq⟧, so it suffices to work in $c$ with one presentation. An operator of the support is $(f - s_j)'(y)$ for a branch $j$ through $f(y)$ (§XV.12). Its reduced restriction is onto ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.surjective_reduced_toIntr_of_isGeneralPositionGerm⟧, by the chart lemma: *every vector $k$ of the fibre $K_z$ has a preimage under the chart operator in $T^R_zO \cap T_zO$* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.exists_reduced_preimage_of_isGeneralPositionGerm⟧. For this lemma, Part I's general position of $(f - s_j)|_O$ gives good position, hence a smooth solution submanifold in general position at $y$ ⟦Chapter5/GeneralPosition · exists_isGeneralPositionGerm_iff⟧; the first lemma gives $\ker + T^R = T$ in the restricted chart; the linearization is onto, so $k$ has a preimage $v = a + b$ with $a$ in the kernel and $b \in T^R$, and $b$ is a preimage; and the derivative of the restricted chart is that of $c$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.scDeriv_restrictTo_subRestrict⟧. Passing from the chart operator to the intrinsic one has two cases, as the intrinsic operator is defined by cases: if the chart operator takes values in the image of the fibre identification, the preimage $b$ is carried to a reduced tangent vector with the right image; otherwise the intrinsic operator is $0$, and the full operator being onto (§XV.10) forces $W_y = 0$, where any operator is onto.

**Theorem 15.2.5, closing sentence** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_generalPosition_hyp⟧. Let $X$ be tame, $f$ with tame germ data, $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$ and $(f, \Lambda)$ in general position at $x$. Then all conclusions of Theorem 15.2.5 hold on a natural representation $U(x)$, and $(f, \Lambda)$ is in general position and in good position at every $y \in U(x)$ with $\Lambda(f(y)) > 0$. *Proof.* *Step 1.* General position at $x$ gives good position at $x$, and Theorem 15.2.5 gives $U_1(x)$, the structure on $O$, the chart and all conclusions. *Step 2, openness of general position.* $O$ is tame, an open subset of the tame $X$ ⟦Chapter11/FaceIntersectionCounterexample · MPolyfold.isTame_restrictOpen⟧. For each branch through $f(x)$, Part I's general position of $(f - s_i)|_O$ at $x$ (the second lemma) is open along the solution set: Part I's Theorem 4.2.11 (3), in the form that a zero in general position of a tame sc-Fredholm section over a tame M-polyfold has an open neighbourhood $W_i$ at whose zeros the section is in general position ⟦Chapter5/GeneralPosition · exists_isOpen_isGeneralPositionGerm⟧. For the other branches $W_i = X$. *Step 3.* Shrink $U_1(x)$ into $\bigcap_iW_i$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.exists_naturalRep_shrink⟧; the conclusions of Theorem 15.2.5 survive the shrinking, as in Step 7 of §XV.13. *Step 4.* At a support point $y \in U(x)$, every branch through $f(y)$ passes through $f(x)$ (last clause of Theorem 15.2.5) and $y \in W_i$, so it is in Part I's general position at $y$; the fourth lemma gives general position of the pair at $y$, and good position is clause (2) of Theorem 15.2.5. *The hypothesis of tameness* is that of Definition 15.3.5, which the text states over tame ep-groupoids, and it is what Part I's openness of general position needs. *Witness* ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_generalPosition_hyp_witness⟧: the example of §XV.12, where the trivial ep-groupoid of $\mathbb R^n$ is tame ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isTame_trivial_rn⟧ and every pair is in general position ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPosition_epSEP_zero⟧. Zero fibres: a consistency witness.

**Witnesses for Theorem 15.2.5.** The hypotheses in good position hold together at every point of the example of §XV.12 (§XV.15) ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_hyp_witness⟧, and the conclusion is obtained there, with good position on all of $U(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_hyp_applies⟧. The example has no boundary and zero fibres, so it does not exercise the corner geometry for which Theorem 15.2.5 is made; Part I's Theorem 3.1.26, on which the tame form rests, has its own witnesses in Part III.

**Remark 15.2.6** (pp. 690–691; nothing to formalize). Prose: with an oriented $(f, o)$ the branches $M_i$ inherit orientations $o_{i,y}$ from the surjective oriented $(f - s_i)'(y)$, recorded in the formal sum $\hat T_{((f,o),\Lambda)}(y) = \sum\sigma_i \cdot (T_yM_i, o_{i,y})$. The local data it needs are in place: the $M_i$ of Theorems 15.2.2 and 15.2.5 and the surjective $(f - s_i)'(y)$ of (2) with the text's reading of §XV.12. The orientations themselves are Theorem 15.4.1 and Definition 15.4.2, formalized at a single point in §XV.34.

### XV.17 The paragraph before Definition 15.3.1, Definition 15.3.1 and Remark 15.3.2 (2017: Definition 15.4, Remark 15.4)

§15.3 opens (p. 691) with the standing data of a perturbation problem: a strong bundle $(P : W \to X, \mu)$ over an ep-groupoid, an sc-Fredholm section functor $f$, and an auxiliary norm $N$ (Definition 12.2.1, which is Definition 8.3.5). An auxiliary norm is defined on $W_{0,1}$; the text extends it by $N(h) = +\infty$ off $W_{0,1}$, so that "$N(f(x)) \le 1$" makes sense for every $x$. The formalization does not extend $N$. It keeps $N$ on the level-$(0,1)$ part $W[1]$ and reads "$N(h) \le r$" as Part I's relation $\mathrm{AuxLe}$: $h \in W_{0,1}$ and the value of $N$ at $h$ is at most $r$ ⟦Chapter5/Compactness · StrongBundle.AuxLe⟧. This is exactly the text's convention, a point with $N(h) = +\infty$ satisfying no inequality $N(h) \le r$.

**Definition 15.3.1** (restated) ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.ControlsCompactness⟧. $(N, U)$ *controls the compactness of* $f$ if

1. $N$ is an auxiliary norm of $(W, \mu)$ (Definition 8.3.5: an auxiliary norm of the strong bundle, invariant under $\mu$);
2. $U \subset X$ is open;
3. $U$ is saturated;
4. $S_f = \{x : f(x) = 0_x\} \subset U$;
5. the closure in $|X|$ of $\pi(\{x \in U : N(f(x)) \le 1\})$ is compact, $\pi : X \to |X|$ the orbit map.

*Readings.* The orbit space "of a set" $A \subset X$ is its image $\pi(A)$. The text places the definition over an ep-groupoid with paracompact $|X|$. Paracompactness is not part of the formal definition, which is therefore more general; the statements that use paracompactness (the structurable addendum of Theorem 15.3.7, Theorem 15.3.9, Corollary 15.3.10) carry it as a hypothesis of their own. The text calls $f$ an sc-Fredholm section functor; the formal predicate takes any $f$, and the theorems that use it supply the Fredholm property.

*Monotonicity* ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.ControlsCompactness.mono⟧. If $(N, U)$ controls the compactness of $f$ and $U' \subset U$ is a smaller saturated open set still containing $S_f$, then $(N, U')$ controls it. *Proof.* Clauses (1)–(4) for $U'$ are the hypotheses. For (5): $\{x \in U' : N(f(x)) \le 1\} \subset \{x \in U : N(f(x)) \le 1\}$, so the closure of its image lies in the closure of the larger image, a compact set; a closed subset of a compact set is compact. The lemma is used wherever a proof shrinks the controlling neighbourhood.

**The paragraph before Definition 15.3.1** (same) ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.exists_controlsCompactness⟧. *Statement.* For an sc-Fredholm section functor $f$ with $|S_f| = \pi(S_f)$ compact and any auxiliary norm $N$, there is a $U$ with $(N, U)$ controlling the compactness of $f$. The text says this follows from "the discussion in Section 12.4".

*Proof.* It is Theorem 12.4.2, the implication (2) $\Rightarrow$ (3), of Part XII: an sc-Fredholm section functor with compact solution set is proper$_{<\infty}$, that is, for every auxiliary norm $N$ there is a saturated open $U \supset S_f$ such that $\operatorname{cl}_{|X|}\pi(\{x \in U : N(f(x)) \le C\})$ is compact for every $0 < C < \infty$ ⟦Chapter12/CompactnessEp · EpStrongBundle.isProperLtInftyFunctor_of_hasCompactSolutionSetEp⟧ ⟦Chapter12/CompactnessEp · EpStrongBundle.IsProperLtInftyFunctor⟧. The formal proof then takes $C = 1$. The proof of the implication, as Part XII retells it, runs in four steps, and we recall it because it is the whole content of the paragraph.

*Step 1, the local step.* At each zero $x$ of $f$ the local step of Theorem 5.2.2 gives an open $V(x) \ni x$ such that $\operatorname{cl}\{y \in V(x) : N(f(y)) \le C\}$ is compact for every $C > 0$ ⟦Chapter12/CompactnessEp · exists_nhds_isCompact_closure_auxLe⟧; this uses only that $f$, as a section of the object M-polyfold, is sc-Fredholm.

*Step 2, a finite cover.* The orbit map is open (Proposition 7.1.8, Part VII) ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_1_8⟧, so the sets $\pi(V(x))$, $x \in S_f$, are an open cover of the compact $|S_f|$; finitely many, $\pi(V(x_1)), \dots, \pi(V(x_m))$, suffice. Let $O$ be their union and $U = \pi^{-1}(O)$: it is open (continuity of $\pi$), saturated (a preimage under $\pi$), and contains $S_f$.

*Step 3, invariance.* If $y \in U$ with $N(f(y)) \le C$, then $\pi(y) = \pi(y')$ for some $y' \in V(x_i)$, that is, there is a morphism $\varphi : y \to y'$. Since $f$ is a section functor and $N$ is $\mu$-invariant, $N(f(y')) = N(\mu(\varphi, f(y))) = N(f(y)) \le C$ ⟦Chapter12/CompactnessEp · EpStrongBundle.auxLe_tgt_of_auxLe_src⟧.

*Step 4, compactness.* Hence $\pi(\{y \in U : N(f(y)) \le C\})$ lies in $K = \bigcup_i\pi(\operatorname{cl}\{y \in V(x_i) : N(f(y)) \le C\})$, a finite union of continuous images of compact sets, compact, and closed because $|X|$ is Hausdorff. The closure of the image lies in $K$ and is compact.

*Departure from the text.* The text's proof of Theorem 12.4.2 shrinks to neighbourhoods with the natural action and uses $\operatorname{cl}_{|X|}|U| = |\operatorname{cl}_XU|$; neither is needed, because the closure lies in the finite union $K$. The paracompactness of $|X|$, which Theorem 12.4.2 assumes, is not used ⟦Chapter12/CompactnessEp · EpStrongBundle.theorem_12_4_2⟧.

**Remark 15.3.2** (nothing to formalize). The remark says that the construction of perturbations needs sc-smooth bump functions in general, and that geometric constructions may replace them at the price of checking compactness by hand. It is a comment. In the formalization bump functions enter as a hypothesis exactly where perturbations are built: Theorem 15.3.7 assumes that $X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions in the pointwise reading (§XV.21), and the cylinder $[0, 1] \times X$ of Corollary 15.3.10 inherits them from $X$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.admitsBumpFunctionsPointwise_cubeProd⟧ (§XV.30). The sentence after Definition 15.3.1, "we also assume that $X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions", is likewise read as a hypothesis of the theorems that construct perturbations, not as part of any definition.

### XV.18 Definition 15.3.3 (2017: 15.5) and the example after it

**Definition 15.3.3** (same) ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.IsAdmissible⟧. An *$(N, U)$-admissible perturbation* for $f$ is a function $\Lambda : W \to \mathbb Q^+$ such that

1. $\Lambda$ is an sc⁺-multisection (Definition 13.2.1, in the 2021 form with local section structures, Part XIII);
2. $N(\Lambda)(x) \le 1$ for every $x \in X$, where $N(\Lambda)(x)$ is the pointwise norm of Definition 13.2.3, the largest value of $N$ on the finite set $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda)(x) = \{w \in W_x : \Lambda(w) > 0\}$ ⟦Chapter13/MultisectionSupport · SBLocalization.pointwiseNorm⟧;
3. $\{x \in X : \exists t \in [-1, 1],\ (t\Lambda)(f(x)) > 0\} \subset U$, where $t\Lambda$ is the scalar multiple of Definition 13.2.10: $(0\Lambda)(w) = 1$ if $w$ is a zero vector and $0$ otherwise, and $(t\Lambda)(w) = \Lambda(w/t)$ for $t \ne 0$ ⟦Chapter13/MultisectionAlgebra · SBLocalization.multisectionSmul⟧.

*Readings.* The text's standing data, $f$ sc-Fredholm with compact $|S_f|$ and $(N, U)$ controlling compactness, are not part of the predicate; they are hypotheses of the theorems that use it (Theorem 15.3.9, the boundary conditions of Corollary 15.3.10). The pointwise norm is defined as a supremum; for an sc⁺-multisection it is attained, the support over a point being finite and nonempty, and the points of the support lie in $W_{0,1}$, where $N$ is defined (Part XIII). Condition (3) with $t = 0$ asks that $S_f \subset U$, since $(0\Lambda)(f(x)) > 0$ exactly when $f(x) = 0_x$; with $t = \pm 1$ it asks that the support of $\Lambda \circ f$ and of $(-\Lambda) \circ f$ lie in $U$. The interval $[-1, 1]$ is what the cobordism argument of Corollary 15.3.10 (3) needs: perturbations $t\Lambda$ along a path stay inside $U$.

**The example after Definition 15.3.3** (same) ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.isAdmissible_of_domSupp_subset⟧. *Statement.* Let $f$ be a section with $S_f \subset U$, and $\Lambda$ an sc⁺-multisection with $N(\Lambda) \le 1$ whose domain support lies in $U$. Then $\Lambda$ is $(N, U)$-admissible. The domain support is $\operatorname{dom\text{-}supp}(\Lambda) = \operatorname{cl}_X\{x : \exists w \in W_x \setminus \{0_x\},\ \Lambda(w) > 0\}$ (Definition 13.2.2 (1)) ⟦Chapter13/MultisectionSupport · SBLocalization.domSupp⟧.

*Proof.* Conditions (1) and (2) are hypotheses; condition (3) is the content, and it goes in three steps.

*Step 1, off the domain support $\Lambda$ sees only the zero vector* ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.eq_zero_of_not_mem_domSupp⟧. If $x \notin \operatorname{dom\text{-}supp}(\Lambda)$ and $w \in W_x$ is not $0_x$, then $\Lambda(w) = 0$: otherwise $x$ would lie in the set whose closure is the domain support.

*Step 2, the same for every scalar multiple* ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.eq_fiberZero_of_multisectionSmul_pos⟧. If $P(w) \notin \operatorname{dom\text{-}supp}(\Lambda)$ and $(t\Lambda)(w) > 0$ for some real $t$, then $w$ is the zero vector of its fibre. For $t = 0$ this is the definition of $0\Lambda$. For $t \ne 0$, $(t\Lambda)(w) = \Lambda(t^{-1}w)$, with $t^{-1}w$ computed in the fibre; if $w \ne 0$ then $t^{-1}w \ne 0$ (multiply back by $t$), so $\Lambda(t^{-1}w) = 0$ by Step 1, a contradiction.

*Step 3.* Let $x \notin U$ with $(t\Lambda)(f(x)) > 0$ for some $t \in [-1, 1]$. Since $\operatorname{dom\text{-}supp}(\Lambda) \subset U$, $x \notin \operatorname{dom\text{-}supp}(\Lambda)$, and $P(f(x)) = x$ because $f$ is a section; by Step 2, $f(x) = 0_x$, so $x \in S_f \subset U$, a contradiction.

The text's argument is Step 1 and Step 3 for $t = 1$; Step 2 makes the argument cover every $t \in [-1, 1]$, including $t = 0$, where $0\Lambda$ is the multisection of the zero section and the claim is $S_f \subset U$. Only the section property of $f$ and $S_f \subset U$ are used: neither the Fredholm property nor the control of compactness enters. Witness of the definition: the zero multisection, whose domain support is empty and whose pointwise norm is $0$ (§XV.21), is admissible for every controlling pair by this example.

### XV.19 The products remark after Definition 15.3.3, and Remark 15.3.4: product ep-groupoids and product strong bundles

After Definition 15.3.3 (pp. 692–693) the text observes that admissible perturbations "behave well under products": for two problems $(W, f, N, U, \Lambda)$ and $(W', f', N', U', \Lambda')$ it takes the product $f \times f'$ as an sc-Fredholm section of $W \times W' \to X \times X'$, the auxiliary norm $(N \times N')(h, h') = \max\{N(h), N'(h')\}$, the product multisection $(\Lambda \times \Lambda')(h, h') = \Lambda(h)\Lambda'(h')$, and checks that $\Lambda \times \Lambda'$ is admissible for $(N \times N', U \times U')$. Remark 15.3.4 adds that the domain support of $\Lambda \times \Lambda'$ lies in $(U \times X') \cup (X \times U')$, not necessarily in $U \times U'$. The text takes the product ep-groupoid, the product strong bundle and its structure map for granted. The formalization builds them: the product ep-groupoid (extra, row V15.17), the product strong bundle of Part I (restated, V15.53), products of sections (same, V15.54), the product over the product ep-groupoid with $\mu \times \mu'$ (same, V15.55), and $N \times N'$ as an auxiliary norm (same, V15.56). What remains of the remark, the sc-Fredholm property of $f \times f'$ and the multisection $\Lambda \times \Lambda'$ with its admissibility and domain support, is gap G.160 (§XV.38). The product ep-groupoid is also the base of the cylinder $[0, 1]^n \times X$ of Corollary 15.3.10 (§XV.30).

**The product ep-groupoid** (extra) ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · EpGroupoid.prod⟧. *Statement.* For ep-groupoids $X$, $X'$, the groupoid with objects $X \times X'$ and morphisms $\mathbf X \times \mathbf X'$, all structure maps (source, target, composition, unit, inverse) taken componentwise ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · GroupoidStr.prod⟧, and the product M-polyfold structures on objects and morphisms (Exposition Lemma 4.D, Part II), is an ep-groupoid (Definition 7.1.3, Part VII). The groupoid axioms hold componentwise. *Proof* of the four conditions of Definition 7.1.3.

*(1)–(2), the étale property and the smooth structure maps.* Products of sc-smooth maps are sc-smooth on products of open sets: $f \times g = (f \circ \mathrm{pr}_1, g \circ \mathrm{pr}_2)$, a pair of composites with the sc-smooth projections ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · MPolyfold.IsScSmoothOn.prodMap⟧. Hence a product of sc-diffeomorphisms between open sets is one, with the product of the inverses as inverse ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · MPolyfold.IsScDiffeoOn.prodMap⟧, and a product of local sc-diffeomorphisms is one: at $(p_1, p_2)$ take the product of the two local inverses ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.prodMap⟧. So $s \times s'$ and $t \times t'$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms, and the unit and inverse maps, products of sc-smooth maps on $\mathrm{univ} \times \mathrm{univ}$, are sc-smooth.

*(3), properness.* At $(x, x')$ take the neighbourhoods $V \ni x$, $V' \ni x'$ of condition (3) for $X$ and $X'$, with $t : s^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}V) \to X$ and $t' : s'^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}V') \to X'$ proper. For $V \times V'$, the closure of a product is the product of the closures, so $(s \times s')^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}(V \times V')) = s^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}V) \times s'^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}V')$, and $t \times t'$ restricted to it is proper: a product of proper maps, composed with the homeomorphism between a product of subsets and the subset of the product ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · isProperMap_domRestrict_prod⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · EpGroupoid.prod_exists_isProperMap⟧.

*(4), sc-smooth composition.* Condition (4) asks that composition be sc-smooth on the fibred product $\mathbf X\,{}_s\!\times_t\mathbf X$; Part VII proves it equivalent to its sheet form: for every sheet $\sigma$ of $s$ (a local inverse of $s$ on an open $V$), the map $\psi \mapsto m(\sigma(t(\psi)), \psi)$ is sc-smooth on $t^{-1}(V)$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · isScSmoothComp_iff_sheet⟧. The formal proof checks the sheet form for the product ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · EpGroupoid.prod_isScSmoothCompSheet⟧. Let $\sigma$ be a sheet of $s \times s'$ over $V$, and $\psi_0 \in (t \times t')^{-1}(V)$. Take sheets $h_1$ of $s$ near the first component of $\sigma(t(\psi_0))$, defined on $U_1$, and $h_2$ of $s'$ near the second, on $U_2$; let $O$ be the open set of $\psi$ near $\psi_0$ with $\sigma(t(\psi)) \in U_1 \times U_2$. On $O$, $s(\sigma(t(\psi))_1) = t(\psi_1)$, and since $h_1$ is a left inverse of $s$ on $U_1$, $\sigma(t(\psi))_1 = h_1(t(\psi_1))$; likewise for the second component. So on $O$ the map is $\psi \mapsto (m(h_1(t\psi_1), \psi_1), m'(h_2(t'\psi_2), \psi_2))$, a pair of maps that are sc-smooth by the sheet form of (4) for $X$ and $X'$, composed with the projections. Sc-smoothness is local, which concludes.

*Consequences.* The projections are sc-smooth functors ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · EpGroupoid.prodFst⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · EpGroupoid.prodSnd⟧. If $X$ and $X'$ are tame, so is $X \times X'$, with $d_{X \times X'}(x, x') = d_X(x) + d_{X'}(x')$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · EpGroupoid.isTame_prod⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · EpGroupoid.degIndex_prod⟧, from the M-polyfold statement ⟦Chapter2/FibredProduct · MPolyfold.isTame_prod⟧. Two objects are isomorphic iff their components are: a morphism of the product is a pair of morphisms ⟦Chapter15/ProductEp · EpGroupoid.prod_π_eq_π_iff⟧. *Reading.* The type of ep-groupoids requires paracompact object and morphism spaces; on the products these are instances that always hold, M-polyfolds being metrizable ⟦Chapter2/FibredProduct · MPolyfold.paracompactSpace_prod⟧.

**The model level: products of strong bundle maps and retracts.** A strong bundle chart of $W$ takes values in $E \triangleleft F$, pairs (base, fibre); for the product the natural model is $(E \oplus E') \triangleleft (F \oplus F')$, base first. The two are related by the swap $((a, a'), (b, b')) \mapsto ((a, b), (a', b'))$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · bundleSwap⟧, which on every level is a continuous linear isomorphism, an sc-operator ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · ScBanach.bundleSwapOp⟧. The product of local maps $\Phi$, $\Phi'$ is $\Phi \times \Phi' := \mathrm{swap} \circ (\Phi \times \Phi') \circ \mathrm{swap}$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · prodBundleMap⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · prodBundleMap_eq⟧, sc-smooth on $(U \times U') \triangleleft (F \oplus F')$ when $\Phi$, $\Phi'$ are, as a composite of the product of sc-smooth maps with two sc-operators ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · isScSmooth_prodBundleMap⟧.

*Products of strong bundle maps* (Definition 2.6.1) ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · IsStrongBundleMap.prod⟧. Each clause of the definition is checked componentwise. $\Phi \times \Phi'$ maps $(U \times U') \triangleleft$ into $(V \times V') \triangleleft$; its base part does not depend on the fibre variable; it is linear in the fibre; it preserves the double filtration, because a pair lies on level $m$ of $E \oplus E'$ iff both entries do ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · ScBanach.mem_range_prod_toBase⟧; it is sc-smooth on $\triangleleft$ by the previous paragraph. For the shifted bundle $\triangleleft[1]$ one needs that the $[1]$-version of the product is the product of the $[1]$-versions: the lift to level $1$ of a pair of level-$1$ points is the pair of the lifts ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · ScBanach.invFun_prod_toBase_one⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · shiftFiber_prodBundleMap⟧, and the $[1]$-maps are sc-smooth by the same composition.

*Retractions and retracts* (Definitions 2.6.1, 2.6.2). For strong bundle retractions $R$, $R'$, $R \times R'$ is idempotent componentwise, so it is a strong bundle retraction ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · IsStrongBundleRetraction.prod⟧; its base retraction is $r \times r'$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · baseRetraction_prod⟧, with retract the product of the base retracts ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · retract_baseRetraction_prod⟧; and its image is the swap preimage of $K \times K'$, $K = R(U \triangleleft F)$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · image_prodBundleMap⟧. Hence $\mathrm{swap}^{-1}(K \times K')$ is a local strong bundle retract of $(C \times C') \triangleleft (F \oplus F')$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · IsStrongBundleRetract.prod⟧. Sc-smooth maps between retracts multiply in the same way: $T \times T'$ is the swap, the product $T \times T'$ of retract maps, and the swap back, three sc-smooth maps between retracts ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · IsScSmoothRetractMap.prodBundleMap⟧. The $[1]$-retract of $\mathrm{swap}^{-1}(K \times K')$ is $\mathrm{swap}^{-1}(K[1] \times K'[1])$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductStrongBundle · strongShiftOne_bundleSwap_preimage⟧.

**The product strong bundle** (restated) ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundle.prod⟧. *Statement.* For strong bundles $P : W \to X$ and $P' : W' \to X'$ over M-polyfolds, $P \times P' : W \times W' \to X \times X'$ is a strong bundle (Definition 2.6.5), with the atlas of products of charts. *Construction.*

*The fibres.* The fibre over $(x, x')$ is in bijection with $P^{-1}(x) \times P'^{-1}(x')$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · prodFiberEquiv⟧; the vector space structure is transported along the bijection, which then is a topological linear isomorphism ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · prodFiberCLE⟧. A product of Banachable spaces is Banachable ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · IsBanachable.prod⟧, and Banachability passes along topological linear isomorphisms ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · IsBanachable.of_equiv⟧.

*The charts.* For charts $\Phi$ of $W$ over $\varphi$ and $\Phi'$ of $W'$ over $\varphi'$, the product chart is $y \mapsto \mathrm{swap}(\Phi(y_1), \Phi'(y_2))$ over $\varphi \times \varphi'$, with fibre model $F \oplus F'$, domain $U \times U'$ and strong bundle retraction $R \times R'$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundleChart.prod⟧; its inverse is the pair of inverses after the swap ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundleChart.prodPartialEquiv⟧, it covers $\varphi \times \varphi'$, and it is linear on fibres, componentwise. Its image is $\mathrm{swap}^{-1}(K \times K')$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundleChart.prod_K⟧. *Compatibility.* The overlap of two product charts is the swap preimage of the product of the overlaps ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundleChart.overlap_prod⟧, and the transition map is the product of the transition maps ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundleChart.transition_prod⟧. Compatibility (Definition 2.6.4) asks four sc-smoothness statements, the transition maps and their inverses on $[0]$ and on $[1]$, and two level-preservation statements. The first four are the product of retract maps of the previous paragraph, on $[1]$ after identifying the $[1]$-map of the product with the product of the $[1]$-maps; the last two hold componentwise ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundleChart.Compatible.prod⟧. *The atlas* consists of the products $\Phi \times \Phi'$ of charts of the two atlases; any two are compatible by what was just shown, and they cover $W \times W'$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundle.prodAtlas⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundle.prod_mem_charts⟧. $W \times W'$ is paracompact, $W[0]$ and $W'[0]$ being metrizable ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundle.paracompactSpace_prod⟧. *Restated*, because the text does not describe the structure; the atlas of products of charts is the one the M-polyfold product of Part II uses.

*The levels.* As M-polyfolds, $(W \times W')[0]$ and $W[0] \times W'[0]$ coincide: the identity is sc-smooth in both directions, being the swap in the charts $\Phi \times \Phi'$ and $\Phi[0] \times \Phi'[0]$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleLevels · StrongBundle.isScSmoothMap_id_prod_zero⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleLevels · StrongBundle.isScSmoothMap_id_prod_zero_symm⟧. The $(0, 1)$-part is the product, $(W \times W')_{0,1} = W_{0,1} \times W'_{0,1}$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleLevels · StrongBundle.mem_oneSet_prod⟧, since in a product chart the level-$1$ lift is the swap of the pair of lifts ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleLevels · StrongBundleChart.liftOne_prod⟧. With their own topologies, $(W \times W')[1]$ and $W[1] \times W'[1]$ are homeomorphic ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleLevels · StrongBundle.prodOneHomeomorph⟧, the right side paracompact ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleLevels · StrongBundle.paracompactSpace_prod_one⟧, and the homeomorphism and its inverse are sc-smooth, again the swap in the $[1]$-charts ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleLevels · StrongBundle.isScSmoothMap_prodOneHomeomorph⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleLevels · StrongBundle.isScSmoothMap_prodOneHomeomorph_symm⟧.

*Products of strong bundle maps over maps of the bases* (§8.3's strong bundle maps). Products of sc-smooth maps of total spaces are sc-smooth on $[0]$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleMap · StrongBundle.isScSmoothMap_prodMap_zero⟧ and, through the homeomorphism of the $[1]$-levels, on $[1]$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleMap · StrongBundle.isScSmoothMap_prodMap_one⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleMap · StrongBundle.oneRestrict_prodMap⟧. If $\Phi$ covers $g$ and $\Phi'$ covers $g'$, then $\Phi \times \Phi'$ is a strong bundle map covering $g \times g'$: it covers componentwise, is linear on fibres, maps $(W_1 \times W'_1)_{0,1}$ into $(W_2 \times W'_2)_{0,1}$ by the product formula for the $(0,1)$-parts, and is sc-smooth on $[0]$ and $[1]$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundleMap · StrongBundle.IsStrongBundleMap.prod⟧.

**Products of sections** (same). $f \times f'$ is a section of $P \times P'$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · IsSection.prodMap⟧. *Sc-smooth* ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundle.IsScSmoothSection.prod⟧: near any point $p$, an sc-smooth section has a chart representative: a chart $\varphi$ of the base around $p_1$, a strong bundle chart $\Phi$ around $f(p_1)$, and an open $V \ni p_1$ on which $\Phi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is an sc-smooth map between retracts ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundle.exists_chart_rep⟧. Do the same for $f'$ at $p_2$; on $V \times V'$ the representative of $f \times f'$ in the product charts is the swap composed with the product of the two representatives, sc-smooth between retracts. *Sc⁺* ⟦Chapter15/ProductBundle · StrongBundle.IsScPlusSection.prod⟧: in a product chart the fibre values lie on level $1$ because both components do, and the representative into the $[1]$-retract $\mathrm{swap}^{-1}(K[1] \times K'[1])$ is again a swap composed with the product of the $[1]$-representatives.

**Over the product ep-groupoid** (same) ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · EpStrongBundle.prod⟧. *Statement.* For strong bundles $(W, \mu)$ over $X$ and $(W', \mu')$ over $X'$, $(W \times W', \mu \times \mu')$ is a strong bundle over $X \times X'$ (Definition 8.3.1), with $(\mu \times \mu')((\varphi, \varphi'), (w, w')) = (\mu(\varphi, w), \mu'(\varphi', w'))$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · EpStrongBundle.prod_μ⟧. *Proof.* The structure map is defined on the pull-back $(\mathbf X \times \mathbf X')\,{}_{s \times s'}\!\times_{P \times P'}(W \times W')$, a strong bundle over the morphism space; $\mu \times \mu'$ is a map on the product of the two pull-backs. The first step identifies the two. The splitting $((\varphi, \varphi'), (w, w')) \mapsto ((\varphi, w), (\varphi', w'))$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · prodPullbackSplit⟧, with inverse the joining map ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · prodPullbackJoin⟧, is a strong bundle map covering the identity of $\mathbf X \times \mathbf X'$, on $[0]$ and on $[1]$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · isStrongBundleMap_prodPullbackSplit⟧: each of its two components is sc-smooth into its pull-back by the universal property of the pull-back (a map into a pull-back is sc-smooth when its two projections are), the projections being the projections of the product composed with the identification $(W \times W')[0] = W[0] \times W'[0]$ above, and likewise on $[1]$ with the homeomorphism of the $[1]$-levels. Its inverse is sc-smooth by the same argument, so it is an sc-diffeomorphism and in particular a local sc-diffeomorphism ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · isLocalScDiffeo_prodPullbackSplit⟧. Then $\mu \times \mu' := (\mu \times \mu') \circ \mathrm{split}$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · EpStrongBundle.prodμ⟧ is: a strong bundle map covering $t \times t'$, as the composite of the splitting with the product of the strong bundle maps $\mu$, $\mu'$; surjective, by joining preimages; a local sc-diffeomorphism, as the composite of the splitting, the identity between the product strong bundle and the product M-polyfold on $[0]$, the product of the local sc-diffeomorphisms $\mu$, $\mu'$, and the identity back; and it satisfies the unit and composition laws componentwise.

*Section functors.* If $f$ and $f'$ satisfy the functor condition $f(t\varphi) = \mu(\varphi, f(s\varphi))$, so does $f \times f'$, componentwise ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · EpStrongBundle.IsFunctorialSection.prod⟧; products of sc-smooth section functors are sc-smooth section functors ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · EpStrongBundle.IsScSmoothSectionFunctor.prod⟧, and products of sc⁺-section functors are sc⁺ ⟦Chapter15/ProductEpBundle · EpStrongBundle.IsScPlusSectionFunctor.prod⟧ (Definition 8.3.4 (1), (2)). The paracompactness instances on the pull-backs and products that the types require are produced by the lemmas above; they always hold.

**$N \times N' = \max(N, N')$ is an auxiliary norm** (same). *Definition* ⟦Chapter15/ProductAuxNorm · StrongBundle.prodAuxNorm⟧: on $(W \times W')[1]$, $(N \times N')(w, w') = \max(N(w), N'(w'))$, read through the homeomorphism $(W \times W')[1] \cong W[1] \times W'[1]$; on a fibre, the level-$(0,1)$ fibre of the product is the product of the fibres ⟦Chapter15/ProductAuxNorm · StrongBundle.prodOneFiberFst⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ProductAuxNorm · StrongBundle.prodOneFiberMk⟧, and the norm is the maximum of the norms of the components ⟦Chapter15/ProductAuxNorm · StrongBundle.prodAuxNorm_toOne⟧. *Statement* ⟦Chapter15/ProductAuxNorm · StrongBundle.isAuxNorm_prodAuxNorm⟧: if $N$, $N'$ are auxiliary norms (Definition 5.1.1), so is $N \times N'$. *Proof*, clause by clause. *Continuity*: a maximum of continuous functions. *On each fibre a complete norm*: (i) if $\max(N(v_1), N'(v_2)) = 0$, both are $0$, since both are non-negative, so $v_1 = 0$, $v_2 = 0$, and $v = 0$ ⟦Chapter15/ProductAuxNorm · StrongBundle.prodOneFiber_ext⟧; (ii) homogeneity, $\max(|t|N(v_1), |t|N'(v_2)) = |t|\max(N(v_1), N'(v_2))$; (iii) the triangle inequality, each component's inequality bounded by the sum of the maxima; (iv) completeness: a sequence Cauchy for the maximum is Cauchy for each component, the components converge to $a$ and $b$ by completeness of $N$ and $N'$, and the sequence converges to the pair $(a, b)$ for the maximum. *Condition (2) of Definition 5.1.1*: if the base points $P(w_k)$ converge to $x$ and $(N \times N')(w_k) \to 0$, then both $N(w_{k,1}) \to 0$ and $N'(w_{k,2}) \to 0$ by squeezing between $0$ and the maximum, condition (2) for $N$ and $N'$ gives $w_{k,1} \to 0_{x_1}$ in $W[1]$ and $w_{k,2} \to 0_{x_2}$ in $W'[1]$, and the inverse of the homeomorphism of the $[1]$-levels carries the pair to $w_k \to 0_x$ in $(W \times W')[1]$. *Over the ep-groupoid* ⟦Chapter15/ProductAuxNorm · EpStrongBundle.isAuxNorm_prodAuxNorm⟧ (Definition 8.3.5): in addition $N \times N'$ is invariant under $\mu \times \mu'$, because each component is invariant under its own structure map.

**What is not formalized** of the remark (gap G.160, §XV.38): (c) $f \times f'$ is sc-Fredholm with tame germ data; Part I has no product of sc-Fredholm germs, only the case of the cube $[0, 1]^n$ as a parameter, which the cylinder uses (§XV.30); (d) $\Lambda \times \Lambda'$ as an sc⁺-multisection, from products of local section structures with weights $\sigma_i\sigma'_j$, the identity $(N \times N')(\Lambda \times \Lambda') = \max(N(\Lambda), N'(\Lambda'))$, the identity $t(\Lambda \times \Lambda') = (t\Lambda) \times (t\Lambda')$ and the admissibility for $(N \times N', U \times U')$, and Remark 15.3.4 on the domain support. The ingredient that the sections of the local structures multiply to sc⁺-sections is `IsScPlusSection.prod` above.

### XV.20 Definition 15.3.5 and Remark 15.3.6 (2017: Definition 15.6, Remark 15.6): general position

**Definition 15.3.5** (restated) ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.IsInGeneralPosition⟧. *Statement.* $(f, \Lambda)$ is *in general position* if for every $x \in X_1$ with $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$, every operator $L$ in the support of the formal sum $T(f, \Lambda)(x) \in \mathrm{GrF}(x)$ (Definition 15.1.7, §XV.8), every chart $\varphi$ of $X$ around $x$ and every presentation $T$ of the partial quadrant $C$ of its model ($C = T^{-1}([0, \infty)^k \times V)$), the restriction of $L : T_xX \to W_x$ to the reduced tangent space $T^R_xX$ is surjective. $T^R_xX$ is Part II's reduced tangent fibre (Definition 2.5.8), read in the chart $\varphi$ and the presentation $T$ ⟦Chapter2/ReducedTangentIntrinsic · MPolyfold.reducedTangentFiber⟧.

*Readings.* (a) The text quantifies over $x \in \operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$; the formal definition takes $x$ in $X_1$, where $T(f, \Lambda)$ is defined. Nothing is lost, because the support lies in $X_1$ (below). (b) The text writes $T(f, \Lambda)(x) = \sum_i\sigma_iL_i$ with $\sigma_i > 0$; these $L_i$ are the elements of the support of the formal sum, the operators with positive coefficient. (c) "$T^R_xX$ (Definition 2.5.8)" is read in every chart and every presentation; since $T^R_xX$ does not depend on them, one suffices (below). (d) The text works over a tame ep-groupoid; tameness is not part of the formal definition, and it enters the statements that need $T^R_xX$ to be the right space, through Part I's results on tame M-polyfolds.

*The support lies in $X_1$* ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.mem_levelSet_one_of_pos⟧. *Statement.* For an sc-Fredholm section functor $f$ and an sc⁺-multisection $\Lambda$, $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$ implies $x \in X_1$. *Proof.* Take a local section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ of $\Lambda$ on an open $O \ni x$ (the 2021 form, Part XI). The count formula gives $\Lambda(f(x)) = \sum_{i : f(x) = s_i(x)}\sigma_i$; the sum is positive, so some $i$ has $f(x) = s_i(x)$. The value $s_i(x)$ of an sc⁺-section lies in $W_{0,1}$, and an sc-Fredholm section functor is regularizing: $x \in X_0$ and $f(x) \in W_{0,1}$ give $x \in X_1$ ⟦Chapter12/CompactnessEp · EpStrongBundle.remark_12_1_1_regularizing_obj⟧ (the remark after Definition 12.1.1, Part XII).

*One chart suffices.* Every level-$1$ point lies in a chart with a presentation of its partial quadrant ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.exists_chart_presentation⟧. The reduced tangent fibre does not depend on the chart and the presentation (Proposition 2.4.10, Part II) ⟦Chapter2/ReducedTangentIntrinsic · MPolyfold.reducedTangentFiber_eq⟧, so surjectivity on it, checked in one chart and presentation at each point, holds in all ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPosition_iff_exists⟧: given the check in $(\varphi, T)$ and another pair $(\psi, T')$, rewrite the reduced fibre of $(\psi, T')$ as that of $(\varphi, T)$.

*The reduced linearization.* The text calls the restriction $T^R_{(f,\Lambda)}(x) = \sum_i\sigma_iL_i|T^R_xX$ the reduced linearization. Formally it is the push-forward of the formal sum along $L \mapsto L|T^R_xX$, in a chart and presentation ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.reducedLinearization⟧. Two distinct operators may have the same restriction; their coefficients then add. With coefficients in $\mathbb Q^+$ nothing cancels, so the support of a push-forward is the image of the support ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · Finsupp.support_mapDomain_nnrat⟧: for $b = g(a)$ with $a$ in the support, the coefficient of $b$ is a sum of non-negative terms one of which is positive. Hence general position is the surjectivity of every operator of the reduced linearization ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPosition_iff_reducedLinearization⟧.

*Witness* ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPosition_witness⟧: over the trivial ep-groupoid of $\mathbb R^n$ with the bundle $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$, the zero section and the zero multisection (the multisection of the zero section, value $1$ at zero vectors) are in general position, and $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$ is all of $\mathbb R^n$. The fibres are $0$, so every operator onto them is surjective. The witness shows that the all-charts form is satisfiable with nonempty support; it has zero fibres and is **weak** as a test of the condition.

**Remark 15.3.6, first sentence** (same) ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.IsInGeneralPosition.surjective⟧. *Statement.* In general position, every operator of the support of $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$, $x \in \operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f) \cap X_1$, is surjective. *Proof.* Choose a chart and a presentation at $x$; for $w \in W_x$ general position gives $\alpha \in T^R_xX$ with $L\alpha = w$, and $\alpha \in T_xX$. "Onto" is read operator by operator, as in Definition 15.2.1 (§XV.12); so general position implies transversality, which the proof of Theorem 15.3.7 uses (§XV.22).

**Remark 15.3.6, second sentence** (narrower; stronger in its range) ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionBranches · SBLocalization.remark_15_3_6_goodPosition_hyp⟧. *Statement.* Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section functor with Part I's tame germ data, $\Lambda$ an sc⁺-multisection, $(f, \Lambda)$ in general position and $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$. Then (a) $(f, \Lambda)$ is in good position at $x$ (Definition 15.2.4, §XV.15); (b) for every local section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ of $\Lambda$ on an open $O \ni x$ and every $i$ with $s_i(x) = f(x)$, the section $(f - s_i)|_O$ of the restricted bundle $W|_O$ (§XV.10) is in general position at $x$ in Part I's sense (Definition 5.3.9). The text states this for $x \in \partial X$, with "good position, in fact even in general position"; (b) is the reading of "even in general position", Definition 15.3.5 being "a natural extension" of Definition 5.3.9. The formal statement holds at every point of the support, on the boundary or not: stronger in that respect.

*Proof.* Four steps, the first two in a chart.

*Step 1, the reduced surjectivity read in a chart* ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionBranches · SBLocalization.exists_reduced_preimage⟧. Let $c$ be a strong bundle chart around $x$ with base chart $\varphi$, retraction $r$ on $U$, fibre retract $K$, and $z$ the level-$1$ point over $\varphi(x)$. Let $L$ be a chart operator $E_0 \to F_0$ whose intrinsic operator $\Phi_x^{-1} \circ L \circ T\varphi$ (§XV.7) is onto $W_x$ on $T^R_xX$. Then every $k$ with $(\varphi(x), k) \in K$ is $Lw$ for some $w$ in the chart's reduced tangent space at $z$ that also lies in the range of $Dr(z)$, the chart tangent space $T_zO$. The intrinsic operator is built from $L$ only when all chart vectors are mapped into the range of the fibre identification; in that case the preimage $\alpha \in T^R_xX$ of $\Phi_x^{-1}(k)$ gives $w$, the chart vector of $\alpha$, which lies in $T_zO$ and, by the chart description of the reduced fibre, in the reduced tangent space. Otherwise the intrinsic operator is $0$ by definition, surjectivity forces $W_x = 0$, and $w = 0$ serves.

*Step 2, the chart step* ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionBranches · SBLocalization.isGeneralPositionGerm_subRestrict⟧. *Statement.* Let $s$ be sc⁺ on an open $O$, $f(x) = s(x)$, and $c$ a **tame** strong bundle chart of $W$ **centred** at $x$ ($\varphi(x) = 0$) with domain in $O$. If the intrinsic operator $(f - s)'(x)$ (§XV.7) is onto $W_x$ on $T^R_xX$, then $(f - s)|_O$ is in general position at $x$ in Part I's sense. *Proof.* Restrict $c$ to a chart $c'$ of $W|_O$, tame because $c$ is ⟦Chapter15/LocalIFT · SBLocalization.scDeriv_restrictTo_subRestrict⟧: in it the derivative at $0$ of the principal part of $(f - s)|_O$ composed with the retraction is the chart operator $D((\hat f - \hat s) \circ r)(0)$ of $W$. The section $(f - s)|_O$ is tame sc-Fredholm (§XV.10) and vanishes at $x$. By Step 1 the linearization $\mathrm{Lin}(0)$ of $(f - s)|_O$ in $c'$ maps the reduced tangent space onto the fibre $K_0$, in particular it is onto. Next, $\ker\mathrm{Lin}(0) + T^R_0 = T_0O$: for $v \in T_0O$, $k = \mathrm{Lin}(0)v$ lies in the fibre of $K$ over $0$, because the derivative of the principal part composed with $r$ is fixed by the fibre projection $\rho$ at a zero; Step 1 gives a reduced $w$ with $\mathrm{Lin}(0)w = k$; and $v = (v - w) + w$ with $v - w \in \ker\mathrm{Lin}(0)$. These two facts are Part I's chart criterion for general position, proved in Part I's chapter on general position ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · isGeneralPositionGerm_of_sup_eq⟧, which concludes.

*Step 3, every branch through $f(x)$* ⟦Chapter15/GoodPositionBranches · SBLocalization.isGeneralPositionGerm_branch⟧. Let $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ be a local structure on $O \ni x$ and $s_i(x) = f(x)$. The point $x$ is smooth, being a zero of the regularizing section $f - s_i$ ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_smoothSet_of_eq⟧, in particular in $X_1$. The tame germ data of $f$ give a tame chart centred at $x$; restricted to $O$ it stays tame and centred with domain in $O$. With the local structure and this chart as local data (§XV.8), $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is their formal sum, so the intrinsic operator $(f - s_i)'(x)$ is in its support, the branch passing through $f(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_support_linSumIntr_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter15/LinearizationIntrinsic · SBLocalization.linearization_eq⟧. General position makes it onto on $T^R_xX$ in this chart, and Step 2 applies.

*Step 4, good position.* Definition 15.2.4 asks three things at $x$. $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$ is the hypothesis. $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ is onto: $x \in X_1$ by the lemma above, and every operator of the support is onto by the first sentence. For some local structure on an open $O \ni x$, given by the sc⁺-multisection, every branch through $f(x)$ is in Part I's good position (Definition 3.6.6): by Step 3 it is in general position, and general position implies good position for a tame sc-Fredholm section at a zero, Part I's Lemma 5.26 ⟦Chapter5/Transversality · StrongBundle.IsGeneralPositionGerm.isGoodPositionGermTame⟧, applied to $(f - s_i)|_O$, which is tame sc-Fredholm ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.isScFredholmSectionTame_subRestrict⟧ and vanishes at $x$ ⟦Chapter15/LocalScPlus · SBLocalization.isZeroAt_subSec_iff⟧.

*Narrower* by the inherited hypothesis: Part I's tame germ data of $f$, the hypothesis of all of §15.2 (§§XV.13–XV.16), inherited from Part I's Theorems 3.1.18 and 3.6.8, without which Theorem 3.6.8 does not hold as we read it (Part III). Here it supplies the tame chart centred at $x$ of Step 2. Witness of all hypotheses together: the zero section of $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$ with the zero multisection, which has tame germ data ⟦Chapter15/InteriorPerturbationWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_2_hyp_witness⟧ and is in general position ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPosition_epSEP_zero⟧; it has zero fibres (weak). No $d_X = 0$ is needed: unlike Remark 15.2.3 (§XV.14), the boundary points are reached through good position.

**Remark 15.3.6, last sentence** (narrower). The text concludes that $\Lambda \circ f$ is a tame branched ep⁺-subgroupoid. Three formal statements carry this.

*Local branching* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.remark_15_3_6_localBranching_hyp⟧. *Statement.* Under the hypotheses of the second sentence, at every $y$ with $\Lambda(f(y)) > 0$ the function $z \mapsto \Lambda(f(z))$ has a local branching structure in the sense of Definition 9.1.2 (2)–(4) (Part IX). *Proof.* By the second sentence $(f, \Lambda)$ is in good position at $y$, so Theorem 15.2.5 (§XV.16) applies at $y$: it gives a natural representation $U(y)$, a local section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ and a chart, such that each $M_i = \{z \in U(y) : f(z) = s_i(z)\}$ is a smooth submanifold properly embedded in $U(y)$, the count $\Lambda(f(z)) = \sum_{i : f(z) = s_i(z)}\sigma_i$ holds on $U(y)$, and only branches through $f(y)$ meet $f$ in $U(y)$. The branching structure is indexed by the branches through $f(y)$, with the sets $M_j$, which contain $y$, and the weights $\sigma_j > 0$. The count identity of Definition 9.1.2 is the count formula with the sum restricted to these branches: the terms of the other branches vanish on $U(y)$ by the last clause of Theorem 15.2.5.

*Branched* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.remark_15_3_6_isBranchedEpSubgroupoid_hyp⟧. *Statement.* If moreover the orbit space $|\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)|$ is paracompact, $\Lambda \circ f$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid of $X$ (Definition 9.1.2). *Proof.* Each clause of the definition: the values are non-negative rationals; $\Lambda \circ f$ is a functor, because $f$ is a section functor and $\Lambda$ is a functor, $\Lambda(f(t\varphi)) = \Lambda(\mu(\varphi, f(s\varphi))) = \Lambda(f(s\varphi))$ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isFunctorial_comp⟧; the support consists of smooth points, the tame germ data making $f - s_i$ regularizing ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_smoothSet_of_pos⟧; the paracompactness of $|\operatorname{supp}|$ is the hypothesis; and the local branching structures are the previous statement. *The added hypothesis*, the paracompactness of the orbit space of the support, is Definition 9.1.2 (1), new in the 2021 edition, which the remark does not address; it is not derived from the text. It is automatic when $|\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)|$ is compact, the situation of Theorem 15.3.7 (§XV.21); witness for $\mathbb R^n$ ⟦Chapter9/Propositions · EpGroupoid.paracompactSpace_orbitSupp_trivial_rn⟧.

*Tame* ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.remark_15_3_6_isTameBranched_hyp⟧. *Statement.* Under the same hypotheses $\Lambda \circ f$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid and tame (Definition 9.3.6). *Proof.* Good position holds at every point of the support (second sentence), and the global form of Theorem 15.2.5 (§XV.16) ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_isTameBranched_hyp⟧ concludes: at each support point Theorem 15.2.5 with "tame" gives a tame local branching structure, a natural representation with the properness property whose sheets $M_j$ carry a tame induced structure (Definition 2.5.18); forgetting the tameness gives the local branching structures of Definition 9.1.2, and the tame structures are Definition 9.3.6. Witness of the tame global form on $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0$, with support everything ⟦Chapter15/TameWitness · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_isTameBranched_hyp_witness⟧ (zero fibres, weak).

*Narrower* in all three only through the inherited tame germ data and, for the global forms, the paracompact support of Definition 9.1.2 (1). The text writes "tame branched ep⁺-groupoid", read as "ep⁺-subgroupoid". The compact form, under the hypotheses of Theorem 15.3.7, is its "in particular" (§XV.21), where compactness supplies the paracompactness.

### XV.21 Theorem 15.3.7 (2017: 15.4): the statement and its "in particular"

Theorem 15.3.7 (pp. 693–698) is the existence theorem for perturbations in general position. Over a tame ep-groupoid with sc-smooth bump functions, it takes an sc-Fredholm section functor $f$ with compact solution set $|S_f|$, a pair $(N, U)$ controlling compactness, and a continuous functor $h : X \to (0, 1]$. It produces an sc⁺-multisection functor $\Lambda$ with four properties, and then adds two claims: "in particular" $\Lambda \circ f$ is a compact, tame, branched ep⁺-subgroupoid, and $\Lambda$ "can be taken to be structurable". The formalization states the theorem as two propositions, one with and one without "structurable", and proves both. The proof is told in §§XV.22–XV.25; the final theorems are in §XV.26.

**Statement** (explicit) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionExistence · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_existence_statement⟧. Suppose:
- $X$ is tame;
- $X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions, in the pointwise reading of Part XII, which Theorem 12.3.2 (1) shows equivalent to bump functions on the object M-polyfold ⟦Chapter12/BumpEp · EpGroupoid.theorem_12_3_2_1⟧;
- $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section functor with the tame germ data of §15.2, and $|S_f|$ is compact;
- $(N, U)$ controls compactness (Definition 15.3.1, §XV.17) ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.ControlsCompactness⟧. That is, $N$ is an auxiliary norm, $U$ is an open saturated set containing $S_f$, and the orbit set of $\{x \in U : N(f(x)) \le 1\}$ has compact closure in $|X|$;
- $h$ is continuous, takes the same value at the source and the target of every morphism, and satisfies $0 < h \le 1$.

Then there is an sc⁺-multisection $\Lambda$ with:
- (1) $N(\Lambda)(x) < h(x)$ for every $x$, where $N(\Lambda)(x)$ is the pointwise norm of Part XIII (Definition 13.2.3), the largest $N(w)$ over the $w \in W_x$ with $\Lambda(w) > 0$;
- (2) domain support in $U$;
- (3) $(f, \Lambda)$ transversal (Definition 15.2.1, §XV.12) ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.IsTransversal⟧;
- (4) $(f, \Lambda)$ in general position (Definition 15.3.5, §XV.20) ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.IsInGeneralPosition⟧.

*The structurable form* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_statement⟧ is the same proposition with $\Lambda$ structurable (Definition 13.3.6). The theorem with its addendum pairs the two: (1)–(4) under the hypotheses above, and the structurable form whenever $X$ has a good system ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionExistence · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7⟧.

*Readings.*
- The text's "$U$ … a saturated subset" is read as open and saturated, as in Definition 15.3.1.
- A "continuous functor $h : X \to (0, 1]$" is read as a continuous function on objects that is constant along morphisms. This is a functor into the trivial category on $(0, 1]$.
- (3) is "$T(f, \Lambda)$ is surjective on $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$", i.e. every operator of the linearization of Definition 15.1.7 (§XV.8) is onto at every support point.
- (4) is formalized as the reduced linearization being onto at every support point. This follows the first sentence of the proof: "Point (4) is equivalent to" that requirement.
- "Structurable" is Definition 13.3.6.

*Explicit*: the only hypothesis not printed in the theorem is the tame germ data of $f$. It is inherited from §15.2 (§XV.16), where the boundary local perturbation needs it. The theorem itself uses no good system and no paracompactness of $|X|$.

**"In particular", compact and branched** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_in_particular_hyp⟧. Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section functor with tame germ data, and let $(N, U)$ control compactness. Let $\Lambda$ be an sc⁺-multisection with $N(\Lambda) \le 1$, domain support in $U$, and $(f, \Lambda)$ in general position. Then $\Lambda \circ f$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid (Definition 9.1.2) with compact support (Definition 9.1.6 (2)).

*Proof.*
1. $f$ is continuous, being an sc⁰ section.
2. *The support is closed* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isClosed_supp_comp⟧. Near any point $x_0$, $\Lambda$ has a local representation $(s_i, \sigma_i)_{i \in I}$ on an open $O \ni x_0$, with positive weights. On $O$, $\Lambda(w) = \sum_{i : s_i(y) = w}\sigma_i$ for $w \in W_y$. Since the weights are positive, $\Lambda(f(y)) > 0$ if and only if $f(y) = s_i(y)$ for some $i$ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.pos_iff_exists_eq⟧. So the complement of the support meets $O$ in $O \cap \bigcap_i\{y : f(y) \ne s_i(y)\}$. Each set $\{f \ne s_i\}$ is open in $O$, because two continuous sections into a Hausdorff bundle disagree on an open set. Hence the complement is open.
3. *Its orbit set is closed* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isClosed_orbitSupp_comp⟧. The support is saturated: $f(\operatorname{tgt}\varphi) = \mu(\varphi, f(\operatorname{src}\varphi))$, and $\Lambda$ is a functor, so $\Lambda \circ f$ is constant along morphisms. Hence the complement of $|\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)|$ is the image of the complement of the support under the orbit map. The orbit map is open (Proposition 7.1.8) ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_1_8⟧, so this image is open.
4. *The support lies in the controlled set* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.supp_comp_subset_controlled⟧. Let $\Lambda(f(x)) > 0$.
   - If $f(x) = 0$, then $x \in S_f \subseteq U$.
   - Otherwise $\Lambda$ is positive at a non-zero vector over $x$, so $x$ is in the domain support, hence in $U$.

   In both cases $f(x)$ lies in $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda)(x)$, so $N(f(x)) \le N(\Lambda)(x) \le 1$.
5. *Compactness* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isCompact_orbitSupp_comp⟧. $|\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)|$ is a closed subset of the compact closure that $(N, U)$ provides.
6. *Branched*. A compact space is paracompact. This gives the paracompact support that Definition 9.1.2 (1) asks for, and Remark 15.3.6 (§XV.20) supplies the local branching structures ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.remark_15_3_6_isBranchedEpSubgroupoid_hyp⟧.

Only (1) (with $h \le 1$), (2) and (4) are used. (3) follows from (4) ⟦Chapter15/ControllingPairs · SBLocalization.IsInGeneralPosition.surjective⟧. *Narrower*: the tame germ data are inherited from §15.2, and here they enter the conclusion, through good position at every support point (§XV.16).

**"In particular", tame** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_in_particular_tame_hyp⟧. Under the same hypotheses, $\Lambda \circ f$ is moreover a tame branched ep⁺-subgroupoid (Definition 9.3.6).

*Proof.* The first two conclusions are the previous theorem. Tameness is the tame form of Remark 15.3.6 (§XV.20) ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.remark_15_3_6_isTameBranched_hyp⟧, applied with the paracompactness that the compact support gives.

**The zero multisection.** Suppose $(f, \Lambda_0)$ is already in general position, where $\Lambda_0$ is the trivial multisection (weight $1$ at the zero vector). Then $\Lambda_0$ has all the conclusions of the structurable form, for every $h > 0$ and every $U$, provided $|X|$ is paracompact (needed for "structurable") ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_of_isInGeneralPosition_zero⟧:
- its pointwise norm is $0$ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.pointwiseNorm_zeroMultisection⟧;
- its domain support is empty ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.domSupp_zeroMultisection⟧.

On the bundle $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$, every pair is in general position, because every operator onto the zero fibre is surjective ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPosition_epSEP_zero⟧. So the structurable form holds there with $\Lambda = \Lambda_0$ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_statement_epSEP_zero⟧. This instance shows that the statement is not vacuous. It is weak: the fibres are zero and there is no boundary.

### XV.22 Proof of Theorem 15.3.7, I: linear families, (15.1), and the assembly

The text's proof:
- builds a family $\Lambda_t$, $t \in \mathbb R^{\bar\ell}$, of multisections from local pieces at the points of $S_f$;
- shows that the parametrized problem is onto on reduced tangent spaces at $\{0\} \times S_f$ ((15.1));
- uses the compactness (15.2) to stay near $S_f$ for small $|t|$;
- picks a small regular value $t_0$ of the projection to the parameter space, by Sard's theorem on the intersections of faces.

The formalized proof of (1)–(4) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionExistence · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_existence⟧ follows this plan in five steps:
- (a) at every point of $S_f$, small sections with (15.1) near that point ("seeds"; §§XV.23–XV.24);
- (b) from the seeds, a family good on a saturated neighbourhood of each point of $S_f$ (§XV.23);
- (c) by compactness of $|S_f|$, one family good on a neighbourhood of $S_f$ (this subsection);
- (d) for this family, general position for almost every small $t$ (§XV.25);
- (e) the choice of $t$ (this subsection).

The structurable form ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionGoodSystem · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_of_goodSystem⟧ has the same five steps with structurable families. This subsection gives the objects the proof works with and steps (c) and (e).

**Linear combinations of sections** ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.paramSec⟧. For sections $s_1, \dots, s_\ell$ and $t \in \mathbb R^\ell$, the section $\sum_jt_js_j$ is taken fibrewise, in the linear structure of $W_y$:
- it is a section, and an sc⁺-section when each $s_j$ is one;
- concatenating the parameters adds the combinations: $\sum_j t_js_j + \sum_k t'_ks'_k$ is the combination of the concatenated sections at the concatenated parameter ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.paramSec_append⟧;
- $N(\sum_jt_js_j(y)) \le \sum_j|t_j|\,N(s_j(y))$, by subadditivity and homogeneity of the auxiliary norm on the fibres ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.normW_paramSec_le⟧.

**Linear families** ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.IsLinearFamily⟧. A family $t \mapsto \Lambda_t$ of multisections, $t \in \mathbb R^\ell$, is *linear* if around every point $x_0$ there are:
- an open $O \ni x_0$;
- sections $s_{ij}$ on $O$ ($i \in I$ finite, $j \le \ell$);
- weights $\sigma_i > 0$ with $\sum_i\sigma_i = 1$;

such that, for every $t$, the sections $\sum_jt_js_{ij}$ with the weights $\sigma_i$ form a local representation of $\Lambda_t$ on $O$. So one domain, one set of sections and one set of weights serve all $t$. This is how the text's $\Lambda_t$ and $\tilde\Lambda(t, w) = \Lambda_t(w)$ are formalized. The text asks that $\tilde\Lambda$ be an sc⁺-multisection of the pull-back of $W$ to $\mathbb R^{\bar\ell} \times X$; a linear family gives that representation directly. At $t = 0$ every branch is the zero section, so $\Lambda_0$ is the trivial multisection.

The pointwise norm of a linear family is controlled by its sections:
- the norm $N(\Lambda)(x)$ is attained at a branch value of any local representation ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.pointwiseNorm_le_of_isLocalRepOn⟧;
- so if $N(s_{ij}) \le b$ then $N(\Lambda_t)(x) \le |t|_1\,b$, where $|t|_1 = \sum_j|t_j|$ ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.pointwiseNorm_le_of_linear⟧.

**(15.1) at a point** ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.IsParamOntoAt⟧. Let $x$ be a level-$1$ point. The family satisfies (15.1) at $x$ if it has a linear representation around $x$ with the following property. For every operator $L$ of the linearization $T(f, \Lambda_0)(x)$ (§XV.8), every chart presentation of the reduced tangent space $T^R_xX$, every branch $i$ and every $w \in W_x$, there are $v \in T^R_xX$ and $\tau \in \mathbb R^\ell$ with
$$Lv + \textstyle\sum_j\tau_js_{ij}(x) = w.$$

The text writes (15.1) as "$T^R_{(\tilde f, \tilde\Lambda)}(0, x)$ is onto". Its local constructions phrase it as: the image of $f'(x)$ on $T^R_xX$, together with the vectors $s_{ij}(x)$, spans $W_x$. Two readings are made:
- $f'(x)$ is read as the operator of $T(f, \Lambda_0)(x)$, which at a zero of $f$ is the linearization of $f$ (§XV.24);
- the $t$-derivative of $f - \sum_jt_js_{ij}$ is $\tau \mapsto -\sum_j\tau_js_{ij}(x)$, and its sign is immaterial for surjectivity.

At points with $d_X(x) = 0$, $T^R_xX = T_xX$, and (15.1) is the text's interior condition. So the interior and boundary constructions of the text become one construction.

**Sums of families** ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.famAdd⟧. For families $\Lambda$ over $\mathbb R^\ell$ and $\Lambda'$ over $\mathbb R^{\ell'}$, the sum over $\mathbb R^{\ell+\ell'}$ is $(\Lambda \oplus \Lambda')_{(t, t')} = \Lambda_t \oplus \Lambda'_{t'}$, the sum of multisections of Definition 13.2.9. This is the text's $\Lambda_t = \bigoplus_i\Lambda^{x_i}_{t_i}$.
- *Local representations of a sum* ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.isLocalRepOn_famAdd⟧. If $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ represents $\Lambda$ and $(s'_{i'}, \sigma'_{i'})$ represents $\Lambda'$ on $O$, then the sections $s_i + s'_{i'}$ with weights $\sigma_i\sigma'_{i'}$ represent the sum. The pairs $(i, i')$ are re-enumerated as one finite index set; the weights sum to $1$; the sums are sc⁺ on $O$. The value of the sum at $w$ is $\sum\{\sigma_i\sigma'_{i'} : s_i(y) + s'_{i'}(y) = w\}$, which is how Definition 13.2.9 computes a sum on a common representation domain.
- *Linearity* ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.IsLinearFamily.famAdd⟧. With linear representations, the branches $\sum_jt_js_{ij} + \sum_kt'_ks'_{i'k}$ are the combinations of the concatenated sections (`paramSec_append` above). So the sum of linear families is linear, on $O \cap O'$.
- *(15.1) for a sum* ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.IsParamOntoAt.famAdd_left⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.IsParamOntoAt.famAdd_right⟧. (15.1) for either summand at $x$ gives it for the sum. At $t = 0$ the sum is $\Lambda_0 \oplus \Lambda_0 = \Lambda_0$, so the operators $L$ are the same. For a branch $(i, i')$ of the sum, solve with the summand that has (15.1), and put $\tau = 0$ on the parameters of the other summand.
- *Two inequalities the text uses silently.*
  - $N(\Lambda \oplus \Lambda')(x) \le N(\Lambda)(x) + N(\Lambda')(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.pointwiseNorm_multisectionAdd_le⟧. A vector in the support of the sum is $a + b$ with $\Lambda(a) > 0$ and $\Lambda'(b) > 0$ ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.exists_of_multisectionAdd_pos⟧, and $N(a + b) \le N(a) + N(b)$ ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.normW_add_le⟧.
  - The domain support of a sum lies in the union of the domain supports ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.domSupp_multisectionAdd_subset⟧. Off both, each summand is trivial, and so is the sum; the domain support is a closure, and the closure of a union of two sets is the union of their closures.

**Families good on a set** ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionExistence · SBLocalization.ScPlusGPFamily⟧. For a set $Q$, a family *good on $Q$* is a linear family $\Lambda$ over some $\mathbb R^\ell$ with:
- every $\Lambda_t$ an sc⁺-multisection;
- $N(\Lambda_t)(x) \le |t|_1\,h(x)$ for all $t$ and $x$;
- domain supports in $U$;
- (15.1) at every level-$1$ point of $S_f \cap Q$.

The structurable twin ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.GPFamily⟧ asks every $\Lambda_t$ to be structurable instead.

The operations on good families:
- A family good on $Q$ is good on every subset of $Q$ ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.GPFamily.mono⟧ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionExistence · SBLocalization.ScPlusGPFamily.mono⟧.
- *The empty family* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionExistence · SBLocalization.ScPlusGPFamily.zero⟧ has $\ell = 0$ and $\Lambda_t = \Lambda_0$, and is good on $\emptyset$. It is linear with one branch, the zero section of weight $1$ ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.isLocalRepOn_zeroMultisection⟧.
  - The structurable empty family ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.GPFamily.zero⟧ needs $\Lambda_0$ to be structurable. With a good system it is, with the zero decoration ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.isStructurable_zeroMultisection_of_goodSystem⟧.
- *Sums* ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionExistence · SBLocalization.ScPlusGPFamily.add⟧. Families good on $Q$ and $Q'$ add to a family good on $Q \cup Q'$:
  - the sum of sc⁺-multisections is one (Definition 13.2.9) ⟦Chapter13/MultisectionAlgebra · SBLocalization.definition_13_2_9⟧;
  - the norm bound adds, $|t|_1h + |t'|_1h = |(t, t')|_1h$;
  - the domain supports stay in $U$;
  - (15.1) holds on $Q$ by `famAdd_left` and on $Q'$ by `famAdd_right`.

  The structurable sum ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.GPFamily.add⟧ is the same, with Proposition 13.3.12 for the structurability of a sum ⟦Chapter13/StructurableMultisection · SBLocalization.proposition_13_3_12⟧.
- By induction on a finite index set, with the empty family as the empty sum, families good on $Q_1, \dots, Q_k$ give a family good on $\bigcup_iQ_i$ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionExistence · SBLocalization.nonempty_scPlusGPFamily_biUnion⟧ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.nonempty_gpFamily_biUnion⟧.
- So without a good system, sums of sc⁺-families need nothing; with structurable families, the empty sum needs a good system. This is the only place where the two forms of the theorem differ.

**Step (c), from local to global** ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionExistence · SBLocalization.exists_scPlusGPFamily_of_compact⟧ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.exists_gpFamily_of_compact⟧. Suppose every $x \in S_f$ lies in an open saturated $Q_x$ carrying a good family. In the structurable form this hypothesis is named ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.HasLocalGPFamilies⟧. Then there is one family good on an open $Q \supseteq S_f$.
- The sets $\pi(Q_x)$ are open in $|X|$, since $\pi$ is open (Proposition 7.1.8), and they cover the compact $|S_f|$. Choose finitely many $x_1, \dots, x_k$ and put $Q = \bigcup_iQ_{x_i}$.
- $S_f \subseteq Q$: a point of $S_f$ has its orbit in some $\pi(Q_{x_i})$, and $Q_{x_i}$ is saturated.
- The family on $Q$ is the sum of the $k$ families.

The sc⁺ version first saturates the open neighbourhoods it is given (§XV.23). This is the text's "From local to global", with $\bar\ell = \ell_{x_1} + \dots + \ell_{x_k}$.

**Steps (d) and (e), the choice of $t$.** Step (d) (§XV.25) gives $\varepsilon > 0$ and a Lebesgue-null set off which $(f, \Lambda_t)$ is in general position for $\|t\| < \varepsilon$ (sup norm on $\mathbb R^\ell$). The hypothesis $N(\Lambda_t) \le |t|_1$ it needs follows from $N(\Lambda_t) \le |t|_1h$ and $h \le 1$; (15.1) holds on $S_f$ because $S_f \subseteq Q$.
- Put $r = \min(\varepsilon, 1/(\ell + 1)) > 0$. A ball of positive radius has positive measure, so it is not contained in a null set. Hence there is $t$ with $\|t\| < r$ and $(f, \Lambda_t)$ in general position ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.exists_norm_lt_of_ae⟧.
- From $\|t\| < 1/(\ell + 1)$: $|t|_1 \le \ell\|t\| < 1$ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.sum_abs_lt_one⟧.
- (1): $N(\Lambda_t)(x) \le |t|_1h(x) < h(x)$, since $h(x) > 0$.
- (2): the family's domain supports lie in $U$.
- (4) is the choice of $t$.
- (3) follows from (4) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.isTransversal_of_isInGeneralPosition⟧. A support point is a level-$1$ point, and an operator that is onto on the reduced tangent space $T^R_xX \subseteq T_xX$ is onto.

*Readings.*
- The text's $\varepsilon_0$, "so that $N(\Lambda_t)(x) < 1$ … provided $|t| \le \varepsilon_0$", is $1/(\ell + 1)$ in the sup norm. The bound actually used is $N(\Lambda_t) \le |t|_1h$, which gives (1) with $h$ and not only with $1$.
- "A set of measure zero … for $t$ in its complement" is "for almost every $t$".
- The text's remark that the complement "contains points arbitrarily close to $0$" is the positive measure of balls.

*Departures from the text's assembly.*
- The text starts from "a large parameter space $\mathbb R^h$, i.e. $h >> 0$". In the formalization the number of parameters is whatever the construction produces, the sum $\ell_{x_1} + \dots + \ell_{x_k}$ of the local ones.
- The text views $\tilde\Lambda$ as an sc⁺-multisection over $\mathbb R^{\bar\ell} \times X$ and $\tilde f(t, x) = (t, f(x))$ as an sc-Fredholm section there. The formalization never forms this pair on the product ep-groupoid. Everything it needs from $\tilde\Lambda$ is in the linear representations: (15.1) at the points of $S_f$, the norm bound, and the domain supports. The product appears only branch by branch, on $\mathbb R^\ell \times O$ with $O$ open in the object M-polyfold (§XV.25), where Part I applies.

**The assembly with the two analytic steps as hypotheses** ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_hyp⟧. Steps (c) and (e) for structurable families, as one statement. Its hypotheses:
- a good system;
- compact $|S_f|$;
- $(N, U)$ controlling compactness;
- $0 < h \le 1$;
- the local families of step (b) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.HasLocalGPFamilies⟧;
- the parametric general position of step (d) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.HasParametricGeneralPosition⟧. This is stated for every linear family of sc⁺-multisections with $N(\Lambda_t) \le |t|_1$, domain supports in $U$ and (15.1) on $S_f$.

Its conclusion is a structurable $\Lambda$ with (1)–(4). The structurable form of the theorem then follows from a good system and the two steps ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionAssembly · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_of_hyp⟧. Both steps are proved from the theorem's hypotheses in §§XV.23–XV.25, so these statements are the skeleton of the final proof, not additional assumptions of it.

### XV.23 Proof of Theorem 15.3.7, II: the local constructions

The text's "Local constructions at $x \in S_f$":
- choose vectors $w_1, \dots, w_\ell \in W_x$ completing the image of $f'(x)$, on $T^R_xX$ at boundary points;
