If $f(x_0) = s^0_a(x_0)$, then $(0, x_0)$ is a zero of $F_{a,i}$, the slice at $t = 0$ being $f - s^0_a$ ⟦Chapter15/RelativeParametric · SBLocalization.sectionAdd_paramSec_zero⟧, $F_{a,i}$ is in general position there by the previous lemma, and Part I's local Sard step, the local form of Theorem 5.3.10 without compactness ⟦Chapter15/LocalSlice · StrongBundle.exists_null_isGeneralPositionGerm_paramSlice_near⟧, gives the neighbourhood and the null set; its slices are the branches. If $f(x_0) \ne s^0_a(x_0)$, the zero set of $F_{a,i}$, closed because $F_{a,i}$ is sc-smooth (Part I's Theorem 3.1.21) ⟦Chapter3/ParamPerturbationG · Polyfold.theorem_3_1_21_tame⟧ ⟦Chapter5/Transversality · isClosed_solutionSet⟧, misses $(0, x_0)$; its complement is $W_{a,i}$ and $C_{a,i} = \emptyset$. The finitely many $W_{a,i}$ contain a product $B_\delta(0) \times V'$, and $C_V = \bigcup_{a,i}C_{a,i}$ is null. For $y \in V'$, $\|t\| < \delta$, $t \notin C_V$ and $(\Lambda_0 \oplus \Lambda_t)(f(y)) > 0$: $y$ is at level $1$; restrict a chart around $y$ to $O$; the sum representation has the branches $s^0_a + \sum_jt_js_{ij}$; each branch through $f(y)$ is in Part I's general position at $y$ by the choice of $W_{a,i}$; and Part I's general position of the branches through $f(y)$ is Definition 15.3.5 at $y$ ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.isReducedOntoAtLevel_of_isGeneralPositionGerm⟧ (§XV.16).

*Relative (15.2)* ⟦Chapter15/RelativeParametric · SBLocalization.exists_pos_supp_rel_subset⟧. If $(N, U)$ controls compactness, $N(\Lambda_0) \le 1$, the domain supports lie in $U$, $N(\Lambda_t) \le |t|_1(1 - N(\Lambda_0))$, and $V$ is a saturated open set containing $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda_0 \circ f)$, then for some $\varepsilon > 0$ every $t$ with $|t|_1 < \varepsilon$ has $\operatorname{supp}((\Lambda_0 \oplus \Lambda_t) \circ f) \subset V$. The text's (15.2) has $S_f$; relative to $\Lambda_0$ the support of $\Lambda_0 \circ f$ takes its place. *Proof*, by contradiction. Suppose there are $t_n$ with $|t_n|_1 < 1/(n + 1)$ and $x_n \notin V$ with $(\Lambda_0 \oplus \Lambda_{t_n})(f(x_n)) > 0$. For $|t|_1 \le 1$, $N(\Lambda_0 \oplus \Lambda_t) \le N(\Lambda_0) + |t|_1(1 - N(\Lambda_0)) \le 1$, so $x_n \in U$ and $N(f(x_n)) \le 1$ ⟦Chapter15/ParametricGeneralPosition · SBLocalization.auxLe_of_pos⟧, using the sum of multisections (Definition 13.2.9) ⟦Chapter13/MultisectionAlgebra · SBLocalization.definition_13_2_9⟧. The orbits $\pi(x_n)$ lie in the compact closure that the control of compactness provides; they have a cluster point $\pi(z)$. The object space is metrizable; along a decreasing basis $B_k$ of neighbourhoods of $z$ pick $n_k \ge k$ and $y_k \in B_k$ in the orbit of $x_{n_k}$ (the orbit map is open, so $\pi(B_k)$ is a neighbourhood of $\pi(z)$ met infinitely often). Then $y_k \to z$, $y_k \notin V$ ($V$ saturated), and $(\Lambda_0 \oplus \Lambda_{t_{n_k}})(f(y_k)) > 0$, since $f$ and the sum are functors. Decompose $f(y_k) = a_k + b_k$ with $\Lambda_0(a_k) > 0$ and $\Lambda_{t_{n_k}}(b_k) > 0$ ⟦Chapter15/RelativeParametric · SBLocalization.exists_of_multisectionAdd_pos_at⟧ ⟦Chapter15/ParamFamily · SBLocalization.exists_of_multisectionAdd_pos⟧; then $N(b_k) \le N(\Lambda_{t_{n_k}})(y_k) \le |t_{n_k}|_1 \le 1/(k + 1)$. Take a local representation $(s^0_i, \sigma^0_i)$ of $\Lambda_0$ on $O_2 \ni z$; for large $k$, $y_k \in O_2$ and $a_k = s^0_i(y_k)$ for some branch $i$; some $i$ occurs infinitely often, and along that subsequence $(f - s^0_i)(y_k) = b_k$ ⟦Chapter15/RelativeParametric · SBLocalization.subSec_eq_of_add⟧. The section $f - s^0_i$ is continuous on $O_2$, being a tame sc-Fredholm section of $W|_{O_2}$, so $(f - s^0_i)(y_k) \to (f - s^0_i)(z)$; and $b_k \to 0_z$, because the $b_k$ lie in $W_{0,1}$, their base points converge to $z$ and their norms to $0$, which for an auxiliary norm forces convergence to the zero vector. Hence $f(z) = s^0_i(z)$, so $\Lambda_0(f(z)) > 0$ and $z \in V$; $V$ being open, $y_k \in V$ for large $k$, a contradiction. The text's analogue for $\Lambda_0 = 0$ is the statement (15.2) of §XV.25; the new point is the branch of $\Lambda_0$ met infinitely often.

*The assembly.* Let $S = \operatorname{supp}(\Lambda_0 \circ f)$. Every $z \in S$ is at level $1$ (§XV.20), so the local step applies at $z$ and gives $V_z$, $\delta_z$, $C_z$. $|S|$ is compact (Step 2 above); finitely many $\pi(V_z)$, $z \in T$, cover it. Let $V_s$ be the saturation of $\bigcup_{z \in T}V_z$, open and saturated, containing $S$. Relative (15.2) gives $\varepsilon_0$ with $\operatorname{supp}((\Lambda_0 \oplus \Lambda_t) \circ f) \subset V_s$ for $|t|_1 < \varepsilon_0$. Choose $\varepsilon > 0$ so that $\|t\| < \varepsilon$ implies $\|t\| < \delta_z$ for $z \in T$ and $|t|_1 < \varepsilon_0$. The union of the $C_z$, $z \in T$, is null. For $t$ off it with $\|t\| < \varepsilon$, and $x$ in the support of $(\Lambda_0 \oplus \Lambda_t) \circ f$: $x \in V_s$, so there are $y \in V_z$ for some $z \in T$ and a morphism $\varphi : y \to x$; the support is saturated, so $y$ is in it; general position holds at $y$ by the local step; and general position at a point is carried along morphisms ⟦Chapter15/ParametricGeneralPosition · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPositionAt_of_mor⟧ (§XV.25). Pointwise general position everywhere on the support is general position ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionLocal · SBLocalization.isInGeneralPosition_iff_forall_at⟧. $\square$ The text discusses a countable cover and then remarks that a finite one suffices; the formal proof uses the finite cover directly, as in §XV.25.

**What remains: the relative local families** (gap G.178). Everything in steps (c)–(d) is proved except the proposition ⟦Chapter15/ChargedExtensionFibres · SBLocalization.relative_local_families_statement⟧ that every point of $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda_0 \circ f)$ has a relative family with domain support in $U \setminus \partial X$ and bound $|t|_1(h - N(\Lambda_0))$, under the hypotheses of the relative statement. It splits in two ⟦Chapter15/RelativeReduction · SBLocalization.hasLocalGPFamiliesRel_of_boundary⟧: at the points of $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda_0 \circ f) \cap \partial X$ the empty family suffices as soon as $(f, \Lambda_0)$ is reducedly onto at the support points of a saturated open neighbourhood, by the empty family of a set on which this holds; at the other points a relative family is needed. The first is the openness of general position near the boundary part of the support, which the text gets from the implicit function theorem (the neighbourhoods $Q(x)$ of its step (c)); the second is the text's "for $x \in U \setminus Q$ … we note that $d_X(x) = 0$ and we can argue as in Theorem 15.3.7": seeds at interior support points as in §XV.23, now making all the operators $(f - s^0_a)'(x)$ of $T(f, \Lambda_0)(x)$ onto at once, with domain support in a small neighbourhood that avoids $\partial X$. What each needs, with estimates, is in §XV.38. Witnesses of the two relative steps: on $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$ every pair is in general position, so the empty family covers everything ⟦Chapter15/RelativeReduction · SBLocalization.hasLocalGPFamiliesRel_epSEP_zero⟧ ⟦Chapter15/RelativeReduction · SBLocalization.hasParametricGeneralPositionRel_epSEP_zero⟧, and the relative statement holds there from them ⟦Chapter15/RelativeReduction · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_relative_statement_epSEP_zero_of_hyp⟧ ⟦Chapter15/RelativeParametric · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_relative_statement_epSEP_zero_of_local⟧; these witnesses have no boundary and zero fibres, so they are **weak**.

### XV.30 The cylinder $[0, 1]^n \times X$, and $d_X \equiv 0$ implies tame (prerequisites for Corollary 15.3.10)

Corollary 15.3.10 (p. 699) and its proof work on "the tame ep-groupoid $[0, 1] \times X$" with the pulled-back strong bundle $\widetilde W \to [0, 1] \times X$, whose fibre over $(t, x)$ is $W_x$, and the section $\tilde f(t, x) = (t, f(x))$. The text takes all of this for granted, and it assumes $d_X \equiv 0$ where Theorems 15.3.7 and 15.3.9, which it applies, ask for a tame $X$. This subsection builds the cylinder and proves the two facts the corollary uses silently: that the cylinder is a tame ep-groupoid with the expected boundary, orbit space and bundle, and that $d_X \equiv 0$ makes $X$ tame.

**The cube instead of the interval.** The formalization builds $[0, 1]^n \times X$ for every $n$, with Part I's cube $[0, 1]^n$ (the M-polyfold of maps $\{1, \dots, n\} \to [0, 1]$); the text's $[0, 1] \times X$ is $n = 1$. The reason is that Part I's parametrized Fredholm theory, which gives the sc-Fredholm property of $\tilde f$, is stated for the cube. Where the boundary or the time coordinate matters, $n = 1$ is fixed.

**The ep-groupoid** (extra) ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.cubeProd⟧. $[0, 1]^n \times X$ is the product (§XV.19) of the trivial ep-groupoid of the cube, whose only morphisms are identities, with $X$: objects $(q, x)$, morphisms $(q, \varphi)$, with source $(q, s(\varphi))$ and target $(q, t(\varphi))$. Two functors connect it with $X$. The projection $(q, x) \mapsto x$, $(q, \varphi) \mapsto \varphi$ is the second projection of the product ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.cubeProj⟧. The inclusion $i_q : x \mapsto (q, x)$, $\varphi \mapsto (q, \varphi)$ at a point $q$ of the cube ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.cubeIncl⟧ is sc-smooth because a constant map with a smooth value is sc-smooth ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · MPolyfold.isScSmoothMap_const_of_mem_smoothSet_poly⟧ and every point of the finite-dimensional cube is smooth ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · cubePolyfold_mem_smoothSet⟧; and $\mathrm{pr} \circ i_q = \mathrm{id}$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.cubeProj_comp_cubeIncl⟧.

*Tameness and the boundary.* If $X$ is tame, so is $[0, 1]^n \times X$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.isTame_cubeProd⟧, by Part I's tameness of products with the cube ⟦Chapter6/CubeSections · prod_cube_isTame⟧. The degeneracy index is additive, $d(q, x) = \#\{i : q_i \in \{0, 1\}\} + d_X(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.degIndex_cubeProd⟧: the first term is the degeneracy index of the cube at $q$, and the sum is Part I's degeneracy index of a product of tame M-polyfolds. For $n = 1$ and $d_X \equiv 0$ the count runs over a one-element index set, so $d(t, x) = 1$ if $t \in \{0, 1\}$ and $d(t, x) = 0$ otherwise ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.degIndex_cubeProd_one_of_degIndex_eq_zero⟧. The boundary is the set of points of positive degeneracy index, so $\partial([0, 1] \times X) = \{0, 1\} \times X$ ⟦Chapter15/RegularPerturbations · SBLocalization.mem_boundary_cubeSEP_iff⟧. This is the fact behind "$\Lambda$ over $i = 0, 1$": the boundary data of Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder are data over the two ends.

*Isomorphism classes and the orbit space.* Since the cube contributes only identities, $(q, x)$ and $(q', x')$ are isomorphic iff $q = q'$ and $x$, $x'$ are isomorphic ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.cubeProd_π_eq_π_iff⟧; hence $S \times U$ is saturated whenever $U$ is ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.isSaturated_prod_cubeProd⟧. The map $(q, |x|) \mapsto |(q, x)|$ from $[0, 1]^n \times |X|$ to the orbit space of the cylinder is well defined by the same criterion ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.cubeOrbitMap⟧. It is continuous ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.continuous_cubeOrbitMap⟧: $\mathrm{id} \times \pi$ is an open quotient map (the orbit map of $X$ is open, Proposition 7.1.8), and composed with it the map is the orbit map of the cylinder, which is continuous. It carries $[0, 1]^n \times |A|$ onto $|[0, 1]^n \times A|$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.image_π_cubeProd⟧, so $|[0, 1]^n \times A|$ is compact when $|A|$ is ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.isCompact_image_π_cubeProd⟧. More is true. The map is injective ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · EpGroupoid.injective_cubeOrbitMap⟧ (the isomorphism criterion again), surjective ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · EpGroupoid.surjective_cubeOrbitMap⟧ (every orbit has a representative $(q, x)$), and open ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · EpGroupoid.isOpenMap_cubeOrbitMap⟧: the image of an open $O \subset [0, 1]^n \times |X|$ is the image under the orbit map of the cylinder of the open set $(\mathrm{id} \times \pi)^{-1}(O)$, and the orbit map of the cylinder is open by Proposition 7.1.8. So it is a homeomorphism $[0, 1]^n \times |X| \cong |[0, 1]^n \times X|$ ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · EpGroupoid.cubeOrbitHomeomorph⟧. A product of a compact space with a paracompact space is paracompact, and paracompactness is carried by homeomorphisms; so the orbit space of the cylinder is paracompact when $|X|$ is ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · EpGroupoid.hasParacompactOrbitSpace_cubeProd⟧. This is the hypothesis "paracompact orbit space" of Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder, derived from the corollary's own hypothesis on $|X|$.

*Bump functions.* If $X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions (Definition 12.3.1, read pointwise), so does $[0, 1]^n \times X$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.admitsBumpFunctionsPointwise_cubeProd⟧: Theorem 12.3.2 (1) passes between the ep-groupoid and its object M-polyfold, and Part I proves bump functions on products with the cube ⟦Chapter6/CubeSections · admitsBumpFunctions_prod_cube⟧.

**The bundle and the section** (narrower). $\widetilde W$ is the pull-back of $W$ along the projection functor ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · SEP.cubeSEP⟧, Chapter 10's pull-back of a strong bundle over an ep-groupoid along a functor. A point of $\widetilde W$ is a pair $((q, x), w)$ with $w \in W_x$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · SEP.cubeVal⟧, and the morphism $(q, \varphi)$ acts by $\tilde\mu((q, \varphi), ((q, x), w)) = ((q, t(\varphi)), \mu(\varphi, w))$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeLift · SBLocalization.cubeVal_fibAct⟧. The section is $\tilde f(q, x) = ((q, x), f(x))$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · SEP.cubeLiftEp⟧, a section of $\widetilde W$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · SEP.isSection_cubeLiftEp⟧. The text writes $\tilde f(t, x) = (t, f(x))$ in the statement and $\tilde f(t, x) = f(x)$ in the proof; both mean this section.

*It is a functor* ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · SEP.isFunctorialSection_cubeLiftEp⟧: at a morphism $(q, \varphi)$ the identity $\tilde f(t(q, \varphi)) = \tilde\mu((q, \varphi), \tilde f(s(q, \varphi)))$ has first component $(q, t(\varphi))$ on both sides, and its second component is $f(t(\varphi)) = \mu(\varphi, f(s(\varphi)))$, the functor property of $f$. *It is sc-smooth* ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · SEP.isScSmoothSectionFunctor_cubeLiftEp⟧, by Part I's pull-back of sc-smooth sections along the sc-smooth projection. *It is sc-Fredholm when $f$ has Part I's tame germ data* ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · SEP.isScFredholmSectionFunctor_cubeLiftEp⟧: the germ of $\tilde f$ at $(q, x)$ is the germ of $f$ at $x$ with the cube coordinates as parameters, and Part I proves that this parametrized germ has tame germ data again ⟦Chapter6/CubeFredholm · StrongBundle.IsScFredholmSectionTame.paramCube⟧, which gives the sc-Fredholm property; the tame germ data of $\tilde f$ are recorded separately, for the theorems that need them on the cylinder ⟦Chapter15/RegularPerturbations · SBLocalization.isScFredholmSectionTame_cubeLiftEp⟧. *Its solution set* is $S_{\tilde f} = [0, 1]^n \times S_f$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · SEP.solutionSet_cubeLiftEp⟧, since the second component of $\tilde f(q, x)$ is $f(x)$ and the zero of $\widetilde W_{(q, x)}$ is $((q, x), 0_x)$; so $|S_{\tilde f}|$ is compact when $|S_f|$ is ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · SEP.hasCompactSolutionSetEp_cubeLiftEp⟧, by the compactness of $|[0, 1]^n \times A|$ above.

*The added hypothesis.* The row is narrower only through the tame germ data of $f$, Part I's hypothesis for its parametrized Fredholm theory (Part I's untamed parametrized case is not formalized; with the 2021 untamed notion Part I's Theorem 3.6.8 does not hold as we read it, Part III). It is inherited, as in all of §15.2 (§XV.10), not new; its witness is the zero section of $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$ with its graph section's tame germ data ⟦Chapter15/InteriorPerturbationWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_2_hyp_witness⟧ ⟦Chapter3/NonVacuityG · isScFredholmSectionTame_graphSection⟧. The rest (tameness, boundary, orbit space, bump functions, compact solution set) holds as the text uses it.

**$d_X \equiv 0$ implies tame** (extra) ⟦Chapter5/DegeneracyZeroTame · EpGroupoid.isTame_of_degIndex_eq_zero⟧. *Statement.* An ep-groupoid whose degeneracy index vanishes at every object is tame; it is the statement for its object M-polyfold ⟦Chapter5/DegeneracyZeroTame · MPolyfold.isTame_of_degIndex_eq_zero⟧. Corollary 15.3.10 assumes $d_X \equiv 0$ and applies Theorems 15.3.7 and 15.3.9, which are stated for tame $X$; the text passes from one to the other without comment.

*Proof, the local step* ⟦Chapter5/DegeneracyZeroTame · isTameRetract_inter_of_degIndex_eq_zero_ty⟧. Let $r : U \to U$ be an sc-smooth retraction of a partial quadrant $C \subset E$, presented by an sc-isomorphism $T : E \cong \mathbb R^k \times W'$ with $C = T^{-1}([0, \infty)^k \times W')$, and let $W$ be open with $d_C = 0$ on $r(U) \cap W$. The claim is that $r(U) \cap W$ is a tame retract (Definition 2.5.2). (i) For $z \in C$, $d_C(z) = 0$ iff all $k$ half-line coordinates of $T(z)$ are positive ⟦Chapter5/DegeneracyZeroTame · degIndexWith_eq_zero_iff_ty⟧ ⟦Chapter5/DegeneracyZeroTame · degIndex_eq_zero_iff_pos_ty⟧, and the set $D$ of such $z$ is open ⟦Chapter5/DegeneracyZeroTame · isOpen_setOf_pos_coord_ty⟧, a finite intersection of open half-spaces. (ii) Restrict $r$ to $U' = U \cap r^{-1}(W) \cap D$. This is still an sc-smooth retraction: $U'$ is relatively open, $r$ maps $U'$ into $r(U) \cap W$, where $d_C = 0$, hence into $D$, and $r \circ r = r$. Its retract is $r(U) \cap W$: a point of $r(U) \cap W$ is fixed by $r$ and lies in $D$. (iii) Definition 2.5.2 (1), $d_C(r(x)) = d_C(x)$ on $U'$, holds because both sides are $0$ there. (iv) Definition 2.5.2 (2) asks, at a smooth point $x$ of the retract, for an sc-complement of $T_xO$ inside the minimal subspace $E_x$ of $E$ spanned by the directions in which no vanishing coordinate is tied down. Since no half-line coordinate of $x$ vanishes, $E_x = E$, and the range of $Dr(x)$ is sc-complemented in $E$ by $\ker Dr(x)$, Part I's sc-splitting of the range of the derivative of a retraction. Hence the restricted retract is tame.

*Proof, the M-polyfold.* At a point $x$ take a chart $\varphi$ whose degeneracy index at $x$ attains $d_X(x) = 0$ (Definition 2.4.1 takes a minimum over charts, and it is attained). The points of its domain with chart degeneracy index $0$ form an open set $s$, by the upper semicontinuity of the chart degeneracy index; the restriction of $\varphi$ to $s$ is again a chart of the structure, and its image is $r(U) \cap W$ for an open $W$. On it $d_C = 0$, so it is a tame retract by the local step, and the M-polyfold is tame by Part I's criterion that every point lie in a chart on a tame retract ⟦Chapter2/TameFaces · MPolyfold.isTame_of_forall_exists_chart⟧. The ep-groupoid is tame when its object M-polyfold is. Gap G.183 is closed.

### XV.31 Corollary 15.3.10 (1) and (2) (2017: Corollary 15.1 (1), (2))

**The setting.** Corollary 15.3.10 (p. 699) assumes a strong bundle over an ep-groupoid with $d_X \equiv 0$ and paracompact orbit space $|X|$, and an sc-Fredholm section functor $f$ with $|S_f|$ compact. Part (1) produces a perturbation for one controlling pair, (2) an auxiliary norm on the cylinder that interpolates two controlling pairs, (3) a perturbation on the cylinder that interpolates two perturbations (§§XV.32–XV.33).

**Definition: regular perturbations** ⟦Chapter15/RegularPerturbations · SBLocalization.IsRegularPerturbation⟧. $(N, U, \Lambda)$ is a structurable regular perturbation of $f$ if $(N, U)$ controls the compactness of $f$ (Definition 15.3.1, §XV.17), $\Lambda$ is structurable (Definition 13.3.6, Part XIII), its domain support lies in $U$, $N(\Lambda)(x) < 1$ for all $x$, and $(f, \Lambda)$ is transversal (Definition 15.2.1, §XV.12). This is the text's definition in (1): "$T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ onto for all $x \in \operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$" is transversality, and the clauses about $\Theta$ are a consequence, not part of the definition.

**Corollary 15.3.10 (1)** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_1_ty⟧. *Statement.* Let $d_X \equiv 0$, $|X|$ paracompact, $X$ admit sc-smooth bump functions, $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section functor with Part I's tame germ data and $|S_f|$ compact, and $(N, U)$ control the compactness of $f$. Given the statement of Theorem 15.3.7 for the bundle, there is a $\Lambda$ such that $(N, U, \Lambda)$ is a structurable regular perturbation, $(f, \Lambda)$ is in general position (Definition 15.3.5), and $\Theta = \Lambda \circ f$ is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid with compact $|\operatorname{supp}\Theta|$. The statement of Theorem 15.3.7 holds for every bundle whose orbit space is paracompact ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionGoodSystem · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_of_paracompact⟧ (§XV.26), which the corollary assumes; so the hypothesis is discharged under the corollary's own assumptions. The two declarations compose; the composite is not stated as one declaration.

*Proof.* (i) *Tameness.* $X$ is tame because $d_X \equiv 0$ (§XV.30). (ii) *Theorem 15.3.7 with $h \equiv 1$.* The constant function $1$ is continuous, constant along morphisms and satisfies $0 < h \le 1$; the statement of Theorem 15.3.7 (§XV.21) then gives a structurable $\Lambda$ with $N(\Lambda) < 1$, domain support in $U$, $(f, \Lambda)$ transversal and in general position. These are the clauses of a regular perturbation, with general position in addition. (iii) *The "in particular".* With $N(\Lambda) \le 1$, domain support in $U$ and general position, Theorem 15.3.7's "in particular" ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_in_particular_hyp⟧ (§XV.21) makes $\Theta$ a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid with compact support; its tame form ⟦Chapter15/TameBranched · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_in_particular_tame_hyp⟧ gives the text's "tame branched". (iv) *Where the hypotheses enter.* $d_X \equiv 0$ is used only for (i), and paracompactness only through Theorem 15.3.7's structurable addendum, which needs a good system, supplied by Theorem 13.1.8 for paracompact $|X|$ (§XV.26). The text's proof says "a special case of Theorem 15.3.7"; the special case is $h \equiv 1$.

*Intermediate form.* The same conclusion with "$X$ tame" as an extra hypothesis in place of its derivation ⟦Chapter15/RegularPerturbations · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_1_hyp⟧; the final form calls it with the tameness of §XV.30.

*Added hypotheses.* Sc-smooth bump functions, which Theorem 15.3.7 needs and the corollary does not state; Remark 15.3.2 says that the theory needs them. And the tame germ data of $f$, inherited from §15.2 (§XV.10). Neither is derived from the corollary's statement; they hold together with the corollary's own hypotheses on the example of §XV.13 over $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$ ⟦Chapter15/InteriorPerturbationWitness · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_2_hyp_witness⟧, where $d_X \equiv 0$ and $|X| = \mathbb R^n$ is paracompact; there the zero section with the zero multisection is a regular perturbation, a degenerate one (zero fibres).

**Corollary 15.3.10 (2)** (same) ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.corollary_15_3_10_2⟧. *Statement.* If $(N^0, U^0)$ and $(N^1, U^1)$ control the compactness of $f$, there are an auxiliary norm $\widetilde N$ of $\widetilde W \to [0, 1] \times X$ and a saturated open $\widetilde U \supset S_{\tilde f}$ such that $(\widetilde N, \widetilde U)$ controls the compactness of $\tilde f$ and restricts to $(N^i, U^i)$ over $t = i$. The text states (2) for regular perturbations $(N^i, U^i, \Lambda^i)$; the $\Lambda^i$ play no role in it, and only the control of compactness is assumed. The text does not give $\widetilde N$; its proof pulls back a single $N$, which is the first step below. The formalization proves both.

*The proof's step: one pair, pulled back.* $\widetilde N(q, x, h) = N(h)$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.cubeAuxNorm⟧ is Part I's pull-back of an auxiliary norm along a map of the base ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · StrongBundle.pullbackAuxNorm⟧; its value at a point of $\widetilde W_{0,1}$ is $N$ of the $W$-component ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.cubeAuxNorm_eq⟧. It is an auxiliary norm of the strong bundle $\widetilde W$ (Definition 5.1.1) ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.isAuxNorm_cubeAuxNorm'⟧, by Part I's lemma that pull-backs of auxiliary norms are auxiliary norms ⟦Chapter5/CylinderPerturbation2021 · StrongBundle.IsAuxNorm.pullback⟧. It is invariant under $\tilde\mu$ (Definition 8.3.5 (3)) ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.isAuxNorm_cubeAuxNorm⟧: if $h = \tilde\mu((q, \varphi), k)$, then the $W$-component of $h$ is $\mu(\varphi, k_2)$ and the cube coordinate is unchanged ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.cubeVal_μ⟧, so $\widetilde N(h) = N(\mu(\varphi, k_2)) = N(k_2) = \widetilde N(k)$ by the invariance of $N$. At the values of $\tilde f$, "$\widetilde N(\tilde f(q, x)) \le r$" is "$N(f(x)) \le r$" ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.auxLe_cubeAuxNorm_iff⟧. Then $(\widetilde N, [0, 1]^n \times U)$ controls the compactness of $\tilde f$ whenever $(N, U)$ controls that of $f$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.controlsCompactness_cube⟧: $[0, 1]^n \times U$ is open, saturated (§XV.30) and contains $S_{\tilde f} = [0, 1]^n \times S_f$; and its sublevel set $\{z \in [0, 1]^n \times U : \widetilde N(\tilde f(z)) \le 1\}$ is $[0, 1]^n$ times the sublevel set $S$ of $(N, U)$. The orbit set of $[0, 1]^n \times S$ lies in the image of $[0, 1]^n \times \operatorname{cl}|S|$ under the continuous map $(q, |x|) \mapsto |(q, x)|$, a compact set, so its closure is compact ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.isCompact_closure_image_π_cube⟧.

*The weights.* $\alpha(s) = \min(1, 3(1 - s))$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.cubeWeight₀⟧ and $\beta(s) = \min(1, 3s)$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.cubeWeight₁⟧ are continuous and non-negative on $[0, 1]$, $\alpha = 1$ on $[0, \tfrac23]$, $\beta = 1$ on $[\tfrac13, 1]$, $\alpha(1) = 0$, $\beta(0) = 0$, and at every $s$ one of them is positive ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.cubeWeight_pos⟧ (for $s \le \frac23$, $\alpha(s) = 1$; otherwise $\beta(s) = 1$). With the time coordinate $t(w)$ of a point of $\widetilde W_{0,1}$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.cubeTime⟧, a continuous function, the interpolated norm is
$$\widetilde N(w) = \max\big(\alpha(t(w))\,\widetilde N^0(w),\ \beta(t(w))\,\widetilde N^1(w)\big)$$
⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.interpAuxNorm⟧, with $\widetilde N^i$ the pull-back of $N^i$, and the interpolated set is $\widetilde U = ([0, \tfrac23) \times U^0) \cup ((\tfrac13, 1] \times U^1)$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.interpSet⟧.

*Step 1, a lemma on maxima.* For auxiliary norms $N_0$, $N_1$ of a strong bundle and constants $a, b \ge 0$, not both $0$, $\max(aN_0, bN_1)$ is an auxiliary norm ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · StrongBundle.isAuxNorm_max_mul⟧. If both are positive, Part I's lemmas that positive multiples and maxima of auxiliary norms are auxiliary norms apply; if $b = 0$, the maximum is $aN_0$, since $aN_0 \ge 0$, and symmetrically for $a = 0$.

*Step 2, $\widetilde N$ is an auxiliary norm of $(\widetilde W, \tilde\mu)$* ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.isAuxNorm_interpAuxNorm⟧. Definition 5.1.1 has three conditions and Definition 8.3.5 adds the invariance. (0) Continuity on $\widetilde W_{0,1}$: products and maxima of continuous functions. (1) On each fibre a complete norm: on the fibre over $z$ the time is the constant $t(z)$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.cubeTime_toOne⟧, so there $\widetilde N$ agrees with $\max(\alpha(t(z))\widetilde N^0, \beta(t(z))\widetilde N^1)$ for constants, which is a complete fibre norm by Step 1; completeness of a fibre norm depends only on the values on that fibre ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · StrongBundle.IsCompleteFiberNorm.congr⟧. (2) The convergence condition, that $w_k \in \widetilde W_{0,1}$ with $\widetilde P(w_k) \to z$ and $\widetilde N(w_k) \to 0$ converge to $0_z$. Let $t_0$ be the time of $z$; one of $\alpha(t_0)$, $\beta(t_0)$ is positive, say $\alpha(t_0)$. By continuity $\alpha(t(w_k)) > \alpha(t_0)/2$ for large $k$, so $\widetilde N^0(w_k) \le (2/\alpha(t_0))\,\widetilde N(w_k) \to 0$, and condition (2) for $\widetilde N^0$ gives $w_k \to 0_z$; symmetrically if $\beta(t_0) > 0$. (3) Invariance: both $\widetilde N^i$ are invariant, and $\tilde\mu$ does not change the time (the same lemma on the cube coordinate as above).

*Step 3, the restrictions.* Over $t = 0$, $\alpha = 1$ and $\beta = 0$, so $\widetilde N = \widetilde N^0$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.interpAuxNorm_of_cubeTime_eq_zero⟧, and $(0, x) \in \widetilde U$ iff $x \in U^0$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.mem_interpSet_zero⟧; over $t = 1$, $\widetilde N = \widetilde N^1$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.interpAuxNorm_of_cubeTime_eq_one⟧ and $(1, x) \in \widetilde U$ iff $x \in U^1$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.mem_interpSet_one⟧. This is "restricts over $i = 0, 1$ to $N^i$, $U^i$".

*Step 4, $(\widetilde N, \widetilde U)$ controls the compactness of $\tilde f$.* $\widetilde U$ is open, a union of two products of open sets. It is saturated: each piece is a product of a set of times with a saturated set (§XV.30), and images and preimages under the orbit map commute with unions. It contains $S_{\tilde f} = [0, 1] \times S_f$: a point $(t, x)$ with $x \in S_f$ lies in the first piece if $t < \tfrac23$, since $S_f \subset U^0$, and in the second otherwise, since then $t > \tfrac13$ and $S_f \subset U^1$. For the compactness, let $(t, x) \in \widetilde U$ with $\widetilde N(\tilde f(t, x)) \le 1$; the value $f(x)$ then lies in $W_{0,1}$, the level of the pull-back being that of $W$. If $(t, x)$ is in the first piece, $\alpha(t) = 1$, so $N^0(f(x)) \le \widetilde N(\tilde f(t, x)) \le 1$ and $x$ lies in the sublevel set $S_0$ of $(N^0, U^0)$; in the second piece, $x$ lies in the sublevel set $S_1$ of $(N^1, U^1)$. So the sublevel set of $(\widetilde N, \widetilde U)$ lies in $([0, 1] \times S_0) \cup ([0, 1] \times S_1)$, whose orbit set has compact closure, by the pulled-back step applied to each piece. A closed subset of a compact set is compact.

*Reading.* The text's (2) asks for one pair restricting to the two given ones; it does not say how. The interpolation is ours; any partition of the time interval into two overlapping pieces works, and the margin between $\tfrac13$ and $\tfrac23$ makes $\widetilde U$ open while each end sees only one of the two pairs. With §XV.30 ($\tilde f$ sc-Fredholm with compact solution set, under the inherited tame germ data), all of (2) is covered.

### XV.32 Corollary 15.3.10 (3) (2017: Corollary 15.1 (3)): the glued boundary data and the partitions of unity of the cylinder

The proof of (3) (pp. 699–700) applies Theorem 15.3.9 on $[0, 1] \times X$ to the multisection over $\partial([0, 1] \times X) = \{0, 1\} \times X$ that is $\Lambda^i$ over $\{i\} \times X$, and concludes from its output. Theorem 15.3.9 in its charged form (§XV.27) asks, of the space, that it be tame with paracompact orbit space, sc-smooth partitions of unity and tame strong bundle charts at every object; and of the boundary data, that they be structurable over the boundary (Definition 14.1.7), charge every boundary fibre, have boundary domain support in $\widetilde U$, satisfy $\widetilde N(\Lambda) < h$ on the boundary, and satisfy the face condition. The text checks none of this explicitly. This subsection proves what can be proved about these hypotheses: tameness and paracompactness were done in §XV.30; here are the glued data with their values, support, norm and charge, the partitions of unity of the cylinder, and the structurability of the glued data up to one analytic statement.

**The glued data** ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.cubeGlue⟧. $\Lambda_\partial(w) = \Lambda^1(w_2)$ if the time of $w$ is $1$, and $\Lambda^0(w_2)$ otherwise, $w_2$ being the $W$-component; so $\Lambda_\partial = \Lambda^0$ over $t = 0$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.cubeGlue_of_zero⟧ and $\Lambda^1$ over $t = 1$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.cubeGlue_of_one⟧. The values at times strictly between $0$ and $1$ are irrelevant: Theorem 15.3.9 looks at its boundary data only over $\partial([0, 1] \times X)$, and $\Lambda$ there is a function on all of $W$ of which only these values enter (§XV.27).

**Boundary domain support** ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.boundaryDomSupp_cubeGlue_subset⟧. If the domain support of $\Lambda^i$ lies in $U^i$, the boundary domain support of $\Lambda_\partial$, the closure of the set of boundary points $z$ over which some nonzero $w$ has positive weight, lies in $\widetilde U$. *Proof.* Let $z$ be such a point, $w \ne 0_z$ with $\Lambda_\partial(w) > 0$. By §XV.30, $z$ has time $0$ or $1$; say $0$. Then $\Lambda^0(w_2) > 0$ and $w_2 \ne 0$ in $W_{z_2}$, since $w$ and $((z, 0_{z_2}))$ differ only in the $W$-component ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.cubeVal_snd_ne_fiberZero⟧; so $z_2$ lies in the domain support of $\Lambda^0$. Hence the set lies in $(\{0\} \times \operatorname{dom-supp}\Lambda^0) \cup (\{1\} \times \operatorname{dom-supp}\Lambda^1)$, which is closed, so its closure does too; and a point of $\{i\} \times \operatorname{dom-supp}\Lambda^i$ lies in $\widetilde U$ by the restriction of $\widetilde U$ over $t = i$ (§XV.31).

**The norm on the boundary.** $\widetilde N(\Lambda_\partial)(0, x) \le N^0(\Lambda^0)(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.pointwiseNorm_cubeGlue_le_zero⟧ and $\widetilde N(\Lambda_\partial)(1, x) \le N^1(\Lambda^1)(x)$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.pointwiseNorm_cubeGlue_le_one⟧. *Proof.* $N(\Lambda)(x)$ is the supremum of the norms of the points of the fibre over $x$ with positive weight (Definition 13.2.3). A point $w$ over $(0, x)$ with $\Lambda_\partial(w) > 0$ has $W$-component $w_2$ over $x$ with $\Lambda^0(w_2) > 0$, and its norm is at most that of $w_2$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.normW_interpAuxNorm_le⟧: on level $1$, $\widetilde N = \widetilde N^0$ over $t = 0$ and $\widetilde N^0(w) = N^0(w_2)$; off level $1$ both sides are the convention value. For an sc⁺-multisection the supremum is attained, so it is at least $N^0(w_2)$. Hence $\widetilde N(\Lambda_\partial) < 1$ on the boundary when $N^i(\Lambda^i) < 1$, which holds for regular perturbations.

**The glued data charge the boundary.** *An sc⁺-multisection charges every fibre* ⟦Chapter15/ChargedExtensionCylinder · SBLocalization.exists_ne_zero_of_isScPlusMultisection⟧: near $x$ it has a local representation by $k$ sections with positive weights summing to $1$, so $k > 0$; the first section gives $w = s_0(x)$ over $x$, and $\Lambda(w)$, the sum of the weights of the sections through $w$, is at least $\sigma_0 > 0$. So the glued data charge $\partial([0, 1] \times X)$ ⟦Chapter15/ChargedExtensionCylinder · SBLocalization.chargesBoundary_cubeGlue⟧ in the sense of Part XIV's charging condition ⟦Chapter14/EmptyIndex · SBLocalization.ChargesBoundary⟧: at a boundary point $(i, x)$ take $((i, x), v)$ with $\Lambda^i(v) \ne 0$. This is the hypothesis that the charged form of Theorem 15.3.9 adds (§XV.27), discharged for the cylinder.

**Partitions of unity on $[0, 1] \times X$** (explicit). Theorem 15.3.9 asks for sc-smooth partitions of unity on the M-polyfold of objects; the text does not say why the cylinder has them. *Step 1, from Urysohn functions to partitions of unity* ⟦Chapter5/CubePartitions · admitsScPartitionsOfUnity_of_urysohn⟧. If any two disjoint closed sets of an M-polyfold are separated by an sc-smooth function with values in $[0, 1]$, the M-polyfold admits sc-smooth partitions of unity: this is the second half of the proof of Theorem 5.5.10. Given an open cover, a bump covering subordinate to it by such functions $f_i$ exists by a general construction in paracompact spaces (Mathlib's subordinate bump coverings with functions from a prescribed class), and $\rho_i = f_i\prod_{j < i}(1 - f_j)$ is the partition of unity; locally only finitely many factors are nontrivial, so each $\rho_i$ is locally a finite product of sc-smooth real functions, hence sc-smooth.

*Step 2, a local separation.* Let $s$, $t$ be disjoint closed sets of $[0, 1]^n \times X$ and $x \in X$. The slices $S = \{q : (q, x) \in s\}$, $T = \{q : (q, x) \in t\}$ are closed in the compact cube, hence compact, and disjoint. A smooth Urysohn function $g_x : \mathbb R^n \to [0, 1]$ is $0$ near $S$ and $1$ near $T$. The points of the cube where $g_x \ne 0$ form a compact set disjoint from $S$, and the tube lemma gives an open $V_x \ni x$ such that $g_x(q) = 0$ whenever $(q, y) \in s$ and $y \in V_x$; likewise $g_x(q) = 1$ whenever $(q, y) \in t$ and $y \in V_x$, after shrinking $V_x$.

*Step 3, gluing over $X$* ⟦Chapter5/CubePartitions · exists_cubeProd_urysohn_w5⟧. Let $(\rho_x)$ be an sc-smooth partition of unity of $X$ subordinate to $(V_x)$, which exists by hypothesis, and
$$F(q, y) = \sum_x\rho_x(y)\,g_x(q).$$
The sum is locally finite, since $\rho$ is, and each term is sc-smooth (an sc-smooth function of $y$ times a smooth function of the cube coordinates); so $F$ is sc-smooth. On $s$, every term with $\rho_x(y) \ne 0$ has $y \in V_x$, so $g_x(q) = 0$, and $F = 0$; on $t$, every such term has $g_x(q) = 1$, so $F = \sum_x\rho_x(y) = 1$; and $F$ takes values in $[0, 1]$ as a convex combination of values in $[0, 1]$. *Conclusion.* $[0, 1]^n \times X$ admits sc-smooth partitions of unity when $X$ does ⟦Chapter5/CubePartitions · admitsScPartitionsOfUnity_cubeProd⟧, and so does the object M-polyfold of the cylinder bundle ⟦Chapter15/CylinderPartitions · SBLocalization.admitsScPartitionsOfUnity_cubeSEP⟧. Gap G.181 is closed. What remains is a hypothesis on $X$: sc-smooth partitions of unity, which Corollary 15.3.10 does not state and Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder needs; witness $\mathbb R^n$ ⟦Chapter7/LocalDiffeo · rnPolyfold_admitsScPartitionsOfUnity⟧. For $X = \mathbb R^n$ the cylinder's partitions of unity have also a direct proof, from Theorem 5.5.10 with the product charts of the cube and $\mathbb R^n$, whose finite-dimensional models have smooth partitions of unity (Proposition 5.5.11) ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · SBLocalization.admitsScPartitionsOfUnity_cube_rn⟧.

**The glued data are structurable over the boundary** (narrower: given one analytic statement). The text treats the data over $\{0, 1\} \times X$ as structurable because the $\Lambda^i$ are. The formalization makes this precise by lifting the structures of $\Lambda^i$ along the projection $[0, 1] \times X \to X$.

*Lifted sections.* For a section $s$ of $W$ (corrected to the zero of the fibre where $s(y)$ does not lie over $y$, a formality), the lift is $\tilde s(q, y) = ((q, y), s(y))$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeLift · SBLocalization.cubeLiftSec⟧, a section of $\widetilde W$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeLift · SBLocalization.P_cubeLiftSec⟧, and $\tilde s(p) = w$ iff $s(p_2) = w_2$ for $w$ over $p$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeLift · SBLocalization.cubeLiftSec_eq_iff⟧. Along a morphism, $\tilde\mu$ acts on the $W$-component by $\mu$ (§XV.30), so the equivariance of lifted sections reduces to that of the sections: if $s'(t(\varphi_2)) = \mu(\varphi_2, s(s(\varphi_2)))$ then $\tilde s'(t(\varphi)) = \tilde\mu(\varphi, \tilde s(s(\varphi)))$ ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.cubeLiftSec_compat⟧. The isotropy group of $z = (q, x)$ maps to that of $x$ by $(q, g) \mapsto g$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeLift · SBLocalization.cubeIso⟧; it is an isomorphism, since the cube contributes only identities.

*The key step: natural representations on a connected neighbourhood* ⟦Chapter15/CubeLift · SBLocalization.cube_Γ_snd⟧. Let $V$ be a natural neighbourhood of $z$ in the cylinder (Theorem 7.1.13), with $V$ connected and lying over the domain of a natural neighbourhood $N$ of $z_2$ in $X$. Then for $g \in G_z$ and $y \in V$, the $X$-part of the morphism $\Gamma_V(g, y)$ is $\Gamma_N(g_2, y_2)$. *Proof.* The maps $a(p) = \Gamma_V(g, p)_2$ and $b(p) = \Gamma_N(g_2, p_2)$ are continuous on $V$ with values in the morphism space of $X$ and have the same source $p_2$. Two such maps agree on an open set, by the étale property ⟦Chapter13/StrongBundlePullMap · isOpen_setOf_eq_of_src⟧, and disagree on an open set, the morphism space being Hausdorff. These two open sets cover $V$; they agree at $z$, where both are $g$ (the natural representation at its centre is the given isotropy element); and $V$ is connected, so they agree on all of $V$. In particular the action of $g$ on $V$ is $\Phi_V(g)(y) = (y_1, \Phi_N(g_2)(y_2))$ ⟦Chapter15/CubeLift · SBLocalization.cube_Φ_eq⟧, and the same holds for the bi-action of isotropy groups on morphisms between two such neighbourhoods ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.cube_biact_snd⟧. The text uses this compatibility of the natural representations of $[0, 1] \times X$ and of $X$ without comment; formally it is the uniqueness of continuous lifts through the source map.

*Lifting one structure* ⟦Chapter15/CubeLift · SBLocalization.liftStructure⟧. A symmetric sc⁺-section structure of $\Lambda$ on $N$ (Definition 13.2.5, Part XIII) — an index set $I$ with an action of $G_{z_2}$, sc⁺-sections $s_i$ on $N$ and weights $\sigma_i$, equivariant, representing $\Lambda$ — gives a boundary symmetric structure (Definition 14.1.3, Part XIV) of any $\widetilde\Lambda$ with $\widetilde\Lambda(w) = \Lambda(w_2)$ over $V \cap \partial$: the same index set and weights, $G_z$ acting through $G_z \cong G_{z_2}$, and the lifted sections $\tilde s_i$. Equivariance follows from that of the $s_i$ with the key step: $\tilde s_{g\cdot i}(\Phi_V(g)(y))$ has $W$-component $s_{g_2 \cdot i}(\Phi_N(g_2)(y_2)) = \mu(\Gamma_N(g_2, y_2), s_i(y_2))$, the $W$-component of $\tilde\mu(\Gamma_V(g, y), \tilde s_i(y))$. The representation: $\widetilde\Lambda(w) = \Lambda(w_2) = \sum_{i : s_i(y_2) = w_2}\sigma_i = \sum_{i : \tilde s_i(y) = w}\sigma_i$. Condition (1) of Definition 14.1.3, that the sections be sc⁺ on the local faces, is taken as given (below). The index set is that of a structure of an sc⁺-multisection, so it is not empty ⟦Chapter13/TightMultisection · SBLocalization.Decoration.nonempty_I⟧.

*The two sides.* A point $p$ of the cylinder is on the side "$t > \frac12$" or "$t < \frac12$" ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.cubeSide⟧; both sides are open ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.isOpen_sideSet⟧, every boundary point lies on its side ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.mem_sideSet_cubeSide⟧, morphisms keep the time and hence the side ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.cubeSide_src⟧, and on the boundary $\Lambda_\partial$ is $\Lambda^{\text{side}}$ ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.cubeGlue_eq_side⟧. A function that is $\Lambda^{\text{side}}(w_2)$ over the boundary is a functor there when the $\Lambda^i$ are ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.isBoundaryWFunctor_of_sides⟧, since morphisms keep the side and act by $\mu$ on the $W$-component.

*The glued structure.* Let $(\mathcal U^b, S^b)$ be decorations of $\Lambda^b$ with correspondences $\tau^b$ (Definition 13.3.6, $\Lambda^b$ structurable). At a boundary point $z$ let $O(z) = \{\text{side of } z\} \times \{p : p_2 \in U^{\text{side}}(z_2)\}$ ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.glueO⟧, an open set containing $z$ ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.isOpen_glueO⟧ ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.mem_glueO⟧. Theorem 14.1.6 (Part XIV) gives a good system for the boundary of the tame cylinder with paracompact orbit space whose neighbourhoods lie in the $O(z)$ ⟦Chapter14/BoundaryMultisection · EpGroupoid.theorem_14_1_6_hyp⟧; its neighbourhoods are connected. Two facts make everything reduce to $X$. (i) A morphism of the good system from $z$ to $z'$ stays on one side, and its $X$-part is a morphism of $\mathcal U^b(z_2, z'_2)$ ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.mor_glue⟧, because its source and target lie in $O(z)$ and $O(z')$. (ii) The structure at $z$ is the lift of the structure of $\Lambda^{\text{side}(z)}$ at $z_2$ ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.glueS⟧. The correspondences are $\tilde\tau_{z,z'}(\varphi) = \tau^b_{z_2, z'_2}(\varphi_2)$ ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.glueTau⟧ (between different sides the full correspondence is put in, but there are no morphisms between them, so it is never used). The conditions of Definition 14.1.7 on correspondences follow from those of $\tau^b$: local constancy and finiteness of the image along the $X$-parts; symmetry under inversion; the diagonal condition at isotropy elements, by the key step $\Gamma_V(g, y)_2 = \Gamma_N(g_2, y_2)$; equivariance under the bi-action of isotropy groups, by its form for morphisms; and the compatibility with the sections, by the equivariance of lifted sections above.

*Structurability* ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.isBoundaryStructurable_of_sides⟧. For tame $X$ with $d_X \equiv 0$ and paracompact $|X|$, structurable $\Lambda^0$, $\Lambda^1$, and the analytic statement below, any $\widetilde\Lambda$ equal to $\Lambda^{\text{side}}(w_2)$ over the boundary is structurable over the boundary: functor by the side lemma, a structure at every boundary point by the lift, the decoration and correspondences as just built. In particular the glued data are ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.isBoundaryStructurable_cubeGlue_w5⟧. Their index sets are those of the $\Lambda^i$, hence not empty, in agreement with the charging above.

*The analytic statement* ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.CubeLiftFace⟧: for an sc⁺-section $s$ on an open $U \subset X$, the lift $\tilde s$ is sc⁺ on the local faces through the points of $([0, 1] \times U) \cap \partial([0, 1] \times X)$, condition (1) of Definition 14.1.3. It is a statement in the text's setting, which the text uses without comment (that the lift of an sc⁺-section along the projection is sc⁺), but it is not proved: Part I's lemma on sc⁺-sections in charts is available only for charts with domain inside the open set, and the pull-back lemma of Part I is stated for sc-smooth, not sc⁺, sections. It is taken as a hypothesis and has no witness; a witness would be the general proof. This is gap G.193.

### XV.33 Corollary 15.3.10 (3): the statement with the charged Theorem 15.3.9, the last paragraph of the proof, and Remark 15.3.11

**Corollary 15.3.10 (3)** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/ChargedExtensionCylinder · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_charged⟧. *Statement.* Let $d_X \equiv 0$, $|X|$ paracompact, $f$ an sc-Fredholm section functor with Part I's tame germ data and $|S_f|$ compact, and $(N^i, U^i, \Lambda^i)$, $i = 0, 1$, structurable regular perturbations of $f$. Assume on the cylinder: the charged statement of Theorem 15.3.9 ⟦Chapter15/ChargedExtensionFibres · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_9_charged_statement⟧ (§XV.27), a tame strong bundle chart at every object, sc-smooth partitions of unity, and, of the glued data $\Lambda_\partial$ of §XV.32, structurability over the boundary and the face condition. Then there is $\widetilde\Lambda$ such that $(\widetilde N, \widetilde U, \widetilde\Lambda)$ is a structurable regular perturbation of $\tilde f$, with $(\widetilde N, \widetilde U)$ of (2), $\widetilde\Lambda = \Lambda^i$ over $\{i\} \times X$, and $\widetilde\Theta = \widetilde\Lambda \circ \tilde f$ a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid with compact $|\operatorname{supp}\widetilde\Theta|$: the text's "compact cobordism $\widetilde\Theta$ between $\Theta_0$ and $\Theta_1$". The text's (3) does not repeat the pairs; it is stated for different $(N^i, U^i)$, as in (2).

*Proof*, as the text's, with every input named. (i) $X$ is tame (§XV.30), hence so is the cylinder, and $\partial([0, 1] \times X)$ lies over $t \in \{0, 1\}$. (ii) $(\widetilde N, \widetilde U)$ controls the compactness of $\tilde f$, by (2) (§XV.31). (iii) The data on the cylinder: $\tilde f$ is an sc-Fredholm section functor with tame germ data and compact solution set, and $|[0, 1] \times X|$ is paracompact (§XV.30). (iv) The boundary data: $\Lambda_\partial$ is structurable over the boundary (hypothesis), charges every boundary fibre, has boundary domain support in $\widetilde U$, and satisfies $\widetilde N(\Lambda_\partial) \le 1$ and $< 1$ on the boundary (§XV.32, the last from $N^i(\Lambda^i) < 1$). (v) Apply the charged Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder with $h \equiv 1$. It returns $\widetilde\Lambda$ structurable, equal to $\Lambda_\partial$ over the boundary, with domain support in $\widetilde U$, $\widetilde N(\widetilde\Lambda) < 1$, $(\tilde f, \widetilde\Lambda)$ transversal, and $\widetilde\Lambda \circ \tilde f$ branched with compact support. (vi) These are the clauses of a regular perturbation; and over $t = i$ the points lie in the boundary (§XV.30), where $\widetilde\Lambda = \Lambda_\partial = \Lambda^i(w_2)$ by §XV.32. The declaration concludes "branched and compact"; the text's "tame" for $\widetilde\Theta$ would come from general position, which the statement of Theorem 15.3.9 does not conclude.

*The hypotheses, discharged and open.* Of the hypotheses that the declaration takes, two are proved for the corollary's data in §XV.32: the partitions of unity of the cylinder from those of $X$, and the structurability of $\Lambda_\partial$ from the structurability of the $\Lambda^i$, given the analytic statement on lifted sections; the declarations compose, and the composite is not stated as one declaration. The remaining inputs are: (a) the charged Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder, which holds given the relative local families on the cylinder ⟦Chapter15/ChargedExtensionFibres · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_9_charged_of_local_rel⟧ (§XV.29; gap G.178); (b) tame strong bundle charts at every object of the cylinder, the product of a tame strong bundle chart of $W$ with the tame charts of $[0, 1]$, which is not formalized (gap G.189); (c) the analytic statement on lifted sections (gap G.193); (d) the face condition of $\Lambda_\partial$ (gap G.180); (e) sc-smooth partitions of unity on $X$, which the corollary does not state. *Reading of (d).* The text's proof says only $\widetilde U = [0, 1] \times U$ and $\tilde f(t, x) = f(x)$ and does not say how the face condition of the glued data is checked; presumably from the transversality of $(f, \Lambda^i)$, since $T^R_{(i,x)}([0, 1] \times X) = \{0\} \times T_xX$ when $d_X \equiv 0$, so that the reduced surjectivity on the face is the surjectivity of $T(f, \Lambda^i)(x)$.

**Remark: the forms with the uncharged statement.** The same conclusion is also proved from the uncharged Lean statement of Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder: with six hypotheses on arbitrary boundary data $\Lambda_b$ ⟦Chapter15/RegularPerturbations · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_hyp⟧; the same with tameness and paracompactness of the cylinder derived ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_ty⟧; for the glued data of two regular perturbations ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_glue_hyp⟧; with the partitions of unity of $X$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderPartitions · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_pu_w5⟧ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderPartitions · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_glue_w5⟧; and with the analytic statement on lifted sections in place of structurability ⟦Chapter15/GlueStructurable · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_struct_w5⟧. That statement, which admits boundary data with empty index sets, does not hold for the cylinder of a nonempty $X$ under the corollary's hypotheses ⟦Chapter15/ChargedExtensionCylinder · SBLocalization.not_theorem_15_3_9_statement_cube_w2⟧: the point $(0, x)$ is a boundary point, $\tilde f$ and the pair $(\widetilde N, \widetilde U)$ of (2) for the pair $(N, U)$ taken twice satisfy its hypotheses, and the general counterexample of §XV.27 applies. So these forms are vacuous for nonempty $X$; this is a property of our formalization, not of the text, whose boundary data are sc⁺-multisections with nonempty index sets. They are the steps at which the lemmas of §§XV.30–XV.32 were proved, and those lemmas discharge the corresponding hypotheses of the charged form above.

*Witnesses, and their limits.* On $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$ with $\Lambda^0 = \Lambda^1 = 0$, every hypothesis of the forms above on the boundary data holds together with tameness, $d_X \equiv 0$ and the paracompactness of the cylinder ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_boundary_witness⟧, and the glued data are structurable over the boundary and satisfy the face condition ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_glue_witness⟧. There the fibres are $0$, so the projection $W \to X$ is injective, every operator onto a fibre is onto ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · SBLocalization.isReducedOntoAtPt_of_injective⟧ and the face condition is automatic ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · SBLocalization.isBoundaryFaceOnto_of_injective⟧; the zero multisection is $1$ at the only point of each fibre ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · SBLocalization.zeroMultisection_eq_one_of_injective⟧, the glued data are the zero multisection of the cylinder, and that is structurable over the boundary ⟦Chapter14/BoundaryStructured · SBLocalization.isBoundaryStructurable_zero⟧. These witnesses are **weak**: zero fibres, and they show only that the hypotheses are consistent. That $\Lambda^i = 0$ are themselves regular perturbations on that example is not rechecked. The analytic statement on lifted sections and the tame strong bundle charts of the cylinder have no witness.

**The last paragraph of the proof** (same). The text closes with: if $(N, U)$ and $(N', U')$ control compactness, so does $(N'', U'') = (\max\{N, N'\}, U \cap U')$, and a perturbation for it is controlled by both pairs, so one can connect $\Lambda$ with $\Lambda''$ and $\Lambda''$ with $\Lambda'$. *Proof.* (i) $\max\{N, N'\}$ is an auxiliary norm of $(W, \mu)$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.isAuxNorm_max_ty⟧: Part I's lemma for the maximum of two auxiliary norms, and invariance from that of $N$ and $N'$. (ii) $(N'', U'')$ controls compactness ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.controlsCompactness_max⟧: $U \cap U'$ is open, saturated (a morphism with source in both saturated sets has its target in both) and contains $S_f$; and its sublevel set $\{x \in U \cap U' : \max\{N, N'\}(f(x)) \le 1\}$ lies in the sublevel set of $(N, U)$, since $N \le \max\{N, N'\}$, whose orbit set has compact closure. (iii) For an sc⁺-multisection, $N(\Lambda) \le \max\{N, N'\}(\Lambda)$ pointwise ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.pointwiseNorm_le_max_left⟧: the supremum defining $N(\Lambda)(x)$ is attained at some $w$, and $N(w) \le \max\{N, N'\}(w) \le \max\{N, N'\}(\Lambda)(x)$. (iv) Hence a regular perturbation for $(N'', U'')$ is one for $(N, U)$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.IsRegularPerturbation.of_max_left⟧ and for $(N', U')$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderGlue · SBLocalization.IsRegularPerturbation.of_max_right⟧: domain support in $U \cap U' \subset U$, norm $N(\Lambda) \le N''(\Lambda) < 1$, structurability and transversality unchanged, and the control of compactness by $(N, U)$ given. *A remark on its role.* The formal (3) takes the two regular perturbations with different pairs $(N^0, U^0)$, $(N^1, U^1)$ from the start, through the interpolated pair of (2), so it does not need this paragraph; the paragraph is proved as printed, and the two-step connection it describes, (3) applied twice, is not stated as a separate declaration.

**Remark 15.3.11** (nothing to formalize) is prose: without orientations the perturbation theory gives only rational chains, and with $f$ oriented, $\Lambda \circ \tilde f$ carries a natural orientation and gives invariants, which is §15.4 (§§XV.34–XV.37).

### XV.34 Oriented formal sums, Theorem 15.4.1 and Definition 15.4.2 (2017: Theorem 15.6, Definition 15.7)

§15.4 opens (p. 700) with a list of standing data, Assumption 15.4: a strong bundle over a tame ep-groupoid, an oriented sc-Fredholm section functor $(f, o)$ with compact $|S_f|$, and an sc⁺-multisection $\Lambda$ with $T(f, \Lambda)$ onto on $\operatorname{supp}(\Lambda \circ f)$, kernels in good position at the boundary, and $\Theta = \Lambda \circ f$ a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid. Theorem 15.4.1 then lifts the tangent functor $T\Theta$ to oriented tangent spaces, using $o$. The text's route has two layers. The first is linear algebra at one point $y$: every summand $(f - s_i)'(y)$ of $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$ inherits an orientation $o_{i,y}$ from $o$, and the oriented formal sum $\hat T_{((f,o),\Lambda)}(y) = \sum_{f(y) = s_i(y)}\sigma_i \cdot ((f - s_i)'(y), o_{i,y})$ does not depend on the local section structure. The second layer is geometry: for $y$ in the support the operators are onto, $o_{i,y}$ orients $\ker(f - s_i)'(y)$, these orientations vary continuously along the branch $M_i = \{f = s_i\}$, and $\hat T_{(\Theta, o)}(y) = \sum\sigma_i \cdot T_y(M_i, o_i)$ is an orientation of $\Theta$ in Chapter 9's sense. The formalization proves the first layer completely, at a chart point, and the identification of the kernel orientation; the second layer is gap G.159 (§XV.38).

**The setting: chart points and $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$.** Part I's orientation theory of sc-Fredholm sections (Chapter 6) is formalized at a *chart point*: a strong bundle chart $c$ around $x$ together with a level-$1$ point $z$ of the model over $\varphi(x)$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint⟧. There $T_xX$ is read as $T_zO = \operatorname{im}Dr(z)$ and the fibre $W_x$ as $K_z = \operatorname{im}\rho(z)$. Part I's $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ (Definition 6.2.1) is the set of operators $T_zO \to K_z$ of the form $(f + s)'(x) + a$, with $s$ an sc⁺-section through $-f(x)$ and $a$ an sc⁺-operator ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.linSet⟧; for one fixed $s$ it is $(f + s)'(x) + \{\text{sc⁺-operators}\}$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.mem_linSet_iff⟧, it is convex ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.convex_linSet⟧, and at a smooth point it is not empty when sc⁺-sections pass through every smooth point of the fibre ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.linSet_nonempty⟧, the standing hypothesis of §12.5. Its members are Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.isFredholm_of_mem_linSet⟧, so the determinant lines form a line bundle $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ over $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.detLin⟧, and $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ is the set of its orientations (Definition 6.6.2) ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.Or⟧. Since $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is convex, hence contractible, an orientation is determined by its value at any one member: $o \mapsto o(L)$ is a bijection of $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ with the two rays of $\det L$ ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.orEquivRay⟧, because two orientations of a line bundle over a preconnected base that agree on one fibre agree everywhere ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · LineOrientation.eq_of_apply_eq⟧.

**Oriented formal sums** (restated). At a chart point $p$, an *oriented member of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$* is a pair $(L, r)$ with $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ and $r$ a ray of $\det L$ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.OrLin⟧. The text's $\widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}_F(x)$ (p. 701) is the set of finite formal sums of oriented operators with weights in $\mathbb Q^+$, read here as finitely supported functions on oriented members ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.GrFHat⟧, as $\mathrm{GrF}(x)$ was read in §XV.1. The forgetful map $f_F$ sends $\sum\sigma \cdot (L, r)$ to $\sum\sigma \cdot L$ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.forgetOr⟧. *The reading*: the text's oriented operators are all sc-Fredholm operators $T_xX \to W_x$; here they are the members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, which are exactly the operators that $o$ can orient, and all operators that occur in $T(f, \Lambda)(x)$ are of this kind (below).

*$f_F$ is 2–1* ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.exists_two_orLin⟧: over every $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ there are exactly two oriented members. *Proof.* $\det L$ is a real line, since $L$ is Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · finrank_fredholmDet⟧, and a real line has exactly two rays, a nonzero vector $v$ and $-v$ spanning them ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.exists_two_rays_of_finrank_eq_one⟧. Two oriented members over the same $L$ are equal iff their rays are.

**The canonical lift of a formal sum.** For $o \in \mathrm{Or}^f_x$ and $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, $(L, o(L))$ is the oriented member $L$ inherits from $o$ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.orLin⟧, and $L \mapsto (L, o(L))$ is injective ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.orLin_injective⟧. The canonical lift of a formal sum $w = \sum\sigma_L \cdot L$ of members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is its push-forward along this map, $\sum\sigma_L \cdot (L, o(L))$ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.canonLift⟧. Four facts follow, each a short computation with push-forwards of finitely supported functions.

- *$f_F$ undoes the lift*: $f_F(\mathrm{lift}_o(w)) = w$, read as a sum of operators ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.forgetOr_canonLift⟧, since $f_F \circ (L \mapsto (L, o(L)))$ is the inclusion of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$. The lift is additive and commutes with finite sums and single terms ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.canonLift_add⟧ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.canonLift_sum⟧ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.canonLift_single⟧.
- *Every summand carries the orientation induced by $o$* ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.snd_eq_of_mem_support_canonLift⟧: the support of a push-forward lies in the image of the support.
- *Uniqueness* ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.canonLift_unique⟧: a formal sum $W$ of oriented members whose image under $f_F$ is $w$ and all of whose summands carry the orientation induced by $o$ equals $\mathrm{lift}_o(w)$. *Proof.* On the support of $W$ the identity agrees with $q \mapsto (q_1, o(q_1))$, so $W$ is the push-forward of itself along that map; this push-forward factors as the push-forward along the first projection, which is $w$, followed by the lift.
- *The lift sees $o$* ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.canonLift_injective_o⟧: two orientations $o$, $o'$ that give the same lift of a nonzero sum $w$ are equal. *Proof.* Take $L$ in the support of $w$. Then $(L, o(L))$ lies in the support of the lift, hence of the lift by $o'$, so by the previous point it is $(L, o'(L))$, and $o(L) = o'(L)$. Since $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is convex, hence preconnected, two orientations of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ that agree at $L$ agree everywhere (Part I, as above).

Since operators of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ are determined by their values, formal sums of members with the same image as sums of operators are equal ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.mapDomain_val_injective⟧, and so have the same lift ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.canonLift_eq_of_mapDomain_eq⟧.

**The kernel orientation of an onto member.** The text identifies $\Lambda^{\max}\ker L$ with $\det L = \Lambda^{\max}\ker L \otimes (\Lambda^{\max}\operatorname{coker}L)^*$ when $L$ is onto (p. 702). Formally, for $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ onto and $N \subset E_0$ the image of $\ker L$ under the inclusion $T_zO \subset E_0$, the ray $o(L)$ is carried to a ray of $\Lambda^{\max}N$ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.orKer⟧ by Part I's map $\det L \cong \Lambda^{\max}\ker L \cong \Lambda^{\max}N$ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · surjRay⟧, built from the determinant of an onto operator (the cokernel being $\{0\}$) and the isomorphism $\ker L \cong N$ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · kerEquivOfMap⟧. Composed with $o \mapsto o(L)$ this is a bijection $\mathrm{Or}^f_x \cong \mathrm{Ray}(\Lambda^{\max}N)$ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.orKerEquiv⟧ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.orKerEquiv_apply⟧: the orientation of $f$ at $x$ and the induced orientation of the kernel determine each other. The kernel is finite-dimensional ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.finiteDimensional_of_mem_linSet⟧, and the ray can be read as an orientation of the subspace $N$ in Mathlib's sense, through Part I's pull-back of rays to orientations ⟦Chapter6/SolutionSetOrientation · pullOr⟧ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.orKerOrientation⟧: a basis $b_1, \dots, b_k$ of $N$ is positive iff $b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b_k$ lies in the ray ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.orientation_eq_orKerOrientation_iff⟧. This orientation still determines $o$ ⟦Chapter15/OrientedLinearizations · ChartPoint.orKerOrientation_injective⟧. *Proof.* Fix a basis $b$ of $N$; its orientation is either the orientation from $o$ or its negative. In the first case the characterization above says that the ray from $o$ is the ray of $b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b_k$, and the same holds for $o'$, whose orientation is the same by hypothesis. In the second case the ray from $o$ is not that of the wedge (the characterization would make the orientations equal, while an orientation is never its negative), so, $\Lambda^{\max}N$ being a line, it is the opposite ray ⟦Chapter6/SolutionSetOrientation · ray_eq_or_eq_neg_of_finrank_eq_one⟧; again the same for $o'$. In both cases the two rays agree, and the bijection $\mathrm{Or}^f_x \cong \mathrm{Ray}(\Lambda^{\max}N)$ gives $o = o'$.

**The operators $(f - s)'(y)$ as members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$.** The bridge between §15.1 and Part I is the chart point at which the linearization of §§XV.7–XV.8 is read: for a chart $c$ around $y \in X_1$, the point $z$ is the level-$1$ lift of $\varphi(y)$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.liftPt⟧. Let $s$ be an sc⁺-section on an open $O$ containing the domain of $c$, with $f(y) = s(y)$. Then $\hat f(\varphi(y)) = \hat s(\varphi(y))$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.principal_eq_of_eq⟧, and the derivative $D((\hat f - \hat s) \circ r)(z)$ of §XV.10 takes values in $K_z$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.subDeriv_mem_K⟧: the principal part of the section $f - s$ maps $r(U)$ into the fibres $K$ of the retract, and at a zero the derivative of such a map lies in $K_z$ (Part I's lemma on derivatives of sections of a strong bundle retract). Restricted to $T_zO$ it is an operator $(f - s)'(y) : T_zO \to K_z$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.subOp⟧ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.coe_subOp⟧; composed with $K_z \subset F$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.toF⟧, an injective operation ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.toF_injective⟧, it is the operator of the chart sum of Theorem 15.1.1 ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.toF_subOp⟧.

**Lemma** (extra) ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.subOp_mem_linSet⟧: at a smooth $y$, under §12.5's standing hypothesis, $(f - s)'(y) \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$. This is what lets $o_y$ orient every summand of $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$; the text takes it from §12.5 (p. 701, "see Section 12.5"). *Proof.* By the standing hypothesis there is an sc⁺-section $s_0$ with $(f + s_0)(y) = 0$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.linSet_nonempty⟧, and by Part I's description for one section it suffices to write $(f - s)'(y) = (f + s_0)'(y) + a$ with $a$ an sc⁺-operator. In the chart, both $s$ and $s_0$ are sc⁺, so their principal parts lift to the shifted fibre $F^1$, and these lifts composed with $r$ are sc-smooth into the shift ⟦Chapter3/IndexLocallyConstantLocal · StrongBundle.HasScPlusSectionsThrough⟧ (for $s$ through Part I's chart lemma for local sc⁺-sections, §XV.10). Put $h = (\hat s_1 + \hat s_{0,1}) \circ r$. On $U$,
$$\hat{(f + s_0)} \circ r = (\hat f - \hat s) \circ r + \iota \circ h ,$$
$\iota : F^1 \to F^0$ the inclusion, an identity checked pointwise from the principal part of a sum of sections and the lifts. Differentiating at $z$ gives $D(\hat{(f + s_0)} \circ r)(z) = D((\hat f - \hat s) \circ r)(z) + \iota \circ Dh(z)$. Here $Dh(z)$ is an sc-operator into the shifted space, because $h$ is sc-smooth and $z$ is smooth; its values composed with $\iota$ lie in $K_z$, being the difference of two derivatives with values in $K_z$. So $b = \iota \circ Dh(z)$ restricted to $T_zO \to K_z$ is an sc⁺-operator, by Part I's criterion for operators that factor through the shift ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.isScPlusOp_of_shift⟧, and $(f - s)'(y) = (f + s_0)'(y) + (-1)b$. The standing hypothesis holds whenever $X$ has sc-smooth bump functions; it is the hypothesis Part XII carries for §12.5.

**The formal sum with members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$.** Let $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ be a local section structure of $\Lambda$ on an open $O$ (Definition 13.2.1) and $c$ a chart with domain in $O$. At a smooth $y$ in the domain, $\sum_{i : s_i(y) = f(y)}\sigma_i \cdot (f - s_i)'(y)$ is a formal sum of members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.linW⟧. Its image as a sum of operators $T_zO \to F$ is the chart sum $\sum_{\hat s_i = \hat f}\sigma_i(\hat f - \hat s_i)'(z)$ of Theorem 15.1.1 in a chart (§XV.7) ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.mapDomain_toF_linW⟧. *Proof.* Term by term. The condition $s_i(y) = f(y)$ is equivalent to $\hat s_i(\varphi(y)) = \hat f(\varphi(y))$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.eq_iff_principal_eq⟧, because the chart is injective on the fibre over $y$ and maps $s_i(y)$, $f(y)$ to $(\varphi(y), \hat s_i(\varphi(y)))$, $(\varphi(y), \hat f(\varphi(y)))$; where it holds, the operator of the term is that of the chart sum (above), and where it fails both terms are $0$.

**Theorem 15.4.1** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.theorem_15_4_1_lift⟧. Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section, $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ a local sc⁺-section structure of $\Lambda$ on an open $O$, $c$ a chart with domain in $O$, $y$ a smooth point of the domain, and $o \in \mathrm{Or}^f_y$ read at the chart point of $y$. Then $\hat T = \mathrm{lift}_o(\sum_{s_i(y) = f(y)}\sigma_i \cdot (f - s_i)'(y))$ satisfies (1) $f_F(\hat T) = T(f, \Lambda)(y)$, the chart sum of Theorem 15.1.1; (2) every summand of $\hat T$ carries the orientation induced by $o$; and $\hat T$ is the only element of $\widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}_F(y)$ with (1) and (2). *Proof.* The general characterization ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.canonLift_spec⟧: for any formal sum $w$ of members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$ whose image as operators is a given $T$, the lift of $w$ maps to $T$ (by $f_F \circ \mathrm{lift}_o = \mathrm{id}$), its summands carry $o$, and any $W$ with these two properties has $f_F(W) = w$, because the passage from formal sums of members to formal sums of operators $T_zO \to F$ is injective (inclusion of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$, then the injective $L \mapsto \iota \circ L$), so the uniqueness of the lift applies. With $w$ the formal sum above and $T$ the chart sum, the hypothesis of the characterization is the previous paragraph. *The formula* is the text's, $\hat T = \sum_{f(y) = s_i(y)}\sigma_i \cdot ((f - s_i)'(y), o((f - s_i)'(y)))$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.canonLift_linW_eq_sum⟧, by additivity of the lift on the finite sum over $i$.

**Independence of the local structure** ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.theorem_15_4_1_indep⟧: two local section structures $(s_i, \sigma_i)$ on $O$ and $(t_j, \tau_j)$ on $O'$, both containing the domain of $c$, give the same $\hat T$. This is the text's argument (p. 701), that the occurring operators do not depend on the choice. *Proof.* By Theorem 15.1.1 in a chart (§XV.7) the two chart sums agree at the point ⟦Chapter15/Linearization · SBLocalization.linSumChart_eq⟧. Both are the images of the corresponding formal sums of members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$, and that passage is injective, so the two formal sums of members agree, and so do their lifts.

**Definition 15.4.2** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.canonicalLift⟧: the canonical lift $\hat T_{((f,o),\Lambda)}(y) \in \widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}_F(y)$, read at the chart point. *The kernel orientations.* For an onto summand, surjectivity onto $K_z$ is the chart surjectivity of §XV.10 ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.surjective_subOp_iff⟧ (onto $K_z$ means: every $k$ in the range of $\rho(z)$ is hit, and $K_z$ is that range), and $o_{i,y}$ is the orientation of $\ker(f - s_i)'(y)$ induced by $o_y$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.branchOr⟧, the kernel-orientation construction above applied to the member $(f - s_i)'(y)$. It determines $o_y$ ⟦Chapter15/CanonicalLift · SBLocalization.branchOr_injective⟧, by the bijection $\mathrm{Or}^f_y \cong \mathrm{Ray}(\Lambda^{\max}N)$.

*Narrower.* Theorem 15.4.1 lifts $T\Theta$, a section functor of oriented tangent planes of $\Theta$, to $\widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}(X)$ of Chapter 9. What is proved is the pointwise layer, in $\widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}_F(y)$ at a chart point: the lift of $T(f, \Lambda)(y)$, its formula, its uniqueness, its independence of the local structure, and the kernel orientations $o_{i,y}$. Not formalized (gap G.159, §XV.38): that the tangent space of $M_i$ at $y$ is the kernel of $(f - s_i)'(y)$, the continuity of $y \mapsto o_{i,y}$ along $M_i$ as an orientation of a submanifold in Chapter 9's sense, the naturality under morphisms ($\varphi_*(L, o) = (\varphi_*L, \varphi_*o)$ in the text's category $\widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}_F(X)$), and the assembly into an orientation of $\Theta$. So Theorem 15.4.3 and Corollary 15.4.4 below take the orientation of $\Theta$ as data. *Hypotheses.* §12.5's standing hypothesis (sc⁺-sections through smooth points), which bump functions give; and $y$ smooth, where $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$ is defined. Neither is new: the text works at smooth points and refers to §12.5 for the orientations. The chart-point reading of $\widehat{\mathrm{Gr}}_F$ is the reading of $\mathrm{GrF}$ in §XV.1, with the operators of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$.

### XV.35 Theorem 15.4.3 (2017: 15.7): branched, compact, Stokes

The theorem (pp. 702–703) has two parts: under (1) $N(\Lambda) \le 1$, (2) $T(f, \Lambda)$ onto on the support and (3) good position at the support points in $\partial X$, $\Theta = \Lambda \circ f$ is a compact, tame, branched ep⁺-subgroupoid, oriented by $o$; and Stokes' theorem holds for it, with the effective version under the local unique continuation property. The first part is a statement of §§15.2–15.3, proved here from them. The second is Part IX's Stokes theorem applied to $\Theta$, once $\Theta$ carries an orientation by oriented tame structures.

**The local branching at a point of good position** ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.localBranching_of_isGoodPositionAt⟧. If $(f, \Lambda)$ is in good position at $y$ (Definition 15.2.4, §XV.15) and $f$ has tame germ data, then $z \mapsto \Lambda(f(z))$ has a local branching structure at $y$ in the sense of Definition 9.1.2 (2)–(4) (Part IX). *Proof.* Theorem 15.2.5 at $y$ (§XV.16) ⟦Chapter15/BoundaryPerturbation · SBLocalization.theorem_15_2_5_hyp⟧ gives a natural representation $U(y)$, a local section structure $(s_i, \sigma_i)_{i \le k}$ and the sets $M_i = \{z \in U(y) : f(z) = s_i(z)\}$, each a smooth submanifold properly embedded in $U(y)$, the count $\Lambda(f(z)) = \sum_{f(z) = s_i(z)}\sigma_i$ on $U(y)$, and the clause that only the branches through $f(y)$ meet $f$ in $U(y)$. The branching structure is indexed by the branches through $f(y)$, $\{i : s_i(y) = f(y)\}$, with the sheets $M_i$ and the weights $\sigma_i$; each sheet contains $y$, is a submanifold and properly embedded. The count is a chain of four rewritings: the count formula as a sum over all $i$ of $\sigma_i$ or $0$; restriction of the sum to the branches through $f(y)$, the others contributing $0$ at points of $U(y)$ by the last clause; and two changes of the index type (a subtype, then its lift to the universe of $X$) which do not change the sum.

**Branched and compact** ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.theorem_15_4_3_isBranched_hyp⟧ (narrower). Let $f$ be an sc-Fredholm section functor with tame germ data, $(N, U)$ control the compactness of $f$ (Definition 15.3.1, §XV.17), and let $\Lambda$ be an sc⁺-multisection with domain support in $U$, $N(\Lambda) \le 1$, transversal (Definition 15.2.1, §XV.12), and in good position at every support point in $\partial X$. Then $\Theta = \Lambda \circ f$, read with values in $\mathbb Q$, is a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid with compact support. *Proof.* The compactness of $|\operatorname{supp}\Theta|$ is that of the "in particular" of Theorem 15.3.7 (§XV.21) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isCompact_orbitSupp_comp⟧: the support lies in the sublevel set $\{x \in U : N(f(x)) \le 1\}$, whose orbit set has compact closure, and is closed. Compactness gives the paracompactness of the orbit space of the support, Definition 9.1.2 (1). $\Theta$ is nonnegative, a functor (because $f$ and $\Lambda$ are) ⟦Chapter15/GeneralPositionBranched · SBLocalization.isFunctorial_comp⟧, and its support consists of smooth points under the tame germ data ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.mem_smoothSet_of_pos⟧. The local branching at a support point $z$ is a case split. If $z \in \partial X$, (3) and the previous paragraph. If not, $d_X(z) = 0$, and Remark 15.2.3 at an interior point of transversality (§XV.14) ⟦Chapter15/Transversality · SBLocalization.remark_15_2_3_hyp⟧ gives the structure. *Readings.* The text's (2) is transversality in the sense of Definition 15.2.1 (the operators of $T(f, \Lambda)$ are onto on the support); its (3), "in good position to $\partial X$", is Definition 15.2.4; "tame" for $\Theta$ is the tame form of §XV.21. The tameness of $X$, which the text assumes, is not used: good position carries what is needed near the boundary points. *Narrower* only through the tame germ data of $f$, inherited from §15.2 (§XV.13).

**Theorem 15.4.3** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.theorem_15_4_3_hyp⟧. Under the hypotheses above, together with sc-smooth partitions of unity on $X$ (Definition 7.5.5) and an orientation $\hat T$ of $\Theta$ (Definition 9.3.x of Part IX: a lift of $T\Theta$ to oriented tangent planes) represented at every support point by an oriented tame structure of dimension $m + 1$, $m \ge 1$: $\Theta$ is a compact branched ep⁺-subgroupoid, and for every $\omega \in \Omega^m_{\mathrm{ep},\infty}(X)$
$$\int_{(\Theta, \hat T)} d\omega = \mu^{\partial\Theta}_\omega(\partial S),$$
the boundary measure of Theorem 9.5.15 of the whole boundary $\partial S = |\operatorname{supp}\partial\Theta|$, which is the text's $\int_{\partial(\Theta, o)}\omega$. *Proof.* The first part is the lemma above; the identity is Part IX's Theorem 9.5.17 ⟦Chapter9/StokesTextHypotheses · EP.theorem_9_5_17⟧, whose hypotheses are exactly these: partitions of unity on $X$, $\Theta$ compact and branched, oriented, and tame of dimension $m + 1$. The boundary measure ⟦Chapter9/StokesTextHypotheses · EP.boundaryMeasure⟧ is defined on the $\sigma$-algebra $L(\partial S)$ of Definition 9.5.14 over the orbit space of the support of $\partial\Theta$ (Definition 9.2.16) ⟦Chapter9/Boundary · EpGroupoid.boundaryTheta⟧.
