*The effective version* ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.theorem_15_4_3_eff_hyp⟧: if moreover $X$ has the local unique continuation property (Definition 7.2.18) ⟦Chapter7/ReducedCriterion · EpGroupoid.IsLUC⟧, then $\oint_{(\Theta, \hat T)}d\omega$ is the effective boundary measure of $\partial S$ (Theorem 9.5.16), by Part IX's Theorem 9.5.18 ⟦Chapter9/StokesTextHypotheses · EP.theorem_9_5_18⟧; the local structures then have the property needed for the effective integral ⟦Chapter9/StokesTextHypotheses · EP.hloc_hasLUC⟧. *Dimension $1$* ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.theorem_15_4_3_dim1_hyp⟧: for $\Theta$ of dimension $1$ and $\omega$ a function, $\int_\Theta d\omega$ is the signed count over the finitely many oriented boundary points ⟦Chapter9/StokesDimOne · EP.boundaryBranchedMeasureDim1⟧, Part IX's Stokes theorem in dimension $1$ ⟦Chapter9/StokesDimOne · EP.theorem_9_5_17_dim1⟧. Together these cover the text's "every sc-differential form of degree $k - 1$" for every index $k \ge 1$, $k = m + 1$.

*Narrower.* (a) The orientation is data: the text takes the canonical orientation of Theorem 15.4.1, and with it the induced orientation of $\partial\Theta$ (Definition 9.3.10). Theorem 15.4.1 is formalized only pointwise (§XV.34, gap G.159), so the orientation $\hat T$ and its oriented tame structures are hypotheses; "tame" and the dimension $m + 1 = k$ are carried by these structures, which is how Part IX's Theorem 9.5.17 reads its hypotheses. (b) Sc-smooth partitions of unity on $X$, a hypothesis of Theorem 9.5.17, inherited; the text's Theorem 15.4.3 does not state it, and Part IX has witnesses for it. (c) The tame germ data of $f$, inherited (§XV.13). The Fredholm index $k$ of the text enters only through the dimension of the oriented tame structures.

### XV.36 Corollary 15.4.4 (2017: 15.2): the invariant and the cobordism argument

The corollary (p. 703) asserts, for $d_X \equiv 0$, paracompact $|X|$, compact $|S_f|$ and an orientation $o$ of $f$, a well-defined map $\Phi_{(f,o)} : H^*_{\mathrm{dR}}(X) \to \mathbb R$ with $\Phi_{(f,o)}([\omega]) = \int_{(\Lambda \circ f, o)}\omega$ for any regular perturbation $(N, U, \Lambda)$, $\Lambda \circ f$ carrying the canonical orientation; and the effective version under the local unique continuation property. Its proof is left to the reader. Read degree by degree, "well defined" says two things: the integral of an exact form over $(\Lambda \circ f, o)$ vanishes, so the integral descends to cohomology; and a closed form has the same integral over any two regular perturbations. The first is Stokes with $\partial\Theta = 0$. The second is the cobordism argument: two regular perturbations are joined by a compact oriented cobordism $\tilde\Theta$ over $[0, 1] \times X$ (Corollary 15.3.10 (3)), and Stokes on $\tilde\Theta$ for the pull-back of a closed form. The formalization proves both steps for an abstract cobordism (this subsection) and then builds the cobordism on the cylinder in the text's order (§XV.37).

**Oriented regular perturbations.** An oriented regular perturbation of dimension $m + 1$ ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.OrientedRegularPerturbation⟧ is a regular perturbation $(N, U, \Lambda)$ of $f$ (Corollary 15.3.10 (1), §XV.31: $(N, U)$ controls compactness, $\Lambda$ structurable, domain support in $U$, $N(\Lambda) < 1$, transversal) ⟦Chapter15/RegularPerturbations · SBLocalization.IsRegularPerturbation⟧, with $\Theta = \Lambda \circ f$ compact and branched, and an orientation $\hat T$ of $\Theta$ represented by oriented tame structures of dimension $m + 1$, the data that Theorem 15.4.1 would provide. Its integral is $\int_{(\Theta, \hat T)}\omega$ for $\omega \in \Omega^{m+1}_{\mathrm{ep},\infty}(X)$ ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.OrientedRegularPerturbation.integral⟧, the branched integral of Definition 9.5.6 (1) ⟦Chapter9/TameOpen · EpGroupoid.FormEval.tameBranchedIntegral⟧.

**The statement** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.corollary_15_4_4_statement⟧. For a predicate $\mathrm{Can}$ on oriented regular perturbations, standing for "the orientation is the canonical one from $(f, o)$": (i) for every $P$ with $\mathrm{Can}(P)$ and every $\eta \in \Omega^m_{\mathrm{ep},\infty}(X)$, $\int_P d\eta = 0$; (ii) for any $P_0$, $P_1$ with $\mathrm{Can}$ and every closed $\omega \in \Omega^{m+1}_{\mathrm{ep},\infty}(X)$, $\int_{P_0}\omega = \int_{P_1}\omega$. Then $\Phi_{(f,o)}([\omega]) = \int_P\omega$ is well defined on $H^{m+1}_{\mathrm{dR}}$, in the degree $m + 1 = \dim\Theta$; on the other degrees the text's $\Phi$ is $0$ by the degree of the integrand, which the formal statement does not spell out. $\mathrm{Can}$ is a parameter because the canonical orientation is formalized only pointwise (§XV.34).

**Exact forms.** *The integral of the zero form vanishes* ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.tameBranchedIntegral_zero⟧, by linearity of the sheet integrals. *If $\partial X \cap \operatorname{supp}\Theta = \emptyset$, every signed measure on $\partial S$ gives $0$ to $\partial S$* ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.signedMeasure_univ_eq_zero_of_boundary⟧: $\operatorname{supp}\partial\Theta \subset \partial X \cap \operatorname{supp}\Theta$ ⟦Chapter9/Boundary · EpGroupoid.supp_boundaryTheta_subset⟧, so the orbit set of $\operatorname{supp}\partial\Theta$ is empty and its whole space is the empty set; in particular the boundary measure vanishes ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.boundaryMeasure_univ_eq_zero⟧. **Lemma** ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.integral_d_eq_zero_of_degIndex_eq_zero⟧: if $d_X \equiv 0$ and $X$ has sc-smooth partitions of unity, then $\int_{(\Theta, \hat T)}d\eta = 0$ for every compact, branched, oriented, tame $\Theta$ of dimension $m + 1 \ge 2$. *Proof.* Theorem 9.5.17 turns the left side into the boundary measure of $\partial S$; $\partial X = \{d_X \ge 1\}$ is empty, so the previous fact applies. In dimension $1$ the same with the dimension-$1$ Stokes theorem ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.integral_d_eq_zero_of_degIndex_eq_zero_dim1⟧.

**The cobordism argument** ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.integral_eq_of_cobordism⟧. Let $F : Y \to X$ be an sc-smooth functor between ep-groupoids (in the text, the projection $[0, 1] \times X \to X$), $Y$ with sc-smooth partitions of unity, $\tilde\Theta$ a compact, branched, oriented, tame ep⁺-subgroupoid of $Y$ of dimension $m + 2$, and $I_0$, $I_1$ two functions on $\Omega^{m+1}_{\mathrm{ep},\infty}(X)$ such that for every $\omega$
$$\mu^{\partial\tilde\Theta}_{F^*\omega}(\partial\tilde S) = I_1(\omega) - I_0(\omega).$$
Then $I_0(\omega) = I_1(\omega)$ for every closed $\omega$. *Proof.* Stokes (Theorem 9.5.17) on $Y$ for the form $F^*\omega$ of degree $m + 1$: $\int_{\tilde\Theta}dF^*\omega = \mu^{\partial\tilde\Theta}_{F^*\omega}(\partial\tilde S)$. The exterior derivative commutes with the pull-back along a functor, $dF^* = F^*d$ on $\Omega^*_{\mathrm{ep},\infty}$ ⟦Chapter8/EpFormsFunctor · EP.epFormsInftyD_comp_epFormsInftyPullback⟧ (Theorem 11.2.1 (2), the functor case, Part XI; on the direct limit it is checked level by level from the same identity for forms of a fixed level). So $dF^*\omega = F^*d\omega = 0$, the left side is the integral of the zero form, $0$, and $I_1(\omega) - I_0(\omega) = 0$. The text's form, with $\partial\tilde\Theta = \Theta_1 \sqcup -\Theta_0$, is the case $I_i = \int_{\Theta_i}$; the lemma separates the analytic content (Stokes and $dF^* = F^*d$) from the identification of the boundary, which is §XV.37.

**Cobordant perturbations** ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.OrientedRegularPerturbation.HasOrientedCobordism⟧. $P_0$ and $P_1$ are joined by an oriented compact cobordism if there are $Y$, $F$, $\tilde\Theta$ as in the lemma with $\mu^{\partial\tilde\Theta}_{F^*\omega}(\partial\tilde S) = \int_{P_1}\omega - \int_{P_0}\omega$ for all $\omega$. **Corollary 15.4.4** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.corollary_15_4_4_hyp⟧: for $d_X \equiv 0$ and $X$ with sc-smooth partitions of unity, in every dimension $m + 1 \ge 1$, the statement holds for every $\mathrm{Can}$ whose members are pairwise cobordant. *Proof.* (i) is the exact-form lemma, split by $m = 0$ (dimension $1$) or $m \ge 1$. (ii): the cobordism between $P_0$ and $P_1$ and the cobordism argument with $I_i = \int_{P_i}$.

*The added hypothesis*, that any two perturbations of the class are cobordant, is not derived here; on the cylinder it is reduced to the oriented end identities (§XV.37). It is satisfiable with a nonempty class: every oriented regular perturbation is cobordant to itself ⟦Chapter15/PerturbedStokesInvariants · SBLocalization.OrientedRegularPerturbation.hasOrientedCobordism_refl⟧, with $Y = X$, $F$ the identity and $\tilde\Theta = 0$, which is branched ⟦Chapter9/Basic · EpGroupoid.isBranchedEpSubgroupoid_zero⟧, compact (its support is empty) and oriented by the zero lift ⟦Chapter9/OrientationBasic · EpGroupoid.isOrientation_zero⟧, with vanishing boundary measure. This witness is **weak**: it shows that the hypothesis can hold, not that it holds for two different perturbations; no oriented regular perturbation with nonempty support exists in the project. *Further hypotheses*: partitions of unity on $X$, for Stokes; the paracompactness of $|X|$, which the corollary assumes, is not used in this form (it enters through the cylinder, §XV.37).

### XV.37 Corollary 15.4.4 on the cylinder: the ends, the boundary measure, the effective version; Remark 15.4.5

The text's argument, "in view of Corollary 15.3.10", has four steps: (a) two regular perturbations $(N^i, U^i, \Lambda^i)$ of $f$ with $\Theta_i = \Lambda^i \circ f$; (b) Theorem 15.3.9 on $[0, 1] \times X$ gives $\tilde\Lambda$ with $\tilde\Lambda = \Lambda^i$ over $\{i\} \times X$, and $\tilde\Theta = \tilde\Lambda \circ \tilde f$ is a compact cobordism between $\Theta_0$ and $\Theta_1$ (Corollary 15.3.10 (3)); (c) $\tilde\Theta$ carries the canonical orientation from $(\tilde f, \tilde o)$, and with the boundary orientation of Definition 9.3.10, $\partial\tilde\Theta = \Theta_1 \sqcup -\Theta_0$; (d) Stokes on $\tilde\Theta$ (§XV.36). The formalization follows this order. Proved: (a), (b) with Theorem 15.3.9 in its charged form (§§XV.27–XV.33), the restriction of $\tilde\Theta$ to the ends as sets and as orbits, the splitting of the boundary measure over the two ends, and (d). Step (c), the oriented identification of each end, is a hypothesis (gap G.182).

Throughout, the cylinder is $[0, 1] \times X$, the case $n = 1$ of $[0, 1]^n \times X$ (§XV.30), with the pulled-back bundle and $\tilde f(t, x) = (t, f(x))$; $\tilde\Lambda$ is any function on the cylinder bundle with $\tilde\Lambda(w) = \Lambda^0(w_2)$ over $t = 0$ and $\tilde\Lambda(w) = \Lambda^1(w_2)$ over $t = 1$, $w_2$ the $W$-component.

**$\tilde\Theta$ on the ends** (same; V15.48). Over $t = 0$, $\tilde\Lambda(\tilde f(t, x)) = \Lambda^0(f(x))$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.theta_cyl_of_time_zero⟧, and over $t = 1$, $\Lambda^1(f(x))$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.theta_cyl_of_time_one⟧: the $W$-component of $\tilde f(t, x)$ is $f(x)$. Hence $\tilde\Theta \circ i_0 = \Theta_0$ and $\tilde\Theta \circ i_1 = \Theta_1$ for the inclusion functors $i_q : X \to [0, 1] \times X$, $x \mapsto (q, x)$ (§XV.30) ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.theta_cubeIncl_zero⟧ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.theta_cubeIncl_one⟧, the text's "restricts to $\{i\} \times X = X$ as $\Theta_i$" (p. 700). **The boundary part of the support** ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.mem_boundary_inter_supp_cyl_iff⟧: for $d_X \equiv 0$, $(t, x) \in \partial([0, 1] \times X) \cap \operatorname{supp}\tilde\Theta$ iff $t = 0$ and $x \in \operatorname{supp}\Theta_0$, or $t = 1$ and $x \in \operatorname{supp}\Theta_1$. *Proof.* $d_X \equiv 0$ makes $X$ tame (§XV.30) ⟦Chapter5/DegeneracyZeroTame · EpGroupoid.isTame_of_degIndex_eq_zero⟧, and then $\partial([0, 1] \times X) = \{0, 1\} \times X$ ⟦Chapter15/RegularPerturbations · SBLocalization.mem_boundary_cubeSEP_iff⟧; on each end the value of $\tilde\Theta$ is that of $\Theta_i$, by the two identities above.

**The ends on orbit spaces.** The orbit space of the cylinder is $[0, 1] \times |X|$ (the homeomorphism of §XV.30) ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · EpGroupoid.cubeOrbitHomeomorph⟧. Its time coordinate, $|(t, x)| \mapsto t$, is defined through the inverse of this homeomorphism ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.cylOrbitTime⟧, takes the value $t$ on the orbit of $(t, x)$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.cylOrbitTime_π⟧ and is continuous ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.continuous_cylOrbitTime⟧. For $\Theta$ on the cylinder, the *end at time $i$* of $\partial S = |\operatorname{supp}\partial\Theta|$ is the set of its points of time $i$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.cylEnd⟧. It is closed, as the preimage of a point under a continuous map ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.isClosed_cylEnd⟧, hence Borel, hence in the $\sigma$-algebra $L(\partial S)$ of Definition 9.5.14, which contains the Borel sets ⟦Chapter9/BoundaryNullSigmaAlgebra · EpGroupoid.borel_le_lebesgueSigmaBoundaryH⟧ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.measurableSet_cylEnd⟧. The map $|(i, x)| \mapsto |x|$ from the end at time $i$ to $|X|$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.cylEndMap⟧ is $|x|$ on the orbit of $(i, x)$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.cylEndMap_π⟧, continuous ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.continuous_cylEndMap⟧ and injective ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.injective_cylEndMap⟧. *Proof of injectivity.* Two points of the end at time $i$ come from objects $(q, x)$, $(q', x')$ of the support with the same time $i$, so $q = q'$ (the cube $[0, 1]^1$ has one coordinate); if $|x| = |x'|$, the two objects are isomorphic in $[0, 1] \times X$, because two objects of the product are isomorphic iff their cube coordinates agree and their $X$-components are isomorphic (§XV.30), and so the two orbits agree. For $d_X \equiv 0$ the end at time $i$ of $|\operatorname{supp}\partial\tilde\Theta|$ maps into $|\operatorname{supp}\Theta_i|$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.cylEndMap_mem_orbitSupp_zero⟧ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.cylEndMap_mem_orbitSupp_one⟧: a point of $\operatorname{supp}\partial\tilde\Theta$ lies in $\partial([0, 1] \times X) \cap \operatorname{supp}\tilde\Theta$ (Definition 9.2.16), so by the description of the boundary part of the support its $X$-component lies in $\operatorname{supp}\Theta_i$ for its time $i$; the other end is excluded because $0 \ne 1$.

**The boundary measure splits** ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.boundaryMeasure_cyl_univ⟧. For $d_X \equiv 0$ and any compact, branched, oriented, tame $\tilde\Theta$ of dimension $m + 2$ on the cylinder, $\mu^{\partial\tilde\Theta}_\omega(\partial S) = \mu^{\partial\tilde\Theta}_\omega(\text{end } 0) + \mu^{\partial\tilde\Theta}_\omega(\text{end } 1)$; the same for the effective boundary measure ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.boundaryMeasureEff_cyl_univ⟧. *Proof.* A general lemma ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.signedMeasure_univ_eq_cylEnds⟧: if every boundary object of the cylinder has time $0$ or $1$, then for every $\sigma$-algebra on $\partial S$ containing the Borel sets and every signed measure $\mu$ on it, $\mu(\partial S) = \mu(\text{end } 0) + \mu(\text{end } 1)$. Every point of $\partial S$ has time $0$ or $1$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · EpGroupoid.cylOrbitTime_eq_zero_or_one⟧, because it is the orbit of a point of $\operatorname{supp}\partial\Theta \subset \partial([0, 1] \times X)$; so $\partial S$ is the union of the two ends, which are disjoint and measurable, and $\mu$ is additive on them. For $d_X \equiv 0$ the boundary objects have time $0$ or $1$ ⟦Chapter15/CylinderEnds · SBLocalization.boundary_cyl_time⟧, and the boundary measures of Theorems 9.5.15 and 9.5.16 live on $L(\partial S)$, which contains the Borel sets.

**Step (c) as a proposition.** *The end identities* ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.IsCylinderBoundaryOf⟧: for oriented regular perturbations $P_0$, $P_1$ of dimension $m + 1$ and a compact, branched, oriented, tame $\tilde\Theta$ of dimension $m + 2$ on the cylinder, for every $\omega \in \Omega^{m+1}_{\mathrm{ep},\infty}(X)$,
$$\mu^{\partial\tilde\Theta}_{pr^*\omega}(\text{end } 1) = \int_{P_1}\omega, \qquad \mu^{\partial\tilde\Theta}_{pr^*\omega}(\text{end } 0) = -\int_{P_0}\omega ,$$
$pr = $ the projection functor to $X$ (§XV.30) ⟦Chapter15/CubeEp · EpGroupoid.cubeProj⟧. This is the text's "$\partial\tilde\Theta = \Theta_1 \sqcup -\Theta_0$", read on the level of the boundary measure, which is what Stokes uses: with the outward normal first (Definition 9.3.10), the outward normal is $+\partial_t$ at $t = 1$ and $-\partial_t$ at $t = 0$, whence the sign. *The orientation statement* ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.CylinderOrientationStatement⟧: every $\tilde\Lambda$ that step (b) can produce, that is, every regular perturbation of $\tilde f$ for the interpolated pair $(\tilde N, \tilde U)$ of Corollary 15.3.10 (2) (§XV.31) ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.interpAuxNorm⟧ ⟦Chapter15/CubeAuxNorm · SEP.interpSet⟧ with $\tilde\Lambda = \Lambda^i$ over $t = i$ and $\tilde\Theta$ compact and branched, carries an orientation by oriented tame structures of dimension $m + 2$ with the end identities. In the text this orientation is the canonical one from $(\tilde f, \tilde o)$; the statement asks only for the properties of it that the argument uses.

**The cobordism from the end identities** ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.hasOrientedCobordism_of_cylinder⟧: for $d_X \equiv 0$ and the cylinder with sc-smooth partitions of unity, a $\tilde\Theta$ with the end identities joins $P_0$ and $P_1$ in the sense of §XV.36, with $Y = [0, 1] \times X$ and $F = pr$. *Proof.* $\mu^{\partial\tilde\Theta}_{pr^*\omega}(\partial S)$ is the sum over the two ends, and the end identities make it $\int_{P_1}\omega - \int_{P_0}\omega$. *Partitions of unity on the cylinder* ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.hasScPartitionsOfUnity_cyl⟧: in the ep-groupoid sense of Definition 7.5.5, from Theorem 7.5.7 ⟦Chapter7/PartitionsOfUnity · EpGroupoid.theorem_7_5_7⟧, given the paracompactness of the orbit space of the cylinder, which follows from that of $|X|$ ⟦Chapter15/Cylinder · EpGroupoid.hasParacompactOrbitSpace_cubeProd⟧, and partitions of unity on the object M-polyfold of the cylinder, which follow from those of $X$ (§XV.32) ⟦Chapter15/CylinderPartitions · SBLocalization.admitsScPartitionsOfUnity_cubeSEP⟧.

**Steps (b) and (c) together** ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.hasOrientedCobordism_cylinder_hyp⟧: for $d_X \equiv 0$, $|X|$ paracompact, $f$ sc-Fredholm with tame germ data and compact $|S_f|$, if the charged Theorem 15.3.9 holds on the cylinder, the cylinder bundle has tame strong bundle charts at every object, its object M-polyfold has sc-smooth partitions of unity, the glued boundary data of $\Lambda^0$, $\Lambda^1$ are structurable over the boundary and satisfy the face condition (§XV.32), and step (c) holds, then $P_0$ and $P_1$ are cobordant. *Proof.* Corollary 15.3.10 (3) in its charged form (§XV.33) ⟦Chapter15/ChargedExtensionCylinder · SBLocalization.corollary_15_3_10_3_charged⟧ produces $\tilde\Lambda$: a regular perturbation of $\tilde f$ for $(\tilde N, \tilde U)$, equal to $\Lambda^i$ over $t = i$, with $\tilde\Theta$ compact and branched. Step (c) gives the orientation and the end identities, and the previous paragraph the cobordism.

**Corollary 15.4.4 along the text's argument** (narrower) ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.corollary_15_4_4_cylinder_hyp⟧: for $d_X \equiv 0$, $|X|$ paracompact, sc-smooth partitions of unity on $X$ and on the object M-polyfold of the cylinder, $f$ sc-Fredholm with tame germ data and compact $|S_f|$, and a class $\mathrm{Can}$: if the charged Theorem 15.3.9 holds on the cylinder, the cylinder bundle has tame strong bundle charts, and for any two members of $\mathrm{Can}$ the glued data are structurable with the face condition and step (c) holds, then the statement of §XV.36 holds. *Proof.* Corollary 15.4.4 from cobordisms (§XV.36), the cobordisms from the previous paragraph. *With Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder reduced* ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.corollary_15_4_4_cylinder_of_rel⟧: the charged Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder follows from the relative statement of steps (c)–(d) there (§XV.29) ⟦Chapter15/ChargedExtensionFibres · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_9_charged_hyp⟧ ⟦Chapter15/TransversalExtension · SBLocalization.theorem_15_3_7_relative_statement⟧, so the corollary rests on that relative statement in place of the theorem.

*Narrower.* Formalized in the text's order: the two regular perturbations, the cylinder perturbation from the charged Theorem 15.3.9, its restriction to the ends, the splitting of the boundary measure, and Stokes with $dF^* = F^*d$. The hypotheses are: (1) step (c), the oriented end identities (gap G.182), which contain the weights on the ends ($\partial\tilde\Theta(i, x) = \Theta_i(x)$, gap G.190; proved here are the values of $\tilde\Theta$, the support and the injectivity of the end maps, not that the end maps are onto $|\operatorname{supp}\Theta_i|$ nor the weights of $\partial\tilde\Theta$) and the canonical orientation on the cylinder (Theorem 15.4.1, gap G.159), so $\mathrm{Can}$ stays a parameter; (2) the charged Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder, hence the relative local families there (gap G.178); (3) tame strong bundle charts on the cylinder (gap G.189); (4) the structurability of the glued data, proved given that lifted sc⁺-sections are sc⁺ on the faces (gap G.193, §XV.32), and their face condition (gap G.180); (5) partitions of unity on $X$, used for Stokes and for those of the cylinder, which the corollary does not state. The paracompactness of $|X|$, which the corollary assumes, is used for the cylinder's partitions of unity. *Witnesses.* Step (c) has **no witness in the non-degenerate case**: the project has no oriented regular perturbation with nonempty support. The remaining hypotheses have the weak witnesses listed with §§XV.29, XV.32–XV.33 (on $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^0 \to \mathbb R^n$, no boundary, zero fibres); tame strong bundle charts on the cylinder have none of their own.

**The effective version** (narrower; V15.49). *Definitions*: the effective integral $\oint_P\omega$ over an oriented regular perturbation, for $X$ with the local unique continuation property (Definition 9.5.6 (2)) ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.OrientedRegularPerturbation.integralEff⟧ ⟦Chapter9/TameOpen · EpGroupoid.FormEval.tameBranchedIntegralEff⟧, and effective cobordisms, as in §XV.36 with $Y$ having the local unique continuation property and the effective boundary measure ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.OrientedRegularPerturbation.HasOrientedCobordismEff⟧. *The statement* ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.corollary_15_4_4_eff_statement⟧: exact forms have effective integral $0$ over every member of $\mathrm{Can}$, and closed forms have the same effective integral over any two, so $\Phi^{\mathrm{eff}}_{(f,o)}([\omega]) = \oint_{(\Lambda \circ f, o)}\omega$ is well defined in degree $m + 1$. *The lemmas*, as in §XV.36: the effective integral of the zero form vanishes ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.tameBranchedIntegralEff_zero⟧; the cobordism argument with Theorem 9.5.18 on $Y$ in place of Theorem 9.5.17 ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.integralEff_eq_of_cobordism⟧; and exact forms ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.integralEff_d_eq_zero_of_degIndex_eq_zero⟧, for $d_X \equiv 0$, by Theorem 9.5.18 and, in dimension $1$, its dimension-$1$ form ⟦Chapter9/EffectiveDimOneLUC · EP.theorem_9_5_18_dim1_isLUC⟧, the boundary measure vanishing because $\partial X = \emptyset$. *Proof of the statement* ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.corollary_15_4_4_eff_hyp⟧, for $d_X \equiv 0$, partitions of unity and the local unique continuation property on $X$, and pairwise effective cobordisms: the two lemmas, in every dimension $m + 1 \ge 1$. The cobordism hypothesis is satisfiable with a nonempty class ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.OrientedRegularPerturbation.hasOrientedCobordismEff_refl⟧ (self-cobordism by $\tilde\Theta = 0$; **weak**, as in §XV.36).

*On the cylinder*: the effective end identities ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.IsCylinderBoundaryEffOf⟧, with the effective boundary measure and $\oint_{P_i}$, give an effective cobordism ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.hasOrientedCobordismEff_of_cylinder⟧ through the splitting of the effective boundary measure; step (c) in effective form ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.CylinderOrientationEffStatement⟧; and the corollary along the text's argument ⟦Chapter15/CylinderCobordism · SBLocalization.corollary_15_4_4_eff_cylinder_hyp⟧, from the charged Theorem 15.3.9 on the cylinder and the hypotheses of the non-effective form, with the local unique continuation property on $X$ and on $[0, 1] \times X$. The latter presumably follows from that on $X$, natural representations of the cylinder at $(t, x)$ being products of those of $X$ at $x$ with the trivial groupoid of $[0, 1]$; it is not derived (gap G.191) and has no witness.

**Remark 15.4.5** (nothing to formalize). The remark mentions another route to invariants, triangulating the weighted solution set into a rational chain, and says it is not carried out; there is nothing to formalize.

### XV.38 What is not formalized

The open gaps of the chapter, with what is proved of each, what is missing, and an estimate of the Lean it needs.

- **Gap G.159** (formalized in part): Theorem 15.4.1 and Definition 15.4.2 as an orientation of $\Theta = \Lambda \circ f$. Proved at single points in Part I's chart reading: $(f - s_i)'(y) \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$, the existence, formula and uniqueness of the canonical lift, its independence of the local structure, and the kernel orientations $o_{i,y}$ (§XV.34). Missing: (a) the tangent spaces of the branches $M_i = \{f = s_i\}$ in good position are the kernels of $(f - s_i)'(y)$ in the chart, 150–250 lines; (b) the continuity of $y \mapsto o_{i,y}$ along $M_i$ as an orientation of a submanifold in Chapter 9's sense, with a bridge from Part I's ray orientations to frames, 300–450; (c) naturality under morphisms, 150–250; (d) the assembly into an orientation of $\Theta$ with independent tangent sums, after which the class of canonically oriented perturbations that Corollary 15.4.4 takes as a parameter, and the orientation that Theorem 15.4.3 takes as data, are defined; 150–250. Together 750–1,200 lines.
- **Gap G.160** (formalized in part): the products remark after Definition 15.3.3 and Remark 15.3.4. Formalized: product ep-groupoids, the product strong bundle and the product over $X \times X'$ with $\mu \times \mu'$, products of sections and section functors, sc-smooth and sc⁺, products of strong bundle maps, the level $1$ of the product, and $\max(N, N')$ as an auxiliary norm (§XV.19). Missing: (c) $f \times f'$ sc-Fredholm with tame germ data, for which Part I has only the cube parameter case: products of filling germs, of basic germs after reordering coordinates, and of the regularizing property, 300–500 lines; (d) $\Lambda \times \Lambda'$ as an sc⁺-multisection, from products of local section structures with weights $\sigma_i\sigma'_j$, its norm $\max$ for $N \times N'$, admissibility for $(N \times N', U \times U')$ and the domain-support inclusion of Remark 15.3.4, 150–300 lines. Together 450–800 lines.
- **Gap G.162** (closed for Theorem 15.3.7): what remains is Theorem 15.3.9 and Corollary 15.3.10 (3), that is, the gaps G.178–G.180, G.189 and G.193 below. Corollary 15.3.10 (1) is proved from Theorem 15.3.7 for paracompact $|X|$ (§XV.31), though the composite is not stated as one declaration.
- **Gap G.178**: Theorem 15.3.9, steps (c)–(d), the relative local families, the one proposition from which the charged Theorem 15.3.9 is proved (§XV.29). Proved: everything else in steps (c)–(d), the relative Sard and compactness steps included, and the trivial families where the support meets only $\partial X$. Missing: (a) seeds at interior support points: one family making all $(f - s^0_a)'(x)$ onto at once, by the bridge of §XV.24 applied to each $f - s^0_a$ and complements of the finitely many cokernels, then openness for each pair of branches, and a seed family with domain support in a small neighbourhood avoiding $\partial X$; (b) openness at boundary support points: the family vanishes near $x$, so the reduced surjectivity of $(f, \Lambda_0)$ at $x$ must persist near $x$, from Part I's openness with $\ell = 0$ and the passage from Part I's general position to reduced surjectivity, about 60–100 lines. Together 400–700 lines.
- **Gap G.179**: the face condition of Theorem 15.3.9 does not depend on the extension. It is asked for every sc⁺ extension of the boundary data (§XV.27). Missing: (a) the restriction of $(f - s_i)'(x)$ to $T^R_xX$ depends only on $s_i$ on the faces through $x$, a germ argument in a tame chart, about 80 lines; (b) two sc⁺ extensions have local representations whose branches agree on the faces up to reindexing, a statement of the kind of Theorem 15.1.1 on faces, with crossing branches and the charts of boundary symmetric structures, 170–320 lines; (b) needs the non-empty index sets that charging gives. Its only witness has zero fibres.

Missing: (a) the weights on the ends, gap G.190; (b) oriented tame structures of $\tilde\Theta$ at $(i, x)$ whose boundary sheets are $\{i\} \times M_j$, with the weights and isotropy of $\Theta_i$; (c) the boundary orientation of $\{i\} \times M_j$ inside $\tilde M_j$, outer normal first (Definition 9.3.10), equal to $(-1)^{i+1}$ times the canonical orientation of $M_j$, Part I's sign bookkeeping of Theorem 6.7.1 for the kernel of $(\tilde f - \tilde s)'$ with $\partial_t$, which needs Theorem 15.4.1 on the cylinder (G.159); (d) the sheet integral of $pr^*\omega$ over $\{i\} \times M$ equals that of $\omega$ over $M$; (e) the transfer of measurability along the end maps and the uniqueness of Theorem 9.5.4 for the push-forward. 1,200–2,200 lines, plus (c) after G.159; a non-degenerate witness, an oriented regular perturbation with nonempty support, 300–600 lines more.

The cylinder bundle is a pull-back whose atlas contains the charts over the identity of a cube-times-chart model; missing is that the products of a tame strong bundle chart of $W$ with the tame charts of the cube are modelled on relatively open subsets of a partial quadrant. 80–250 lines.

Proved: $\tilde\Theta(i, x) = \Theta_i(x)$, the boundary part of the support is the two ends, and each end maps injectively into $|\operatorname{supp}\Theta_i|$ (§XV.37). The independence of the sc-structures of $T_zO$ and $K_z$ from the chart, not used since the sc-Fredholm property holds in every chart (§XV.11). "Tame" in the conclusions of Theorem 15.3.9 and Corollary 15.3.10 (3): the formal conclusions say branched and compact; the perturbations built are in general position, so the tame form of the "in particular" of Theorem 15.3.7 (§XV.21) applies to them, but the combination is not stated.

Every other hypothesis of the Part has a witness, named in its subsection.

### XV.39 What the formalization taught us

*§15.1 is topology plus Part I's chain rule.* The proof of Theorem 15.1.1 is a statement about finitely many continuous maps and their germs, and it holds in that generality: two finite families of branches with the same weighted count of every value at every point have the same formal sums of (value, germ invariant) pairs at every point, as soon as the germ invariants vary continuously (§XV.7). Lemmas 15.1.4, 15.1.5, Proposition 15.1.3 and Remark 15.1.6 are pure topology, and Lemma 15.1.5 needs only the observation that two continuous maps into a Hausdorff space differ on an open set, so it is proved pair by pair without Lemma 15.1.4 (§XV.5). Written this way, two places of the text needed a reading. The derivative of an sc¹ map is continuous only on level $1$, and there pointwise; so the argument runs in the level-$1$ topology, where it holds equally, and the text's "weak topology" is pointwise convergence. And the final display of the text sums over all branches, as if every $s_i(0)$ equalled $f(0)$; comparing pairs (value, derivative) for all branches and selecting the value $f(0)$ at the end avoids this. Separating the two families together, rather than their union with halved weights, gives the comparison in one step, and it lets $x_0$ itself serve as a separated point. So Proposition 15.1.3, which asks for $x_k \ne 0$ converging to $0$ and does not hold as we read it at an isolated point, is not needed. The step "without loss of generality $X = O$" is the independence of the intrinsic operator $(f - s)'(x)$ from the chart, which Part I's chain rule gives at a zero of $f - s$ made a global section (§XV.7). The functor property, for which the text gives no argument, is the same chain rule once more: a local structure near $s(\varphi)$ is carried to one near $t(\varphi)$ by the local strong bundle isomorphism of the sheet of $\varphi$, and in the carried chart $T\varphi$ is the identity on chart vectors, so the intrinsic operators are conjugate by $\mu(\varphi, \cdot)$ (§XV.9).

*§15.2 is Part I branch by branch, and so inherits Part I's hypothesis.* A local sc⁺-section on $O$ is a global sc⁺-section of $W|_O$, and $(f - s_i)|_O$ is an sc-Fredholm section there, so Part I's Theorems 3.1.18, 3.1.26 and 3.6.8 apply to each branch (§XV.10). This gives the sc-Fredholm summands of $T(f, \Lambda)$ in the chart reading, the local solution sets, their tameness, and good position along them. The price is Part I's tame germ data, without which Theorem 3.6.8 does not hold as we read it; it is inherited, not new, and it is the same hypothesis that §12.5 and the cylinder carry. Definition 15.2.1 asks for less than it says: "nonzero" and "sc-Fredholm" are automatic, so transversality is the surjectivity of every summand (§XV.12). The proof of Theorem 15.2.2, which writes $f(x) = s_i(x)$ for all $i$, presumably means the branches through $f(x)$; the others have empty solution sets near $x$ (§XV.13). "The ep-groupoid $U(x)$" is the translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$, and on it the paracompactness of the support, which Definition 9.1.2 (1) asks of a branched ep⁺-subgroupoid since 2021, is automatic, its orbit map being closed with finite fibres; on $X$ it is a hypothesis that the remarks do not address (§XV.14).

*General position is Part I's general position of each branch.* On $T^R_xX$ the intrinsic operator of a branch is the derivative of the branch in a transported chart of $W|_O$, so surjectivity there is Part I's general position of $(f - s_i)|_O$; that gives good position by Part I and persists near $x$. This is why Remark 15.3.6 holds at every point of the support and not only at $\partial X$, and why it needs no $d_X = 0$ (§§XV.16, XV.20). General position at a point is invariant under morphisms, which the text uses silently when it passes to saturations "by equivariance" (§XV.25).

*The existence theorems separate into an assembly and Part I.* The assembly of Theorem 15.3.7 is finite covers of $|S_f|$, sums of linear families, the bounds $N(\Lambda \oplus \Lambda') \le N(\Lambda) + N(\Lambda')$ and on domain supports that the text uses silently, and a small parameter off a null set (§XV.22). The local families are Part XIII's atomic multisections built from seeds, linear in the parameter and carried along morphisms (§XV.23). Parametric transversality is Part I's local Sard step branch by branch: in a tame chart a branch of $\Lambda_t$ is the slice at $t$ of a Part I parametrized section, and (15.1) for the branch is Part I's general position of that section at $(0, x)$ (§XV.25). The one bridge the text takes for granted is between (15.1), which uses $T^R_xX$, and Part I's conditions (i)–(ii), which use the full tangent space; in a tame chart centred at the zero the two are equivalent by two lines of linear algebra in each direction, and the text's appeal to the implicit function theorem for the openness of (15.1) is Part I's openness of general position on the product with $\mathbb R^\ell$ (§XV.24). "Structurable" contains a good system, so the addendum of Theorem 15.3.7 needs one; (1)–(4) do not, with the sums of Definition 13.2.9 in place of structurable ones, which is Remark 15.3.8 (§XV.26).

*Boundary data must charge the boundary.* Theorem 15.3.9 is Theorem 14.1.9 followed by Theorem 15.3.7 relative to the boundary. Stated with the index sets of the formal Definition 14.1.3, which admits empty ones, it fails with boundary: the zero function with empty index sets is structurable over $\partial X$, and no structurable extension vanishes there (§XV.27). The text's boundary multisection has non-empty index sets; with it, the charged statement, the theorem is proved from one open proposition. A witness on a space without boundary could not reveal this, which is why every hypothesis here is asked for a witness in the non-degenerate case. Step (a), the cut-off $h_0$, uses the upper semicontinuity of $N(\Lambda)$ along $\partial X$, which holds when the bundle has tame charts at every object and which the text uses without comment (§XV.28). Steps (c)–(d) are Theorem 15.3.7 with the operators of $T(f, \Lambda_0)$ in place of those of $T(f, 0)$, and the parametric part carries over branch by branch (§XV.29).

*The cylinder needs more than the text says.* The product with $[0, 1]$ is built as the product with Part I's cube, whose parametrized Fredholm theory is available; $d_X \equiv 0$ makes $X$ tame, a step the text takes without comment (§XV.30); the auxiliary norm of Corollary 15.3.10 (2), which the text does not give, is the interpolation $\max(\alpha(t)N^0, \beta(t)N^1)$ (§XV.31). The partitions of unity of $[0, 1] \times X$ are a product construction, $\sum_x\rho_x(y)g_x(q)$, and the structurability of the glued boundary data comes from lifting the structures of the $\Lambda^i$ along $[0, 1] \times X \to X$, where two continuous lifts that agree at one point agree on a connected neighbourhood (§XV.32). The text's proof does not say how the face condition of the glued data is checked; presumably from the transversality of $(f, \Lambda^i)$, since $T^R_{(i,x)}([0, 1] \times X) = \{0\} \times T_xX$ when $d_X \equiv 0$ (§XV.33).

*In §15.4 the argument is short and the data are hard.* The canonical lift is pointwise linear algebra once the operators $(f - s_i)'(y)$ are seen to be in Part I's $\mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$, because $f - s_i$ differs from $f$ by an sc⁺ term (§XV.34). The cobordism argument for the invariants is Stokes' theorem with $dF^* = F^*d$ (§XV.36), and Theorem 15.4.3 does not use the tameness of $X$, good position carrying what is needed at boundary points (§XV.35). What is hard is the data the argument takes: the continuity of the kernel orientations along the branches, and on the cylinder the weights and signs on the ends, where Part I's orientation bookkeeping has to meet Chapter 9's boundary orientation (§XV.37, gaps G.159, G.182, G.190).

## Part XVI. Polyfolds (HWZ Chapter 16, §§16.1–16.6)

Chapter 16 (Springer 2021, pp. 705–740; 2017 numbers in parentheses) passes from ep-groupoids to polyfolds. A polyfold is a topological space $Z$ together with an equivalence class of ep-groupoid structures on it, and every notion of the earlier chapters (bump functions, partitions of unity, the degeneracy index, tameness, the tangent, sc-differential forms, strong bundles, auxiliary norms, sections, branched ep⁺-subgroupoids, sc⁺-multisections, sc-Fredholm sections, orientations and the invariants of Chapter 15) is carried to the class. The method is uniform: a notion of a polyfold is a notion of one structure in the class, and a theorem of invariance under equivalences of ep-groupoids, or under generalized isomorphisms, shows that it does not depend on the structure. §16.1 defines polyfold structures, their equivalence and polyfolds (Definitions 16.1.1–16.1.3 (2017: Definitions 16.1–16.3)), shows that bump functions and partitions of unity are invariant (Proposition 16.1.4, Definition 16.1.5 (2017: Proposition 16.2, Definition 16.4)), defines the maps between polyfolds (Definitions 16.1.6, 16.1.8, 16.1.10, 16.1.11, Remarks 16.1.7, 16.1.9 (2017: Definitions 16.5–16.8, Remarks 16.1, 16.2)), transports the degeneracy index, the boundary and tameness (Lemma 16.1.13, Definitions 16.1.14, 16.1.17, Lemma 16.1.19, Definition 16.1.20 (2017: Lemma 16.1, Definitions 16.9, 16.11, Lemma 16.2, Definition 16.12)), and introduces the raised polyfolds $(Z, c)^i$. It also treats the lifts $Z_i$, subpolyfolds and faces (Proposition 16.1.12, Definition 16.1.15, Remark 16.1.16, Example 16.1.18, Definition 16.1.21, Proposition 16.1.22), which are not formalized. §16.2 builds the tangent $T(Z, c)$, the tangent functor and the complex of sc-differential forms. §16.3 defines strong polyfold bundles, their maps, auxiliary norms, reflexivity, mixed convergence and sections. §16.4 defines branched finite-dimensional suborbifolds of a polyfold, their orientations and integrals, and proves Stokes' theorem. §16.5 defines sc⁺-multisections of strong polyfold bundles and proves the extension theorem 16.5.7. §16.6 defines sc-Fredholm sections, their compactness properties and orientations, and states the integration theorem 16.6.6.

This Part follows the book's order. §§XVI.1–XVI.6 treat §16.1: polyfold structures and polyfolds with the metrizability remark (§XVI.1), the uniqueness statement after Definition 16.1.2 and Remark 16.1.7 (§XVI.2), Proposition 16.1.4 and Definition 16.1.5 (§XVI.3), the maps of polyfolds (§XVI.4), the degeneracy index, boundary and tameness (§XVI.5) and the raised polyfolds (§XVI.6). §§XVI.7–XVI.10 treat §16.2: Lemma 16.2.1 (§XVI.7), the tangent $T(Z, c)$ and the projection $\tau_Z$ (§XVI.8), Theorem 16.2.4 (§XVI.9) and sc-differential forms with Theorem 16.2.6 (§XVI.10). §§XVI.11–XVI.16 treat §16.3: strong polyfold bundles (§XVI.11), their maps (§XVI.12), auxiliary norms (§XVI.13), reflexivity and mixed convergence (§XVI.14), Theorems 16.3.15, 16.3.17 and Proposition 16.3.16 (§XVI.15), and sections with the zero section (§XVI.16). §§XVI.17–XVI.20 treat §16.4: branched suborbifolds (§XVI.17), Proposition 16.4.3 (§XVI.18), orientations and integrals (§XVI.19) and Stokes' theorem (§XVI.20). §§XVI.21–XVI.23 treat §16.5: sc⁺-multisections and (16.8) (§XVI.21), structurability (§XVI.22) and Theorem 16.5.7 (§XVI.23). §§XVI.24–XVI.26 treat §16.6: sc-Fredholm sections and Theorem 16.6.4 (§XVI.24), orientations (§XVI.25) and Theorem 16.6.6 (§XVI.26). Then come the witnesses (§XVI.27), what is not formalized (§XVI.28) and what the formalization taught us (§XVI.29).

**What is proved, and what is not.** All six sections of Chapter 16 are formalized, except Proposition 16.1.12, the subpolyfolds and faces of §16.1 and Remark 16.2.7.

*Formalized as printed.* Definitions 16.1.1, 16.1.2, 16.1.3, 16.1.5, 16.1.6, 16.1.8, 16.1.14, 16.1.17 and 16.1.20, Remark 16.1.9 and Lemma 16.1.13 (§§XVI.1, XVI.3–XVI.5). The remark after Definition 16.1.1 that $Z$ is metrizable (§XVI.1). The construction of $T(Z, c)$ with the maps $T\alpha$ and (16.5), Lemma 16.2.2 and Definition 16.2.3 (§XVI.8). Definition 16.2.5 with the remark before it, and Theorem 16.2.6 in both parts, the complex and the pull-back by sc-smooth maps (§XVI.10). In §16.3: Definitions 16.3.1, 16.3.3, 16.3.4, 16.3.6, 16.3.7, 16.3.8, 16.3.12, 16.3.13, 16.3.14 and 16.3.18, Lemma 16.3.2, Proposition 16.3.10, Theorem 16.3.15, Proposition 16.3.16 (2), Theorem 16.3.17 (1), the parenthetical of Definition 16.3.12 that the model does not matter, the independence of the model of mixed convergence and of reflexive auxiliary norms, and the zero section (§§XVI.11–XVI.16). In §16.4: Definitions 16.4.1, 16.4.2, 16.4.4 and 16.4.5, Proposition 16.4.3 and the integrals of p. 732 on classes (§§XVI.17–XVI.19). In §16.5: Definitions 16.5.1, 16.5.4 and 16.5.6, Remark 16.5.3 and (16.8) with the continuity of $n(\lambda)$ (§§XVI.21–XVI.22). In §16.6: the claim before Definition 16.6.1, Definitions 16.6.1, 16.6.2 and 16.6.3, and Theorem 16.6.4 (§XVI.24). Where the text asserts that a relation is an equivalence relation, or lists a condition that the others imply, the relation is proved and the condition derived.

*Restated.* The raised polyfolds $(Z, c)^i$ and the projection $\tau_Z$, with $(Z, c)^1$ a space injecting into $Z$ with image $Z_1$ (§§XVI.6, XVI.8). Definitions 16.2.5, 16.4.1 and 16.4.4, whose representatives are made explicit as pairs (§§XVI.10, XVI.17, XVI.19). Definition 16.3.5 (2), (3) through representatives, Definition 16.1.21 not being formalized (§XVI.11). Definition 16.3.9 with $n$ a function on $Y$ whose values on $Y_{0,1}$ matter (§XVI.13). Definition 16.3.19 as the sc-smooth sections with an sc⁺ functor (§XVI.16). Definition 16.5.2 with $y \ne 0_z$, since the set as printed is all of $Z$; Definition 16.5.5 with the pull-back over $\partial X$ in orbit form (§§XVI.21–XVI.22).

*Stronger.* Proposition 16.1.4 with the text's sketch of part (2) written out (§XVI.3); Lemma 16.1.19 as an equivalence (§XVI.5); Proposition 16.3.16 (1) for every auxiliary norm, without reflexivity (§XVI.15). The metrizability of $Z$ is proved without the Nagata–Smirnov theorem (§XVI.1).

*Narrower.* Definition 16.1.11: the polyfold category is built on effective polyfolds, since as we read Definition 16.1.10 the composite is not defined on all of them (§XVI.4). Theorem 16.2.4: a functor on the category of polyfold structures, well defined on sc-smooth maps of all polyfolds, and a functor on the category of effective polyfolds, the tangent of an effective polyfold being effective (§XVI.9). Theorem 16.3.17 (2), with the reflexive local step of Theorem 12.2.13 as a hypothesis, which Part XII discharges for tame bases (§XVI.15). Definition 16.6.5: an orientation on one representative, carried to every other along any diagram under the standing hypotheses of the M-polyfold theory on the bundles of the diagram (§XVI.25). Theorem 16.6.6: the integrals live on the polyfold and depend only on $[\tau]$; their independence of $\lambda$ is proved from cobordisms between perturbations with the inherited orientation, both taken as inputs (§XVI.26). Proposition 16.4.3 and the integrals on classes are proved as printed; only the boundary integrals on classes are not wrapped (§XVI.19).

*With an added hypothesis.* Theorem 16.4.6, Stokes' theorem, with sc-smooth partitions of unity, which the Chapter 9 Stokes theorem it reduces to assumes (§XVI.20); Theorem 16.6.6 likewise (§XVI.26). Theorem 16.5.7, with tame strong bundle charts in the models and $\lambda$ with non-empty index sets, which is the text's notion (§XVI.23).

*Does not hold as we read it.* Five statements, all by one mechanism: Theorem 10.3.19 (Part X) does not hold as we read it, on the ep-groupoid $\mathbb Z/3 \times \mathbb R \rightrightarrows \mathbb R$ with the trivial action, which satisfies (ZHOU) and has a paracompact orbit space, so it is a polyfold structure in the exact sense of Definition 16.1.1. (1) The sentence after Definition 16.1.2, that the generalized isomorphism $f$ with $\alpha = \beta \circ |f|$ is unique as a consequence of (ZHOU) (§XVI.2). (2) Remark 16.1.7, that for a homeomorphism $h$ there is at most one generalized isomorphism $f$ with $h \circ \alpha = \beta \circ |f|$, together with the sentence on pp. 709–710 that an isomorphism $(f, \mathfrak f)$ of polyfold structures is determined by $f$ (§XVI.2). (3) Lemma 16.2.1 (§XVI.7), which holds on orbit spaces, the form §16.2 uses. (4) The claim of Definition 16.1.10 that the composite does not depend on the choices, on the middle structure $(\mathbb Z/3)^2 \times \mathbb R \rightrightarrows \mathbb R$ with the trivial action (§XVI.4). (5) The uniqueness of $f$ and $F$ after Definition 16.3.3, on the strong bundle $\mathbb R \times \mathbb R^k \to \mathbb R$ over $\mathbb Z/3 \times \mathbb R \rightrightarrows \mathbb R$ (§XVI.11). All five hold when the target, or the middle structure, is effective, and each such form is proved. The class-level notions of §§16.3–16.6 do not depend on the non-unique isomorphisms: a section is determined by its map $f$, a multisection by its function $\lambda$, a branched suborbifold by its function $\theta$ (§§XVI.16, XVI.21, XVI.26).

*Not formalized.* The second sentence of Remark 16.1.7, on continuous maps, which has no formal content beyond an example; Remark 16.3.11, which is prose. *Not yet formalized:* Proposition 16.1.12, Definition 16.1.15, Remark 16.1.16, Example 16.1.18, Definition 16.1.21, Proposition 16.1.22 and Remark 16.2.7; the boundary integrals of p. 732 as functions on classes; weak face structure under generalized isomorphisms.

*Remaining gaps* (§XVI.28). G.153: Stokes' theorem on polyfolds without partitions of unity. G.175, in part: the orientation of $\lambda \circ f$ inherited from $(f, o)$ on the polyfold, and the cobordism of Corollary 15.4.4 on the polyfold. G.176, in part: the independence of the transported orientation of the diagram, and the transfer of tameness, bump functions and tame germ data along strong bundle equivalences. G.187: general position of $(f, \lambda)$ does not depend on the model. G.188: Theorem 16.6.6 in index $0$.

**The decisions that shape the chapter.**

(1) *Polyfolds as quotients.* A polyfold structure is a Lean structure holding the ep-groupoid, its two properties (paracompact orbit space, (ZHOU)) and the homeomorphism; a polyfold on $Z$ is an element of the quotient of the polyfold structures on $Z$ by the equivalence of Definition 16.1.2. Every notion of a polyfold is "some structure in $c$ has the property", and it comes with the theorem that then every structure in $c$ has it. The same pattern gives strong polyfold bundles (quotients of strong polyfold bundle structures), sc-smooth maps (quotients of morphisms of PS), forms, sections, branched suborbifolds and multisections (quotients of representatives).

(2) *Bump functions on the objects.* "Admits sc-smooth bump functions" in Proposition 16.1.4 (1) and Definition 16.1.5 (1) is read for the object M-polyfold of the ep-groupoid, pointwise (Definition 5.3.1), as the text's proof uses it; by Theorem 12.3.2 (1) (Part XII) this is equivalent to Definition 12.3.1 in the pointwise reading. Partitions of unity are read in the ep-groupoid sense of Definition 7.5.5, and shown equivalent to partitions of unity of the orbit space whose pull-backs to the objects are sc-smooth.

(3) *A base structure instead of a gluing.* The text builds $T(Z, c)$, and the raised polyfold $(Z, c)^1$, by gluing over all structures of $c$ along canonical maps. The formalization chooses one structure $(X_0, \alpha_0)$ of $c$ (the representative chosen by the quotient) and takes $T(Z, c) = |TX_0|$, $(Z, c)^1 = |X_0^1|$; every other structure is attached to it by the maps $T\alpha$, $\alpha^1$, which are proved independent of every choice. This avoids the gluing and makes visible that what the gluing needs is a canonical map on orbit spaces, not a canonical generalized isomorphism.

(4) *Effective polyfolds for composition.* As we read it, Definition 16.1.10 does not give a well-defined composite on all polyfolds (§XVI.4). The formalization keeps the category PS of polyfold structures for all structures, keeps sc-smooth maps of all polyfolds and everything that is defined map by map (the tangent of a map, the pull-back of forms), and builds the category of polyfolds on the effective ones, where Theorem 10.3.19 holds and the composite is well defined.

(5) *Functions determine the class-level objects.* In §§16.3, 16.5 and 16.6 the relation between representatives is stated with a generalized strong bundle isomorphism, which need not be unique. The formalization proves in each case that the relation holds iff the functions on $Y$ or $Z$ agree (the section $f$, the multisection $\lambda$, the function $\theta = |\Theta| \circ \alpha^{-1}$), so the non-uniqueness of the isomorphisms does not reach these notions.

(6) *Added hypotheses are named and witnessed.* Where the text's proof reduces to a statement of an earlier chapter that carries a hypothesis the polyfold statement does not print (partitions of unity in Stokes' theorem; tame strong bundle charts in Theorem 14.1.9; the reflexive local step of Theorem 12.2.13), the hypothesis is added to the polyfold statement, named, and witnessed (§XVI.27).

**Map.**

Throughout, a generalized map $\mathfrak f = [X \xleftarrow{F} A \xrightarrow{\Phi} Y]$ is a morphism of Chapter 10's localization of the category $\mathcal{EP}$ of ep-groupoids at the equivalences; its orbit map is $|\mathfrak f| = |\Phi| \circ |F|^{-1} : |X| \to |Y|$, and it is a generalized isomorphism if it is invertible in the localization. (ZHOU) is Zhou's condition of Chapter 7, (LR) the local regularity property of Chapter 10, and an ep-groupoid is effective if the only isotropy element acting trivially near its object is the identity (Definition 7.2.1).

### XVI.1 Definitions 16.1.1–16.1.3 (2017: 16.1–16.3): polyfold structures and polyfolds, pp. 705–707

**Statement** (same). *Definition 16.1.1* (p. 705) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure⟧: a polyfold structure on a topological space $Z$ is a pair $(X, \beta)$ of an ep-groupoid $X$ and a homeomorphism $\beta : |X| \to Z$ such that (1) the orbit space $|X|$ is paracompact and (2) $X$ satisfies (ZHOU). *Definition 16.1.2* (p. 707) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.Equiv⟧: two polyfold structures $(X, \alpha)$, $(Y, \beta)$ on $Z$ are equivalent if there is a generalized isomorphism $f : X \to Y$ with $\alpha = \beta \circ |f|$. *Definition 16.1.3* (p. 707) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldClass⟧: a polyfold is a pair $(Z, c)$ with $c$ an equivalence class of polyfold structures on $Z$. *The remark after Definition 16.1.1* (same) ⟦Chapter16/TangentPolyfold · PolyfoldStructure.metrizableSpace⟧: if $Z$ carries a polyfold structure, $Z$ is metrizable.

*Readings.* $Z$ lives in the universe of the object and morphism sets of $X$, so that $\beta$ is a homeomorphism between types of one universe; a polyfold on $Z$ is therefore a class of structures whose ep-groupoids live in that universe. The 2017 Definition 16.1 had neither (1) nor (2); both are part of the formal structure, and every theorem of this Part that needs (LR), (LUC), metrizability or the existence of auxiliary norms obtains it from them. The pair $(X, \beta)$ is an orbit chart in the sense of Remark 10.3.18 ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.toOrbitChart⟧, and Definition 16.1.2 is the relation of Remark 10.3.18 on orbit charts ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.equiv_iff_rel⟧.

**Proof that Definition 16.1.2 is an equivalence relation.** The text calls the relation an equivalence relation without proof; it is proved in three steps.

*Step 1, reflexivity* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.Equiv.refl⟧. The identity $1_X$ of the localization is a generalized isomorphism and $|1_X| = \mathrm{id}_{|X|}$, so $\alpha = \alpha \circ |1_X|$.

*Step 2, symmetry* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.Equiv.symm⟧. If $f : X \to Y$ is a generalized isomorphism with $\alpha = \beta \circ |f|$, its inverse $f^{-1}$ in the localization is a generalized isomorphism with $|f^{-1}| = |f|^{-1}$ (Proposition 10.3.11, Part X). Then $\beta = \alpha \circ |f|^{-1} = \alpha \circ |f^{-1}|$.

*Step 3, transitivity* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.Equiv.trans⟧. For $f : X \to Y$ and $g : Y \to V$ with $\alpha = \beta \circ |f|$ and $\beta = \gamma \circ |g|$, the composite $g \circ f$ is a generalized isomorphism with $|g \circ f| = |g| \circ |f|$ (Proposition 10.3.11), so $\alpha = \gamma \circ |g \circ f|$.

The quotient by this relation ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.setoid⟧ is the type of polyfolds on $Z$. A consequence used throughout: if $(X, \alpha) \sim (Y, \beta)$ through $f$, then $|f| = \beta^{-1} \circ \alpha$ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.orbitMap_eq_of_equiv⟧, since $\beta$ is a bijection. So the orbit map of a realizing generalized isomorphism is determined by the two structures, even though (§XVI.2) the generalized isomorphism itself is not.

**(ZHOU) gives (LR)** ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.isLR⟧. *Proof.* Proposition 7.4.22 (Part VII) ⟦Chapter7/SmoothRegularAssembly · proposition_7_4_22_of_isZhou⟧ shows that an ep-groupoid with (ZHOU) has the local regularity property. This is the hypothesis the text has in mind when it cites Theorem 10.3.19 after Definition 16.1.2, and the hypothesis of Proposition 10.1.10 and Proposition 11.2.9, which carry §16.2 (§§XVI.7–XVI.10).

**Proof of the remark: polyfolds are metrizable.** *Step 1.* $|X|$ is paracompact by Definition 16.1.1 (1). *Step 2.* Theorem 7.3.1 (Part VII) gives that $|X|$ is Hausdorff, regular and locally metrizable; with paracompactness, $|X|$ is metrizable ⟦Chapter7/OrbitTopology · theorem_7_3_1_metrizable⟧. *Step 3, the metrization step.* It is the theorem of Chapter 2 (Part II) that a paracompact Hausdorff space which is locally metrizable is metrizable ⟦Chapter2/Metrizable · metrizableSpace_of_locally⟧, proved through the pull-back of a metrizable topology along an embedding ⟦Chapter2/Metrizable · metrizableSpace_of_pullback⟧. The Nagata–Smirnov theorem, which the text's appeal to metrization theorems suggests, is not needed. *Step 4.* $\beta$ is a homeomorphism, so the metrizable topology of $|X|$ carries over to $Z$. The text's 2017 Proposition 16.1 is this remark.

**The polyfold $\mathbb R$ with isotropy $\mathbb Z/3$.** This example is the witness of every definition of §16.1 and the counterexample of §XVI.2, so it is built with care. Let $X = \mathbb Z/3 \times \mathbb R \rightrightarrows \mathbb R$ be the action groupoid of the trivial action of $\mathbb Z/3$ on $\mathbb R$: objects $\mathbb R$, morphisms $\mathbb Z/3 \times \mathbb R$, source and target the projection.

*Step 1, the orbit space.* The orbit map $\pi : \mathbb R \to |X|$ is injective, since every orbit is a point ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · EpGroupoid.Examples.injective_π_trivialZ3⟧. It is continuous and open (Proposition 7.1.8, Part VII), and surjective, hence a homeomorphism ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · EpGroupoid.Examples.isHomeomorph_π_trivialZ3⟧. Its inverse gives $|X| \cong \mathbb R$ ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · EpGroupoid.Examples.trivialZ3OrbitHomeomorph⟧.

*Step 2, paracompactness.* $\mathbb R$ is paracompact, hence so is $|X|$ ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · EpGroupoid.Examples.hasParacompactOrbitSpace_trivialZ3⟧.

*Step 3, (ZHOU).* Every isotropy element acts trivially, so for every $x$ the natural representation of $G_x$ is trivial and the conditions of (ZHOU) hold with the whole of $\mathbb R$ as the neighbourhood ⟦Chapter7/Zhou · EpGroupoid.Examples.isZhou_trivialZ3⟧.

*Step 4, the structure.* With $\beta$ the inverse of the homeomorphism of Step 1, $(X, \beta)$ is a polyfold structure on $\mathbb R$ in the exact sense of Definition 16.1.1 ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.z3PolyfoldStructure⟧, and its class is a polyfold ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.z3Polyfold⟧.

*Step 5, not effective.* The non-trivial elements of $\mathbb Z/3$ act as the identity near every object, so $X$ is not effective ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.not_isEffective_z3PolyfoldStructure⟧. This is what makes the example a counterexample to the uniqueness statements, and why their effective forms hold.

*Where Lean departs from the text.* The text states Definitions 16.1.1–16.1.3 and treats the relation of Definition 16.1.2 as evidently an equivalence relation; the formalization proves the three properties from Proposition 10.3.11, the only input being that orbit maps of generalized maps compose and invert. The universe in which $Z$ lives is implicit in the text; the formalization fixes it to be that of the object and morphism sets of $X$, which costs nothing because every construction of the chapter stays inside one universe or moves up by one (the tangent). The metrizability remark is proved by a different route from the one the 2017 text suggests: instead of a general metrization theorem for the orbit space, Theorem 7.3.1 provides local metrizability, and the Chapter 2 theorem for paracompact Hausdorff spaces finishes. The polyfold $\mathbb R$ with isotropy $\mathbb Z/3$ is not in the text; it is the example of Part X carried to polyfolds, and it serves both as the universal witness of the definitions and as the example of §XVI.2.

### XVI.2 The uniqueness after Definition 16.1.2, Remark 16.1.7 (2017: Remark 16.1), and the sentence on pp. 709–710

**Statement** (does not hold as we read it; holds for an effective target). After Definition 16.1.2 (p. 707) the text says that the generalized isomorphism $f$ with $\alpha = \beta \circ |f|$ is necessarily unique as a consequence of (ZHOU), citing Theorem 10.3.19: for generalized isomorphisms $f, f' : X \to Y$, $|f| = |f'|$ implies $f = f'$ if one of the ep-groupoids has (LR). The claim in Lean ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.Uniqueness_16_1_2⟧: for polyfold structures $(X, \alpha)$, $(Y, \beta)$ on $Z$, at most one generalized isomorphism $f$ has $\alpha = \beta \circ |f|$. Remark 16.1.7 (p. 711) ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.Remark_16_1_7⟧: for a homeomorphism $h : Z \to W$, a polyfold structure $(X, \alpha)$ on $Z$ and one $(Y, \beta)$ on $W$, at most one generalized isomorphism $f$ has $h \circ \alpha = \beta \circ |f|$. The sentence on pp. 709–710: an isomorphism $(f, \mathfrak f)$ of polyfold structures in the category PS is determined by $f$.

*Verdict.* The uniqueness after Definition 16.1.2 does not hold as we read it ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.not_uniqueness_16_1_2⟧, nor does Remark 16.1.7 ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.not_remark_16_1_7⟧, nor the sentence on pp. 709–710. All three hold when the target ep-groupoid is effective ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.uniqueness_16_1_2_of_isEffective⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldStructure · PolyfoldStructure.remark_16_1_7_of_isEffective⟧ ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.uniqueness_16_1_2_of_forall_isEffective⟧.

**Proof that the uniqueness does not hold as we read it.** *Step 1, the structure.* Take the polyfold structure $(X, \beta)$ on $\mathbb R$ of §XVI.1, with $X = \mathbb Z/3 \times \mathbb R \rightrightarrows \mathbb R$ and the trivial action, as both $(X, \alpha)$ and $(Y, \beta)$. All hypotheses of Definition 16.1.1 hold: paracompact orbit space, (ZHOU), and a homeomorphism to $\mathbb R$ ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.uniqueness_16_1_2_counterexample⟧.

*Step 2, two generalized isomorphisms.* Let $\mathrm{Inv} : X \to X$ be the functor that is the identity on objects and inverts morphisms; since $\mathbb Z/3$ is abelian and acts trivially, $\mathrm{Inv}$ is a functor, and it is an equivalence. Take $f = [1_X]$ ⟦Chapter10/LocalizationLRCounterexample · LocalizationLRCounterexample.genId⟧ and $f' = [X \xleftarrow{1} X \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Inv}} X]$ ⟦Chapter10/LocalizationLRCounterexample · LocalizationLRCounterexample.genInv⟧. Both are generalized isomorphisms ⟦Chapter10/LocalizationLRCounterexample · LocalizationLRCounterexample.isGeneralizedIso_genInv⟧.

*Step 3, both realize the equivalence.* Both functors are the identity on objects, so both orbit maps are the identity of $|X|$, and $\beta = \beta \circ |f|$ ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.β_eq_β_comp_orbitMap_genId⟧ and $\beta = \beta \circ |f'|$ ⟦Chapter16/ZhouUniquenessCheck · PolyfoldStructure.β_eq_β_comp_orbitMap_genInv⟧.

*Step 4, they differ* ⟦Chapter10/LocalizationLRCounterexample · LocalizationLRCounterexample.genInv_ne_genId⟧. Two morphisms of the localization represented by functors $X \to X$ through the identity leg agree only if the functors are connected by a natural transformation after a refinement. A natural transformation from $1$ to $\mathrm{Inv}$ would be a family $\tau_x \in \mathbb Z/3$ with $\tau_x g = g^{-1}\tau_x$, that is $g = g^{-1}$, for every $g$; this fails for a generator. The argument is the one of Part X, where it shows that Theorem 10.3.19 does not hold as we read it ⟦Chapter10/LocalizationLRCounterexample · LocalizationLRCounterexample.not_theorem_10_3_19⟧.

*Step 5, conclusion.* (ZHOU) gives (LR) (§XVI.1), so the text's citation of Theorem 10.3.19 applies to this $X$, and the example shows that (LR) does not give the uniqueness. For Remark 16.1.7, take $h = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbb R}$ in the same example. For the sentence on pp. 709–710, the pairs $(\mathrm{id}, f)$ and $(\mathrm{id}, f')$ are two isomorphisms of PS with the same continuous map.

**Proof of the effective form.** *Step 1.* If $Y$ is effective, Theorem 10.3.19 holds ⟦Chapter10/LocalizationLRCounterexample · EPLocalization.EPLoc.theorem_10_3_19_of_isEffective⟧ (Part X): an effective target rules out isotropy acting trivially, which is what Step 4 above uses. *Step 2.* Two generalized isomorphisms $f, f'$ with $\beta \circ |f| = h \circ \alpha = \beta \circ |f'|$ have $|f| = |f'|$, because $\beta$ is injective. *Step 3.* By Step 1, $f = f'$. The form for $h = \mathrm{id}$ is the uniqueness after Definition 16.1.2; the form quantified over all effective polyfold structures is a corollary.

**What depends on the uniqueness.** Definitions 16.1.2 and 16.1.3 do not: an equivalence of structures asks only that some generalized isomorphism exist. Nor do Definition 16.1.6, which carries its generalized isomorphisms as data, the invariance statements of §16.1, or any of the class-level definitions of §§16.3–16.6 (decision (5)). The uniqueness is used in the text in three places: Lemma 16.2.1 and the gluing of $T(Z, c)$ (§§XVI.7–XVI.8), where the orbit form suffices; the claim of Definition 16.1.10 (§XVI.4), which does not hold as we read it; and the uniqueness after Definition 16.3.3 (§XVI.11), which does not hold as we read it either. The second sentence of Remark 16.1.7, that for a continuous map there may be none or many generalized maps, is an observation without formal content beyond an example and is not formalized.

*Where Lean departs from the text.* The text's argument is one sentence: (ZHOU), then Theorem 10.3.19. The formalization splits it into its two steps and tests each. The first, (ZHOU) gives (LR), is Proposition 7.4.22 and holds. The second, (LR) gives the uniqueness, is Theorem 10.3.19 and does not hold as we read it; the example of Part X satisfies every hypothesis of Definition 16.1.1, so the polyfold statement inherits the gap exactly. The effective form keeps the text's two steps and replaces Theorem 10.3.19 by its effective form. The formalization does not attempt to strengthen (ZHOU) or (LR) to a condition that would restore uniqueness without effectiveness; effectiveness is the condition under which Part X proves Theorem 10.3.19, and it is the one the rest of this Part uses.

### XVI.3 Proposition 16.1.4 (2017: Proposition 16.2) and Definition 16.1.5 (2017: Definition 16.4), p. 708

**Statement.** *Proposition 16.1.4 (1)* (same) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldBump · PolyfoldStructure.proposition_16_1_4_one⟧: for equivalent polyfold structures $(X, \alpha) \sim (Y, \beta)$, the object M-polyfold of $X$ admits sc-smooth bump functions iff that of $Y$ does. *Proposition 16.1.4 (2)* (explicit) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · PolyfoldStructure.proposition_16_1_4_two⟧: $X$ admits sc-smooth partitions of unity in the sense of Definition 7.5.5 iff $Y$ does. Both together ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · PolyfoldStructure.proposition_16_1_4⟧. *Definition 16.1.5* (same) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldBump · PolyfoldClass.AdmitsBumpFunctions⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · PolyfoldClass.AdmitsScPartitionsOfUnity⟧: a polyfold admits sc-smooth bump functions, or sc-smooth partitions of unity, if some structure in $c$ does; then every structure does ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldBump · PolyfoldClass.definition_16_1_5_one⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · PolyfoldClass.definition_16_1_5_two⟧. *Verdict* for (2): "explicit", because the text's proof of (2) is a sketch, calling a step an easy exercise; the steps below fill it.

**Proof of (1).** *Step 0, reduction to one equivalence.* An equivalence of structures is realized by a diagram $X \xleftarrow{F} A \xrightarrow{G} Y$ of equivalences of ep-groupoids, so it suffices to show that bump functions pass in both directions along one equivalence $F : A \to X$ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldBump · EpFunctor.IsEquivalence.admitsBumpFunctions_iff⟧.

*Step 1, bump functions are local.* Call a point a bump point if there are sc-smooth bump functions at it, in every neighbourhood. An M-polyfold admits bump functions iff every point is a bump point. Sc-smoothness of a real function is local ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldBump · MPolyfold.isScSmoothMap_real_of_locally⟧, so a function that is sc-smooth near its support and $0$ elsewhere is sc-smooth.

*Step 2, bump points along sc-diffeomorphisms of open sets* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldBump · MPolyfold.IsScDiffeoOn.hasBumpAt⟧. Let $\varphi : U \to U'$ be an sc-diffeomorphism of open sets with $\varphi(a) = b$, and $b$ a bump point. For a neighbourhood $V$ of $a$, choose a bump function $g$ at $b$ supported in a small neighbourhood inside $\varphi(V \cap U)$ whose closure is inside $U'$; then $g \circ \varphi$ on $U$, extended by $0$, is sc-smooth by Step 1 and is a bump function at $a$ supported in $V$.

*Step 3, along an equivalence* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldBump · EpFunctor.IsEquivalence.hasBumpAt_of_hasBumpAt_obj⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldBump · EpFunctor.IsEquivalence.hasBumpAt_obj_of_hasBumpAt⟧. An equivalence is a local sc-diffeomorphism on objects (Chapter 10), so Step 2 carries bump points from $F(a)$ to $a$ and from $a$ to $F(a)$.

*Step 4, essential surjectivity* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldBump · EpGroupoid.hasBumpAt_tgt⟧. Every $y \in X$ is the target of a morphism $\psi : F(a) \to y$. The local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\psi = t \circ (s|_{U(\psi)})^{-1}$ of the morphism, defined near $F(a)$, sends $F(a)$ to $y$, so by Step 2 bump points are invariant under $\hat\psi$, and $y$ is a bump point if $F(a)$ is. With Step 3 every object of $X$ is a bump point if every object of $A$ is; the converse is Step 3 alone.

**Proof of (2).** *Step 1, read on the orbit space.* Definition 7.5.5 holds for $X$ iff every open cover of $|X|$ has a subordinate partition of unity $(\sigma_\lambda)$ of $|X|$ with every $\sigma_\lambda \circ \pi$ sc-smooth ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · EpGroupoid.HasOrbitScPartitionsOfUnity⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · EpGroupoid.hasScPartitionsOfUnity_iff_orbit⟧. The proof has three ingredients. An invariant continuous function on the objects descends to a continuous function on $|X|$ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · EpGroupoid.descendP3Z⟧, so an ep-groupoid partition of unity, which is invariant, gives one of $|X|$. Closures commute with $\pi^{-1}$, because $\pi$ is open ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · EpGroupoid.preimage_closure_π⟧, so subordination to a saturated cover upstairs is subordination to the image cover downstairs. And a partition of unity of $|X|$ pulls back along the continuous map $\pi$ to a family that is again locally finite with sum $1$ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · PartitionOfUnity.comapP3Z⟧.

*Step 2, the text's "easy exercise"* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · EpFunctor.IsEquivalence.isScSmoothMap_comp_π_of_comp_obj⟧. For an equivalence $F : A \to X$ and $g : |X| \to \mathbb R$: if $g \circ \pi_X \circ F$ is sc-smooth on the objects of $A$, then $g \circ \pi_X$ is sc-smooth on the objects of $X$. Near a point $F(a)$, $g \circ \pi_X = (g \circ \pi_X \circ F) \circ F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{-1}$ with $F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{-1}$ a local inverse of $F$, which exists because $F$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism. Near a point $y$ isomorphic to $F(a)$ through $\psi$, $g \circ \pi_X = (g \circ \pi_X) \circ \hat\psi^{-1}$ near $y$, because $\pi_X$ is invariant under $\hat\psi$; so sc-smoothness near $F(a)$ gives it near $y$. The converse direction, that $g \circ \pi_X$ sc-smooth gives $g \circ \pi_X \circ F$ sc-smooth, is the chain rule.

*Step 3, transport.* $|F| : |A| \to |X|$ is a homeomorphism (Chapter 10, Part X), so partitions of unity of $|X|$ and of $|A|$ correspond under composition with $|F|$, and $\sigma \circ \pi_X \circ F = \sigma \circ |F| \circ \pi_A$. With Step 2 the property of Step 1 passes from $A$ to $X$ and back ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldPartitions · EpFunctor.IsEquivalence.hasScPartitionsOfUnity_iff⟧, and along a diagram by two applications.

**Proof of Definition 16.1.5.** By Proposition 16.1.4 applied to any two structures of $c$. *Where Lean departs from the text.* The text's proof of (1) goes through local inverses and $\hat\psi$ as here. Its proof of (2) indicates the reduction to the orbit space; Steps 1–3 are the details. The reading of bump functions on the object M-polyfold is decision (2).

*Why the reading on the objects.* Proposition 16.1.4 (1) could be read for the ep-groupoid in the sense of Definition 12.3.1, with bump functions that are themselves invariant. The text's proof works with bump functions on the object M-polyfold and moves them by local inverses and by $\hat\psi$, which does not preserve invariance; so the reading on the objects is the one the proof supports. By Theorem 12.3.2 (1) the two readings agree pointwise, so nothing is lost. For partitions of unity the opposite holds: the text's Definition 7.5.5 is the ep-groupoid notion, and the formalization keeps it, proving the orbit-space form as a lemma rather than replacing the definition.

### XVI.4 Definitions 16.1.6–16.1.11 (2017: Definitions 16.5–16.8) and Remark 16.1.9 (2017: Remark 16.2): maps of polyfolds, pp. 709–711

**Statement.** *The category PS* (p. 709, same) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSCat⟧: objects are polyfold structures; a morphism $(X, \alpha) \to (Y, \beta)$ is a pair $(f, \mathfrak f)$ of a continuous map $f : Z \to W$ and a generalized map $\mathfrak f : X \to Y$ with $f \circ \alpha = \beta \circ |\mathfrak f|$ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom⟧. *Definition 16.1.6* (p. 710, same) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.Equiv⟧: $(f, \mathfrak f) \sim (f', \mathfrak f')$ if $(f', \mathfrak f') \circ (h, \mathrm{Id}_Z) = (k, \mathrm{Id}_W) \circ (f, \mathfrak f)$ for isomorphisms $(h, \mathrm{Id}_Z)$, $(k, \mathrm{Id}_W)$ of PS. *Definition 16.1.8 and Remark 16.1.9* (p. 711, same) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PolyfoldClass.ScMap⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PolyfoldClass.ScMap.remark_16_1_9⟧: an sc-smooth map $(Z, c) \to (W, d)$ is an equivalence class $[(f, \mathfrak f)]$ of morphisms between structures of $c$ and $d$, and its underlying continuous map is $f$. *Definition 16.1.10* (p. 711, does not hold as we read it; holds for an effective middle structure) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.Definition_16_1_10⟧ ⟦Chapter16/CompositionCounterexample · CompositionCounterexample.not_definition_16_1_10⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.Equiv.comp_of_isEffective⟧: $\hat g \circ \hat f = [(g \circ f, \mathfrak g \circ \mathfrak f)]$ for representatives with a common middle structure, and the text states that this does not depend on the choices. *Definition 16.1.11* (p. 711, narrower) ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · EffPolyfold⟧: the category of effective polyfolds and sc-smooth maps.

**Proof that PS is a category.** *Step 1, the continuous map is determined* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.f_eq⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.continuous_f⟧: from $f \circ \alpha = \beta \circ |\mathfrak f|$, $f = \beta \circ |\mathfrak f| \circ \alpha^{-1}$, a composite of continuous maps, since orbit maps of generalized maps are continuous (Part X). So the text's requirement that $f$ be continuous is a consequence, and a morphism is determined by its generalized map ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.ext⟧; every generalized map defines a morphism ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.ofGen⟧.

*Step 2, identities and composition* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.id⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.comp⟧: $(\mathrm{id}_Z, 1_X)$, and $(g, \mathfrak g) \circ (f, \mathfrak f) = (g \circ f, \mathfrak g \circ \mathfrak f)$, which is a morphism because $|\mathfrak g \circ \mathfrak f| = |\mathfrak g| \circ |\mathfrak f|$ (Proposition 10.3.11). *Step 3, the laws* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.comp_assoc⟧: componentwise, from those of the localization.

*Step 4, isomorphisms over the identity* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.IsIdIso⟧: a morphism $(h, \mathrm{Id}_Z)$ between structures on one space $Z$ with $h$ a generalized isomorphism. They have inverses of the same kind ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.IsIdIso.inv⟧, compose ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.IsIdIso.comp⟧ and include the identities ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.isIdIso_id⟧; for one of them, $\alpha = \beta \circ |h|$ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.IsIdIso.β_eq⟧, so two structures are related by one iff they are equivalent in the sense of Definition 16.1.2, and one exists between any two equivalent structures ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.exists_isIdIso⟧. For two structures of one class the formalization fixes one such isomorphism ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PolyfoldClass.transport⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PolyfoldClass.transport_isIdIso⟧; it is used to define composites of representatives below.

**Proof of Definition 16.1.6 and Definition 16.1.8.** *Step 1, the continuous maps agree* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.Equiv.f_eq⟧: comparing the continuous components of the square, $f' \circ \mathrm{Id}_Z = \mathrm{Id}_W \circ f$. *Step 2, an equivalence relation* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.Equiv.refl⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.Equiv.symm⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.Equiv.trans⟧: reflexive with $h = 1$, $k = 1$; symmetric with the inverses $h^{-1}$, $k^{-1}$, multiplying the square by them; transitive by pasting two squares, with the composites $h' \circ h$, $k' \circ k$ of isomorphisms over the identity. The text states the relation without proof. *Step 3, the representatives* ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PolyfoldClass.MapRep⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PolyfoldClass.MapRep.setoid⟧: morphisms of PS from a structure of $c$ to a structure of $d$, with the relation; composing a representative with isomorphisms over the identity on either side stays in its class ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.equiv_comp_left⟧ ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PSHom.equiv_comp_right⟧. *Step 4, Definition 16.1.8.* An sc-smooth map is a class ⟦Chapter16/PolyfoldMaps · PolyfoldClass.ScMap.mk⟧.
